passages.title: Measuring Kinase Activity with Kemptide
text: Protein kinases transfer the terminal phosphate of ATP to the hydroxyl group of serine, threonine or tyrosine residues. Kinase activity is often measured with a short synthetic peptide that the enzyme recognizes. Kemptide (Leu-Arg-Arg-Ala-Ser-Leu-Gly) is a standard substrate for protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates its single serine. A useful assay must separate the phosphorylated product from the unreacted peptide so that each can be measured.

Researchers used capillary electrophoresis for this purpose. A sample is drawn into a thin capillary filled with buffer, and a voltage is applied so that charged molecules move toward the electrode of opposite charge. The capillary wall was chemically coated to stop the bulk flow of buffer that normally occurs in uncoated glass, so a molecule moved only if it carried a net charge. Positively charged peptides moved toward the negative electrode, where the detector was placed, and a larger net charge for a given size gave a shorter migration time. Charges at each pH were calculated from these pKₐ values: N-terminus 8.0, C-terminus 3.1, arginine side chain 12.5, phosphate group 1.5 and 5.8.
The researchers ran three peptides in buffer at pH 7.4 and in buffer at pH 2.5 (Table 1). The third peptide was a variant in which the serine was replaced by alanine (Ser→Ala).

The method has advantages over older assays that use radioactive ATP, because no radioactive waste is produced and both substrate and product are measured directly in the same run. It requires only a few nanoliters of sample, so many time points can be taken from one small reaction.

To follow the reaction, kemptide (0.2 mM) was mixed with PKA and ATP at pH 7.4 and 30 °C. At each time point a sample was removed and added to an equal volume of cold pH 2.5 buffer, which stopped the reaction, and the sample was then run at pH 2.5. A parallel mixture contained PKA that had been heated to 95 °C for 10 minutes, and a third contained the Ser→Ala peptide with active PKA (Table 2).

qs.q: Why was phospho-kemptide not detected in the run at pH 7.4?
o: It was too large to enter the capillary
Not quite. One phosphate barely changes the peptide's size.
It raced toward the positive electrode
Not quite. With a net charge of 0, it moves toward neither electrode.
PKA removed the phosphate during the run
Not quite. The reaction was stopped before the run; no enzyme was active.
Its net charge was zero, so it did not move
Correct: +2 from the peptide plus −2 from the phosphate gives 0, so it doesn't move.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the capillary wall was coated to stop the usual flow of buffer, so a molecule moves only if it has a net charge. Table 1 gives phospho-kemptide a net charge of 0 at pH 7.4. Here's where that comes from. Kemptide carries +2 at pH 7.4, from its two arginines and N-terminus, minus the C-terminus. Adding a phosphate adds about −2, because at pH 7.4 both of its acidic groups (pKₐ 1.5 and 5.8) have lost their protons. +2 + (−2) = 0. With no charge and no buffer flow to carry it, it just sits near where it was loaded and never reaches the detector. Why the others are wrong: One phosphate barely changes the size of a seven-residue peptide; a net charge of 0 means it doesn't move toward either electrode, including the positive one; the reaction was stopped in cold acid before the run, so no enzyme was working. Trap: Forgetting the coating removed the buffer flow that would otherwise sweep neutral molecules to the detector.

qs.q: Why did the researchers analyze the reaction samples at pH 2.5 rather than at pH 7.4?
o: PKA works faster at pH 2.5
Not quite. The cold pH 2.5 buffer was used to stop the reaction.
Kemptide carries no charge at pH 7.4
Not quite. Kemptide carries +2 at pH 7.4.
Both forms are positive and give separate peaks
Correct: at pH 2.5 both are positive (+2.8 and +1.9), so both reach the detector at different times.
Phosphate groups lose their negative charge entirely at pH 2.5
Not quite. The phosphate still carries about −0.9 at pH 2.5.
qs.x: Correct: At pH 2.5, Table 1 shows both forms are positive: kemptide is +2.8 and phospho-kemptide is +1.9. Why? At pH 2.5 the C-terminus (pKₐ 3.1) is mostly protonated, and the phosphate's second group (pKₐ 5.8) is fully protonated, leaving only about −0.9 from its first group (pKₐ 1.5). Both peptides move toward the negative electrode where the detector sits, and because their charges differ, they arrive at different times (4.6 and 6.8 min). That lets the researchers measure substrate and product in the same run and calculate percent converted. At pH 7.4 the product has zero charge and never shows up. Why the others are wrong: Kemptide carries +2 at pH 7.4, not zero; the phosphate still carries about −0.9 at pH 2.5, which is why the two forms differ; the acid buffer was used to stop PKA, not speed it up. Trap: Assuming the separation must run under the same conditions as the reaction.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the heated-PKA mixture?
o: To show that PKA is stable when heated
Not quite. Heating destroyed PKA's activity.
To show that the conversion needs active enzyme
Correct: with dead enzyme, almost no product formed, so active PKA is required.
To show that heat phosphorylates kemptide
Not quite. Essentially no product formed with heated PKA.
To measure the rate of the reaction at 95 °C
Not quite. The reaction still ran at 30 °C; only the enzyme was preheated.
qs.x: Correct: Heating PKA to 95 °C denatures it, meaning it unfolds and loses its shape and activity. So the heated mixture has everything the real reaction has, ATP, peptide, buffer, except a working enzyme. Table 2 shows almost no product, 1% at most after 40 minutes, against 88% with active PKA. That's a negative control: it proves the phosphorylation comes from the enzyme, not from ATP reacting with the peptide by itself. Why the others are wrong: Showing PKA is stable when heated is backwards, since heating destroyed its activity; measuring the rate at 95 °C is wrong, because the heated enzyme was used in a reaction at 30 °C; heat phosphorylating kemptide is wrong, since essentially no product formed. Trap: Misreading a negative control as a separate experiment about temperature.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the Ser→Ala results?
o: PKA phosphorylates the serine and no other site
Correct: swapping serine for alanine wiped out all product, so serine is the only site.
PKA requires arginine to bind its substrate
Not quite. Both peptides have the same arginines, so their role wasn't tested.
The Ser→Ala peptide inhibits PKA
Not quite. Inhibition of PKA wasn't tested here.
Alanine is phosphorylated more slowly
Not quite. Alanine has no hydroxyl, so it can't be phosphorylated at all.
qs.x: Correct: Kinases put a phosphate on a hydroxyl (−OH) group, and serine has one. Alanine's side chain is just a methyl group (−CH₃), with no hydroxyl. Table 1 shows the Ser→Ala peptide has the same charge and migration time as kemptide, so it could be measured just as easily. Yet Table 2 shows 0% phosphorylation at every time point. Since nothing else in the peptide changed, the serine must be the only site PKA modifies. Why the others are wrong: Saying PKA needs arginine can't be tested here, since both peptides have the same arginines; saying alanine is phosphorylated more slowly is wrong, since alanine has no hydroxyl to accept a phosphate at all; saying the Ser→Ala peptide inhibits PKA wasn't tested, because no other substrate was present. Trap: Drawing a conclusion about a residue the experiment didn't change.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the slower rise in product between 20 and 40 minutes?
o: PKA was denatured by the pH 2.5 buffer
Not quite. Only samples already removed touched the acid.
Less unreacted kemptide was left
Correct: by 20 min, 66% was used up, so less substrate meant a slower rate.
Heating the enzyme slowed the reaction
Not quite. The active-enzyme mixture was never heated.
The phospho-peptide migrated too fast to detect
Not quite. It was detected fine at 6.8 min at pH 2.5.
qs.x: Correct: Work out the rate in each stretch: rate = change in % phosphorylated ÷ time. From Table 2, 0 to 10 min: (41 − 0) ÷ 10 = 4.1% per minute. 20 to 40 min: (88 − 66) ÷ 20 = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1% per minute. The reaction slowed to about a quarter of its early speed. By 20 minutes, 66% of the kemptide was already used up, so only 34% was left. With less substrate around, the enzyme meets it less often and the rate drops. Why the others are wrong: PKA wasn't denatured by the pH 2.5 buffer during the reaction, because only samples already removed met the acid; the phospho-peptide wasn't too fast to detect, since it showed up at 6.8 min; the active mixture was never heated. Trap: Blaming the measurement method for a change that happened in the reaction itself.

passages.title: Ketone Bodies from Excess Acetyl-CoA in Fasting
text: During a prolonged fast, the liver oxidizes fatty acids released from adipose tissue faster than it can use the resulting acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle. Much of the extra acetyl-CoA is converted in the mitochondrial matrix to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate (β-HB), the ketone bodies. These leave the liver and are taken up by heart, skeletal muscle and, after several days of fasting, the brain, which convert them back to acetyl-CoA. The liver itself cannot use ketone bodies because it lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase, the enzyme that activates acetoacetate.

Long-chain fatty acids cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly. In the cytosol, a fatty acid is first activated to its acyl-CoA. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1), on the outer membrane, then transfers the acyl group to carnitine, and the acyl-carnitine enters the matrix, where the acyl group is returned to CoA (Figure 1). CPT1 is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, which is abundant in the cytosol after a meal.

Researchers isolated liver mitochondria from rats that had been fed or fasted for 24 hours. The mitochondria were incubated with ATP, CoA, the enzyme that activates fatty acids, and the substrates listed in Table 1. Ketone body output (acetoacetate plus β-HB) was measured after 10 minutes. Each value is the mean of four preparations, and the standard deviation was less than 10% of the mean in every condition.

In a pilot experiment, the researchers confirmed that the mitochondria were intact by showing that they consumed oxygen rapidly when ADP was added and slowly when it was absent. Damaged mitochondria lose this coupling between electron transport and ATP synthesis. Preparations that failed this test were discarded before the ketone measurements.

The researchers noted that malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol and is lost when mitochondria are isolated, so any difference between fed and fasted mitochondria must come from the mitochondria themselves.

qs.q: Why did malonyl-CoA block ketone production from palmitate but not from palmitoyl-carnitine?
o: It converts palmitoyl-carnitine back
Not quite. Malonyl-CoA doesn't reverse the CPT1 reaction.
It competes directly with palmitate for the same enzymes
Not quite. Then palmitoyl-carnitine would have been slowed too.
It inhibits HMG-CoA synthase in the matrix
Not quite. A block inside the matrix would stop both substrates.
It inhibits the step that forms acyl-carnitine
Correct: malonyl-CoA blocks CPT1, and palmitoyl-carnitine already skips that step.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says CPT1 is the enzyme that attaches a fatty acyl group to carnitine so it can enter the mitochondrial matrix, and malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT1. Table 1 compares two starting points. With palmitate plus carnitine plus malonyl-CoA, ketone output fell to 1.4 nmol/min per mg (from 10.2). With palmitoyl-carnitine plus malonyl-CoA, it was 9.8, basically normal. Palmitoyl-carnitine is already the product of the CPT1 step, so it skips the blocked enzyme. The block must be at CPT1. Why the others are wrong: Inhibiting HMG-CoA synthase in the matrix would also block palmitoyl-carnitine, since both end up there; competing with palmitate for enzymes would slow palmitoyl-carnitine too, which didn't happen; malonyl-CoA doesn't convert palmitoyl-carnitine back to palmitate. Trap: Putting the block downstream when the bypass result shows it's upstream.

qs.q: What does the condition without added carnitine show?
o: Carnitine inhibits ketone body formation
Not quite. Output was far higher with carnitine than without.
Palmitate is toxic without carnitine
Not quite. Toxicity wasn't measured.
Palmitate needs carnitine to enter
Correct: without carnitine, output fell to 0.9, near the 0.5 baseline.
Carnitine is oxidized to ketone bodies
Not quite. Carnitine alone gave only 0.5, so it isn't the fuel.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says long-chain fatty acids can't cross the inner mitochondrial membrane on their own; they ride in as acyl-carnitine. Table 1 shows that with 1.0 mM palmitate and carnitine, output was 10.2 nmol/min per mg. Remove carnitine and it drops to 0.9, close to the 0.5 seen with no substrate at all. Without carnitine, palmitate can't get into the matrix to be oxidized. Why the others are wrong: Carnitine being turned into ketone bodies doesn't fit, since carnitine alone gave only 0.5; palmitate being toxic wasn't measured anywhere; carnitine inhibiting ketone formation is backwards, because output was much higher with it. Trap: Treating a needed carrier like carnitine as if it were a fuel.

qs.q: Why did mitochondria from fasted rats produce more ketone bodies from the same substrate?
o: Fasting raised their ketogenic enzyme levels
Correct: malonyl-CoA was lost on isolation, so the mitochondria themselves must differ.
Fasted mitochondria received more palmitate
Not quite. Both got the same 1.0 mM palmitate.
Fasted mitochondria held more malonyl-CoA
Not quite. Malonyl-CoA would lower output, and it's lost on isolation.
Fasted mitochondria lacked CPT1
Not quite. Without CPT1, output would be near zero.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows fasted-rat mitochondria made 18.5 nmol/min per mg from 1.0 mM palmitate, against 10.2 from fed-rat mitochondria. Paragraph 5 says malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol and is lost when mitochondria are isolated. So the difference can't be due to malonyl-CoA; it must come from the mitochondria themselves. During fasting, hormones like glucagon (high) and insulin (low) increase the amount of enzymes such as CPT1 and the ketone-making enzymes, so the fasted mitochondria simply have more machinery. Why the others are wrong: Fasted mitochondria holding more malonyl-CoA would lower output, not raise it, and it's lost on isolation anyway; both groups got the same 1.0 mM palmitate; lacking CPT1 would drop output near zero, not raise it. Trap: Using a whole-body explanation that the isolation step rules out.

qs.q: Between 0.5 and 1.0 mM palmitate, ketone output rose by much less than two fold. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The enzymes involved were nearing saturation
Correct: doubling substrate raised output only 1.3 times, a sign of saturation.
Palmitate was converted into glucose instead
Not quite. Fatty acids can't be used to make net glucose.
Ketone bodies were used by the liver mitochondria
Not quite. The liver lacks the enzyme to use ketone bodies.
The mitochondria ran out of carnitine
Not quite. Carnitine was supplied, and output was still rising.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows output going from 4.1 at 0.25 mM to 7.6 at 0.5 mM to 10.2 at 1.0 mM palmitate. From 0.5 to 1.0 mM the substrate doubled, but output rose by only 10.2 ÷ 7.6 ≈ 1.3 times. That's the classic sign of enzymes nearing saturation. When nearly every enzyme molecule is already busy, adding more substrate barely speeds things up, and the rate levels off toward its maximum. Why the others are wrong: Palmitate turning into glucose can't happen, because fatty acids break down to acetyl-CoA, which can't make net glucose; liver mitochondria using the ketones can't happen, since paragraph 1 says the liver lacks the activating enzyme; running out of carnitine would make output drop, but carnitine was supplied and output was still climbing. Trap: Expecting the rate to stay proportional to substrate at every concentration.

qs.q: A patient has an inherited deficiency of CPT1 in the liver. After an overnight fast, which finding is most likely?
o: High blood ketone bodies with normal glucose
Not quite. Making ketones needs CPT1 to bring fatty acids in.
Normal ketone levels because the brain makes them
Not quite. The brain uses ketones but doesn't make them.
High blood glucose from extra glycogen breakdown
Not quite. Liver glycogen runs low overnight.
Low blood glucose with low ketone bodies
Correct: no fat can enter liver mitochondria, so no ketones and poor glucose making.
qs.x: Correct: Without liver CPT1, long-chain fatty acids can't get into liver mitochondria. That means no β-oxidation, the process that breaks fatty acids into acetyl-CoA. No acetyl-CoA means no ketone bodies. β-oxidation also supplies the ATP and NADH the liver needs to make new glucose during a fast. So after an overnight fast, this patient has low blood glucose without the rise in ketones you'd normally expect. Why the others are wrong: High ketones with normal glucose can't happen, since making ketones requires CPT1; high glucose from extra glycogen breakdown is wrong, because liver glycogen runs low overnight; normal ketones from the brain is wrong, because the brain uses ketones but doesn't make them; the liver does. Trap: Assuming low blood sugar always comes with high ketones.

passages.title: Repressor and Operator Control of the lac Operon
text: In Escherichia coli, the lac operon contains the lacZ, lacY and lacA genes, which are transcribed together from one promoter. The lacI gene, located just upstream, encodes a repressor protein that binds the operator (lacO), a DNA sequence that overlaps the promoter, and blocks RNA polymerase. When lactose is present, some of it is converted to allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. A second level of control acts through the catabolite activator protein (CAP). When glucose is scarce, cyclic AMP rises and binds CAP, and the CAP–cAMP complex helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter (Figure 1).

Researchers measured β-galactosidase (the lacZ product) in several strains grown in a medium with glycerol as the carbon source. Some cultures received isopropyl β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG), a compound that binds the repressor like allolactose but cannot be broken down by the cell. Some also received glucose. The strains carried these mutations: lacI⁻, which makes no functional repressor; lacOᶜ, an operator that the repressor cannot bind; and lacIˢ, which makes a repressor that binds the operator but cannot bind inducer.

Two strains were partial diploids. Each carried a small F′ plasmid with a second copy of the lac region, so the cell had one copy on the chromosome and one on the plasmid. In these strains, the chromosome copy is written first and the plasmid copy after the slash. Activity is reported in Miller units, a standard measure of β-galactosidase activity.

Mutants like these were used in the original studies of the operon. Researchers could not see the repressor or the operator directly, so they inferred which parts of the system were proteins and which were DNA sites by asking whether a second copy of a gene could correct a defect in the other copy. A gene product that can correct a defect on another DNA molecule is said to act in trans; a site that controls only the genes on its own DNA molecule acts in cis.
Before each assay, cells were grown for at least six generations in the stated medium so that enzyme levels had reached a steady state. Each value in Table 1 is the mean of three cultures.

qs.q: What does the lacI⁻ / F′ lacI⁺ result show about the repressor?
o: It is needed to activate the transcription
Not quite. The lacI⁻ strain has high expression, so the repressor blocks transcription.
It diffuses and can act on either copy
Correct: the plasmid's repressor fixed the chromosome's operon, so it acts in trans.
It cannot bind IPTG when made from a plasmid
Not quite. Induction with IPTG worked normally (1,490).
It acts only on the DNA molecule that encodes it
Not quite. The plasmid gene controlled the chromosome's operon.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 explains the test: if a second copy of a gene can fix a defect on a different DNA molecule, its product acts in trans, meaning it can travel. Here the chromosome is lacI⁻, which alone gives 1,480 Miller units even without IPTG, because no repressor exists. Add lacI⁺ on the plasmid, and Table 1 shows activity drops to 3 without IPTG and rises normally to 1,490 with it. The repressor protein made from the plasmid must have diffused over and bound the chromosome's operator. Why the others are wrong: Acting only on its own DNA would leave the chromosome's operon stuck on; the repressor doesn't activate transcription, since losing it raises expression; the plasmid-made repressor still responded to IPTG, as induction was normal. Trap: Mixing up proteins, which can act in trans, with DNA sites, which act in cis.

qs.q: Why is activity low without IPTG in the lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ / F′ lacOᶜ lacZ⁻ strain?
o: The repressor cannot bind the lacOᶜ operator anywhere
Not quite. The chromosome's normal operator still binds the repressor.
The lacZ⁻ copy makes a protein that blocks the other copy
Not quite. Nothing suggests the lacZ⁻ copy interferes.
The faulty operator controls only the lacZ⁻ copy
Correct: operators act in cis, so lacOᶜ only affects the broken lacZ⁻ beside it.
IPTG is needed for any lacZ gene to be transcribed
Not quite. The lacOᶜ strain gave 900 units without IPTG.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says a DNA site like an operator controls only the genes on its own DNA molecule; it acts in cis. In this strain, the broken operator lacOᶜ sits on the plasmid next to lacZ⁻, a lacZ gene that makes no working enzyme. That copy may be transcribed all the time, but it produces nothing measurable. The working lacZ⁺ is on the chromosome, next to a normal operator that the repressor still binds. So without IPTG, activity stays low at 2, and with IPTG it rises to 1,500. Why the others are wrong: Saying the repressor can't bind any lacOᶜ operator misses that the chromosome has a normal operator it does bind; nothing suggests the lacZ⁻ copy makes a blocking protein; IPTG isn't needed for transcription in general, as the lacOᶜ strain alone gave 900 without it. Trap: Assuming a broken operator switches on every lacZ gene in the cell.

qs.q: What would a lacIˢ / F′ lacI⁺ strain most likely show with 1 mM IPTG?
o: High activity, because the normal repressor responds to IPTG
Not quite. The mutant repressor stays bound even when the normal one lets go.
High activity, because two lacI copies cancel each other
Not quite. Repressors don't cancel each other out.
Low, because the mutant repressor stays bound
Correct: the lacIˢ repressor ignores IPTG and stays bound, so it's dominant.
Activity of about 750, half of wild type
Not quite. The mutant protein blocks the operon, so it isn't half on.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says lacIˢ makes a repressor that binds the operator but can't bind inducer. So IPTG can't pull it off. Table 1 shows lacIˢ alone stays at 3 Miller units even with IPTG. Since a repressor is a protein that diffuses and acts in trans, the lacIˢ protein can sit on the operator no matter where the normal repressor is made. The normal repressor lets go when IPTG binds, but the stuck mutant one keeps the operator blocked. So expression stays low. This makes lacIˢ dominant. Why the others are wrong: High activity because the normal repressor responds misses that the mutant one stays bound; about 750, half of wild type, is wrong because the mutant protein can block the operon, not just half of it; repressors don't cancel each other out. Trap: Assuming a normal copy always masks a mutant one.

qs.q: Why did glucose lower activity in the lacI⁻ strain, which has no repressor?
o: Glucose converts IPTG into allolactose
Not quite. IPTG can't be broken down or converted.
Glucose restores a working repressor
Not quite. lacI⁻ makes no working repressor to restore.
Glucose binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Not quite. Sugars don't bind DNA sites like the operator.
Glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is inactive
Correct: glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP can't help, even with no repressor.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 describes a second control system, CAP. When glucose is scarce, cAMP rises, binds CAP, and helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter. When glucose is present, cAMP stays low and CAP can't help. Table 1 shows glucose cuts activity about 10-fold in every induced strain. In lacI⁻: 1,510 ÷ 150 ≈ 10. Since lacI⁻ has no repressor at all, the drop can't involve the repressor. It must go through CAP. This is called catabolite repression. Why the others are wrong: Glucose doesn't bind the operator or any DNA site; glucose doesn't convert IPTG, which can't be broken down; glucose can't repair a mutant gene, and lacI⁻ makes no working repressor. Trap: Explaining all lac control through the repressor alone.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use IPTG instead of lactose as the inducer?
o: Cells cannot break it down
Correct: cells can't break down IPTG, so its level stays steady.
It is a stronger carbon source than glucose
Not quite. IPTG isn't used as food at all.
It binds the operator directly
Not quite. IPTG binds the repressor, not the operator.
It activates CAP in place of cAMP
Not quite. CAP responds to cAMP, not IPTG.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says IPTG binds the repressor like allolactose but can't be broken down by the cell. Lactose, the natural inducer, gets used as food and has to be converted to allolactose by β-galactosidase first. So its level would fall over time and would vary between strains with different amounts of enzyme. IPTG stays at the same concentration the whole time in every culture, which makes the comparisons fair. Why the others are wrong: IPTG isn't a carbon source at all, since cells can't break it down; IPTG binds the repressor, not the operator; IPTG doesn't activate CAP, which responds to cAMP. Trap: Assuming the natural inducer is always the best choice for an experiment.

passages.title: Methanol Poisoning and Alcohol Dehydrogenase
text: Methanol poisoning is dangerous because the body oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde and then to formic acid, which causes metabolic acidosis and damages the optic nerve. The first step is catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), the same liver enzyme that oxidizes ethanol. Two treatments are used. One is fomepizole, a drug that binds the ADH active site. The other, used when fomepizole is unavailable, is ethanol itself. Both slow the conversion of methanol to its toxic products while the kidneys and dialysis remove the unchanged methanol.

Researchers studied purified human liver ADH to compare fomepizole with two experimental compounds. They measured the initial rate of NADH formation at 340 nm with ethanol as the substrate at several concentrations, with each inhibitor at a fixed concentration, and fit the data to the Michaelis–Menten equation. Compound N was known from crystal structures to bind a pocket far from the active site. Compound U had been found in a screen and had no known binding site. The fitted constants are shown in Table 1.

To check the fits, the researchers also drew double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) plots of 1/rate against 1/[ethanol] for each condition (Figure 1). Each point is the reciprocal of a measured rate at one ethanol concentration (0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 and 10 mM). In a second experiment, they measured the rate with methanol as the substrate. ADH oxidized methanol with a Kₘ of about 7 mM and a Vₘₐₓ about one-tenth of that for ethanol. When ethanol (5 mM) was added to a reaction containing methanol (5 mM), the rate of formaldehyde formation fell by about 75%.

Because the three inhibitors were tested at different concentrations, the researchers cautioned that the table should not be used to rank their potency. A fair comparison would require the inhibition constant (Ki) of each compound, measured from several inhibitor concentrations.

The researchers concluded that fomepizole is well suited to treatment because it acts at low concentration and does not itself produce a toxic product, whereas ethanol must be kept at a high blood level for many hours and causes intoxication.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which type of inhibition does fomepizole show toward ethanol oxidation?
o: Irreversible
Irreversible binding removes enzyme and lowers Vₘₐₓ, but Vₘₐₓ stayed at 100.
Competitive
Correct: Kₘ rose from 1.0 to 4.0 mM while Vₘₐₓ stayed at 100.
Noncompetitive
Noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ, and Vₘₐₓ didn't change.
Uncompetitive
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ. Here Kₘ went up.
qs.x: Correct: Look at the fomepizole row of Table 1. The apparent Kₘ (the substrate concentration that gives half the top rate) went from 1.0 mM to 4.0 mM, which is 4.0 ÷ 1.0 = 4 times higher, while Vₘₐₓ (the top rate) stayed at 100. That's the fingerprint of a competitive inhibitor. It sits in the active site, so the enzyme needs more ethanol to reach half speed, but with enough ethanol the substrate wins the site back and the full top rate returns. Paragraph 1 agrees: fomepizole binds the ADH active site. Why the others are wrong: noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ and leaves Kₘ alone, which is what Compound N does; uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ, which is what Compound U does; an irreversible inhibitor takes enzyme out of action for good, so Vₘₐₓ would fall. Trap: Assuming a drug that works at a tiny dose must bind irreversibly.

qs.q: At 1 mM ethanol, what is the expected rate with fomepizole present, in µmol/min per mg?
o: This uses Compound N's values: 50 × 1 ÷ (1 + 1) = 25.
That's the rate with no inhibitor, where 1 mM equals the normal Kₘ.
This puts Kₘ on top instead of [S]: 100 × 4 ÷ 5 = 80.
qs.x: Correct: Use the Michaelis–Menten equation, rate = Vₘₐₓ × [S] ÷ (Kₘ + [S]), where [S] is the substrate concentration. With fomepizole present, Table 1 gives Vₘₐₓ = 100 µmol/min per mg and apparent Kₘ = 4.0 mM, and the stem gives [S] = 1 mM ethanol. Plug in: rate = 100 × 1 ÷ (4.0 + 1). The top is 100 × 1 = 100. The bottom is 4.0 + 1 = 5. So rate = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 µmol/min per mg. The mM units cancel top and bottom, so the answer keeps Vₘₐₓ's units. Why the others are wrong: 25 uses Compound N's numbers, 50 × 1 ÷ (1.0 + 1) = 50 ÷ 2 = 25; 50 is the rate with no inhibitor, since 1 mM equals the normal Kₘ of 1.0 mM and the rate at Kₘ is half of 100; 80 puts Kₘ on top instead of [S], 100 × 4 ÷ 5 = 80. Trap: Using the uninhibited Kₘ of 1.0 mM after the inhibitor has raised it to 4.0 mM.

qs.q: How would the Lineweaver–Burk line for compound N compare with the line for no inhibitor?
o: Identical, because Kₘ is unchanged
Vₘₐₓ fell from 100 to 50, so the y-intercept moved.
Same y-intercept, x-intercept closer to zero
That's the competitive pattern, Kₘ up and Vₘₐₓ unchanged, like fomepizole.
Same x-intercept, higher y-intercept
Correct: Kₘ stayed at 1.0 mM (same x-intercept) and Vₘₐₓ halved (y-intercept doubled).
Parallel to it, shifted upward
Parallel lines are the uncompetitive pattern, like Compound U.
qs.x: Correct: A Lineweaver–Burk plot graphs 1/rate against 1/[S]. Its y-intercept (where the line crosses the vertical axis) is 1/Vₘₐₓ, and its x-intercept is −1/Kₘ. Table 1 and Figure 1 show Compound N cut Vₘₐₓ from 100 to 50 but left Kₘ at 1.0 mM. Half the Vₘₐₓ means double the y-intercept: 1/100 = 0.01 becomes 1/50 = 0.02. An unchanged Kₘ means the same x-intercept, −1/1.0 = −1 per mM. So the Compound N line crosses the x-axis at the same point and rises to a higher y-intercept, making a steeper line. That's the noncompetitive pattern, which fits Compound N binding a pocket far from the active site (paragraph 2). Why the others are wrong: the same y-intercept with the x-intercept moved toward zero is the competitive pattern, like fomepizole; a parallel line shifted up is the uncompetitive pattern, like Compound U; the lines can't be identical because Vₘₐₓ was halved. Trap: Mixing up which intercept reports Kₘ and which reports Vₘₐₓ.

qs.q: What do the data suggest about where compound U binds?
o: Only to the enzyme–substrate complex
Correct: Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ both fell by half, the uncompetitive pattern.
Only to the free enzyme's active site
That's competitive inhibition, which would raise Kₘ, not lower it.
To the ethanol molecule before it reaches ADH
Tying up ethanol acts like lowering [S], which would raise the apparent Kₘ.
Equally to free enzyme and the complex
That's noncompetitive, which leaves Kₘ unchanged, as with Compound N.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows Compound U cut Kₘ from 1.0 to 0.5 mM and Vₘₐₓ from 100 to 50, so both fell by the same factor of 2. That's uncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor can only grab the enzyme after substrate is already bound, forming a stuck enzyme–substrate–inhibitor complex. Trapping that complex lowers Vₘₐₓ, because those enzymes can't finish the reaction. It also pulls more enzyme into the substrate-bound form, so the enzyme looks like it holds substrate more tightly and the apparent Kₘ drops. So U's binding site probably only exists once ethanol is in place. Why the others are wrong: binding only the free enzyme's active site is competitive inhibition and would raise Kₘ; binding free enzyme and the complex equally is the noncompetitive pattern of Compound N, which leaves Kₘ unchanged; soaking up ethanol before it reaches ADH acts like lowering [S], which would raise the apparent Kₘ, not lower it. Trap: Reading a lower Kₘ as a sign that the inhibitor is helping the enzyme.

qs.q: Why should Table 1 not be used to rank the potency of fomepizole, compound N and compound U?
o: The inhibitors were tested at different concentrations
Correct: the effect depends on both potency and concentration, so the two are mixed together.
The Michaelis–Menten equation cannot be fitted to inhibited enzyme
Not quite. The passage says all conditions were fit to that equation.
No uninhibited enzyme was measured as a baseline for comparison
Not quite. The first row of Table 1 is the uninhibited enzyme.
The rates were measured with methanol instead of ethanol as substrate
Not quite. The Table 1 constants came from ethanol; methanol was a second experiment.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says the three inhibitors were tested at different concentrations: 2 µM fomepizole, 50 µM compound N and 20 µM compound U. How much an inhibitor changes Kₘ or Vₘₐₓ depends on how tightly it binds and on how much of it is present, so a bigger change can come from a stronger drug or just from more of it. Because concentration differs between rows, potency and dose are tangled together. A fair ranking needs the inhibition constant Kᵢ, measured at several inhibitor concentrations. Why the others are wrong: the uninhibited row is in Table 1 as the baseline; the Michaelis–Menten fit was applied to every condition; and the Table 1 constants came from ethanol, with methanol used only in the second experiment. Trap: Comparing effects as if every treatment were given at the same dose.

graph.title: Figure 1. Lineweaver–Burk plot for ADH with ethanol as substrate under four conditions

passages.title: Ribonuclease Refolding After Urea Denaturation
text: A protein's amino acid sequence contains the information needed for it to fold. In a classic set of experiments, ribonuclease was fully unfolded in concentrated urea with a reducing agent that breaks its four disulfide bonds. When both were removed, the enzyme refolded and regained nearly all of its activity. Folding is driven mainly by burying hydrophobic side chains away from water, while hydrogen bonds, ion pairs and disulfide bonds add further stability.

Researchers studied a 128-residue enzyme with one disulfide bond, between Cys30 and Cys115, and a single tryptophan buried in its hydrophobic core. When the protein unfolds, the tryptophan becomes exposed to water, and its fluorescence emission peak shifts from 334 nm to 352 nm. The researchers used this shift to measure the fraction of protein unfolded at each urea concentration (Figure 1). From these curves they calculated the urea concentration at which half the protein is unfolded (the midpoint) and the free energy of unfolding in the absence of urea (ΔG). A larger ΔG means a more stable protein. The midpoints and ΔG values are listed in Table 1. They tested the wild type and three mutants: C30A/C115A, which lacks the disulfide; L58A, in which a core leucine is replaced by alanine; and K12A, in which a lysine on the surface is replaced by alanine. All four had the same activity at 25 °C without urea.

In a second experiment, wild-type enzyme was unfolded in 8 M urea with 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), a reducing agent. In procedure 1, the urea was removed first by dialysis and the DTT was removed afterward, in air. In procedure 2, the DTT was removed first while the protein was still in 8 M urea, and then the urea was removed. Procedure 1 restored 92% of the original activity; procedure 2 restored 3%. Mass spectrometry showed that after procedure 2, most molecules had a disulfide bond, but often between Cys30 and one of the protein's two other cysteines, which are normally free.

qs.q: Why does the tryptophan emission shift when the protein unfolds?
o: The peptide bonds near tryptophan are cut
Unfolding changes the shape, not the peptide bonds of the backbone.
The tryptophan becomes exposed to water
Correct: it moves from the nonpolar core into polar water, shifting its emission to longer wavelength.
Urea forms a covalent bond with tryptophan
Urea works through noncovalent effects. It doesn't bond to side chains.
Tryptophan is converted to a different amino acid
The residue is still tryptophan. Only its surroundings changed.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the single tryptophan sits in the protein's hydrophobic core, a nonpolar pocket with no water. When the protein unfolds, that side chain ends up surrounded by water, which is polar. Fluorescence (light given off after a molecule absorbs light) depends on the surroundings, and in a polar environment the light comes out at a longer wavelength: here the peak moves from 334 nm to 352 nm. The residue itself hasn't changed at all, only its neighborhood. Why the others are wrong: urea unfolds proteins through noncovalent effects and doesn't bond to side chains; unfolding loosens the 3D shape but leaves the peptide bonds of the chain intact; tryptophan stays tryptophan, since nothing changes the sequence. Trap: Treating a change in shape as a chemical change in the residue.

qs.q: Why did the L58A substitution lower stability much more than K12A?
o: L58A removes the disulfide bond
The disulfide is between Cys30 and Cys115, untouched by L58A.
Lysine is hydrophobic, so its loss stabilizes the protein
Lysine is charged and polar, not hydrophobic.
Alanine cannot be part of an α-helix
Alanine is one of the strongest helix formers.
Leu58 is buried in the hydrophobic core
Correct: losing a buried core residue weakens the hydrophobic effect, while a surface lysine adds little.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says folding is driven mainly by burying hydrophobic side chains away from water. Leu58 sits in the core, so swapping its large, greasy side chain for alanine's tiny methyl group leaves a hole there and weakens that main driving force. Table 1 shows ΔG of unfolding dropping from 6.8 to 3.4 kcal/mol, a loss of 6.8 − 3.4 = 3.4 kcal/mol, half the stability. Lys12 is on the surface, already in water, so losing its side chain costs only 6.8 − 6.6 = 0.2 kcal/mol. Why the others are wrong: lysine is positively charged and polar, not hydrophobic; alanine is actually one of the best helix-forming amino acids; the disulfide links Cys30 and Cys115, so changing residue 58 doesn't touch it. Trap: Assuming every mutation hurts stability equally, no matter where the residue sits.

qs.q: What best explains the low activity after procedure 2?
o: Urea changed the amino acid sequence
Urea never changes the amino acid sequence.
Disulfides formed before the chain folded
Correct: disulfides formed while the chain was unfolded, locking in wrong cysteine pairs.
Removing urea first harms the protein
Procedure 2 removed urea last, not first.
DTT permanently denatured the enzyme
Procedure 1 also used DTT and restored 92% of activity.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 compares two orders of steps. In procedure 2, DTT (the reducing agent that keeps cysteines from bonding) was removed while the chain was still floppy in 8 M urea. Air then oxidized the cysteines into disulfide bonds before the chain had folded, so whichever cysteines happened to bump into each other got linked, often the wrong pairs. Mass spectrometry confirmed Cys30 bonded to one of the normally free cysteines. When the urea was then removed, those wrong bonds locked the chain into non-native shapes, and only 3% of activity came back. In procedure 1, urea came out first, so the chain folded, Cys30 and Cys115 ended up side by side, and the correct bond formed: 92% activity. Why the others are wrong: urea doesn't change the sequence; procedure 1 also used DTT and worked fine; procedure 2 removed urea last, not first. Trap: Deciding the sequence lacks folding information when the order of steps caused the problem.

qs.q: Which interactions does concentrated urea mainly disrupt to unfold the protein?
o: Covalent bonds within the amino acid side chains
Urea leaves side chains chemically unchanged.
Peptide bonds of the backbone
Breaking peptide bonds needs a protease or strong acid.
Hydrogen bonds and other noncovalent forces
Correct: urea weakens noncovalent forces, unfolding the protein without breaking covalent bonds.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines
Disulfides need a reducing agent such as DTT.
qs.x: Correct: Urea is a denaturant, a chemical that unfolds proteins. It hydrogen-bonds with the protein and makes it easier for water to surround nonpolar groups, which weakens the noncovalent forces (hydrogen bonds and the hydrophobic effect) that hold the folded shape together. It doesn't break covalent bonds. That's why the experiments in paragraphs 1 and 3 needed a separate reducing agent, DTT, to break the disulfide bond. Why the others are wrong: peptide bonds stay intact, since breaking them takes a protease or strong acid; disulfide bonds need a reducing agent such as DTT; side chains come out of urea chemically unchanged. Trap: Assuming a denaturant breaks every kind of bond in the protein.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1 and Table 1, which proteins are mostly unfolded at 3 M urea?
o: L58A and C30A/C115A
Correct: their midpoints, 2.6 M and 2.1 M, are below 3 M.
Wild type and K12A
Their midpoints, 4.2 and 4.1 M, are above 3 M, so they stay mostly folded.
All four proteins
Wild type and K12A have midpoints above 3 M and stay mostly folded.
Only L58A
C30A/C115A's midpoint of 2.6 M is also below 3 M.
qs.x: Correct: The midpoint in Table 1 is the urea concentration at which half the protein is unfolded. Above its midpoint, more than half of that protein is unfolded. So compare each midpoint with 3 M. C30A/C115A has a midpoint of 2.6 M and L58A has 2.1 M. Both are below 3 M, so at 3 M both are mostly unfolded. Wild type (4.2 M) and K12A (4.1 M) are above 3 M, so they're still mostly folded. Figure 1 agrees: at 3 M the points for those two sit below 0.5, and the points for the other two sit above 0.5. Why the others are wrong: wild type and K12A have midpoints above 4 M, so they stay mostly folded at 3 M; picking only L58A misses the disulfide mutant, whose midpoint of 2.6 M is also below 3 M; not all four, since wild type and K12A stay mostly folded. Trap: Forgetting that removing the disulfide also destabilizes the protein.

graph.title: Figure 1. Fraction of protein unfolded at each urea concentration for the wild type and three mutants

passages.title: Reading Vmax and Km from a Saturation Curve
text: An enzyme's rate rises with substrate concentration and then levels off. Two numbers describe the curve: the rate it approaches at high substrate, and the substrate concentration at which it reaches half that rate. The first depends on how much enzyme is present and how fast each molecule works; the second describes how tightly the substrate is held.

Because the two are independent, a reduced rate at some particular substrate concentration can arise from a lower ceiling or from a higher half saturation concentration, and the rate at one concentration cannot say which.
The two parameters were determined for four enzyme preparations, along with rates measured over a wide range of substrate concentrations, including 0.5 mM (Figure 1 and Table 1).

The reference approaches 100 units at high substrate, is half saturated at half a millimolar, and therefore produces 50 units at half a millimolar. C3 repeats it, so its curve overlaps the reference's in Figure 1.

C1 approaches 48 with an unchanged half saturation concentration, and its enzyme content is 47 hundredths of the reference. Its ceiling has fallen in proportion to the amount of enzyme present, and its substrate binding is unaffected.

C2 approaches 99 with a half saturation concentration of 4.8 mM, and its enzyme content is normal. At half a millimolar it produces nine units, far below C1, even though its ceiling is essentially normal.

The measurement at half a millimolar therefore ranks C2 as the worse preparation while the ceiling ranks C1 as the worse, and neither ranking is wrong: they answer different questions. At a substrate concentration of 50 mM the ranking would reverse again, because C2 would approach its normal ceiling and C1 could not.

Two qualifications apply. Both parameters were obtained by fitting the measured rates to a curve, so each carries the uncertainty of the fit as well as of the individual rate measurements, and the half saturation concentration is the less well determined of the two when few points lie below it. And the enzyme present was quantified by total protein of the expected size rather than by activity, so inactive enzyme is counted.

qs.q: Why can the rate at one substrate concentration not identify the change?
o: The two parameters are not independent of each other
C1 and C2 each changed only one parameter.
Two parameters set that rate
Correct: both the ceiling and the half saturation concentration set that rate.
It can identify the change
C1 and C2 are both low for different reasons.
Only the ceiling influences the rate measured
Half saturation matters too, as C2's low rate shows.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says two numbers shape the curve: the ceiling (the rate approached at high substrate, called Vₘₐₓ) and the half saturation concentration (Kₘ, the substrate level giving half the ceiling). The rate at any one substrate level depends on both. Paragraph 2 says a low rate could come from a lower ceiling or a higher Kₘ. Figure 1 shows both: at 0.5 mM, C1 makes 24 units because its ceiling fell to 48, and C2 makes 9 units because its Kₘ rose to 4.80 mM. One rate can't tell those apart; you need the whole curve. Why the others are wrong: the half saturation concentration also affects the rate, as C2 shows; the two vary separately, since C1 changed only its ceiling and C2 only its Kₘ; one rate can't identify the change, because C1 and C2 are both low for different reasons. Trap: Trying to read a curve described by two numbers from a single point on it.

qs.q: Why would the ranking of C1 and C2 reverse at high substrate?
o: C1 has the higher ceiling
C1 has the lower ceiling, 48.
Both would approach the same rate at high substrate
Their ceilings differ, 99 against 48.
C2 reaches its normal ceiling
Correct: at high substrate C2 nears 99 units while C1 is capped at 48.
C1's half saturation concentration would fall
C1's half saturation stays at 0.52 mM.
qs.x: Correct: At very high substrate, every enzyme runs near its ceiling, so the half saturation concentration stops mattering. Table 1 gives C2 a ceiling of 99 units and C1 a ceiling of only 48. At 50 mM, about 10 times C2's Kₘ of 4.80 mM, C2 runs near 99 while C1 can't get past 48. So C2, which looked worse at 0.5 mM (9 units against 24), becomes the better one. Paragraph 7 makes this point. Why the others are wrong: C1's half saturation concentration is a fixed property, 0.52 mM, and doesn't change with substrate; their ceilings differ about two-fold, 99 against 48, so they won't meet; C1 has the lower ceiling, not the higher one. Trap: Assuming a comparison made at one substrate level holds at every level.

qs.q: Why is C1's maximum rate reduced to about half of the reference's?
o: Less active enzyme is present in sample C1
Correct: it has 0.47 of the normal enzyme, matching its 48% ceiling.
Its substrate binding is weaker
Not quite. Its half saturation is unchanged at 0.52 mM.
The fit underestimates its ceiling
Not quite. The fit's weak point is the half saturation concentration, not the ceiling.
Each enzyme molecule works more slowly
The lower enzyme amount explains the drop fully.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the ceiling depends on how much enzyme there is and how fast each molecule works. Table 1 shows C1 has 0.47 of the reference's enzyme and a ceiling of 48 out of 100, or 0.48 of the reference. Those match, so less enzyme explains the whole drop, with no need for each molecule to be slower. Its half saturation concentration, 0.52 mM, is basically the reference's 0.50 mM, so substrate binding is normal (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: its substrate is held normally, the half saturation concentration barely changed; the lower enzyme content already accounts for the fall, so each molecule isn't slower; and the fit is least certain for the half saturation concentration, not the ceiling. Trap: Blaming a change in enzyme quality when a change in amount explains it.

qs.q: A researcher wants to know whether a preparation's low rate at 0.5 mM comes from a lower ceiling or a higher half saturation concentration. Which experiment is best?
o: Measure rates over many substrate concentrations
Correct: the whole curve shows both the ceiling and the half saturation concentration.
Repeat the 0.5 mM measurement several more times
Not quite. Repeats tighten that one rate but still cannot say which parameter changed.
Measure the rate only at a very high substrate concentration
Not quite. That finds the ceiling but says nothing about the half saturation concentration.
Double the amount of enzyme in every reaction tube
Not quite. That raises every rate and does not separate the two parameters.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says a low rate at one substrate concentration can come from a lower ceiling or from a higher half saturation concentration, and one rate cannot say which. The fix is to measure the whole curve. Figure 1 does this: the curve for C1 flattens at 48 units while the curve for C2 rises late but reaches 99. Measuring only low and high concentrations together would then show both numbers. Why the others are wrong: repeating one concentration just narrows the error on that one rate; measuring only at very high substrate reveals the ceiling and leaves the half saturation concentration unknown; and doubling the enzyme raises both curves without telling you which parameter was responsible. Trap: Collecting more of the same measurement when the question needs a different one.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, by what factor is C2's rate at 0.5 mM below the reference's?
o: That's C1's factor: 50 ÷ 24 ≈ 2.1.
Correct: 50 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.6.
That's C2's rate, not the factor.
That's the ratio of half saturation values, 4.80 ÷ 0.50.
qs.x: Correct: A factor is a ratio, so divide: factor = reference rate ÷ C2's rate, both at 0.5 mM. From Figure 1, the reference makes 50 units at 0.5 mM and C2 makes 9 units. Plug in: 50 ÷ 9. Nine goes into 45 five times (9 × 5 = 45), leaving 5, and 5 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.56. So 50 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.56, about 5.6. Units cancel. Why the others are wrong: 9.0 is C2's rate itself, not the factor; 2.1 is C1's factor, 50 ÷ 24 ≈ 2.1; 9.6 is the ratio of half saturation concentrations, 4.80 ÷ 0.50 = 9.6, not of rates. Trap: Using the wrong column or reporting a rate when a ratio is asked for.

graph.title: Figure 1. Rate versus substrate concentration for four enzyme preparations (label: rate at 0.5 mM)

passages.title: Lipid Composition and Membrane Fluidity
text: A biological membrane is a fluid in two dimensions: its lipids diffuse within the plane of the bilayer while rarely crossing from one leaflet to the other. How readily they diffuse is its fluidity, and it depends on the lipids' composition and on the temperature.

Two features of the fatty acid chains control it. A chain with a double bond has a kink that prevents close packing and raises fluidity, and a shorter chain has less surface in contact with its neighbors and also raises it. Cholesterol acts in both directions: it reduces fluidity above the transition temperature and prevents the ordered packing that would occur below it.

Function depends on fluidity rather than merely accompanying it. A transport protein needs a degree of freedom to change shape, and an organism moved to a colder environment adjusts its lipid composition to keep the fluidity in the range its proteins require.

Fluidity and transport were measured in membranes of varying composition. Table 1 lists the composition of each membrane type, and Figure 1 plots fluidity against transport rate for five preparations of each type (the legend gives the mean of each type).

Raising unsaturation increased fluidity to 1.46 and transport to 1.38; raising cholesterol reduced them to 0.71 and 0.62; and doing both returned fluidity to 1.02 and transport to 0.98. The transport rate tracked the fluidity in every condition rather than tracking either compositional variable.

The last row is what establishes that fluidity rather than composition is the relevant variable, because its composition differs from the reference in both respects and its fluidity and function match it.

Two qualifications apply. Fluidity is measured by the rotation of a fluorescent probe inserted into the bilayer, which reports the environment the probe occupies and may not sample the bilayer uniformly, particularly if cholesterol creates regions the probe avoids. And cholesterol binds some transport proteins directly, so a change in transport with cholesterol could in principle be a direct effect, which the last row argues against without excluding entirely.

qs.q: According to the passage, why does a double bond in a fatty acid chain raise membrane fluidity?
o: It shortens the chain, reducing contact with neighboring chains
Not quite. Shorter chains do raise fluidity, but a double bond doesn't shorten the chain. It bends it.
It puts a kink in the chain that prevents close packing
Correct: the kink keeps chains from packing closely, so they move more freely.
It strengthens van der Waals contacts between chains
Not quite. Stronger contacts would lower fluidity. The kink actually weakens those contacts.
It raises the transition temperature of the bilayer
Not quite. That's backwards. Unsaturation lowers the transition temperature, which helps keep the membrane fluid.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. A double bond puts a fixed kink in a fatty acid chain. Straight chains can pack tightly side by side, like pencils in a box. Kinked chains can't, so they're held less tightly and move around more. That freedom is fluidity, how easily the lipids slide past each other. Table 1 and Figure 1 show the effect: raising unsaturated chains from 42% to 68% raises fluidity from 1.00 to 1.46. Why the others are wrong: a double bond doesn't shorten the chain, it bends it (shorter chains raise fluidity for a different reason); the kink weakens van der Waals contacts instead of strengthening them; and unsaturation lowers the transition temperature, it doesn't raise it. Trap: Hunting for a change in size or charge when the real change is in packing.

qs.q: Which comparison best supports the claim that membrane fluidity, rather than lipid composition, determines the transport rate?
o: Reference vs high unsaturation
Not quite. Fluidity and transport both rose, but composition changed too, so this can't tell the two apart.
Reference vs high cholesterol
Not quite. Both fell together, but cholesterol changed too, so composition could still be the cause.
High unsaturation vs high unsaturation and cholesterol
Not quite. Only cholesterol differs, and fluidity and transport fall together, so composition is still a possible cause.
Reference vs high unsaturation and cholesterol
Correct: composition differs in both ways, but fluidity and transport both match the reference.
qs.x: Correct: The last row in Table 1 has more unsaturated chains (67% against 42%) and more cholesterol (34 against 18 mol %) than the reference, so its composition differs in both ways. Those two changes cancel out: fluidity is 1.02 (Figure 1), about the reference's 1.00. And transport is 0.98, about the reference's 1.00. Different makeup, same fluidity, same function. So function follows fluidity, not either ingredient on its own (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: the reference against high unsaturation shows fluidity and transport rising together, but composition changed too, so it can't separate the two; reference against high cholesterol has the same problem in the other direction; and high unsaturation against the combined membrane changes cholesterol along with fluidity, so composition is still a suspect. Trap: Linking function to one ingredient when a physical property in between is doing the work.

qs.q: The passage suggests the fluidity measurements could be biased because the fluorescent probe:
o: rotates more slowly in a stiffer bilayer
Not quite. That's how the method works, not a flaw in it.
changes the fluidity of the bilayer it enters
Not quite. The passage doesn't raise this. Its worry is where the probe sits.
may avoid the regions that cholesterol creates in the bilayer
Correct: cholesterol can create patches the probe avoids, skewing its reading.
binds directly to transport proteins
Not quite. The passage says cholesterol, not the probe, binds transport proteins.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says fluidity was measured by watching how fast a fluorescent probe spins inside the bilayer. The probe only reports on the spot where it sits. Cholesterol can create patches packed differently from the rest of the membrane, and if the probe avoids those patches, it reports the fluidity of the remaining bilayer instead of a true average. Why the others are wrong: rotating more slowly in a stiffer bilayer is how the method works, not a flaw; the passage never says the probe changes the bilayer; and it's cholesterol, not the probe, that binds transport proteins. Trap: Assuming a reporter molecule spreads evenly through a patchy material.

qs.q: By what factor did transport differ between the high unsaturation and high cholesterol membranes?
o: That's the high cholesterol rate, not a factor.
That's the high unsaturation rate, not a factor.
That's a fluidity value, not a transport factor.
qs.x: Correct: By what factor means divide: factor = high unsaturation transport ÷ high cholesterol transport. From the means in the Figure 1 legend, the transport rate is 1.38 for high unsaturation and 0.62 for high cholesterol. Plug in: 1.38 ÷ 0.62. Multiply top and bottom by 100 to clear the decimals: 138 ÷ 62. 62 goes into 124 twice, leaving 14, and 14 ÷ 62 ≈ 0.23, so 138 ÷ 62 ≈ 2.23, about 2.2. Why the others are wrong: 1.38 is the high unsaturation rate itself; 0.62 is the high cholesterol rate itself; 1.46 is a fluidity value, from the wrong axis. Trap: Reading across into the fluidity column.

qs.q: A critic claims cholesterol lowered transport by acting on the transport protein itself, not by lowering fluidity. How do the results bear on this claim?
o: They argue against it but cannot fully rule it out
Correct: with extra unsaturation, 34 mol % cholesterol gave normal transport (0.98), which argues against a direct effect. But cholesterol binds some proteins directly, so it can't be excluded.
They rule it out, because transport tracked fluidity in every membrane
Not quite. Tracking fluidity argues against a direct effect, but cholesterol binds some transport proteins, so it isn't fully excluded.
They support it, because high cholesterol alone lowered transport to 0.62
Not quite. Fluidity fell just as much, and the combined membrane had the same cholesterol with normal transport.
They cannot address it, because cholesterol does not bind proteins
Not quite. The passage says cholesterol binds some transport proteins.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says cholesterol binds some transport proteins directly. So cholesterol might change transport by acting on the protein itself, not only by changing fluidity. The last row argues against that: with high cholesterol (34 mol %), transport is 0.98, near normal, because the extra unsaturation brought fluidity back to 1.02. If cholesterol were mainly acting directly, transport should have stayed low. But that's evidence, not proof, so a direct effect can't be ruled out completely. Why the others are wrong: the results don't fully rule it out, because cholesterol can bind proteins directly; the drop to 0.62 doesn't support it, since fluidity fell just as much and the combined membrane had normal transport (0.98) at the same cholesterol level; and the passage says cholesterol does bind some transport proteins. Trap: Treating a result that fits your idea as proof that rules out the alternative.

graph.title: Figure 1. Transport rate against fluidity in membrane preparations of four compositions (5 preparations each)

passages.title: Coupling Unfavorable Steps Through a Shared Intermediate
text: A reaction proceeds spontaneously only if it releases free energy. A step that absorbs free energy can still be made to happen by coupling it to a step that releases more, provided the two share an intermediate so that the second cannot occur without the first. Coupling without a shared intermediate leaves the unfavorable step as unfavorable as before.

The combined free energy change of a coupled pair is the sum of the two, so the pair proceeds when the sum is negative, however unfavorable the first step is on its own. The size of the surplus determines how far the pair can be driven, not whether it proceeds.

Free energy changes were calculated and the extent of reaction reached was measured for five coupled pairs. Table 1 lists the two steps of each pair, and Figure 1 plots the extent reached against the combined free energy change (the sum of the two steps).

The reference couples a step absorbing 14 kJ a mole to one releasing 31, shares an intermediate, and reaches 96%. B3 repeats it. The sum is negative by 17 kJ a mole, and the pair goes nearly to completion.

B1 has the same two steps and no shared intermediate, and reaches 2%, the extent expected from the unfavorable step alone. The energy released by the second step is therefore unavailable to the first unless the two are linked chemically.

B2 shares an intermediate but the favorable step releases only 9 kJ a mole. The sum is positive by five, and the pair reaches 11%, which is more than B1 but far from completion. A shared intermediate is necessary and not sufficient.

B4 shares an intermediate and has a sum negative by 3 kJ a mole, and reaches 63%. Comparing B4 with the reference shows that the extent reached rises with the size of the surplus rather than switching between two states, so the surplus sets how far and the sign sets whether.

Two qualifications apply. The free energy changes were calculated for standard concentrations of all participants, and the actual concentrations in the reaction mixtures differ, so the values describe a reference condition rather than the mixtures themselves. And the extent reached was recorded after a fixed interval of two hours, which is long enough for these pairs to approach their limits but does not guarantee that the slowest had stopped changing.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, why does the coupled reaction in B1 proceed only to 2%?
o: Its unfavorable step absorbs more than B4's
B1 absorbs 14 kJ/mol. B4 absorbs more, 28.
Nothing links the two steps
Correct: With no shared intermediate, the favorable step's energy can't reach the unfavorable one.
It reaches 96%
That's the reference. B1 reached only 2%.
Its favorable step releases too little energy
It releases 31 kJ/mol, the same as the reference.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says an unfavorable step (one that absorbs free energy) can be driven by a favorable one only if they share an intermediate, a molecule made by one step and used by the other. B1 has the same two steps as the reference, +14 and −31 kJ/mol, but nothing links them. So the favorable step just runs on its own, and its energy never reaches the unfavorable one. B1 reaches 2%, about what the unfavorable step manages alone (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: the favorable step releasing too little is wrong, it releases 31, same as the reference; absorbing more than B4 is wrong, B1 absorbs 14 and B4 absorbs 28; reaching 96% is the reference, B1 reached 2%. Trap: Assuming two reactions in the same tube are automatically coupled.

qs.q: B2 shares an intermediate between its two steps, yet it barely proceeds. Why is a shared intermediate not sufficient for coupling?
o: Sharing an intermediate makes the sum negative
Sharing an intermediate passes energy across but doesn't change the sum.
B2 lacks an enzyme
Nothing mentions a missing enzyme. B2's sum is simply positive.
B2 lacks a shared intermediate entirely
Table 1 says B2 does share an intermediate.
The sum may still be positive
Correct: B2 shares an intermediate, but +14 + (−9) = +5, still positive.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says a coupled pair's total free energy change is the sum of its two steps. The formula: ΔG(total) = ΔG(unfavorable) + ΔG(favorable). For B2 in Table 1, that's +14 + (−9) = +5 kJ/mol. The sum is still positive, so even with a shared intermediate the pair doesn't go far: 11% (paragraph 6). Sharing an intermediate lets the energy pass across, but it doesn't add any energy. Why the others are wrong: sharing an intermediate making the sum negative is wrong, it doesn't change either number; B2 lacking a shared intermediate is false, the table says Yes; B2 lacking an enzyme isn't mentioned anywhere, the passage blames the positive sum. Trap: Treating something that's needed as if it were enough by itself.

qs.q: What does comparing the extent of reaction in B4 with that of the reference show?
o: Extent rises with the surplus
Correct: A −3 surplus reached 63%, a −17 surplus reached 96%. Bigger surplus, further reaction.
Their extents are identical
B4 reached 63% and the reference 96%.
Extent depends on the favorable step alone
Not quite. B4's favorable step matches the reference's; the surplus, not one step, sets the extent.
A larger unfavorable step prevents reaction
B4 absorbs 28 kJ/mol and still reaches 63%.
qs.x: Correct: Work out each sum with ΔG(total) = ΔG(unfavorable) + ΔG(favorable). Reference: +14 + (−31) = −17 kJ/mol, reaching 96%. B4: +28 + (−31) = −3 kJ/mol, reaching 63%. Both sums are negative, so both go forward, but B4's small surplus gets it only part of the way. Paragraph 7 sums it up: the sign of the sum decides whether, the size of the surplus decides how far. Why the others are wrong: extent doesn't depend on the favorable step alone, it's the overall surplus that matters; a larger unfavorable step preventing reaction is wrong, B4 absorbs 28 and still reaches 63%; identical extents is false, 63 versus 96. Trap: Thinking a negative sum means the reaction goes all the way to completion.

qs.q: Why do the tabulated energies describe a reference condition?
o: The extent was recorded after two hours
Not quite. That's a separate caveat about the extent measurement, not the energies.
They were measured in the mixtures themselves
Not quite. They were calculated for standard conditions, not measured in the mixtures.
They assume standard concentrations
Correct: They were calculated for standard concentrations, and the real mixtures had different ones.
They describe the mixtures exactly here
Not quite. The mixtures weren't at standard concentrations, so the values don't fit them exactly.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says the free energy values were calculated for standard concentrations of everything in the reaction. But free energy change depends on the real concentrations, and the actual mixtures weren't at standard concentrations. So the table's numbers are a common yardstick, not the exact energy in each tube. Why the others are wrong: being measured in the mixtures is wrong, they were calculated for standard conditions; the two hour recording time is true, but it's a separate caveat about the extent measurement, not about the energies; describing the mixtures exactly contradicts paragraph 8. Trap: Reading a standard value as if it were the value in the actual tube.

qs.q: By how many kilojoules a mole is B4's combined change negative?
o: Correct: +28 + (−31) = −3 kJ/mol.
+5 is B2's sum (14 − 9), and it's positive.
−17 is the reference's sum (14 − 31).
28 is B4's unfavorable step alone. Add the −31.
qs.x: Correct: The total change = ΔG(unfavorable) + ΔG(favorable). Table 1 gives B4's unfavorable step as +28 kJ/mol and its favorable step as −31 kJ/mol. Plug in: +28 + (−31) = 28 − 31 = −3 kJ/mol. So the pair is negative by 3, matching paragraph 7. That small surplus is why B4 goes forward but stops at 63%. Why the others are wrong: 5 is B2's sum (+14 − 9), and it's positive, not negative; 17 is the reference's surplus (+14 − 31 = −17); 28 is only B4's unfavorable step, before adding the favorable one. Trap: Quoting one step's value instead of adding both steps together.

graph.title: Figure 1. Extent of reaction reached against combined free energy change for five coupled pairs

passages.title: Double Bonds, Chain Packing and Lipid Melting
text: A lipid built from long hydrocarbon chains packs tightly when the chains are straight and loosely when they contain a bend. A single double bond in the chain introduces a fixed bend, so one such bond lowers the temperature at which the lipid melts considerably, and further bonds lower it less steeply.

Chain length acts in the opposite direction. A longer chain has more surface in contact with its neighbors and melts at a higher temperature, so a long chain with one double bond can melt at the same temperature as a short saturated one. The melting temperature alone therefore does not report either property.

Chain length, double bond number, melting temperature and area per molecule were measured for five lipids (Table 1 gives chain length and double bonds; Figure 1 plots melting temperature against area per molecule).

The reference has 18 carbons and no double bonds and melts at 69 degrees, occupying 0.42 square nanometers per molecule. P1 adds one double bond at the same length and melts at 13 degrees, a fall of 56 degrees, with the area rising to 0.61.

P2 adds a second double bond and melts at minus five, a further fall of 18 degrees. The first bond therefore accounts for most of the effect, and the area rises only slightly between P1 and P2, which is consistent with the packing already being disrupted.

P3 is saturated and four carbons shorter, and melts at 54 degrees with an area nearly equal to the reference's. Shortening the chain lowers the melting temperature without changing how the chains pack, which separates the two causes.

P4 has 22 carbons and one double bond and melts at 34 degrees, higher than P1 by 21 degrees. A lipid of unknown composition melting at 34 degrees could be a long chain with a bend or a shorter saturated chain, and the area per molecule distinguishes them because it responds to bends and not to length.

Two qualifications apply. Melting temperature was determined as the midpoint of a transition that spans several degrees, and the width of that transition differs between the lipids, so the midpoints are comparable while the onsets are not. And area per molecule was measured in a film spread on a water surface at a fixed pressure, which reproduces the packing of one layer rather than the arrangement within a solid lipid.

qs.q: Why does the first double bond lower the melting temperature most?
o: All bonds lower it equally
Not quite. The drops are 56 and 18 degrees, not equal.
The first bond lengthens the chain considerably
Not quite. A double bond doesn't lengthen the chain. P1 still has 18 carbons.
Later bonds introduce larger bends than the first
Not quite. The bends are similar in size.
It introduces the first bend
Correct: The first bend breaks the tight packing, so later bends have less to disrupt.
qs.x: Correct: Straight chains pack tightly, like pencils in a box. Paragraph 1 says a double bond puts a fixed bend in the chain. The first bend wrecks that neat packing, so the melting temperature drops a lot: 69 to 13 degrees, a fall of 56 (paragraph 4). Once the packing is already messed up, a second bend has much less left to disturb, so it only drops it another 18 degrees, 13 to −5 (paragraph 5). The area per molecule tells the same story: 0.42 to 0.61 for the first bond, then only to 0.66. Why the others are wrong: the bends are about the same size, the second isn't bigger; a double bond doesn't make the chain longer, P1 still has 18 carbons; the drops aren't equal, 56 versus 18 degrees. Trap: Assuming each identical change adds the same amount.

qs.q: Why can two lipids melting at the same temperature differ in composition?
o: Length and bends act oppositely
Correct: Length raises and bends lower the melting point, so they can balance out.
Only chain length sets the melting temperature
Not quite. Double bonds lower it sharply too.
Melting temperature fixes the composition
Not quite. Two different lipids can share one melting point.
Bends raise melting temperature
Not quite. Bends lower the melting temperature.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. Two things change the melting temperature in opposite directions. A longer chain touches its neighbors more and melts higher. A double bond bends the chain and makes it melt lower. So a long chain with a bend can land at the same melting temperature as a shorter straight chain. Paragraph 7 gives the example: P4 (22 carbons, one double bond) melts at 34 degrees, which a shorter saturated chain could also do. Why the others are wrong: chain length isn't the only factor, one double bond dropped the melting point 56 degrees; melting temperature alone can't pin down the composition, since two different lipids can share it; bends lower the melting temperature, they don't raise it. Trap: Trying to read two unknowns from one measurement.

qs.q: Why does measuring the area per molecule help separate the two possible explanations of a 34 degree melting point?
o: It responds to film pressure
Not quite. Film pressure was held fixed.
It responds to bends alone
Correct: It changes with bends but not with length.
It responds to neither property
Not quite. It rises with double bonds, 0.42 to 0.61.
It responds to chain length alone
Not quite. P3 is shorter but has nearly the same area as the reference.
qs.x: Correct: The area per molecule is how much surface each lipid takes up in a single layer. Figure 1 shows it reacts to bends: adding one double bond raises it from 0.42 to 0.61 nm². But it ignores length: P3 is 4 carbons shorter than the reference and still has 0.43, basically the same 0.42 (paragraph 6). So the area tells you about bends without being confused by length, which lets it split two lipids that melt at the same temperature (paragraph 7). Why the others are wrong: it doesn't respond to length, P3 matches the reference; it does respond to something, it rises with double bonds; pressure was held fixed during the measurement (paragraph 8). Trap: Missing that a second measurement sensitive to only one cause can untangle two causes.

qs.q: Why are the onsets of melting not comparable?
o: The transitions differ in width
Correct: The melting ranges differ in width, so midpoints are used instead.
The midpoints were not determined for each lipid
Not quite. Midpoints were found for each lipid.
Area was measured at a fixed pressure
Not quite. That's the other caveat, about area.
The onsets are comparable
Not quite. The widths differ, so onsets aren't comparable.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says each lipid melts over a range of several degrees, not at one exact point, and that range is wider for some lipids than others. The midpoint, the middle of the melting range, is a fair comparison point. The onset, where melting starts, isn't: a lipid with a wide range starts melting much earlier relative to its midpoint than one with a narrow range. So onsets can't be compared fairly. Why the others are wrong: midpoints were found for every lipid; the fixed pressure is the other caveat, about area, not melting; the onsets aren't comparable, because the widths differ. Trap: Comparing where broad and narrow transitions start as if they were the same shape.

qs.q: By how many degrees does P4 melt above P1?
o: Not quite. 13 °C is P1's melting temperature.
Not quite. 20 is the gap between P3 and P4, 54 − 34.
Correct: 34 − 13 = 21 degrees.
Not quite. 34 °C is P4's melting temperature.
qs.x: Correct: Difference = P4's melting temperature − P1's melting temperature. From Figure 1, P4 = 34 °C and P1 = 13 °C. Plug in: 34 − 13 = 21 degrees. Both have one double bond, so the difference comes from P4's extra length: 22 − 18 = 4 more carbons per chain. Why the others are wrong: 13 is P1's melting temperature by itself; 20 is the gap between P3 and P4 (54 − 34), a different pair; 34 is P4's melting temperature by itself. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of rows.

graph.title: Figure 1. Melting temperature against area per molecule for five lipids

passages.title: Cholesterol-Rich Lipid Rafts in the Bilayer
text: Lipids in a bilayer are not uniformly mixed. Mixtures containing cholesterol and lipids with long saturated chains separate into regions that are more tightly packed than the surrounding membrane, and particular proteins partition preferentially into one region or the other.

The partitioning concentrates proteins that need to interact. Two proteins that both favor the ordered regions encounter each other far more often than their average concentrations in the membrane would predict, so a domain raises a reaction rate without changing how much of either protein is present.

The regions are not permanent structures. They form and disperse on a timescale of seconds and are small enough to be below the resolution of ordinary microscopy, which is why their existence was argued about for many years and why most evidence for them is indirect.

Protein association was measured in membranes of two compositions (Figure 1). Figure 1 plots the association rate against the share of protein 1 in ordered regions for five membranes of each condition that had ordered regions (group means in the legend). Cholesterol depleted membranes have no ordered regions and are not plotted; their rate was 0.14.
