Depleting cholesterol abolished the ordered regions and reduced the association rate to 0.14, and restoring cholesterol restored both. Removing the anchor that directs protein 1 into the ordered regions left the regions intact and the other protein in them, and reduced the rate to 0.19.

The last condition separates the domain's existence from the protein's partitioning into it. The regions were present and one protein was excluded from them, and the rate fell almost as much as when the regions were abolished, so what matters is the co-localization rather than the regions themselves.

Two qualifications apply. Cholesterol depletion removes cholesterol from the whole membrane, including any that is bound to the proteins, so the fall in rate in that condition has more than one possible cause and the anchor experiment is the more informative one. And the percentages in ordered regions are measured by separating a detergent-resistant fraction, a procedure performed in the cold that may itself promote the separation it is used to detect.

qs.q: According to the passage, ordered regions raise the association rate of two proteins that both favor them mainly by:
o: increasing the total amount of each protein in the membrane
Not quite. The passage says the amounts stay the same.
raising the local concentration of both proteins
Correct: crowding both partners into small patches makes them meet far more often.
lowering the activation energy of the binding step
Not quite. Nothing changes the binding step itself. Only where the proteins sit changes.
slowing the lateral diffusion of both proteins
Not quite. Slower movement would make meetings rarer, not more common.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. The ordered regions are small patches of membrane. If two proteins both prefer those patches, they get crowded into a small area. Their total amounts in the membrane don't change, but their local concentration goes up, so they bump into each other far more often. More encounters means a faster reaction. Figure 1 backs this: with 81% and 76% of proteins 1 and 2 in the regions, the association rate is 1.00; abolish the regions and it falls to 0.14. Why the others are wrong: the total amount of each protein doesn't change, the passage says so; nothing alters the binding step or its activation energy, only the proteins' location; and slower diffusion would lower the meeting rate, not raise it. Trap: Explaining a rate change by the total amount instead of the local concentration.

qs.q: Why does the passage treat the anchor-removal experiment as more informative than cholesterol depletion?
o: It abolished the ordered regions
Not quite. That's what cholesterol depletion did. The anchor experiment left the regions in place.
It produced a larger drop in the association rate
Not quite. Its drop was slightly smaller: to 0.19, against 0.14 for depletion.
It moved protein 2 out of the ordered regions
Not quite. Protein 2 stayed in the regions (77%). Protein 1 was the one moved out (12%).
It left the ordered regions intact
Correct: the regions stayed, so only protein 1's location changed.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says cholesterol depletion pulls cholesterol from the whole membrane, including any bound to the proteins. So its drop to 0.14 could have more than one cause. The anchor experiment changes just one thing: where protein 1 sits. The regions stay put and protein 2 stays in them (77%), while protein 1 in the regions falls from 81% to 12% (Figure 1). The rate still falls to 0.19. So losing co-localization, the two proteins being in the same place, is what lowers the rate (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: abolishing the regions is what cholesterol depletion did, not the anchor experiment; the anchor drop (to 0.19) was slightly smaller than depletion's (0.14), not larger; and protein 1 is the one that moved out (12%), while protein 2 stayed in (77%). Trap: Preferring the change with the biggest effect over the one with the fewest side effects.

qs.q: Which feature of the method used to measure partitioning could help create the ordered regions it is meant to detect?
o: Depleting cholesterol before the fraction is prepared
Not quite. Depletion was a test condition, not part of the measuring method.
Measuring association at body temperature
Not quite. The passage worries about the cold step, not body temperature.
Preparing the fraction in the cold
Correct: cold favors ordered packing, so it may create some of the separation.
Anchoring protein 1 into the ordered regions
Not quite. The anchor belongs to protein 1 itself. It isn't part of the measurement.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the ordered-region percentages came from a detergent-resistant fraction prepared in the cold. Cold makes lipids pack more tightly and orderly. So the cold step itself could push lipids into ordered patches that weren't there at body temperature. That means the method might create some of what it's trying to measure, and the percentages could run high. Why the others are wrong: cholesterol depletion was one of the test conditions, not part of the measuring method; body temperature isn't what the passage worries about, the cold step is; and the anchor belongs to protein 1, it isn't part of the measurement. Trap: Using a preparation step that produces the very state it's meant to detect.

qs.q: By what factor did removing the anchor reduce the association rate?
o: That's the cholesterol-depleted rate.
That's the reduced rate, not a factor.
That's protein 1's percent in the regions, not a factor.
qs.x: Correct: By what factor means divide: factor = standard rate ÷ rate with the anchor removed. From Figure 1, the standard membrane's association rate is 1.00 and the anchor-removed rate is 0.19. Plug in: 1.00 ÷ 0.19. Multiply top and bottom by 100 to clear the decimal: 100 ÷ 19. 19 goes into 95 five times, leaving 5, and 5 ÷ 19 ≈ 0.26, so 100 ÷ 19 ≈ 5.26, about 5.3. Why the others are wrong: 0.19 is the reduced rate itself, not a factor; 0.14 is the cholesterol-depleted rate, a different condition; 12 is the percent of protein 1 left in the ordered regions, from the wrong axis. Trap: Reading across into the partitioning axis.

qs.q: According to the passage, why was the existence of ordered membrane regions debated for many years?
o: They are too small and brief to image directly
Correct: they're too small and brief for ordinary microscopes, so evidence is indirect.
They appear only in artificial membranes
Not quite. The passage describes them in real membranes. The issue is their size and speed.
They form only when cholesterol is removed
Not quite. It's the reverse. Removing cholesterol abolished them.
They contain no membrane proteins
Not quite. Proteins partition into them. That's how they bring partners together.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says the regions form and break up within seconds and are smaller than ordinary microscopes can resolve. You can't simply take a picture of something that small and short-lived. So the evidence for them had to be indirect, and indirect evidence leaves room for other explanations, which kept the debate going for years. Why the others are wrong: the passage describes these regions in real membranes, not only artificial ones; they need cholesterol, and removing it abolished them; and they do hold proteins, that's how they concentrate partners. Trap: Expecting something that can't be seen directly to be easy to prove.

graph.title: Figure 1. Association rate against protein 1 in ordered regions (5 membranes per condition)

passages.title: Buffer Ratio and Resistance to pH Change
text: A buffer resists a change in acidity because it holds both a proton donor and its conjugate acceptor, and added acid or base is taken up by one of them. The resistance is greatest when the two are present in similar amounts, which occurs when the pH equals the acid's pKₐ, and it falls as the pH moves away in either direction.

Buffer concentration acts separately. A concentrated buffer far from its pKₐ may resist less than a dilute one at its pKₐ, because the limiting factor is the amount of the species that is in short supply rather than the total.
Four buffers were prepared and the pH change produced by a fixed addition of acid was measured (Figure 1 plots the pH change against concentration; Table 1 gives each buffer's pKₐ and starting pH).

The reference is 50 mM at its pKₐ and changes by eight hundredths of a pH unit. U3 repeats it. U1 is the same concentration at a pH 1.2 units below its pKₐ and changes by 67 hundredths, more than eight times as much.

U2 raises the concentration four fold at the same unfavorable pH and changes by 10 hundredths. Concentration therefore compensates partially: 200 mM away from the pKₐ still performs worse than 50 mM at it.

U4 is 12 mM at its pKₐ and changes by 35 hundredths, worse than the reference and better than U1. Comparing U2 with U4 shows that neither proximity to the pKₐ nor concentration dominates in all cases, so a buffer must be chosen on both.

The practical rule that follows is to choose an acid whose pKₐ lies within about one unit of the intended pH and then set the concentration by how much acid or base is expected, rather than compensating for a poor choice of acid with a high concentration.

Two qualifications apply. The pH change was measured after a single addition, so the figures describe the response to that amount and a larger addition would exhaust the buffers unevenly. And pKₐ values were taken from tabulated data at 25 degrees and at low ionic strength, while the measurements were made in the prepared solutions, so the effective values differ slightly.

qs.q: Why is resistance greatest when the pH equals the pKₐ?
o: It is greatest away from the pKₐ
Not quite. U1, away from its pKₐ, changes over eight times as much.
Donor and acceptor are matched
Correct: At the pKₐ the acid and its conjugate base are equal, so neither runs short.
Only the donor is present at that pH
Not quite. At the pKₐ both forms are present in equal amounts.
The total concentration is highest there
Not quite. Concentration is set separately from the pH.
qs.x: Correct: A buffer is a mix of a weak acid (the proton donor) and its conjugate base (the proton acceptor). Added acid gets soaked up by the base, and added base gets soaked up by the acid. Paragraph 1 says the resistance is best when the two are present in similar amounts, and that happens when pH = pKₐ. At that point neither one is in short supply, so whichever you add, there's plenty of partner to react with. Figure 1 backs this up: the reference buffer at its pKₐ moves only 0.08. Why the others are wrong: at the pKₐ both forms are present in equal amounts, not just the donor; total concentration is a separate setting (paragraph 2), not something the pKₐ decides; resistance is worst away from the pKₐ, since U1 changes by 0.67, over eight times the reference. Trap: Thinking the total amount of buffer is what matters, when the limit is whichever of the two forms runs out first.

qs.q: What does U2 show about compensating with concentration?
o: It restores the response to the reference value
Not quite. U2 changes by 0.10, still more than the reference's 0.08.
It makes no difference to the response
Not quite. It drops the change from 0.67 (U1) to 0.10.
Concentration is irrelevant here
Not quite. U2 does better than U1, so concentration matters.
It helps but does not suffice
Correct: 0.10 is much better than U1's 0.67 but still worse than the reference's 0.08.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 and Figure 1 answer this. U1 and U2 are both at pH 6.0, which is 1.2 units below the pKₐ of 7.2. U1 is 50 mM and changes by 0.67. U2 is 200 mM, four times as concentrated, and changes by only 0.10. So the extra concentration helped a lot. But it still doesn't match the reference, which is 50 mM at its pKₐ and changes by just 0.08. Concentration makes up for a bad pH only partly. Why the others are wrong: it doesn't get back to the reference, because 0.10 is still more than 0.08; it clearly does make a difference, dropping the change from 0.67 to 0.10; and that same drop shows concentration is not irrelevant. Trap: Assuming you can always fix a poor buffer choice by just adding more of it.

qs.q: Which added experiment would best test the claim that raising the concentration only partly makes up for a poor pKₐ match?
o: Make the pH 6.0 buffer 400 mM and add the same acid
Correct: A higher concentration at the same unfavorable pH shows whether the gap to the reference keeps closing.
Repeat U4 with twice the acid addition while keeping it at 12 mM
Not quite. A larger addition tests how fast a buffer is used up, not what concentration does at a poor pKₐ match.
Prepare a 50 mM buffer at pH 8.4, 1.2 units above its pKₐ
Not quite. That tests the other side of the pKₐ, not the effect of concentration.
Measure the pH of the reference before any acid is added
Not quite. That is only a baseline reading. It tests nothing about concentration.
qs.x: Correct: The claim in paragraph 5 is that concentration helps at a poor pKₐ match but does not fully make up for it: U2 at 200 mM and pH 6.0 changes by 0.10, still more than the reference's 0.08 (Figure 1). To test it, change only the concentration and keep everything else the same. A 400 mM buffer at pH 6.0 given the same fixed addition of acid shows whether the change keeps shrinking and whether it ever reaches the reference. Why the others are wrong: doubling the acid with U4 changes the addition, not the concentration at a poor match; a buffer at pH 8.4 tests the other side of the pKₐ; measuring the starting pH of the reference is only a baseline. Trap: Picking an experiment that is related to buffers but changes a different variable than the one in the claim.

qs.q: Why do the tabulated pKₐ values differ from the effective ones?
o: Tables ignore the acid used
Not quite. The tables do list each acid.
A single addition of acid was used
Not quite. The single addition is a separate caution about the pH changes.
Conditions differ from the tables
Correct: The tables were for 25 degrees and low ionic strength, unlike the prepared solutions.
The values were measured in these solutions
Not quite. They came from tables, not from these solutions. That's the source of the mismatch.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says the pKₐ values came from tables measured at 25 degrees and low ionic strength (ionic strength is roughly how many ions are floating around). The real buffer solutions weren't under those exact conditions, so the effective pKₐ in each solution shifts a little from the table value. Why the others are wrong: the values weren't measured in these solutions, they were looked up in tables, which is exactly the problem; the single addition of acid is the other qualification in paragraph 8, about the pH changes, not the pKₐ; and the tables do list each acid separately. Trap: Using a reference number without checking whether the conditions match the ones it was measured under.

qs.q: By what factor is U1's pH change larger than U3's?
o: Not quite. That's U3's own pH change, not a ratio.
Not quite. That's U1's own pH change, not a ratio.
Not quite. That's 0.67 ÷ 0.10, which compares U1 with U2.
qs.x: Correct: "By what factor" means divide. The formula is factor = U1's pH change ÷ U3's pH change. From Figure 1, U1 changes by 0.67 and U3 by 0.08. Plug in: 0.67 ÷ 0.08. To make it easier, multiply top and bottom by 100: 67 ÷ 8. 8 × 8 = 64, which leaves 3, and 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, so 67 ÷ 8 = 8.375, about 8.4. U1's change is about 8.4 times U3's, which fits paragraph 4's "more than eight times." Why the others are wrong: 0.08 is just U3's own change; 0.67 is just U1's own change; 6.7 is 0.67 ÷ 0.10, which divides U1 by U2, the wrong pair. Trap: Picking a number straight from the graph when the question asks for a ratio of two numbers.

graph.title: Figure 1. pH change on adding a fixed amount of acid against total buffer concentration

passages.title: The Four-Ring Steroid Framework and Its Substituents
text: The steroids share a framework of four fused rings, and the differences between them are in the substituents attached to it and in a small number of modifications to the rings themselves. Because the framework is rigid and largely non-polar, all steroids are lipid soluble and cross membranes readily.

Small changes to the substituents produce large changes in which receptor a steroid binds. Hormones with quite different actions differ by a single hydroxyl group or a single double bond, and the enzymes that make them are correspondingly specific.

The same lipid solubility that lets steroids enter cells freely creates a transport problem outside them. A steroid is poorly soluble in plasma and is carried bound to a protein, and only the small unbound fraction is available to enter tissues, so the total concentration in plasma is a poor guide to the active amount.

Properties were compared for four steroids: the parent, variant 1 (one hydroxyl added), variant 2 (one double bond added) and variant 3 (one methyl removed). Figure 1 plots each steroid's bound percentage against its free concentration and shows which receptor it bound.

Adding a single hydroxyl group changed the receptor bound from A to B, and adding a single double bond left the receptor unchanged while raising the bound fraction to 97.4 percent and lowering the free concentration to 5.1 nanomoles per liter. Removing a methyl group abolished receptor binding altogether and left 62 percent bound to plasma protein.
The free concentrations span 14-fold across steroids whose total concentrations were matched, so two steroids present in equal total amounts differ greatly in how much is available to act.

Two qualifications apply. The bound percentage is measured at a single total steroid concentration, and the binding protein is saturable, so at a higher total concentration the bound percentage falls and the free concentration rises more than proportionally. And receptor binding was tested against a panel of two receptors, so variant 3, recorded as binding none, may bind a receptor that was not included in the panel.

qs.q: Why does a single hydroxyl change the receptor bound?
o: Binding is highly specific
Correct: Receptors fit their ligands tightly, so one −OH can switch which receptor binds.
The framework is altered
The four-ring framework is the same; only a side group changed.
It changes plasma binding only
The receptor changed too, from A to B.
The hydroxyl makes the steroid water soluble
Paragraph 1 says all steroids stay lipid soluble.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says small changes to a steroid's side groups make big changes in which receptor it binds. A receptor's binding site fits its ligand closely, like a lock and key, so adding one hydroxyl group (an −OH) can spoil the fit to one receptor and create a fit to another. Figure 1 shows variant 1, with one hydroxyl added, switching from receptor A to receptor B. Why the others are wrong: one −OH doesn't make a steroid water soluble, paragraph 1 says the rigid ring framework keeps all steroids lipid soluble; the four-ring framework itself is unchanged; and the receptor did change, from A to B, so it isn't only plasma binding. Trap: Expecting a small chemical change to have only a small biological effect.

qs.q: According to the passage, why is the total plasma concentration of a steroid hormone a poor guide to its activity?
o: Total concentration includes inactive metabolites
Not quite. The passage blames protein binding, not metabolites: only the free part acts.
Only the free part acts
Correct: Only the free part acts, and the bound share varies from 62% to 97.4%.
It is a good guide
Not quite. Paragraph 3 calls the total a poor guide to the active amount.
All steroids are equally bound
Not quite. Figure 1 shows bound shares from 62% to 97.4%.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says steroids travel in plasma mostly bound to a carrier protein, and only the small free (unbound) part can enter tissues and act. Figure 1 shows the bound share ranges from 62% to 97.4%, so the free part differs a lot between steroids. Paragraph 6 says that with matched totals, free concentrations still span 14-fold. So the total tells you little about how much is available to work. Why the others are wrong: metabolites aren't the issue the passage raises, protein binding is; steroids aren't equally bound, the range is 62% to 97.4%; and the passage says the total is a poor guide, not a good one. Trap: Comparing total concentrations of molecules that bind their carrier to different degrees.

qs.q: Why does a higher total concentration raise the free fraction disproportionately?
o: The carrier protein becomes saturated
Paragraph 7 says the bound share falls, so the free fraction rises.
The carrier is destroyed at high concentration
The carrier isn't destroyed. Its sites are just full.
The carrier saturates
Correct: Once carrier sites fill up, extra steroid stays free, so free rises faster than total.
It rises proportionally
Paragraph 7 says free rises more than proportionally.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the binding protein is saturable, meaning it has a limited number of binding sites. At low total steroid, most steroid finds a site. Once the sites are mostly filled, every extra steroid molecule has nowhere to go, so all of it stays free. That makes the free concentration climb faster than the total, more than proportionally, and the bound percentage falls. Why the others are wrong: the passage doesn't say the carrier is destroyed, it's just full; the free fraction isn't constant, it rises as the carrier fills; and the rise is more than proportional, per paragraph 7. Trap: Assuming the bound percentage stays the same at every concentration.

qs.q: How many fold do the free concentrations of variant 2 and variant 3 differ?
o: Not quite. That's variant 2's free concentration, not the ratio.
Not quite. That's variant 3's percent bound, a different axis.
Not quite. That's variant 3's free concentration, not the ratio.
qs.x: Correct: Fold difference = larger ÷ smaller. From Figure 1, variant 3's free concentration is 71.0 nmol/L and variant 2's is 5.1 nmol/L. Plug in: 71.0 ÷ 5.1. Estimate: 5.1 × 14 = 71.4, which is very close to 71.0, so the answer is about 14 (more exactly 13.9). That matches paragraph 6, which says free concentrations span 14-fold. Why the others are wrong: 71.0 is variant 3's free concentration, not the ratio; 5.1 is variant 2's free concentration; 62 is variant 3's percent bound to plasma protein, a different axis. Trap: Quoting one concentration when the question asks how many times bigger one is than the other.

qs.q: Variant 3 bound neither receptor tested. Why might it still bind a receptor in the body?
o: It binds none
Not quite. "None" only covers the two receptors that were tested.
Its binding was below detection
Not quite. The assay detected binding fine; the panel held only two receptors.
All receptors were included
Not quite. Paragraph 7 says only two receptors were in the panel.
The panel had two receptors
Correct: Only two receptors were tested, so it may bind one that wasn't.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says receptor binding was tested against only two receptors. Variant 3's "none" means it didn't bind those two. It says nothing about the many receptors that weren't tested, and variant 3 might bind one of them. A negative result only covers what was actually checked. Why the others are wrong: detection wasn't the problem, the assay picked up binding for the other variants; not all receptors were included, only two; and "binds none" is only true for the two in the panel. Trap: Reading "no binding" against a small panel as "binds nothing at all."

graph.title: Figure 1. Plasma protein binding and free concentration of four steroids, grouped by receptor bound

passages.title: DNA Melting Followed by Absorbance
text: A DNA duplex is held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases and by stacking between neighboring base pairs, and heating a solution of duplex DNA eventually separates the two strands. The separation is followed by absorbance at 260 nanometers, which rises as the strands come apart because the bases absorb more strongly when they are not stacked on one another.

The temperature at which half of the duplex has separated is called the melting temperature. It depends on the proportion of guanine and cytosine pairs, because those pairs make three hydrogen bonds rather than two, and it also depends on the salt concentration of the solution, because the two strands carry negative charges that repel one another and dissolved cations screen that repulsion.

A set of synthetic duplexes of equal length but differing composition was melted in two salt conditions, and the results are collected in Figure 1: panel A plots the melting temperatures against guanine and cytosine content and panel B shows the width of each transition. Each value is the mean of three independent melts of the same preparation.

Across the four uninterrupted duplexes the melting temperature rose with guanine and cytosine content in both salt conditions, and raising the salt added about 13 degrees to every duplex regardless of its composition. The width of the transition, measured between the temperatures at which a tenth and nine tenths of the duplex had separated, was five to seven degrees for those four.

D5 has the same composition as D2 but carries its guanine and cytosine pairs in two long blocks rather than distributed along the molecule. It melts three to four degrees lower than D2 and its transition is almost twice as wide, because the composition averaged over the whole molecule no longer describes any particular region of it, and the weaker region opens before the stronger one.

Two qualifications apply. The absorbance measurement reports the fraction of bases that are unstacked rather than the fraction of molecules that have fully separated, and a partially opened molecule contributes to the signal, so the midpoint is not exactly the point at which half the molecules have come apart. And the values are means of three melts of a single preparation rather than of independent preparations, so they measure the reproducibility of the melt and not the reproducibility of the synthesis.

qs.q: Why does a higher guanine and cytosine content raise the melting temperature?
o: Guanine and cytosine are physically larger bases than the others
The pairs are about the same size. The passage points to bonding.
Those pairs stack less tightly
G-C pairs stack more tightly, not less.
Those pairs make three hydrogen bonds
Correct: a G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds; an A-T pair has two.
Those pairs resist the salt in the solution
Salt acts on the backbone charges, not on particular pairs.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says a guanine-cytosine pair, or G-C pair, is held by three hydrogen bonds, while an adenine-thymine pair, or A-T pair, has only two. More bonds means more energy is needed to pull the strands apart, so the duplex has to get hotter before it melts. Figure 1A shows the trend: as G-C content goes 28, 42, 56, 70%, the low-salt melting temperature goes 58, 65, 72, 79 °C. Why the others are wrong: each pair is one big base with one small base, so the pairs are about the same size, and size isn't the reason the passage gives; salt acts on the negative charges of the backbone, not on particular pairs; G-C pairs actually stack more tightly, not less. Trap: Reaching for a size argument when the difference in bonding is what matters.

qs.q: Why does added salt raise every melting temperature by a similar amount?
o: It screens the backbone charges
Correct: it shields the backbone's negative charges, which every duplex has equally.
It binds specifically to guanine and cytosine pairs
The shift is 13 °C for every duplex, whatever its G-C content.
It changes the number of hydrogen bonds in each pair
Salt doesn't change the hydrogen bonds in each pair.
It lowers them
Every melting temperature rose by 13 °C.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the two strands carry negative charges that repel each other, and dissolved cations (positive ions) screen, or shield, that repulsion. Those charges are on the phosphate backbone, one per nucleotide, whatever the base is. So every duplex gets about the same help from salt. Check Figure 1A: D1 goes 71 − 58 = 13, D2 78 − 65 = 13, D3 85 − 72 = 13, D4 92 − 79 = 13, D5 74 − 61 = 13. The same 13 °C every time. Why the others are wrong: salt doesn't change how many hydrogen bonds a pair makes; if salt bound G-C pairs specifically, G-C-rich duplexes would shift more, but the shift is the same for all; the melting temperatures go up with salt, not down. Trap: Assuming anything that stabilizes DNA must work through the base pairs.

qs.q: Why does D5 melt lower than D2 despite the same composition?
o: Its bases are chemically modified
Nothing suggests a chemical modification.
It does not in fact melt any lower
It melts about 4 degrees lower, 61 against 65 °C.
It carries fewer base pairs in total than D2 does
All the duplexes are the same length.
Its weak block unzips first on heating
Correct: its A-T-rich region opens first, pulling the midpoint down.
qs.x: Correct: D5 has the same overall G-C content as D2, 42%, but paragraph 5 says its G-C pairs are bunched into two long blocks. That leaves the rest of the molecule much richer in A-T pairs than the average. That A-T-rich stretch is weaker, so it opens at a lower temperature and drags the midpoint down: D5 melts at 61 °C against D2's 65 °C in low salt, and 74 against 78 in high salt, about 4 degrees lower. Why the others are wrong: paragraph 3 says all the duplexes are the same length; nothing in the passage mentions a chemical modification; the figure clearly shows D5 melting lower. Trap: Treating the average composition as if it described every part of the molecule.

qs.q: Why is D5's melting transition nearly twice as wide as D2's?
o: Wide transitions follow from high salt alone
D2 saw the same salt and stayed at 6 °C.
Two regions melt at different temperatures
Correct: its weak and strong regions melt at different temperatures.
Its measurement was made less carefully than the others
All duplexes were melted by the same method.
It is the longest duplex
The duplexes are all about the same length.
qs.x: Correct: The width is the temperature range over which the duplex goes from 10% to 90% separated (paragraph 4). In a duplex with evenly spread G-C pairs, the whole molecule melts at about the same temperature, so the range is narrow, 5 to 7 °C. D5 has a weak A-T-rich region and a strong G-C-rich block. The weak part opens first and the strong part only later, so the absorbance rise is spread over both, giving 11 °C, almost twice D2's 6 °C. Why the others are wrong: every duplex was melted the same way, so careless measurement doesn't explain one odd result; D2 saw the same salt conditions and stayed at 6 °C, so salt isn't the cause; all the duplexes are about the same length. Trap: Blaming a broad transition on the measurement instead of on the molecule itself.

qs.q: By how many degrees does high salt raise D3's melting temperature?
o: Correct: 85 − 72 = 13 degrees.
56 is the G-C percentage.
72 °C is the low-salt value itself.
85 °C is the high-salt value itself.
qs.x: Correct: The rise is: change = high-salt melting temperature − low-salt melting temperature. From the D3 points in Figure 1A, high salt = 85 °C and low salt = 72 °C. Plug in: 85 − 72 = 13 degrees. That matches the roughly 13-degree shift paragraph 4 describes for every duplex. Why the others are wrong: 72 is D3's low-salt melting temperature itself; 85 is its high-salt value; 56 is D3's G-C percentage, not a temperature. Trap: Reading a single value off the graph when the question asks for the difference between two.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Melting temperature against guanine and cytosine content in two salt conditions
Figure 1B. Width of the melting transition

passages.title: Supercoiling of Circular DNA
text: Circular DNA in a cell is usually not relaxed. Its two strands are wound about each other either more or less than they would be if the molecule were free to adjust, and that excess or deficit of winding is taken up as a writhing of the whole circle in space. A molecule wound less than the relaxed state is negatively supercoiled, and that is the usual condition inside a cell.

Supercoiling matters because opening the duplex, which every process that reads the sequence must do, is easier in a molecule that is already underwound. The underwinding is stored strain, and local separation of the strands relieves some of it, so the energetic cost of opening a region is lower than it would be in a relaxed circle.

Supercoiling is changed by enzymes that cut one or both strands, allow the ends to turn or pass through one another, and reseal them. Researchers treated a plasmid preparation with three such enzymes (A, B and C), using the untreated plasmid and a heat denatured copy of enzyme A as controls, and separated the products on a gel in which more compact, more supercoiled molecules travel further. The enzyme was the variable they changed, and the superhelical density and the distance traveled were what they measured (Figure 1). Enzyme B and enzyme C need ATP, and enzyme A does not.

The untreated plasmid had a superhelical density of about minus six hundredths, which is the value usually found in bacterial cells. Enzyme A moved it towards zero and enzyme B moved it further negative, and both produced a ladder of several resolved species (9 for enzyme A and 7 for enzyme B, each plotted in Figure 1) rather than a single band, because the enzymes act in steps and a population caught after 30 minutes contains molecules that have undergone different numbers of steps.

Enzyme C changed neither the density nor the distance traveled, although it does require ATP. An enzyme can consume ATP while altering a property the gel does not report, and an activity that passes one duplex region through another changes how two circles are linked to each other without changing the winding of either, which this gel cannot distinguish.

Two qualifications apply. Superhelical density is calculated from the position of the band against a calibration run on the same gel, and because very compact molecules run close together the calculation is least precise exactly where the molecules are most supercoiled. And the heat denatured control shows only that the change requires an intact protein, not that the protein responsible is the one intended, since a contaminating activity would also be destroyed by heat.

qs.q: Why is opening a region easier in an underwound molecule?
o: Underwound molecules carry weaker hydrogen bonds between bases
The hydrogen bonding is the same.
Underwinding adds base pairs
No base pairs are added.
Strand separation relieves strain
Correct: opening a region releases some of the stored strain.
Underwinding removes base pairs from the circle
The base pairs are all still there.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says an underwound (negatively supercoiled) circle is holding stored strain, a bit like a twisted rubber band. Pulling the strands apart in one region lets some of that strain go. So the circle actually "wants" to open a little, and the energy cost of opening is lower than in a relaxed circle. Why the others are wrong: underwinding doesn't change the hydrogen bonds between bases; the base pairs are all still there, none are removed; nothing adds base pairs either. Trap: Looking for a change in the base pairs when the answer is the strain in the whole molecule.

qs.q: Why does a 30-minute reaction give a ladder of species?
o: The enzyme acts in sequential steps
Correct: molecules caught at 30 minutes have gone through different numbers of steps.
The gel separates molecules by their length
The plasmids are one length. The gel sorts by compactness.
Ladders indicate a failed gel
The ladder is the expected result of a stepwise reaction.
Several different enzymes are present in the preparation
Only one enzyme was added.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says these enzymes work in steps. Each time the enzyme acts, it changes the winding by a small fixed amount. Stop the reaction at 30 minutes and some molecules have been acted on once, some twice, some many times. Each group has a slightly different compactness, so each runs to a different spot on the gel, giving a ladder: 9 bands for enzyme A and 7 for enzyme B. Why the others are wrong: only one enzyme was added to each reaction; the plasmids are all the same length, and the gel is separating them by compactness; the ladder isn't a failure, it's a record of the stepwise reaction. Trap: Reading several bands as contamination when they show a reaction caught partway through.

qs.q: Why might enzyme C consume ATP yet change nothing on this gel?
o: It is inactive
Not quite. A blank gel doesn't prove the enzyme is inactive.
It may alter linking between circles
Correct: it may change how circles are linked, which this gel can't see.
An enzyme that uses ATP must change the density
Not quite. Using ATP doesn't mean it must change the density.
The ATP was omitted from that reaction
Not quite. C is recorded as needing ATP, not as lacking it.
qs.x: Correct: Enzyme C left the density at −0.06 and the distance at 42 mm, the same as untreated, yet it needs ATP. Paragraph 5 explains: an enzyme can pass one stretch of DNA through another and change how two circles are linked together, like separating two interlocked rings, without changing the winding of either circle. This gel only reports winding, so that activity leaves no trace. Why the others are wrong: using ATP doesn't mean an enzyme must change the density, it could change something else; C is recorded as needing ATP, not as lacking it; an ATP requirement points to a working enzyme, and a blank gel doesn't prove it's inactive. Trap: Deciding an enzyme does nothing because one test shows nothing.

qs.q: What does the heat-denatured copy of enzyme A establish about the change in supercoiling?
o: That the enzyme needs no ATP
ATP wasn't tested in this control.
That enzyme A and no other protein caused the change
Heat would destroy a contaminating protein too.
That the plasmid is heat stable at that temperature
The enzyme was heated, not the plasmid.
An intact protein is required
Correct: it shows an intact protein is needed, not which protein it is.
qs.x: Correct: Heating destroys a protein's folded shape. Heat-treated enzyme A did nothing: density stayed at −0.06, the same as untreated. So the change needs an intact protein, not just something in the buffer. But paragraph 6 points out the limit: any contaminating protein in the prep would be destroyed by heat too. So the control can't show which protein did the work. Why the others are wrong: heat would also kill a contaminant, so it can't single out enzyme A; the enzyme was heated, not the plasmid; ATP wasn't what this control varied. Trap: Treating a heat control as proof of which protein is active.

qs.q: By how many hundredths does enzyme B change the superhelical density?
o: Correct: −0.11 − (−0.06) = −0.05, a change of 5 hundredths.
−0.06 is the starting density.
−0.11 is the final density, not the change.
55 mm is the distance traveled.
qs.x: Correct: The change is: change = final density − starting density. From Figure 1, enzyme B ends at −0.11 and the untreated plasmid starts at −0.06. Plug in: −0.11 − (−0.06). Subtracting a negative is adding: −0.11 + 0.06 = −0.05. So the density moved by 0.05, which is 5 hundredths, in the negative direction (more underwound). Why the others are wrong: 11 hundredths is the final density, not the change; 6 hundredths is the starting density; 55 is the distance traveled in mm, not a density. Trap: Reporting an endpoint when the question asks for the change between two values.

graph.title: Figure 1. Superhelical density and distance traveled on the gel for the plasmid before and after each treatment

passages.title: GC Content and Duplex Melting Temperature
text: Two strands of nucleic acid held together by paired bases separate when heated, and the temperature at which half of them have separated depends on the composition of the pairs. Pairs joined by three hydrogen bonds hold more strongly than pairs joined by two, so a duplex rich in the former separates at a higher temperature.

Length acts separately. A longer duplex has more pairs contributing, so it separates at a higher temperature than a short duplex of the same composition, and the effect of length is steep in short duplexes and shallow in long ones.
Composition, length and separation temperature were measured for five duplexes in the same solution (Figure 1).

The reference has 24 pairs, half of them of the stronger type, and separates at 61 degrees. X1 and X2 keep the length and vary the composition from 20 to 80%, which moves the temperature from 52 to 71 degrees.

X3 and X4 keep the composition and vary the length from 12 to 96 pairs, which moves the temperature from 41 to 73 degrees. Quadrupling the length from 24 to 96 adds 12 degrees, while halving it from 24 to 12 removes 20, which is the shallowing effect of length at large sizes.

The width of the transition behaves differently. It narrows as length increases, from 7.8 degrees at 12 pairs to 1.6 at 96, because a long duplex separates as a unit once enough pairs have opened, while a short one opens gradually.

A duplex of unknown composition and length therefore cannot be characterized from its separation temperature, but the width of its transition reports its length with little dependence on composition, which is why both numbers are recorded.

Two qualifications apply. Separation was followed by the rise in absorbance that accompanies strand separation, which reports the fraction of pairs opened rather than the fraction of duplexes fully separated, and the two differ most in long duplexes. And all measurements were made in one salt concentration, and separation temperatures shift with salt, so the figures compare the duplexes without being transferable to other solutions.

qs.q: According to the passage, why does composition affect the separation temperature at a fixed length?
o: The heavier bases need more heat
Bond strength is the reason, not base mass.
The two pair types differ in strength
Correct: three-bond pairs hold more strongly than two-bond pairs.
Composition changes the pair count
Length sets the pair count; X1 and X2 both have 24.
Only length affects the temperature
X1 and X2 differ by 19 degrees at the same length.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says some pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds and others by two (these are G-C and A-T pairs). Three-bond pairs hold more strongly, so a duplex with more of them needs more heat to come apart. Figure 1A shows it with length held at 24 pairs: 20% three-bond pairs separates at 52 °C, 50% at 61 °C, and 80% at 71 °C. Why the others are wrong: the number of pairs is set by length, and X1 and X2 both have 24; length isn't the only factor, since X1 and X2 differ by 71 − 52 = 19 degrees at the same length; the passage explains it by bond strength, not base mass. Trap: Crediting the effect to the thing that was held constant.

qs.q: Why does the effect of length on separation temperature become shallow at large sizes?
o: Length has no effect beyond 24 pairs
Going to 96 pairs still added 12 degrees.
Long duplexes separate as a unit
Not quite. That explains the narrower width, not the smaller temperature gain.
Longer duplexes contain weaker pairs
Composition was held at 50%.
Each added pair contributes less
Correct: each added pair adds less; quadrupling gives only 12 degrees.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 compares changes in length at 50% composition. Going from 24 to 96 pairs (four times longer) adds 73 − 61 = 12 degrees. Going from 24 down to 12 pairs (half as long) removes 61 − 41 = 20 degrees. So the extra 72 pairs add less than the 12 pairs taken away. Each extra pair helps less once the duplex is already long. Why the others are wrong: composition was held at 50%, so the longer duplex doesn't have weaker pairs; length still matters past 24 pairs, since 96 pairs added 12 degrees; and separating as a unit explains the narrower width, not the smaller temperature gain. Trap: Assuming that because a value keeps rising, it rises by the same amount each time.

qs.q: Why does the width of the transition report a duplex's length?
o: Long duplexes separate as a unit
Correct: long duplexes separate as a unit, short ones gradually.
Width follows composition
X1 and X2 have nearly the same width.
Width rises with length
Width falls with length, from 7.8 to 1.6.
Width follows the salt concentration
Not quite. Salt was held constant, so it can't explain the width differences.
qs.x: Correct: The width is the temperature range over which a duplex goes from mostly paired to mostly separated. Paragraph 6 says a long duplex comes apart all at once after enough pairs open, so its range is narrow. A short duplex opens bit by bit, so its range is wide. Figure 1B and 1C: 12 pairs gives 7.8 degrees and 96 pairs gives 1.6. Composition barely changes it: X1, the reference and X2 are 4.4, 4.1 and 3.9. Why the others are wrong: width falls with length, from 7.8 to 1.6; composition barely moves the width, since X1 and X2 have nearly the same width; and salt was held constant, so it can't explain the differences. Trap: Assuming the only useful thing about a transition is where it happens.

qs.q: Why does the absorbance method differ from counting separated duplexes?
o: It reports fully separated duplexes only
It reports opened pairs, not separated duplexes.
It reports pairs opened instead
Correct: absorbance tracks opened pairs, not fully separated duplexes.
It measures length directly
Absorbance doesn't measure length.
All measurements used one salt concentration
That's the other, separate limitation.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says absorbance rises as pairs open. It counts opened pairs, not fully separated duplexes. In a long duplex, many pairs can open while the two strands still hang together, so the absorbance can show lots of opening even though few duplexes have fully come apart. That's why the two differ most in long duplexes. Why the others are wrong: the method reports opened pairs, not only fully separated duplexes; the single salt concentration is a real limit but a separate one; absorbance doesn't measure length. Trap: Treating a light signal as if it were the exact structural event you want.

qs.q: How many degrees separate X1 from X2?
o: 61 − 52 = 9 compares X1 with the reference.
Correct: 71 − 52 = 19 degrees.
73 − 41 = 32 compares X4 with X3.
52 °C is X1's own temperature.
qs.x: Correct: The gap is: difference = X2's temperature − X1's temperature. From Figure 1A, X2 separates at 71 °C and X1 at 52 °C. Plug in: 71 − 52 = 19 degrees. Both are 24 pairs long, so that whole gap comes from composition, 20% against 80% three-bond pairs. Why the others are wrong: 9 is X1 compared with the reference, 61 − 52; 52 is X1's own temperature; 32 compares the two length variants, 73 − 41. Trap: Comparing the wrong pair of duplexes.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Separation temperature against three-bond pairs in 24-pair duplexes
Figure 1B. Separation temperature against length in duplexes with 50% three-bond pairs
Figure 1C. Width of the transition

passages.title: Staged Acclimatization to High Altitude
text: At high altitude, the barometric pressure is lower, so each breath delivers oxygen at a lower partial pressure. At 4,300 m, inspired PO₂ is about 60% of its sea-level value. The body responds in stages. Within minutes, breathing increases. Over several days, the kidneys adjust the acid–base balance of the blood. Over weeks, red blood cell production rises in response to erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone released by the kidney when its oxygen supply falls.

To study these stages, investigators enrolled 64 healthy adults who lived near sea level and were about to spend three weeks at a research station at 4,300 m. No participant had been above 2,000 m in the previous year, and none took acetazolamide or any other drug to prevent altitude sickness. Measurements were taken at sea level the day before departure (day 0) and on days 1, 3 and 21 at altitude. Arterial blood was sampled from the radial artery at rest, and minute ventilation was measured with a mouthpiece while participants sat quietly. Plasma volume was estimated with a dye-dilution method. Gases, ventilation and bicarbonate are plotted in Figure 1; the other measures are in Table 1.

Each participant also completed a symptom questionnaire every morning, and the investigators recorded sleep quality, because breathing during sleep at altitude often becomes irregular, with pauses followed by rapid breaths. This periodic breathing is thought to result from the push and pull between the drive from low oxygen and the brake from low carbon dioxide.

New red blood cells take about five to seven days to mature in the bone marrow and enter the circulation after EPO rises. Six participants developed headache and nausea on day 1, consistent with acute mountain sickness; their symptoms resolved by day 4 and their data were kept in the analysis. The investigators noted that the study had no comparison group remaining at sea level, but argued that the large changes seen were unlikely to occur in healthy adults over three weeks without a change in altitude.

qs.q: Which receptors are most directly responsible for the rise in ventilation on day 1?
o: Carotid body chemoreceptors
Correct: arterial PO₂ fell from 95 to 45 mmHg, and the carotid bodies are the sensors for low oxygen.
Pulmonary stretch receptors
Not quite. Stretch receptors sense lung inflation and help end a breath; they don't drive breathing up.
Central chemoreceptors in the medulla
Not quite. These respond to CO₂ and H⁺, and both fell on day 1.
Aortic baroreceptors
Not quite. Baroreceptors sense blood pressure, not oxygen.
qs.x: Correct: Look at the arterial PO₂ curve in Figure 1A. It drops from 95 mmHg at sea level to 45 mmHg on day 1. The only receptors that sense low oxygen in the arterial blood directly are the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (small clusters of sensor cells where the carotid artery splits in the neck). When PO₂ falls this far, they fire hard and tell the brainstem to breathe more, which is why minute ventilation jumps from 7.0 to 9.8 L/min. Why the others are wrong: central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to CO₂ and H⁺, and both went down (PCO₂ 40 to 33, pH 7.40 to 7.47), so they would actually push breathing down; pulmonary stretch receptors sense lung inflation and help stop a breath, they don't drive it; aortic baroreceptors sense blood pressure, not oxygen. Trap: Picking the central chemoreceptors because they set breathing most of the time at sea level.

qs.q: What best explains why arterial pH returned close to 7.40 by day 21 even though PCO₂ kept falling?
o: Breathing slowed, CO₂ retained
Not quite. Ventilation kept rising and PCO₂ kept falling, so CO₂ wasn't retained.
The kidneys excreted more bicarbonate
Correct: plasma HCO₃⁻ fell from 24 to 17 mEq/L, which offset the low PCO₂.
The lungs excreted bicarbonate
Not quite. The lungs get rid of CO₂. Bicarbonate is handled by the kidneys.
Red cells produced lactic acid
Not quite. The passage gives no lactate data, and this doesn't fit the steady HCO₃⁻ drop.
qs.x: Correct: Breathing harder blows off CO₂, so PCO₂ falls (40 to 28 mmHg in Figure 1A). Less CO₂ means less acid in the blood, so pH rises. That's a respiratory alkalosis, and you can see it on day 1 at pH 7.47. Paragraph 1 says that over several days the kidneys adjust the acid–base balance. They do it by getting rid of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻, the main base in plasma) in the urine. The HCO₃⁻ curve in Figure 1C falls from 24 to 17 mEq/L, and with less base around, pH drifts back to 7.41 by day 21 even though PCO₂ stays low. Why the others are wrong: breathing slowed and CO₂ was retained is the opposite of the data, since ventilation kept rising and PCO₂ kept falling; the lungs remove CO₂, not bicarbonate, so they can't excrete it; nothing in the passage measures lactic acid, and red cells making it isn't part of this story. Trap: Expecting the lungs to fix a pH problem that the lungs themselves caused.

qs.q: What most likely explains the rise in hemoglobin between day 0 and day 3?
o: EPO caused a burst of new red cells within hours
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says new red cells take five to seven days to appear.
Low PO₂ increased the hemoglobin in each red cell
Not quite. Mature red cells have no nucleus, so they can't make extra hemoglobin.
The spleen destroyed fewer red cells at altitude
Not quite. The passage gives no data on red cell destruction.
Less plasma water concentrated the red cells
Correct: plasma volume fell to 89% by day 3, so the same red cells sat in less fluid.
qs.x: Correct: Hemoglobin here is a concentration, grams per deciliter of blood. That number can rise in two ways: make more red cells, or have less fluid around the same cells. Table 1 shows plasma volume falling to 89% of day 0 by day 3, an 11% drop (100 − 89 = 11). Same red cells in less water means a higher concentration, so hemoglobin rises from 14.5 to 15.4 g/dL. New red cells can't explain it yet: paragraph 4 says they take five to seven days to mature and enter the blood after EPO rises, so they explain the later climb to 16.8 g/dL by day 21. Why the others are wrong: a burst of new red cells within hours doesn't fit the five to seven day maturation time; mature red cells have no nucleus, so they can't make more hemoglobin each; no data on red cell breakdown by the spleen are given. Trap: Blaming every rise in hemoglobin on new red cells, when less plasma can do it too.

qs.q: Climbers were measured at each altitude stage over the course of the ascent. Which description best fits this study's design?
o: A case-control study
Not quite. Participants weren't chosen because they already had an outcome.
A randomized controlled trial
Not quite. No one was randomly assigned to altitude or sea level.
A prospective repeated-measures study
Correct: one group was followed forward and measured four times.
A cross-sectional survey
Not quite. A cross-sectional study measures once; each person here was measured four times.
qs.x: Correct: Prospective means the study starts now and follows people forward in time. Repeated-measures means the same people are measured more than once. Paragraph 2 says the same 64 adults were measured on day 0 and on days 1, 3 and 21 at altitude, so each person acts as their own baseline. Paragraph 4 also says there was no comparison group left at sea level and no one was assigned to anything at random. Why the others are wrong: a randomized controlled trial would randomly put some people at altitude and others at sea level, which didn't happen; a case-control study picks people because they already have an outcome and looks back, but these people were picked before they went up; a cross-sectional survey measures each person once, but here each person was measured four times. Trap: Calling any study with planned measurements an experiment or a trial.

qs.q: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the kidney and speeds acclimatization. Which mechanism best explains this?
o: It raises the oxygen affinity of hemoglobin in the lungs
Not quite. Acetazolamide works on the kidney enzyme, not on hemoglobin.
It blocks the carotid body response to low oxygen
Not quite. Blocking the carotid bodies would lower ventilation.
It stops the kidneys from releasing EPO
Not quite. Blocking EPO would slow acclimatization, not speed it.
Bicarbonate loss in urine drives breathing further
Correct: losing bicarbonate makes a mild acidosis, which removes the brake on breathing.
qs.x: Correct: Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme that helps the kidney tubule reclaim bicarbonate. Block it, and bicarbonate spills into the urine, which makes the blood a little acidic (a mild metabolic acidosis). Why does that help? On day 1 the low PCO₂ makes the blood alkaline (pH 7.47), and that alkalosis acts as a brake on breathing, since the central chemoreceptors read low acid as a reason to slow down. Paragraph 3 calls this the brake from low carbon dioxide. Acetazolamide does in a day what the kidneys did slowly from day 1 to day 21 (HCO₃⁻ 24 down to 17), so the brake comes off sooner and breathing can rise further. Why the others are wrong: raising hemoglobin's oxygen affinity isn't what this drug does; stopping EPO release would slow acclimatization, not speed it; blocking the carotid body response would cut the drive to breathe. Trap: Forgetting that the early alkalosis itself holds breathing back.

passages.title: Slow-Twitch and Fast-Twitch Muscle Fibers
text: Human skeletal muscle contains a mixture of fiber types. Type I (slow-twitch) fibers have a slow form of myosin ATPase, many mitochondria, abundant myoglobin and a dense capillary supply; they resist fatigue and rely on oxidative phosphorylation. Type II (fast-twitch) fibers have a fast myosin ATPase and generate high force and power, but many of them rely heavily on glycolysis and fatigue quickly. Each motor neuron innervates fibers of only one type, and the proportion of each type in a muscle varies widely among people.

Investigators took needle biopsies from the vastus lateralis (a thigh muscle) of 12 elite sprinters, 12 elite distance runners and 12 untrained adults of similar age. Fibers were typed by staining for myosin ATPase activity. Mitochondrial volume was measured by electron microscopy, and capillaries were counted in cross sections. Each participant also performed a cycling test to measure maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max) and a 6-second sprint to measure peak power. Fiber type, VO₂max and peak power of each man are plotted in Figure 1, with the group means labeled; mitochondrial volume and capillaries per fiber are in Table 1.

To see how much of these differences could be produced by training, the untrained participants then completed 12 weeks of supervised endurance cycling, five sessions a week. Their biopsies were repeated at the end (Table 2).

All participants were men aged 21 to 30, and none had used anabolic steroids, which were screened for in urine. Training sessions lasted 45 minutes at about 70% of each person's VO₂max, and attendance averaged 94%. Diet was not controlled, but body mass changed by less than 1 kg on average over the 12 weeks.

The investigators noted that studies of twins suggest that fiber type proportion is strongly inherited, while mitochondrial content and capillary density respond to training in people of any genetic background. They also noted that a biopsy samples only a few hundred fibers from one site, and that fiber proportions can vary somewhat between the surface and the deeper parts of the same muscle.

qs.q: Why would distance runners benefit from their high mitochondrial volume and capillary density?
o: They store creatine phosphate for sprints
Not quite. Creatine phosphate is a short-term store, not held by capillaries or mitochondria.
They support aerobic ATP production
Correct: mitochondria and capillaries let muscle keep making ATP with oxygen for a long time.
They allow faster glycolysis without lactate
Not quite. Glycolysis runs in the cytosol and doesn't need mitochondria.
They increase the force of each contraction
Not quite. Force depends on fiber size and myosin type, not mitochondria.
qs.x: Correct: Running a long race means making ATP for a long time, and the steady way to do that is oxidative phosphorylation (making ATP in mitochondria using oxygen). That needs two things: lots of mitochondria to do the work, and lots of capillaries to bring oxygen in. Table 1 shows distance runners have the most of both (8.3% mitochondrial volume and 2.9 capillaries per fiber), and Figure 1A shows the highest VO₂max, a mean of 74 mL/kg/min, which is the most oxygen they can use. Why the others are wrong: the force of each contraction comes from myosin type and fiber size, not mitochondria; glycolysis happens in the cytosol and doesn't need mitochondria at all; creatine phosphate is a quick few-second energy store for sprints, not something capillaries or mitochondria hold. Trap: Linking mitochondria to strength instead of endurance.

qs.q: What do the results for the untrained group after training suggest about how training changed their muscle?
o: Training made the untrained group equal to distance runners
Not quite. They stayed far below distance runners, for example 49 vs 74 VO₂max.
Training converted most type II fibers to type I
Not quite. Type I fibers rose only from 52% to 54%.
Training improved the fibers already present
Correct: mitochondria, capillaries and VO₂max rose, but type I % barely moved.
Training raised VO₂max to the runners' level
Not quite. VO₂max rose but stayed at 49 against the runners' 74.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the two columns of Table 2. After 12 weeks of endurance cycling, mitochondrial volume rose from 4.5% to 6.6%, capillaries from 1.8 to 2.3 per fiber, and VO₂max from 42 to 49 mL/kg/min. But type I fibers only went from 52% to 54%, a 2-point change (54 − 52 = 2). So the muscle didn't swap fiber types. It upgraded the fibers it already had. Paragraph 5 agrees: fiber proportion is strongly inherited, while mitochondria and capillaries respond to training. Why the others are wrong: converting most type II fibers to type I would need a big jump in type I %, not 2 points; reaching the runners' VO₂max is wrong, 49 against 74; being equal to distance runners is wrong because they stayed well below (54% vs 79% type I). Trap: Assuming endurance training turns fast fibers into slow ones.

qs.q: What limits the conclusion that sprint training caused the low type I percentage seen in sprinters?
o: Fast-fibered people may choose sprinting
Correct: people born with more fast fibers may choose sprinting, so training may not be the cause.
Sprinters were biopsied from the wrong muscle
Not quite. Every group was biopsied from the same thigh muscle.
Sprinters were trained for too short a time
Not quite. Training length isn't the issue; people with fast fibers may choose sprinting.
Sprinters had a lower VO₂max than distance runners
Not quite. A lower VO₂max is a finding, not a limit on the conclusion.
qs.x: Correct: The athlete comparison in Figure 1 is cross-sectional: it looks at groups that already exist at one moment. It can show sprinters have few type I fibers (24%), but not why. Maybe sprint training changed their fibers, or maybe people born with lots of fast fibers were quick as kids and chose sprinting. That second idea is called selection. Two clues point toward selection: Table 2 shows 12 weeks of training barely moved fiber proportion (52% to 54%), and paragraph 5 says twin studies suggest fiber type is strongly inherited. Why the others are wrong: biopsying the wrong muscle isn't true, since every group was sampled from the vastus lateralis; a lower VO₂max in sprinters is a result, not a flaw in the reasoning; and training length isn't raised, the problem is that people may choose a sport to suit their fibers. Trap: Reading cause and effect into a comparison of groups that already exist.

qs.q: Which feature best explains the sprinters' high peak power?
o: A larger mitochondrial volume in each fiber
Not quite. Sprinters had the lowest mitochondrial volume, 4.1%.
A higher VO₂max than the other groups
Not quite. Distance runners had the highest VO₂max, 74 vs 52.
Their high density of capillaries
Not quite. Sprinters had the fewest capillaries, 1.6 per fiber.
Fast myosin ATPase in type II fibers
Correct: fast myosin ATPase means faster cross-bridge cycling, so more power.
qs.x: Correct: Power is force times speed, so a powerful muscle has to shorten fast while pulling hard. Paragraph 1 says type II fibers have a fast myosin ATPase. That enzyme splits ATP quickly, so cross-bridges (the myosin heads grabbing and pulling actin) cycle faster and the fiber shortens faster. Sprinters have only 24% type I, so 100 − 24 = 76% type II, and Figure 1B shows them with the highest peak power, a mean of 22 W/kg. Why the others are wrong: high capillary density doesn't fit, since sprinters had the fewest (1.6 per fiber); a larger mitochondrial volume doesn't fit, since sprinters had the lowest (4.1%); a higher VO₂max doesn't fit either, since distance runners had the highest (74 vs 52). Trap: Crediting power to aerobic features, which support endurance instead.

qs.q: During a 30-second all-out sprint, sprinters' type II fibers produce lactate. Why?
o: Pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺
Correct: making lactate regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep running.
Lactate is made to store glucose for later
Not quite. Glucose is stored as glycogen, not lactate.
Mitochondria convert pyruvate directly into lactate
Not quite. Lactate is made in the cytosol by lactate dehydrogenase, not in mitochondria.
Lactate is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain
Not quite. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain.
qs.x: Correct: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and, along the way, turns NAD⁺ into NADH. One glycolysis enzyme, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, needs NAD⁺ to work. In an all-out sprint, glycolysis runs so fast that mitochondria can't turn the NADH back into NAD⁺ quickly enough, and fast type II fibers have few mitochondria to begin with (sprinters 4.1% in Table 1). So the cell uses lactate dehydrogenase in the cytosol: it hands NADH's electrons to pyruvate, making lactate and giving back NAD⁺. That keeps glycolysis, and its quick ATP, going. Why the others are wrong: lactate isn't the last electron acceptor of the electron transport chain, oxygen is; glucose is stored as glycogen, not lactate; mitochondria don't make lactate, because lactate dehydrogenase works in the cytosol. Trap: Thinking lactate is just useless waste.

passages.title: Aerobic Respiration Versus Fermentation in Yeast
text: Brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, can obtain ATP from glucose in two ways. In aerobic respiration, glucose is fully oxidized to CO₂, and the NADH formed is reoxidized by the electron transport chain, with O₂ as the final electron acceptor. In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde and CO₂, and acetaldehyde is then reduced to ethanol by NADH, regenerating NAD⁺. Fermentation yields 2 ATP per glucose, while respiration yields about 30.

In the nineteenth century, Louis Pasteur observed that yeast consumes much less sugar when air is present, a finding now called the Pasteur effect. Later work showed a second effect: at high glucose concentrations, many yeast strains ferment even when oxygen is plentiful. This is called the Crabtree effect, and it is the reason yeast in sugary dough or grape juice produces ethanol even when it is well aerated.

Researchers grew yeast in liquid medium and measured, per gram of cells per hour, the glucose consumed, the oxygen consumed, and the ethanol and CO₂ released. In some flasks they added sodium cyanide, which binds cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). Figure 1 shows the results. Each point is labeled by its condition: "Aerobic" for the aerobic flasks with 0.1% glucose, "No O₂" for the nitrogen-flushed flasks, "Cyanide" for the aerobic flasks with cyanide, and "Aerobic 5%" for the aerobic flasks with 5% glucose. In Figure 1A the number in parentheses is the glucose used. The dashed lines show what complete fermentation of the glucose used would give (2 ethanol and 2 CO₂ per glucose) and what complete respiration would give (6 O₂ used and 6 CO₂ released per glucose). All flasks were held at 30 °C and pH 5.0, and each value is the mean of three flasks.

Before the measurements, cells were taken from a starter culture, washed to remove any ethanol, and suspended at the same density in every flask. Dissolved oxygen was monitored with an electrode; in the aerobic flasks it stayed above 50% of air saturation throughout, and in the no-oxygen flasks, which were flushed with nitrogen, it stayed below the limit of detection.

The researchers also measured cell growth. Over 8 hours, cells in the aerobic, low-glucose flasks gained about four times as much mass per mole of glucose consumed as cells without oxygen. They proposed that respiration supplies more ATP per glucose and therefore supports more growth for the same amount of sugar.

qs.q: Why did yeast use about six times more glucose without oxygen?
o: Ethanol speeds up glycolysis directly
Nothing in the passage says ethanol speeds up glycolysis. It's just the end product.
Each glucose yields far less ATP by fermentation
Correct: Fermentation gives 2 ATP per glucose instead of about 30, so the cell burns much more sugar to keep up.
Oxygen inhibits glucose transport into cells
The cyanide flask had oxygen and still used 5.8 mmol of glucose, so oxygen isn't blocking uptake.
Fermentation produces more ATP per glucose
It's the reverse: fermentation makes 2 ATP per glucose, respiration about 30.
qs.x: Correct: Fermentation gets only 2 ATP from each glucose, while respiration gets about 30 (paragraph 1). A cell still needs the same amount of ATP to live, so when oxygen is gone it has to push sugar through glycolysis (the first, sugar-splitting stage) much faster to recover as much of the lost ATP as it can. That's why Figure 1A shows glucose use jumping from 1.0 mmol with oxygen to 6.0 mmol without it, and 6.0 ÷ 1.0 = 6 times as much. This is the Pasteur effect from paragraph 2 seen from the other side. Why the others are wrong: oxygen blocking glucose transport doesn't fit the cyanide flask, which had plenty of oxygen and still used 5.8 mmol; fermentation making more ATP per glucose is backwards, since it's 2 versus about 30; ethanol speeding up glycolysis has no support anywhere in the passage, and ethanol is just a waste product here. Trap: Thinking a cell that can't respire needs less fuel. It needs more, because each glucose is worth so much less.

qs.q: Why do the cyanide results closely match the no-oxygen results?
o: Cyanide removes oxygen from the medium
The oxygen was still in the flask. Cyanide stops the cells from using it.
Cyanide inhibits pyruvate decarboxylase
Pyruvate decarboxylase is needed to make ethanol, and these cells made plenty of it.
Cyanide stops O₂ from being used
Correct: Cyanide jams complex IV, so O₂ can't take electrons. Respiration stops even with oxygen present, and the cells ferment.
Cyanide breaks down ethanol
Ethanol output was high (11.2 mmol), so it wasn't being broken down.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says cyanide binds cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), the last protein in the electron transport chain, the one that hands electrons to O₂. With that step jammed, the whole chain stops, so the cells can't use oxygen even though it's sitting right there. Figure 1 shows it: O₂ use drops from 5.4 to 0.1 mmol, and glucose, ethanol and CO₂ (5.8, 11.2, 11.4) land right next to the no-oxygen flask (6.0, 11.6, 11.8). The cells are forced to ferment. Why the others are wrong: cyanide removing oxygen is wrong because the oxygen stayed in the flask, it just couldn't be used; cyanide blocking pyruvate decarboxylase can't be true, since that enzyme is needed to make ethanol and ethanol output was high; cyanide breaking down ethanol doesn't fit the 11.2 mmol of ethanol that piled up. Trap: Mixing up having no oxygen with being unable to use the oxygen you have.

qs.q: Why must yeast make ethanol when oxygen cannot be used?
o: To produce additional ATP from pyruvate
The steps from pyruvate to ethanol make no ATP. All the ATP comes from glycolysis.
To regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis
Correct: Reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol turns NADH back into NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs to keep running.
To provide carbon for the citric acid cycle
The citric acid cycle needs a working electron transport chain, which these cells don't have.
To store energy for later aerobic use
Making ethanol is about recycling NAD⁺, not saving energy for later.
qs.x: Correct: Glycolysis turns NAD⁺ into NADH as it splits glucose. A cell only has a small stock of NAD⁺, so if nothing turns the NADH back into NAD⁺, glycolysis runs out and stops. Normally the electron transport chain does that job by passing the electrons to O₂. When oxygen can't be used, paragraph 1 gives the backup: acetaldehyde takes the electrons from NADH and becomes ethanol, which hands back NAD⁺. So ethanol is made to keep glycolysis, and its 2 ATP, going. Why the others are wrong: making extra ATP from pyruvate is wrong because the steps from pyruvate to ethanol make no ATP at all; storing energy for later misses the point, since the step exists to recycle NAD⁺; feeding the citric acid cycle fails because ethanol isn't sent there, and the cycle can't run without the electron transport chain recycling NAD⁺. Trap: Assuming every step of a pathway is there to make ATP.

qs.q: In the aerobic flask with 5% glucose, yeast still produced ethanol. What does this result show?
o: Yeast cannot use oxygen at high glucose levels
The yeast still used 1.2 mmol of oxygen, so it could use oxygen. It just used less.
The flask ran out of oxygen
Paragraph 4 says oxygen stayed above 50% of air saturation in every aerobic flask.
Cyanide was present in that flask
Cyanide went only into the flask labeled with it, not this one.
High glucose suppresses respiration
Correct: With plenty of oxygen, high sugar cut O₂ use from 5.4 to 1.2 and raised ethanol to 7.0. That's the Crabtree effect.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the two aerobic points in Figure 1. Both had oxygen, and paragraph 4 says it stayed above 50% saturation. But at 5% glucose, O₂ use fell from 5.4 to 1.2 mmol and ethanol rose from 0.2 to 7.0 mmol. So with lots of sugar around, the yeast turned respiration down and fermented even though it could have respired. Paragraph 2 names this the Crabtree effect, the reason yeast in sweet dough or grape juice makes alcohol even with air. Why the others are wrong: yeast being unable to use oxygen doesn't fit, since it still used 1.2 mmol; the flask running out of oxygen is ruled out by the electrode readings in paragraph 4; cyanide being present is wrong because only the cyanide flask got it. Trap: Assuming ethanol always means there's no oxygen. Here oxygen was plentiful and the yeast fermented anyway.

qs.q: About how much ATP per gram per hour do cells without oxygen make from glucose?
o: 2 mmol
2 is the ATP from one glucose. Multiply it by the 6.0 mmol of glucose used.
6 mmol
6 mmol is the glucose used, not the ATP. Each glucose gives 2 ATP.
12 mmol
Correct: ATP = glucose used × 2 = 6.0 mmol × 2 = 12 mmol.
180 mmol
This is 6.0 × 30, the respiration yield. Without oxygen, each glucose gives only 2 ATP.
qs.x: Correct: The formula is ATP made = glucose used × ATP per glucose. Without oxygen, all the ATP comes from fermentation, which paragraph 1 says gives 2 ATP per glucose. Figure 1A shows the no-oxygen cells used 6.0 mmol of glucose per gram per hour. Plug in: ATP = 6.0 mmol × 2 = 12 mmol of ATP per gram per hour. Why the others are wrong: 2 mmol is just the yield per glucose (2 ATP), not the total; 6 mmol is the glucose used, before multiplying by the ATP each one gives; 180 mmol comes from 6.0 × 30, but 30 ATP per glucose needs respiration, and these cells had no oxygen. Trap: Using the respiration yield of about 30 ATP for cells that can only ferment.
