passages.title: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema in COPD
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) combines two kinds of damage. In chronic bronchitis, the small airways become inflamed and narrowed by mucus and thickened walls. In emphysema, the walls between alveoli are destroyed, which reduces the surface area for gas exchange and removes the elastic tissue that normally pulls the small airways open. During a forced exhalation, pressure outside the airways rises, and airways that have lost this support collapse early, trapping air in the lungs.

Spirometry measures the volume a person can exhale in the first second of a forced breath (FEV₁) and the total volume exhaled (forced vital capacity, FVC). An FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70 after a bronchodilator indicates airflow obstruction. The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) measures how readily gas crosses from the alveoli into the blood, and residual volume (RV) is the air left in the lungs after a full exhalation.

Researchers tested 1,200 adults aged 40 to 75 from one city who answered a mailed invitation. Each person was tested once. Participants were grouped as never smokers, former smokers who had quit at least five years earlier, and current smokers, with 520, 380 and 300 participants and a mean FEV₁/FVC of 0.78, 0.73 and 0.68 (Figure 1). Among current smokers, the prevalence of obstruction was 17% in those with fewer than 20 pack-years, 30% in those with 20 to 40 pack-years, and 49% in those with more than 40 pack-years (Figure 1C). One pack-year equals one pack a day for one year.

The researchers also asked about symptoms. Chronic cough with sputum on most days for at least three months in each of two years was reported by 4% of never smokers, 11% of former smokers and 27% of current smokers. Some participants with obstruction on spirometry reported no symptoms at all, which is common in early disease.

Former smokers had smoked for an average of 19 years before quitting, while current smokers had smoked for an average of 31 years. The researchers cautioned that the study could not show when the lung changes began relative to smoking, and that people who agree to take part in a lung study may differ from those who do not.

qs.q: Why does airflow obstruction lower FEV₁ more than it lowers FVC?
o: The lungs hold less total air in people with COPD
Not quite. COPD often increases lung volume by trapping air.
Narrowed airways slow how fast air leaves
Correct: narrow, collapsing airways slow airflow, so the first second is hit hardest.
Less oxygen reaches the blood
Not quite. Oxygen transfer is measured by DLCO; it doesn't set airflow speed.
Inspiratory muscles are weakened in COPD
Not quite. FEV₁ measures breathing out, not in.
qs.x: Correct: FEV₁ is how much air you can blow out in the first second; FVC is the total you can blow out with no time limit (paragraph 2). In COPD, the airways are narrowed and, as paragraph 1 says, collapse early during a forced breath. That slows how fast air can leave, so the first second suffers most. Given enough time, though, a lot of the air still gets out, so FVC drops less. That's why the FEV₁/FVC ratio falls, from 0.78 in never smokers to 0.68 in current smokers. Why the others are wrong: the lungs holding less air is backwards, since COPD often traps air and raises lung volumes (residual volume 128%); weak inspiratory muscles don't fit, since FEV₁ measures breathing out; less oxygen reaching the blood is a gas exchange problem (DLCO), which doesn't set airflow speed. Trap: Thinking obstruction mainly shrinks how much air the lungs hold, rather than how fast it leaves.

qs.q: What best explains the higher residual volume in current smokers?
o: Smokers inhale more deeply than people who never smoked
Not quite. Residual volume is measured after a full exhalation, so inhaling deeply doesn't matter.
Alveoli fill with fluid in COPD
Not quite. Fluid in the alveoli would lower the air volume.
Smoking strengthens the chest wall
Not quite. Nothing supports a stronger chest wall.
Airways collapse before the lungs can empty
Correct: unsupported airways close early, so air gets trapped.
qs.x: Correct: Residual volume is the air still left in the lungs after you breathe out as hard as you can (paragraph 2). Paragraph 1 explains why it rises in COPD: emphysema destroys the elastic tissue that holds small airways open, so when you push air out, those airways collapse early. The air behind them is trapped. Figure 1B shows residual volume rising from 102% of predicted in never smokers to 128% in current smokers. Why the others are wrong: inhaling more deeply doesn't matter, since residual volume is measured after a full exhalation; alveoli filling with fluid would leave less room for air, not more; nothing in the passage says smoking strengthens the chest wall. Trap: Assuming bigger lung volumes mean healthier lungs.

qs.q: Why is the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) lowest in current smokers?
o: Alveolar walls are lost, reducing exchange area
Correct: losing alveolar walls shrinks the surface area for diffusion.
Carbon monoxide is already bound to their hemoglobin
Not quite. Standard DLCO testing corrects for CO already in the blood.
Their airways are too narrow for CO to enter
Not quite. Narrow airways slow airflow, but gas still reaches the alveoli.
Smoking thickens red blood cell membranes
Not quite. This isn't a recognized effect of smoking.
qs.x: Correct: DLCO measures how easily gas crosses from the alveoli into the blood (paragraph 2). The rate gas diffuses across a membrane depends on how much surface area there is. Paragraph 1 says emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli, and with them the capillaries, so the exchange surface shrinks. That's why DLCO falls from 98% of predicted in never smokers to 74% in current smokers. Why the others are wrong: carbon monoxide already bound to hemoglobin is accounted for in standard DLCO testing; airways being too narrow for CO to enter doesn't work, because narrowing slows airflow but gas still reaches the alveoli during the slow breath hold of the test; smoking thickening red cell membranes isn't a recognized effect. Trap: Blaming airway narrowing for a problem that's really in the alveoli.

qs.q: Which finding most strengthens the argument that smoking causes the obstruction?
o: Never smokers had a mean ratio of 0.78
Not quite. That's the baseline value, not evidence of cause.
Each person was tested only the once
Not quite. Testing once is a limitation, not support.
Obstruction rises with pack-years
Correct: obstruction rose from 17% to 30% to 49% with more pack-years, a dose–response gradient.
Participants answered a mailed invitation
Not quite. Mailed recruitment raises a selection concern.
qs.x: Correct: A dose–response gradient means more of the exposure goes with more of the outcome. Paragraph 3 shows exactly that among current smokers: obstruction was 17% below 20 pack-years, 30% at 20 to 40, and 49% above 40. A pack-year is one pack a day for one year. When an effect climbs step by step with the dose, chance or a single hidden factor is a less likely explanation, so this is good support for cause, even though a one-time study can't show which came first. Why the others are wrong: a never-smoker ratio of 0.78 is just the reference value, not evidence of cause; being tested only once is a limitation of the study; recruiting by mailed invitation raises a selection concern (paragraph 5), which weakens rather than strengthens the case. Trap: Mistaking a description of how the study was done for evidence of causation.

qs.q: Which is a plausible alternative explanation for why former smokers had better values than current smokers?
o: Former smokers were tested with a different machine
Not quite. The passage describes no difference in how people were tested.
Former smokers had smoked fewer years in total
Correct: former smokers averaged 19 years of smoking vs 31, so less total exposure.
Current smokers were younger on average
Not quite. The passage gives no age difference between groups.
Quitting fully reverses emphysema
Not quite. Destroyed alveolar walls don't regrow.
qs.x: Correct: To compare two groups fairly, they should differ only in the thing you're testing, here quitting. Paragraph 5 says former smokers had smoked for an average of 19 years before quitting, while current smokers had smoked for 31 years. That's 31 − 19 = 12 more years of exposure for current smokers. So former smokers' better numbers (FEV₁/FVC 0.73 vs 0.68, obstruction 18% vs 31%) could come from smoking less in total, not only from stopping. Why the others are wrong: a different testing machine isn't described anywhere in the passage; quitting fully reversing emphysema is false, because destroyed alveolar walls don't regrow; current smokers being younger isn't stated, since the passage gives no age breakdown by group. Trap: Crediting a group difference to the label that defines the groups while ignoring other ways they differ.

Figure 1C. Airflow obstruction among current smokers by pack-years

passages.title: Short Sleep, Attention Lapses and Memory
text: Sleep supports attention and memory in different ways. Even one night of short sleep slows reaction time and increases lapses, moments when a person fails to respond at all. Sleep also helps consolidate newly learned material; slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, is linked in particular to strengthening memories for facts and word lists. Adolescents are at special risk of short sleep. At puberty, the evening release of melatonin shifts later, so teenagers tend to feel alert late at night, yet school often begins early in the morning.

Researchers asked 150 students aged 14 to 17 to wear wrist actigraphs, devices that estimate sleep from movement, for the two weeks before final exams. Students were grouped by their average nightly sleep. During the second week, each student completed a 10-minute psychomotor vigilance task (PVT), pressing a button whenever a counter appeared on a screen at random intervals. A response slower than 500 ms was scored as a lapse. On the same evening, students studied a list of 30 unrelated words for five minutes and were asked to recall as many as they could the next morning. Each also rated sleepiness on a 9-point scale. Figure 1 shows the design and Table 1 gives the results.

The actigraph data also showed that, on average, students slept about 90 minutes longer on weekend nights than on school nights, a pattern sometimes called social jet lag. Students in the shortest-sleep group had the largest weekend difference, about two and a half hours.

20 students in the shortest-sleep group reported drinking a caffeinated energy drink before the PVT. Their mean reaction time (286 ms) was close to that of the middle group, but their next-morning recall (14.0 words) did not differ from the rest of their group. The researchers also found that students in the shortest-sleep group reported more evening screen time and higher exam anxiety than the other students.

qs.q: Looking at how the groups were formed in Figure 1, which description best fits the design of this study?
o: Case-control, because students were grouped by their sleep
Not quite. Case-control studies group people by an outcome. These students were grouped by sleep, the exposure.
Longitudinal, because performance was followed for years
Not quite. The study covered two weeks before exams, not years.
Experimental, because sleep was the independent variable
Not quite. Sleep was the grouping variable, but nobody manipulated it. Students chose their own sleep.
Correlational; sleep was measured, not assigned
Correct: Sleep was measured as it happened, not assigned, so this is correlational.
qs.x: Correct: In a correlational study the researchers measure things as they naturally happen and look at how they move together. Here the students slept however much they slept, and the actigraphs (wrist devices that guess sleep from movement) just recorded it. In Figure 1, the actigraph step comes before the grouping step: students were grouped by their average nightly sleep, but nobody told anyone how long to sleep. Putting people into named groups after the fact doesn't turn a study into an experiment, because the researchers never controlled the variable. Why the others are wrong: an experiment would need the researchers to assign sleep amounts, and they didn't; a case-control study picks people by an outcome (say, poor exam scores) and looks back for causes, but these students were grouped by sleep, the exposure; a longitudinal study follows people over a long stretch, and this one lasted two weeks. Trap: Calling a study experimental just because its groups have labels that look like conditions.

qs.q: Which alternative explanation could account for the poorer recall in the shortest-sleep group?
o: The word lists differed by group
Not quite. The passage describes one 30-word task for all students.
Actigraphs measure sleep perfectly
Not quite. Measuring sleep perfectly would remove error. It wouldn't create a third variable.
Anxiety could cut sleep and hurt memory
Correct: Anxiety was higher in this group and could both shorten sleep and hurt memory.
The PVT took longer for some students
Not quite. Every PVT lasted 10 minutes, so its length can't explain anything.
qs.x: Correct: An alternative explanation here means a third variable, something that could drive both short sleep and poor recall, so sleep wouldn't have to be the cause. Paragraph 4 hands you one: the shortest-sleep group reported higher exam anxiety (and more evening screen time). Anxiety can keep a teenager awake, and it can also make it harder to learn and remember a word list. So anxiety alone could produce the link between less sleep and fewer words recalled. Why the others are wrong: the PVT (the button-pressing vigilance task) lasted 10 minutes for everyone, so its length can't differ; nothing in the passage suggests the word lists differed between groups, and the same 30-word task is described for all; perfect sleep measurement would make the data better, not create a confound. Trap: Missing the confounds that the study's own results point out.

qs.q: What does the caffeine subgroup suggest?
o: Caffeine aids alertness, not memory
Correct: Reaction time improved to 286 ms, but recall stayed at 14.0 words.
Caffeine prevents slow-wave sleep entirely
Not quite. Actigraphs only track movement, so sleep stages weren't measured.
Caffeine improves both attention and memory
Not quite. Recall stayed at 14.0 words, no better than the rest of the short-sleep group.
Short sleep does not affect reaction time
Not quite. The short-sleep group averaged 342 ms, much slower than 268 ms for 8 hours or more.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says the 20 short sleepers who had an energy drink reacted in 286 ms, close to the middle group's 291 ms in Table 1 and much faster than the 342 ms average for their own group. So caffeine helped alertness in the moment. But their next-morning recall was 14.0 words, about the same as their group's 14.1. Caffeine didn't help memory. That makes sense: memory consolidation (the brain firming up new learning) happens during sleep, and a stimulant can't do that job. Why the others are wrong: improving both attention and memory fails because recall stayed near 14 words; saying short sleep doesn't affect reaction time ignores the 342 ms short-sleep average versus 268 ms for 8 hours or more; caffeine preventing slow-wave sleep can't be judged, since actigraphs don't measure sleep stages. Trap: Thinking that feeling alert means the effects of lost sleep are gone.

qs.q: Why do many adolescents struggle to fall asleep early on school nights?
o: Melatonin is released later
Correct: The evening melatonin rise comes later at puberty, so sleepiness arrives later.
Adolescents have no circadian rhythm
Not quite. Teens still have a circadian rhythm. It's shifted later, not lost.
Melatonin levels stop rising at night
Not quite. Melatonin still rises at night. The rise is delayed, not gone.
Adolescents need less sleep than adults
Not quite. Teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours, more than adults, not less.
qs.x: Correct: Melatonin is the hormone that signals the body it's time to sleep. Paragraph 1 says that at puberty, the evening release of melatonin shifts later. So a teenager's internal clock (circadian rhythm, the body's roughly 24-hour cycle) runs late, and they feel wide awake at a time when adults are getting sleepy. School still starts early, so sleep gets squeezed from both ends. Why the others are wrong: teenagers actually need more sleep than adults, about 8 to 10 hours, not less; melatonin still rises at night, it just rises later; the circadian rhythm isn't lost, it's shifted. Trap: Blaming late bedtimes only on choices like phones, when biology is pushing the clock later too.

qs.q: Which sleep stage is most closely linked to consolidating word lists?
o: Stage N1 sleep
Not quite. N1 is light, transitional sleep, not the stage tied to word-list memory.
Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
Not quite. REM is linked more to skills and emotional memory. Word lists go with slow-wave sleep.
Slow-wave (N3) sleep
Correct: The passage links slow-wave (N3) sleep to memory for facts and word lists.
Wakefulness
Not quite. This kind of consolidation happens mainly during sleep, not while awake.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says it directly: slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage of non-REM sleep (also called N3), is linked to strengthening memories for facts and word lists. Facts and word lists are declarative memory, the kind you can say out loud. During slow-wave sleep the brain replays and firms up what you learned that day. That's why the study tested word recall the morning after. Why the others are wrong: N1 is the light, drifting-off stage, too brief and shallow to do this work; REM sleep is linked more to skills and emotional memories, so saying REM only leaves out the stage the passage names; while you're awake, new memories are fragile, and this kind of consolidation mostly happens during sleep. Trap: Assuming all memory consolidation happens in REM sleep.

graph.title: Figure 1. Design of the sleep, attention and memory study

passages.title: Attachment Styles in the Strange Situation
text: Attachment theory describes the emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. In the strange situation procedure, a 12-month-old infant and caregiver enter a playroom; a stranger joins them, the caregiver leaves twice, and the infant's behavior at each reunion is observed. Securely attached infants explore freely, may be upset when the caregiver leaves, and are quickly comforted when the caregiver returns. Insecure-avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver at reunion. Insecure-resistant infants are very distressed and are hard to comfort, often seeking and resisting contact at once. Disorganized infants show contradictory or confused behavior, such as freezing or approaching the caregiver with their head turned away.

Researchers followed 180 infants from a community sample. Each was classified in the strange situation at 12 months and again at 24 months by coders who did not see the earlier result. At 12 months, 108 infants (60%) were secure, 36 (20%) insecure-avoidant, 18 (10%) insecure-resistant and 18 (10%) disorganized (Figure 1). When the children were 6 years old, their first-grade teachers rated each child's competence with peers on a 1–5 scale. The teachers did not know about the study's attachment results. Parents reported major family stress, such as job loss, serious illness or divorce, at each visit.

Classifications at both ages were made from video recordings by trained coders. A second coder independently rated a random 20% of the recordings, and the two coders agreed on 88% of cases. 12 families moved away before the age-6 assessment; their children's 12-month classifications did not differ from those of the families who stayed.

Of the 19 children who changed from secure at 12 months to insecure at 24 months, 13 (68%) had families that reported a major stress between the two visits, compared with 22% of children whose secure classification was stable. The researchers also noted that infant temperament, measured by parent questionnaire at 6 months, was modestly related both to attachment classification and to later peer ratings.

qs.q: What behavior at reunion best identifies a securely attached infant?
o: Ignores the caregiver and keeps playing
Not quite. Ignoring the caregiver is the avoidant pattern.
Seeks the caregiver and is soon comforted
Correct: Seeking the caregiver and settling quickly shows a secure base.
Clings but pushes the caregiver away
Not quite. Seeking and resisting at once is the resistant pattern.
Freezes or approaches with head away
Not quite. Freezing or turning away is the disorganized pattern.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 describes a securely attached infant: they may get upset when the caregiver leaves, but when the caregiver comes back, they go to them and calm down quickly, then return to playing. The caregiver acts as a secure base, a safe spot to come back to. Why the others are wrong: ignoring the caregiver and playing on is the insecure-avoidant pattern; clinging while also pushing away is the insecure-resistant pattern, seeking and resisting contact at once; freezing or approaching with the head turned away is the disorganized pattern. Trap: Thinking an infant who isn't upset must be secure. Calm indifference at reunion is actually the avoidant pattern.

qs.q: What do the stress data suggest about why attachment classification can change?
o: Attachment is fixed at birth by genes
Not quite. Many classifications changed over a year.
Secure infants become insecure as they age
Not quite. 82% of secure infants stayed secure.
Coders made more errors at 24 months
Not quite. Coders were blind and agreed on 88% of cases.
Family stress can disrupt attachment
Correct: 68% of children who shifted had family stress, versus 22% of stable ones.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says that of the 19 children who went from secure to insecure, 13 (68%) had a major family stress between visits, compared with 22% of children who stayed secure. That's about three times as common (68 ÷ 22 ≈ 3.1). Stress like job loss or divorce can make caregiving less sensitive, and attachment reflects that ongoing relationship. So attachment can shift. Why the others are wrong: attachment being fixed at birth by genes doesn't fit, since many classifications changed; coders making more errors at 24 months has no support, coders were blind and agreed on 88% of cases; secure infants becoming insecure with age is false, 82% of secure infants stayed secure. Trap: Treating attachment as a permanent label.

qs.q: What most limits the conclusion that secure attachment causes better peer competence?
o: The sample was drawn from a community
Not quite. A community sample helps generalization.
Temperament may influence both measures
Correct: Temperament is linked to both, so it could explain the connection.
Teachers did not know the attachment results
Not quite. Blind teachers are a strength.
Attachment was assessed twice
Not quite. Two assessments improve measurement.
qs.x: Correct: This study is correlational: nobody was assigned to an attachment type. Paragraph 4 says infant temperament was related to both attachment and later peer ratings. That makes temperament a possible confound, a third factor behind both. An easygoing baby might be more likely to form a secure attachment and also get along better with peers, with no direct link between the two. Why the others are wrong: teachers not knowing attachment results is a strength, it prevents bias; assessing attachment twice improves measurement; a community sample helps the results apply more widely. Trap: Picking a strength of the study when the question asks for a limitation.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use teacher ratings rather than parent ratings of peer competence?
o: Teachers saw the sessions
Not quite. Teachers didn't attend the sessions.
Parents cannot rate social behavior
Not quite. Parents often rate social behavior.
Teachers were unaware of attachment status
Correct: Teachers didn't know attachment status, so their ratings are less likely to be biased.
Teachers know the children better than the parents do
Not quite. Parents usually know their children best.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says teachers didn't know the attachment results. Parents took part in the strange situation themselves, and how they see their child might be tied to their own relationship with them. If parents rated both, any bias could show up in both measures and create a fake link. Teachers who don't know give an independent measure. Why the others are wrong: teachers knowing children better is unlikely, parents usually know their own children best; parents being unable to rate social behavior is false, they often do; teachers seeing the sessions is false, they weren't there. Trap: Assuming the closest observer always gives the best measure.

qs.q: About how many of the 180 children had the same classification at 12 and 24 months?
o: About 90
Not quite. That's only the stable secure children (about 89).
About 108
Not quite. That's the number of secure infants at 12 months.
About 130
Correct: 89 + 22 + 10 + 9 = 130 children.
About 150
Not quite. That's more stability than Figure 1A shows.
qs.x: Correct: For each group, number stable = group size × percent stable. From Figure 1A and paragraph 2: secure 108 children, 82% stable; avoidant 36, 61%; resistant 18, 56%; disorganized 18, 50%. Change percents to decimals by dividing by 100 (82% = 0.82). Secure: 108 × 0.82 = 88.56 ≈ 89. Avoidant: 36 × 0.61 = 21.96 ≈ 22. Resistant: 18 × 0.56 = 10.08 ≈ 10. Disorganized: 18 × 0.50 = 9. Add them: 89 + 22 = 111, 111 + 10 = 121, 121 + 9 = 130. So about 130 children, which is 130 ÷ 180 ≈ 0.72, or 72%. Why the others are wrong: about 90 counts only the stable secure children; about 108 is just the number of secure infants at 12 months; about 150 is more stability than Figure 1A shows. Trap: Averaging the four percentages without weighting by group size.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Infants keeping the same attachment classification from 12 to 24 months
Figure 1B. Teacher-rated peer competence at age 6 (1 to 5 scale)

passages.title: Place Coding Along the Basilar Membrane
text: Sound waves enter the ear canal, move the eardrum and the ossicles, and set up a traveling wave along the basilar membrane of the cochlea. The membrane is narrow and stiff at the base, near the oval window, and wide and flexible at the apex. High frequencies produce their largest vibration near the base and low frequencies near the apex, an arrangement called tonotopy. Hair cells on the membrane convert vibration into neural signals. Loud sound can damage these cells, and in mammals they do not regenerate. The ear canal itself acts as a resonating tube that amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz.

Researchers measured hearing thresholds in three groups of workers at one manufacturing company: office staff with little noise exposure, machine operators with at least 10 years of work in areas averaging 95 dB who seldom wore hearing protection, and machine operators with similar exposure whose earplug use was logged by supervisors at more than 90% of shifts. Workers chose whether to wear earplugs. Each person's hearing threshold at each frequency was measured in a sound booth after at least 16 hours away from work. A higher threshold, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), means worse hearing. The groups had 60, 85 and 70 workers respectively, and the mean thresholds are plotted in Figure 1.

Because hearing tests depend on the listener's responses, the researchers repeated the 4,000 Hz measurement in each ear on a second day. The two measurements differed by no more than 5 dB in 94% of ears, and the average of the two was used. Workers with a history of ear surgery or frequent ear infections were excluded.

In a separate test, 20 operators had their hearing measured at the end of an unprotected shift. Their threshold at 4,000 Hz was on average 15 dB higher than their own baseline, but it returned to baseline after 16 hours of quiet. The researchers noted that the average age of the three groups was similar (44 to 46 years).

qs.q: Why is the loss in seldom-protected operators greatest at 4,000 Hz?
o: Low-frequency hair cells are the most fragile
Not quite. Losses at 500 Hz were small, 10 against 5 dB HL.
The ear canal boosts sound near this frequency
Correct: The ear canal amplifies 2,000 to 4,000 Hz, so those hair cells take the most energy.
Noise damages the ossicles at 4,000 Hz
Not quite. The passage says noise damages hair cells.
The cochlear apex receives the most energy
Not quite. The apex responds to low frequencies.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the ear canal acts like a resonating tube that amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz. So the hair cells tuned to that range get the strongest push from loud noise, and they're damaged first. Figure 1 shows the result: seldom-protected operators have a threshold of 48 dB HL at 4,000 Hz, compared with 10 for office staff. That dip is the classic noise notch. Why the others are wrong: low-frequency hair cells being most fragile doesn't fit, since losses at 500 Hz were small (10 against 5); the apex getting the most energy is wrong, since the apex handles low frequencies; noise damaging the ossicles isn't what the passage says, since it names hair cells as the site of damage. Trap: Assuming noise harms every frequency equally.

qs.q: Where along the basilar membrane is the 4,000 Hz damage most likely located?
o: At the apex
Not quite. The apex codes the lowest frequencies.
In the semicircular canals
Not quite. The semicircular canals sense head rotation.
Toward the base
Correct: High frequencies map to the stiff, narrow base.
Evenly along the whole membrane
Not quite. The 4,000 Hz notch shows the damage is localized.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 describes tonotopy, the idea that each spot on the basilar membrane responds best to one frequency. The base, near the oval window, is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies. The apex is wide and floppy and responds to low ones. 4,000 Hz is a high frequency, so the damaged hair cells sit toward the base. Why the others are wrong: the apex is where the lowest frequencies are coded; damage spread evenly doesn't fit the sharp notch at 4,000 Hz; the semicircular canals are part of the balance system and sense head rotation, not sound. Trap: Flipping the map and putting high frequencies at the apex.

qs.q: What is the most important limitation in concluding that earplugs prevented hearing loss?
o: Thresholds were measured after 16 hours of quiet
Not quite. Waiting 16 hours removes temporary shifts. That's a strength.
Office staff were included as a comparison
Not quite. A low-noise comparison group is a strength.
Thresholds were measured in a sound booth
Not quite. A sound booth improves accuracy.
Workers chose whether to wear earplugs
Correct: Self-chosen groups may differ in other ways that affect hearing.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says workers chose for themselves whether to wear earplugs. That's not random assignment. People who choose earplugs might also avoid loud music, take better care of their health, or work at quieter machines. Any of those could explain their better hearing (16 dB HL at 4,000 Hz against 48). So the data support a protective effect, but can't rule out these other differences. Why the others are wrong: testing after 16 hours of quiet is a strength, since it removes temporary shifts (paragraph 4); including office staff is a strength, since it gives a low-noise comparison; using a sound booth improves accuracy. Trap: Picking a design feature that helps the study when the question asks for a weakness.

qs.q: Why is a temporary threshold shift after a shift an important warning sign?
o: It shows the eardrum has ruptured
Not quite. Hearing returned to baseline, so the eardrum wasn't ruptured.
Repeated stress can kill hair cells
Correct: Repeated stress can kill hair cells, which don't regrow, so temporary can become permanent.
It means the auditory nerve has been cut
Not quite. Function recovered, so the nerve wasn't cut.
It shows that hearing loss is always temporary
Not quite. Seldom-protected operators have lasting loss.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says thresholds at 4,000 Hz rose 15 dB after an unprotected shift, then returned to baseline after 16 hours of quiet. That's a temporary threshold shift: the hair cells were stressed but recovered. Paragraph 1 says hair cells in mammals don't regenerate. Stress repeated over years can kill them, and dead hair cells mean permanent loss, like the 48 dB HL in seldom-protected operators. Why the others are wrong: a ruptured eardrum is wrong, since hearing came back in 16 hours; hearing loss always being temporary is wrong, since the seldom-protected group has lasting loss; a cut auditory nerve is wrong, since function recovered. Trap: Treating a change that recovers as harmless.

qs.q: Why do even office staff show their highest threshold at 8,000 Hz?
o: Aging affects high pitches first
Correct: Aging hits high frequencies first, and these workers are in their mid-40s.
The ear canal amplifies 8,000 Hz most
Not quite. The ear canal amplifies 2,000 to 4,000 Hz.
Office noise is concentrated at 8,000 Hz
Not quite. Office staff had little noise exposure.
Thresholds at 8,000 Hz cannot be measured
Not quite. Figure 1 shows 8,000 Hz thresholds.
qs.x: Correct: Office staff have little noise exposure, yet their worst threshold is at 8,000 Hz (15 dB HL in Figure 1). Paragraph 4 notes everyone is about 44 to 46 years old. Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) hits the highest frequencies first. One reason is that every sound passes the base of the cochlea, where high frequencies are coded, so those hair cells wear out soonest over a lifetime. Why the others are wrong: office noise being concentrated at 8,000 Hz is wrong, since office staff had little exposure; the ear canal amplifying 8,000 Hz most is wrong, since it boosts 2,000 to 4,000 Hz; 8,000 Hz not being measurable is wrong, since Figure 1 shows it. Trap: Assuming every high-frequency loss comes from noise.

graph.title: Figure 1. Hearing thresholds by test frequency in three worker groups

passages.title: Following a Reaction by Thin-Layer Chromatography
text: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is a quick way to follow the progress of a reaction. A small spot of the mixture is placed near the bottom of a glass plate coated with silica gel, a polar stationary phase whose surface is covered with Si–OH groups. The plate is stood in a shallow pool of solvent, the mobile phase, which climbs the plate by capillary action. Compounds that bind the silica strongly, especially through hydrogen bonds, move only a short distance; less polar compounds stay dissolved in the solvent and travel farther. The retardation factor, Rf, is the distance a spot travels divided by the distance the solvent front travels.

A student reduced benzophenone, a ketone, to diphenylmethanol, a secondary alcohol, using sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in methanol at room temperature. To follow the reaction, the student removed a drop of the mixture at 0, 10 and 30 minutes and spotted it on silica plates next to standards of pure starting material and pure product, which served as reference controls (Table 1). In one lane, the 10-minute sample was spotted directly on top of a spot of the product standard, a technique called co-spotting. The plates were run in 4:1 hexane:ethyl acetate, and the solvent front traveled 8.0 cm on every plate. Spots were seen under ultraviolet light, where both compounds absorb because of their aromatic rings.

Before choosing the solvent, the student compared both standards in three hexane:ethyl acetate mixtures (Figure 1). Ethyl acetate is more polar than hexane, so mixtures richer in it compete more effectively with the compounds for the silica surface.

A single plate cannot prove what a compound is. Two different substances can happen to have the same Rf in one solvent, so a match is stronger evidence when it holds in more than one solvent system. For a firm identification, chemists confirm the structure by a spectroscopic method such as nuclear magnetic resonance or infrared spectroscopy.

After 30 minutes, the student added dilute acid to destroy the remaining NaBH₄, extracted the product into ethyl acetate and evaporated the solvent, leaving white crystals that gave a single spot at Rf 0.35.

qs.q: What is the Rf of diphenylmethanol on the reaction plates?
o: Correct: 2.8 cm ÷ 8.0 cm = 0.35.
Not quite. That divides by the benzophenone spot (5.2 cm), not the solvent front.
Not quite. 0.65 is benzophenone's Rf.
Not quite. That flips the ratio. Rf can't be more than 1.
qs.x: Correct: Rf = distance the spot travels ÷ distance the solvent front travels (paragraph 1). From Table 1, the diphenylmethanol spot is at 2.8 cm, and paragraph 2 says the solvent front went 8.0 cm on every plate. Plug in: Rf = 2.8 cm ÷ 8.0 cm. The cm cancel. 2.8 ÷ 8 = 0.35. That matches the 4:1 point in Figure 1 (0.35), which makes sense because the plates were run in 4:1. Why the others are wrong: 0.54 divides by the benzophenone spot (2.8 ÷ 5.2) instead of the solvent front; 0.65 is benzophenone's Rf (5.2 ÷ 8.0); 2.86 flips the fraction (8.0 ÷ 2.8), and an Rf can never be more than 1, since a spot can't pass the solvent front. Trap: Flipping the ratio or dividing by the wrong distance.

qs.q: Why does diphenylmethanol travel a shorter distance than benzophenone?
o: Its O–H group binds the silica
Correct: Its O–H donates a hydrogen bond to the silica, so it sticks more.
It has a much larger molar mass
Not quite. The masses differ by only 2 g/mol.
It does not absorb ultraviolet light
Not quite. Both absorb UV through their aromatic rings, and both were seen.
It is less polar than benzophenone
Not quite. The alcohol is the more polar one.
qs.x: Correct: Silica is covered in Si–OH groups, and compounds that hydrogen bond to them stick and move less (paragraph 1). Diphenylmethanol is an alcohol, so it has an O–H that can donate a hydrogen bond to the silica. Benzophenone is a ketone; its C=O can only accept hydrogen bonds, not donate them. The alcohol grips the plate harder, so it travels only 2.8 cm versus 5.2 cm (Table 1). Why the others are wrong: the masses barely differ, reduction just adds two hydrogens, so 182 vs 184 g/mol; the alcohol is the more polar compound, not the less polar one; both absorb ultraviolet light because of their aromatic rings, and both were seen. Trap: Explaining TLC movement by mass instead of polarity.

qs.q: Which solvent gives the best separation of the two compounds?
o: 9:1, because both spots stay near the origin
Not quite. The product barely moves (Rf 0.12), so the spots are poorly resolved.
All three separate the compounds equally well
Not quite. The gaps are 0.26, 0.30 and 0.14, so they differ.
4:1, because the Rf values differ the most
Correct: 0.65 − 0.35 = 0.30, the biggest gap, with both spots mid-plate.
1:1, because both spots travel the farthest
Not quite. Both crowd near the front with only a 0.14 gap.
qs.x: Correct: Good separation means the two spots are far apart and both sit in the middle of the plate. Gap = Rf of benzophenone − Rf of diphenylmethanol, from Figure 1. 9:1: 0.38 − 0.12 = 0.26. 4:1: 0.65 − 0.35 = 0.30. 1:1: 0.88 − 0.74 = 0.14. The 4:1 gap, 0.30, is the biggest, and both spots land mid-plate, where they're easy to see and measure. Why the others are wrong: in 9:1 the product barely leaves the starting line (Rf 0.12), and spots crowded near the bottom are hard to read; in 1:1 both spots crowd up near the solvent front with only a 0.14 gap; the three gaps clearly differ. Trap: Picking the solvent that makes spots travel farthest instead of the one that spreads them apart most.

qs.q: What does the 30-minute plate show?
o: Both compounds are present in equal amounts
Not quite. Only one spot is seen, so both can't be there equally.
The product has broken down
Not quite. The product spot is still there.
No reaction has taken place
Not quite. The starting spot vanished, so a reaction happened.
The benzophenone has been used up
Correct: Only the product spot at 2.8 cm remains, so the ketone is used up.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows the 30-minute lane has only one spot, at 2.8 cm, which matches the diphenylmethanol standard. The spot at 5.2 cm, benzophenone, is gone. So the starting ketone has been used up and turned into the alcohol. Why the others are wrong: the reaction clearly happened, since the starting spot disappeared and the product spot appeared; the product hasn't broken down, its spot is right there; there's only one spot, so both compounds can't be present in equal amounts. Trap: Missing that a spot disappearing tells you as much as a new spot appearing.

qs.q: What does the co-spotted lane add to the analysis?
o: It shows that NaBH₄ has been used up
Not quite. NaBH₄ isn't what's being tested on the plate.
It confirms the new spot is the product
Correct: One round spot means the sample and standard run identically.
It measures how much product has formed
Not quite. Spot size here only gives a rough idea of amount.
It shows the product is more polar than the solvent
Not quite. Co-spotting compares the sample with a standard, not the solvent.
qs.x: Correct: Co-spotting means putting the reaction sample right on top of the pure product standard (paragraph 2). If the new spot in the reaction were a different compound that just happened to run close by, the two would usually smear into a long or double spot. Table 1 shows one round spot at 2.8 cm, so they run identically, which supports that the new spot really is diphenylmethanol. Paragraph 4 adds that this still isn't proof; spectroscopy confirms it. Why the others are wrong: spot size on a simple plate only gives a rough idea of amount; NaBH₄ isn't what's being tested and doesn't show up on the plate; co-spotting compares the sample with a standard, not with the solvent. Trap: Assuming matching Rf values in separate lanes always prove two compounds are the same.

passages.title: Respiratory Control: Oxygen Use Tied to ATP Demand
text: In most cells, the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the mitochondrial matrix, and the protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving ATP production. The rate of oxygen use is therefore tied to the demand for ATP: when ADP is scarce, ATP synthase slows, the proton gradient builds up, and electron transport slows. Brown adipose tissue (BAT), found in newborns, hibernating animals and small amounts in adults, breaks this link. Its mitochondria contain uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which lets protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase. The energy of the gradient is released as heat. Purine nucleotides such as GDP bind UCP1 and close it, while fatty acids released during cold exposure open it.

Researchers housed wild-type mice and mice lacking the UCP1 gene (UCP1 knockout) either at 30 °C, where mice do not need to produce extra heat, or at 4 °C for 7 days, after which BAT had grown and become more active. They isolated BAT mitochondria and measured oxygen use with succinate as the fuel, first without ADP, then with ADP, and in a separate sample without ADP but with GDP. They also measured the membrane potential across the inner membrane, a measure of the proton gradient, without ADP. Table 1 gives the mean oxygen use of each group of mitochondria, and Figure 1 plots oxygen use without ADP against membrane potential for the individual preparations (6 per group, each from a different mouse).

The researchers checked that the isolated mitochondria were intact before each measurement by confirming that oxygen use rose when ADP was added and fell again once the added ADP had been converted to ATP. Preparations that did not show this response were discarded.

In a separate experiment, mice that had been kept at 30 °C were moved directly to 4 °C. After 6 hours, wild-type mice had a body temperature of 35.5 °C, while UCP1 knockout mice had cooled to 29 °C and were shivering vigorously. Knockout mice that were first moved to 18 °C for a week before the 4 °C test maintained their body temperature, a finding the researchers attributed to slower adaptations such as increased shivering capacity.

qs.q: Why is oxygen use high without ADP in wild-type mitochondria from cold-adapted mice?
o: Protons leak back through UCP1
Correct: Protons leak back through UCP1, so the gradient never builds up and the chain keeps running and using O₂.
Succinate is oxidized without the chain
Oxygen is used only at the end of the electron transport chain, so the chain must be running.
GDP opens UCP1
Paragraph 1 says GDP binds UCP1 and closes it.
ATP synthase keeps working without ADP
ATP synthase needs ADP to make ATP. Without ADP it stops.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 explains that oxygen use normally tracks ATP need. With no ADP, ATP synthase sits idle, protons pile up outside the matrix, and the electron transport chain slows. Brown fat is different because UCP1 gives protons a side door back into the matrix. Cold-adapted brown fat has lots of UCP1, so the gradient keeps draining, the chain never gets backed up, and oxygen use stays high: 210 without ADP in Table 1, almost the same as 230 with ADP. The energy comes off as heat. Why the others are wrong: ATP synthase working without ADP is impossible, because ADP is what it turns into ATP; succinate being oxidized without the chain doesn't work, since the chain is what uses oxygen; GDP opening UCP1 is backwards, paragraph 1 says GDP closes it. Trap: Assuming high oxygen use means lots of ATP is being made.

qs.q: What happens when GDP is added to these mitochondria?
o: Oxygen use rises; GDP is a fuel
GDP isn't a fuel here. It blocks UCP1, and oxygen use dropped.
The membrane potential falls
Closing the leak lets protons build up, so the potential would rise, not fall.
Oxygen use falls as the leak closes
Correct: GDP closes UCP1, the gradient builds up, the chain slows, and O₂ use falls from 210 to 70.
ATP synthesis rises without ADP
There's still no ADP, so ATP synthase has nothing to make ATP from.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says GDP binds UCP1 and closes it. With the side door shut, protons can't leak back, so the gradient builds up. A full gradient pushes back on the pumps, the electron transport chain slows, and oxygen use falls. Table 1 shows it in cold-adapted wild-type mitochondria: 210 without GDP down to 70 with GDP. Why the others are wrong: GDP acting as a fuel is wrong because here it works as a blocker, and oxygen use fell rather than rose; ATP synthesis rising doesn't work, since there's still no ADP to turn into ATP; the membrane potential falling is backwards, because closing the leak lets the gradient, and so the potential, build up. Trap: Treating every nucleotide like an energy source. GDP here is a signal that shuts a channel.

qs.q: Why is the membrane potential lowest in cold-adapted wild-type mitochondria?
o: ADP was present in these samples
Not quite. The text says the potential was measured without ADP.
Cold mitochondria pump more protons
Not quite. Pumping more protons would raise the potential. A leak is what lowers it.
The knockout has more UCP1
Not quite. The knockout has no UCP1, and it has the highest potential, 175 mV.
The proton leak discharges it
Correct: Protons leaking back through plentiful UCP1 drain the gradient, giving the lowest potential, 120 mV.
qs.x: Correct: Membrane potential measures the proton gradient across the inner membrane, the voltage set up by protons pumped out. Every proton that slips back through UCP1 takes a little of that away. Cold-adapted wild-type brown fat has the most UCP1, so it leaks the most and has the lowest potential in Figure 1, 120 mV. Wild type at 30 °C, with less UCP1, sits at 160 mV, and the knockout, with no UCP1 at all, is highest at 175 mV. Why the others are wrong: cold mitochondria pumping more protons would push the potential up, not down; the knockout having more UCP1 is false, it has none; ADP being present is wrong because Figure 1 shows potentials measured without ADP. Trap: Assuming the mitochondria using the most oxygen must have the biggest gradient. Here the leak drains it as fast as it's built.

qs.q: Why did knockout mice moved directly to 4 °C become hypothermic despite shivering?
o: They could not shiver
Paragraph 4 says the knockout mice were shivering vigorously.
They could not make heat in brown fat
Correct: Without UCP1, brown fat can't leak protons to make heat, so the mice had only shivering and cooled to 29 °C.
Their mitochondria could not take up oxygen
Not quite. Knockout mitochondria used oxygen; they lacked the protein that lets protons leak back as heat.
Their brown fat used too much oxygen
Knockout brown fat used little oxygen (55 without ADP), not too much.
qs.x: Correct: Brown fat makes heat by letting protons leak through UCP1, so the chain burns fuel and gives off heat instead of making ATP. Knockout mice have no UCP1, so their brown fat can't do this. Table 1 backs it up: knockout brown fat used only 55 without ADP, versus 210 in wild type. Paragraph 4 says that when moved straight into the cold, these mice had only shivering to rely on, and their body temperature fell to 29 °C while wild-type mice held 35.5 °C. Given a week at 18 °C first, slower changes like stronger shivering let them cope. Why the others are wrong: not being able to shiver is wrong, paragraph 4 says they shivered hard; brown fat using too much oxygen is backwards, knockout brown fat used little; and their mitochondria could take up oxygen, they lacked the leak that makes heat. Trap: Assuming shivering alone can keep a body warm in a sudden cold snap.

qs.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol carries protons across the inner membrane. Which effect would it most likely have in a person?
o: Lower body temperature from reduced respiration
Not quite. A proton leak speeds respiration and releases more heat, not less.
More oxygen use and a higher temperature
Correct: It leaks protons in every cell, like UCP1 everywhere, so the chain speeds up, O₂ use rises and heat is released.
Higher ATP production in every cell
Protons go around ATP synthase, so ATP production falls.
Lower oxygen use; the chain stops
Draining the gradient makes the chain run faster, not stop.
qs.x: Correct: Dinitrophenol is a chemical that carries protons across the inner membrane, the same job UCP1 does, but in every cell of the body and with no off switch. Protons skip ATP synthase, so less ATP gets made. With the gradient always draining, the electron transport chain runs as fast as it can, burning more fuel and using more oxygen. That energy becomes heat, so body temperature rises, sometimes dangerously. It was once sold for weight loss and killed people. Why the others are wrong: higher ATP production is backwards, because protons bypass ATP synthase; lower oxygen use with the chain stopping is the opposite of what a leak does, it speeds the chain up; and a lower temperature is backwards too, the energy is released as heat. Trap: Thinking that burning fuel faster must mean making more ATP.

passages.title: p53 and the DNA Damage Checkpoint
text: A cell that has damaged DNA must repair it before replication, or the damage will be copied into both daughter cells. The protein p53 coordinates this response. After damage, p53 escapes its normal rapid destruction and accumulates. It acts as a transcription factor, switching on genes such as CDKN1A, which encodes the protein p21. p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, so the cell cannot pass from G1 into S phase. If the damage is too severe to repair, p53 also switches on genes that trigger apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death in which the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into small fragments, and the remains are cleared by neighboring cells.

Researchers compared two human cell lines: line A, which carries two normal copies of TP53, and line B, which carries a mutation in both copies that prevents the protein from binding DNA. Both lines were exposed to 5 gray of ionizing radiation, which creates double-strand breaks. 24 hours later, the fraction of cells in each phase of the cycle was measured by flow cytometry, which sorts cells by DNA content. Apoptotic cells were counted by a stain that detects cut DNA ends. Each condition was run in four independent dishes (Figure 1). The means across the dishes were: line A untreated, 58% in G1, 26% in S, 16% in G2/M and 2% apoptotic; line A irradiated, 86%, 4%, 10% and 18%; line B untreated, 55%, 28%, 17% and 2%; line B irradiated, 52%, 25%, 23% and 3%.

Protein levels were also measured. Four hours after radiation, line A showed a six fold rise in p53 protein and a five fold rise in p21, while line B showed a five fold rise in p53 protein but no rise in p21. TP53 mRNA levels changed little in either line.

The researchers noted that flow cytometry measures DNA content rather than the phase directly: a cell with the DNA content of G1 could in principle be an arrested cell or one preparing to divide. To check their reading of the data, they repeated the experiment with a chemical that labels cells actively copying DNA, and found that the fraction of labeled cells matched the S-phase fractions in Figure 1.
When line B was given a plasmid carrying a normal TP53 gene before radiation, the G1 fraction rose to 81% and apoptosis to 15%, close to the values for line A.

qs.q: Why did line A accumulate in G1 after radiation?
o: The cells entered mitosis and stopped
The G2/M fraction fell from 16% to 10%, so cells didn't stall in mitosis.
p53 directly copied the damaged DNA
p53 is a transcription factor; it switches genes on, it doesn't copy DNA.
p21 blocked the kinases that start S phase
Correct: p21 blocked the kinases that start S phase, so the G1 checkpoint held.
Radiation destroyed the cells in S phase
Killing S-phase cells wouldn't raise G1 to 86%; apoptosis was only 18%.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 lays out the chain. DNA damage lets p53 build up. p53 is a transcription factor (a protein that switches genes on), and it turns on CDKN1A, which makes p21. p21 blocks the cyclin-dependent kinases, the enzymes that push a cell from G1 into S phase. With those kinases blocked, the cell can't start copying its DNA, so it waits in G1. Figure 1A shows it: after radiation, line A's G1 fraction jumps from 58% to 86% and S drops from 26% to 4%. Why the others are wrong: if radiation had simply killed S-phase cells, that wouldn't push G1 up this much, and apoptosis is only 18%; p53 doesn't copy DNA, it switches genes on; and cells didn't pile up in mitosis, since the G2/M fraction fell from 16% to 10%. Trap: Assuming every cell cycle arrest happens at mitosis.

qs.q: What does the rise in p53 protein without a rise in TP53 mRNA show?
o: p53 protein is made from p21 mRNA
Each protein comes from its own gene; p53 isn't made from p21 mRNA.
TP53 is transcribed faster after damage
TP53 mRNA barely changed, so transcription didn't speed up.
Radiation stabilizes every protein
p21 didn't rise in line B, so this isn't a general effect on all proteins.
p53 is controlled by its destruction rate
Correct: p53 builds up because it's destroyed more slowly, not made faster.
qs.x: Correct: Protein levels can rise two ways: make more mRNA (transcription) or let the protein last longer. Paragraph 3 says p53 protein rose about six-fold in line A, but TP53 mRNA barely changed. So the extra protein didn't come from more transcription. Paragraph 1 gives the answer: p53 is normally destroyed quickly, and after damage it escapes that destruction and builds up. Why the others are wrong: faster transcription of TP53 would raise its mRNA, which didn't happen; p53 is made from its own gene's mRNA, not from p21's; and radiation doesn't stabilize every protein, since p21 didn't rise at all in line B. Trap: Assuming more protein always means more transcription.

qs.q: Why did p21 fail to rise in line B?
o: Mutant p53 cannot bind DNA
Correct: Mutant p53 can't bind DNA, so it can't switch on the p21 gene.
Line B lacks the CDKN1A gene
Adding normal TP53 restored the response, so CDKN1A must be there.
Line B does not make p53 protein
Line B's p53 rose five-fold, so it does make the protein.
Radiation destroys p21 protein
p21 rose five-fold in line A under the same radiation.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says line B's p53 has a mutation that stops it from binding DNA. A transcription factor has to bind DNA to switch on a gene. So even though line B's p53 rose five-fold (paragraph 3), it couldn't turn on CDKN1A, and no extra p21 was made. Without p21, the G1 checkpoint never kicked in. Why the others are wrong: line B does make p53, its level rose five-fold; nothing suggests line B lacks CDKN1A, and adding a normal TP53 gene restored the response (paragraph 5); and radiation doesn't destroy p21, since p21 rose five-fold in line A under the same dose. Trap: Assuming that having more of a transcription factor means it's working.

qs.q: What is the purpose of giving line B a normal TP53 gene?
o: To repair the radiation damage directly
TP53 makes a transcription factor; it doesn't repair DNA directly.
To increase the amount of p53 protein
Line B already builds up p53; its p53 just doesn't work.
To show that plasmids cause G1 arrest
The effect came from the TP53 gene the plasmid carried.
To show the defect lies in TP53
Correct: Restoring TP53 restored the response, so the defect is in TP53.
qs.x: Correct: Line A and line B are different cell lines, so they could differ in many ways, not just TP53. Paragraph 5 puts a working TP53 gene back into line B. Afterward, the G1 fraction rose to 81% and apoptosis to 15%, close to line A's 86% and 18%. Bringing back one gene brought back the response, which shows the TP53 mutation is what caused line B's defect. This is called a rescue experiment. Why the others are wrong: line B already builds up plenty of p53, the problem is that it doesn't work; TP53 makes a transcription factor, which doesn't repair DNA itself; and the arrest came from the gene the plasmid carried, not from the plasmid. Trap: Treating a rescue experiment as just another treatment rather than a test of cause.

qs.q: Based on the passage, how would loss of p53 function most likely contribute to tumor formation?
o: Cells divide more slowly without p53
Line B kept cycling at about its normal pace.
Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing
Correct: Damaged cells keep dividing; both the checkpoint and apoptosis are lost.
Cells without p53 cannot replicate DNA
Line B still had 25% of its cells in S phase.
p53 normally promotes entry into S phase
p53 blocks entry into S phase after damage.
qs.x: Correct: Normally p53 does two jobs after DNA damage: it pauses the cycle so the damage can be repaired, and if the damage is too bad, it triggers apoptosis. Without working p53, neither happens. Figure 1 shows line B after radiation kept cycling almost as if nothing happened (52% G1, 25% S) with only 3% apoptosis. Cells that keep dividing with damaged DNA pile up mutations, and some of those mutations can drive cancer. Why the others are wrong: cells without p53 don't divide more slowly, line B cycled about normally; p53 doesn't promote entry into S phase, it blocks it after damage; and cells without p53 can still copy DNA, line B had 25% in S phase. Trap: Assuming a gene that holds growth back must be needed for growth.

passages.title: Cone Types and Color Vision Deficiency
text: Human color vision normally depends on three cone types with peak sensitivities near 420 nm (S, short), 530 nm (M, medium) and 560 nm (L, long). The brain compares their outputs, so a color is identified by the pattern of activity across cone types rather than by any one cone alone. The genes for the M and L pigments sit next to each other on the X chromosome and are very similar in sequence, which makes unequal crossing over between them relatively common. The S pigment gene is on chromosome 7.

Because the M and L genes are X-linked, a man with a defective copy has no second copy to compensate, while a woman is affected only if both of her X chromosomes carry a defect. Anomalous trichromacy, in which one pigment's peak is shifted rather than missing, is more common than the complete loss of a cone type.

Researchers tested 600 men and 600 women with two methods. In the Rayleigh match, the observer mixes red and green light to match a yellow reference; people with a shifted M or L pigment need an unusual proportion of red. In the Ishihara plates, numbers are formed by dots that differ in color but not in brightness. Participants also named the colors of 20 standard samples under controlled lighting (Figure 1 shows the design and Table 1 the results).

Color vision deficiency affects everyday tasks unevenly. Traffic signals are distinguished partly by position, so they cause little trouble, while reading a colored map, judging whether meat is cooked, or noticing a rash can be harder. Some occupations, such as commercial piloting, require a color vision test.

Among the 49 men with an abnormal match, 36 could still distinguish red from green samples under bright light but made errors with pale or dim colors, while 13 made errors under all conditions. The researchers also noted that about 15% of women in the sample had one normal and one anomalous gene by DNA testing but normal color vision on every test.

qs.q: Table 1 shows an abnormal Rayleigh match in 8.2% of men but only 0.7% of women. Why is red-green color vision deficiency much more common in men?
o: The S pigment gene is X-linked too
Not quite. The S gene is on chromosome 7.
Men have fewer cone cells in the retina than women
Not quite. Cone numbers aren't the explanation.
The M and L genes lie on the X chromosome
Correct: The M and L genes are on the X, and men have only one X.
Men's lenses absorb more red light
Not quite. Lens absorption isn't the cause.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the M and L pigment genes sit on the X chromosome. Men have one X, so one faulty copy is enough to cause the deficiency. Women have two X chromosomes and are affected only if both carry a faulty gene (paragraph 2), which is much rarer. Table 1 matches: abnormal Rayleigh match in 8.2% of men against 0.7% of women (4 of 600). In fact, 0.08 × 0.08 = 0.0064, about 0.6%, close to what you'd expect if a woman needs two faulty copies. Why the others are wrong: men having fewer cones isn't stated or the cause; the S gene being X-linked is wrong, since it's on chromosome 7; men's lenses absorbing more red isn't the explanation. Trap: Blaming a general sex difference instead of X-linked inheritance.

qs.q: In Figure 1, 36 of the 49 men with an abnormal match erred only with pale or dim colors. What do these 36 men most likely have?
o: A shifted pigment, not a missing cone
Correct: A shifted pigment blurs faint differences but keeps strong ones.
No M cones at all
Not quite. Missing M cones would confuse bright red and green too.
Normal color vision, poor attention
Not quite. Their Rayleigh matches were abnormal.
A defect in the S pigment
Not quite. S pigment defects affect blue-yellow vision.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 describes anomalous trichromacy: all three cone types are there, but one pigment's peak is shifted, so the M and L signals look more alike than normal. Strongly different colors still give different patterns, so bright red and green can be told apart. Faint differences get lost, so pale or dim colors cause errors. Paragraph 5 says that's what the 36 men show. A missing cone type would cause errors in every condition, like the other 13 men. Why the others are wrong: no M cones at all would also confuse bright red and green; an S pigment defect affects blue-yellow vision, not red-green; normal vision with poor attention is wrong, since their Rayleigh matches were abnormal on an objective test. Trap: Treating color deficiency as all or nothing.

qs.q: Why do the Ishihara plates use dots that differ in color but not brightness?
o: So normal viewers also fail
Not quite. People with normal vision pass.
So the test measures visual acuity instead
Not quite. Acuity is measured separately.
So the plates print cheaply
Not quite. Cost isn't the reason.
So brightness cannot replace color
Correct: Equal brightness means only color can reveal the number.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says the Ishihara numbers are made of dots that differ in color but not in brightness. If the number were also lighter or darker than the background, someone who can't tell the hues apart could still read it using brightness. Matching brightness removes that backup clue and forces the viewer to rely on color alone. Why the others are wrong: printing cost isn't the reason; making normal viewers fail is wrong, since they read the plates correctly; measuring acuity is wrong, since acuity (sharpness of vision) is a different test. Trap: Missing that a good test removes any other clue that could give the answer.

qs.q: What do the 15% of women with one anomalous gene and normal vision illustrate?
o: Color vision genes are not inherited
Not quite. The genes are on the X and are inherited.
One normal copy is enough
Correct: One normal copy is enough, so the trait is recessive.
X inactivation removes all anomalous cones
Not quite. X inactivation is random, so some cones still use the anomalous gene.
The anomalous gene is dominant in women
Not quite. These women see normally, so it isn't dominant.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says about 15% of women carry one normal and one anomalous gene but test normally on everything. They're carriers. The normal gene on one X is enough to build a normal set of cones, so the trait doesn't show. That's what X-linked recessive means. The 15% also fits the math: if 8% of X chromosomes carry the defect, the chance of one faulty and one normal X is 2 × 0.08 × 0.92 ≈ 0.15. Why the others are wrong: the anomalous gene being dominant in women is wrong, since these women see normally; color vision genes not being inherited is wrong, since they're on the X; X inactivation removing all anomalous cones is wrong, since random inactivation leaves some cones using each gene. Trap: Assuming a carrier must show a mild version of the trait.

qs.q: Why does the brain need more than one cone type to identify a color?
o: Cones cannot respond to dim light
Not quite. Cones still respond. Rods take over only in very dim light.
One cone type gives an ambiguous signal
Correct: One cone type's signal mixes up wavelength and brightness. Comparing cones resolves it.
Each cone type sends signals to a different eye
Not quite. Both eyes have all cone types.
A single cone type responds to only one wavelength
Not quite. Each cone type responds over a broad range.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says color is identified by the pattern across cone types, not by any one cone. Each cone type responds to a broad range of wavelengths. So one cone could give the same response to a dim light at its favorite wavelength and a bright light at a less favored one. On its own, that signal is ambiguous. Comparing two or more cone types settles it, because a change in wavelength shifts their outputs relative to each other, while a change in brightness doesn't. Why the others are wrong: a cone responding to only one wavelength is wrong, since each covers a broad band; cones not responding to dim light is wrong, since cones still respond, though rods take over in very dim light; each cone type going to a different eye is wrong, since both eyes have all three. Trap: Thinking each cone reports one color.

passages.title: Sensitivity and Criterion in Signal Detection
text: Signal detection theory separates two influences on a yes-or-no judgment. Sensitivity (d′) reflects how well a person can tell signal trials from noise trials. The criterion (c) reflects how willing the person is to say "yes." A criterion of 0 is neutral, a negative value is liberal (more "yes" responses), and a positive value is conservative. Both are calculated from the hit rate (the proportion of signal trials called "yes") and the false-alarm rate (the proportion of noise trials called "yes"). Sensitivity is unaffected by shifts in criterion.

Researchers asked 40 radiology residents to judge whether each of 200 chest X-rays showed a lung nodule. Half of the images contained a nodule confirmed by later CT scanning. In the first session, held at the start of a day shift, residents read one block under neutral instructions. They then read one block after being told that missed nodules lead to delayed cancer diagnoses (liberal instructions) and one block after being told that false alarms lead to unnecessary biopsies (conservative instructions). Block order was counterbalanced. In a second session, the same residents read a neutral block at the end of a 12-hour overnight shift. Figure 1 shows the design, and mean results are shown in Table 1.

The residents also rated their confidence on each image from 1 (certainly no nodule) to 5 (certainly a nodule). By treating each confidence level as a separate cutoff, the researchers plotted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for each block, showing the hit rate against the false-alarm rate at each cutoff. The three start-of-shift curves fell almost on top of one another, while the end-of-shift curve lay closer to the diagonal line that represents guessing. A curve that bends farther toward the upper left corner indicates higher sensitivity at every criterion.
The researchers noted that hospitals often track only the number of nodules a reader finds, and that this figure rose after the liberal instructions.

qs.q: What did the change from neutral to liberal instructions mainly alter?
o: The difficulty of the images
Not quite. The same kinds of images were used throughout.
The residents' criterion for answering "yes"
Correct: c fell from 0.00 to −0.46 while d′ barely changed.
The number of images with a nodule
Not quite. Half the images had nodules in every block.
The residents' ability to actually see the nodules
Not quite. d′ stayed near 1.6 to 1.7, so ability didn't change.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 splits a yes/no judgment into two parts. Sensitivity (d′) is how well someone can tell nodule images from normal ones. The criterion (c) is how willing they are to say "yes": lower c means more "yes" answers. In Table 1, going from neutral to liberal, hits rose (0.80 to 0.90) and false alarms rose too (0.20 to 0.36). Both going up together is the sign of a lower criterion, and c fell from 0.00 to −0.46. Meanwhile d′ barely moved (1.68 to 1.64). So the residents just said "yes" more; they didn't get better at seeing nodules. Why the others are wrong: their ability to see nodules didn't change, since d′ stayed around 1.6 to 1.7; the number of nodule images was fixed at half in every block; nothing suggests the images got easier or harder. Trap: Reading more hits as better detection.

qs.q: What best describes the effect of the overnight shift?
o: The criterion became much more liberal
Not quite. c moved slightly the other way, to +0.12, which is more conservative.
Sensitivity rose but fewer "yes" answers
Not quite. d′ fell, it didn't rise.
Both sensitivity and criterion were unchanged
Not quite. d′ dropped a lot, from 1.68 to 1.05.
Sensitivity fell, with little change in criterion
Correct: d′ dropped from 1.68 to 1.05, while c only moved to +0.12.
qs.x: Correct: At the end of the 12-hour shift (Table 1), hits fell (0.80 to 0.66) while false alarms rose (0.20 to 0.26). When hits go down and false alarms go up at the same time, the reader is getting worse at telling the two kinds of image apart, which means lower sensitivity. d′ dropped from 1.68 to 1.05. The criterion moved only a little, from 0.00 to +0.12. Paragraph 3 agrees: the end-of-shift ROC curve sat closer to the guessing line. Why the others are wrong: a much more liberal criterion is wrong, since c moved slightly in the conservative (positive) direction; both staying unchanged is wrong, since d′ dropped a lot; sensitivity rising is wrong, since d′ fell. Trap: Looking only at the falling hit rate, which a conservative shift could also cause. Check false alarms too.

qs.q: The hospital wants residents to miss fewer nodules without making more false alarms. Which approach is most likely to work?
o: Rewarding residents for each nodule they report
Not quite. This lowers the criterion, trading misses for false alarms.
Telling residents to report only obvious nodules
Not quite. This raises the criterion and adds misses.
Improving image quality or adding rest breaks
Correct: Both act on sensitivity, which can cut misses and false alarms together.
Telling residents to report any doubtful shadow
Not quite. This lowers the criterion and raises false alarms too.
qs.x: Correct: Fewer misses means more hits. Getting more hits and fewer false alarms at the same time needs better sensitivity (d′), not a different criterion. Clearer images make nodules easier to tell from normal tissue. Rest breaks help because the end-of-shift data show fatigue lowers d′ (1.68 to 1.05). Why the others are wrong: telling residents to report any doubtful shadow lowers the criterion, which raises false alarms too, as the liberal block shows (0.20 to 0.36); rewarding each nodule reported does the same thing, since it also just encourages "yes"; reporting only obvious nodules raises the criterion, which cuts false alarms but adds misses, as the conservative block shows (hits fall to 0.64). Trap: Assuming instructions or rewards can cut both kinds of error at once. They only trade one error for the other.

qs.q: A resident has a hit rate of 0.95 and a false-alarm rate of 0.60. Compared with the start-of-shift neutral average, this resident most likely has:
o: a more conservative criterion and higher sensitivity
Not quite. A 60% false-alarm rate can't come from a conservative criterion.
a more liberal criterion and lower sensitivity
Correct: 60% false alarms is liberal, and d′ ≈ 1.64 − 0.25 = 1.39, below 1.68.
the same criterion and higher sensitivity
Not quite. A 60% false-alarm rate means the criterion is clearly liberal.
a more liberal criterion and higher sensitivity
Not quite. The criterion is liberal, but d′ ≈ 1.39 is below the average 1.68.
qs.x: Correct: Start with the criterion. Saying "yes" to 60% of normal images (false alarms 0.60, against 0.20 on average) is very liberal. Now sensitivity. The formula is d′ = z(hit rate) − z(false-alarm rate), where z turns a proportion into a distance on a standard normal curve. Values: hit rate = 0.95, so z(0.95) ≈ 1.64; false-alarm rate = 0.60, so z(0.60) ≈ 0.25. Plug in: d′ ≈ 1.64 − 0.25 = 1.39. That's below the neutral average of 1.68 (Table 1). So: more liberal, lower sensitivity. Why the others are wrong: a more conservative criterion with higher sensitivity is ruled out by the very high false-alarm rate; the same criterion with higher sensitivity is wrong, since 60% false alarms is clearly liberal; a more liberal criterion with higher sensitivity is wrong on the second half, since d′ ≈ 1.39 is lower. Trap: Treating a high hit rate as proof of high sensitivity.

qs.q: Why might counting nodules found be a misleading measure of reader quality?
o: It rises with a liberal criterion alone
Correct: Saying "yes" more often raises the count with no gain in skill.
It cannot rise when the instructions change
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the count rose under liberal instructions.
It ignores the number of images each resident read
Not quite. Every resident read the same images.
It depends only on sensitivity, not on criterion
Not quite. Hits depend on both sensitivity and criterion.
qs.x: Correct: The number of nodules found is just the number of hits. Hits go up any time a reader says "yes" more often, even with no gain in skill. Paragraph 4 says the count rose after liberal instructions. But Table 1 shows d′ stayed flat (1.68 to 1.64) and false alarms jumped from 0.20 to 0.36, which means more unnecessary biopsies. So the count can look better while reading quality doesn't improve. Why the others are wrong: ignoring how many images each resident read isn't the problem, since everyone read the same set; depending only on sensitivity is wrong, since hits depend on both sensitivity and criterion; not being able to rise when instructions change is wrong, since paragraph 4 says it rose. Trap: Trusting one outcome measure without checking false alarms.
