passages.title: Mania and Depression in Bipolar I Disorder
text: Bipolar I disorder is defined by at least one manic episode: a week or more of elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, rapid speech, racing thoughts and risky behavior. Depressive episodes usually occur as well, and across the course of the illness patients typically spend more days depressed than manic. Lithium reduces the frequency of episodes but has a narrow therapeutic range: levels below about 0.6 mmol/L often fail to prevent episodes, while levels above about 1.2 mmol/L cause tremor, confusion and kidney injury. Lithium is cleared by the kidney, and it is reabsorbed along with sodium, so dehydration or a low-sodium state raises its blood level.

Researchers followed 240 adults with bipolar I disorder for two years at four clinics. All had been stable for at least a month when they entered. Treatment was chosen by each patient and clinician, not assigned by the researchers. Blood lithium was measured every three months in those taking it. An episode was counted when a psychiatrist who did not know the patient's treatment judged that full criteria were met (Figure 1). The groups were 96 patients on lithium at a mean level of 0.8 mmol/L, 38 on lithium at a mean level of 0.5 mmol/L, 64 on valproate and 42 on no mood stabilizer. The no-stabilizer group is not shown as stopping treatment because those patients were not on treatment.

Adherence was estimated from pharmacy refill records. Patients who filled at least 80% of their prescribed doses were counted as adherent; this was true of 71% of the lithium group and 66% of the valproate group. Episodes were more common among non-adherent patients in both groups.

Among the 42 patients taking no mood stabilizer, 29 had declined one and 13 had stopped because of side effects. Patients in this group had been ill for fewer years on average than those taking lithium. Three patients on lithium developed levels above 1.5 mmol/L; in two of these, the rise followed a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting, and in the third it followed the start of a thiazide diuretic, which increases sodium loss.

qs.q: Why does a thiazide diuretic raise blood lithium?
o: Lost sodium drives reabsorption of lithium
Correct: Sodium loss makes the kidney reabsorb more sodium, and lithium comes back with it.
The diuretic blocks lithium metabolism in the liver
Not quite. Lithium isn't metabolized by the liver.
The diuretic binds lithium in the blood
Not quite. No such binding occurs.
The diuretic increases lithium absorption from food
Not quite. Absorption from food is unchanged.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says lithium is reabsorbed by the kidney along with sodium. A thiazide diuretic makes the body lose sodium (paragraph 4). When sodium runs low, the kidney works harder to pull sodium back into the blood, and lithium comes back with it. Less lithium leaves in the urine, so blood levels climb. That's what happened to the third patient who went above 1.5 mmol/L. Why the others are wrong: blocking liver metabolism doesn't apply, lithium is a simple ion that isn't metabolized, it leaves unchanged through the kidney; the diuretic binding lithium in the blood doesn't happen; absorption from food isn't changed. Trap: Explaining how the body handles an ion with liver metabolism.

qs.q: What is the most important limitation of this study's comparison of treatments?
o: Episodes were judged by a blinded psychiatrist
Not quite. Blinded judging is a strength.
Patients were not randomly assigned
Correct: Without random assignment, groups may differ from the start.
The study lasted two years
Not quite. Two years is a reasonable length.
Blood levels were measured every three months
Not quite. Every three months is reasonable monitoring.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says treatment was chosen by each patient and clinician, not randomly assigned. So the groups could differ before treatment even started. Paragraph 4 gives one example: the no-stabilizer group had been ill for fewer years. Differences like that could change episode rates by themselves. A blinded psychiatrist judging episodes helps, but it can't make the groups alike to begin with. Why the others are wrong: a blinded psychiatrist is a strength; blood levels every three months is reasonable monitoring; two years is a reasonable length. Trap: Choosing a strength when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: What do the two lithium groups together suggest?
o: Lithium is less effective than no treatment
Not quite. Both lithium groups did better than the no-stabilizer group's 79%.
Higher levels are always safer
Not quite. Above about 1.2 mmol/L lithium becomes toxic.
Lithium works equally at any dose
Not quite. Episode rates differ sharply between the two levels.
Benefit depends on the blood level
Correct: 34% vs 61% with episodes, so benefit depends on blood level.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1 shows two lithium groups. At a mean level of 0.8 mmol/L, 34% had an episode and the mean was 0.6 episodes per patient. At 0.5 mmol/L, 61% had an episode and the mean was 1.3. Paragraph 1 says levels below about 0.6 mmol/L often fail. So how well lithium works depends on its blood level, which is why doctors check blood levels and not just the dose. Why the others are wrong: lithium working equally at any dose is false, the episode rates differ sharply; higher levels always being safer is false, levels above about 1.2 mmol/L cause tremor, confusion and kidney injury; lithium being worse than no treatment is false, both lithium groups beat the 79% of the no-stabilizer group. Trap: Thinking a drug simply works or doesn't, without asking about its concentration.

qs.q: Comparing lithium at a mean level of 0.8 mmol/L with valproate in Figure 1, which statement do the data support?
o: Lithium at 0.8 mmol/L had fewer episodes than valproate on both measures
Correct: In Figure 1A, 34% of lithium patients had an episode versus 41% on valproate, and Figure 1B shows 0.6 versus 0.8 mean episodes.
Valproate patients stopped treatment less often than patients in either lithium group
Not quite. In Figure 1A, 25% of valproate patients stopped, more than the 22% and 18% in the lithium groups.
Valproate patients had more mean episodes than patients on no mood stabilizer
Not quite. In Figure 1B, valproate averaged 0.8 episodes and the no-stabilizer group averaged 2.1.
Lithium at 0.5 mmol/L did better than valproate on both measures
Not quite. At 0.5 mmol/L, 61% had an episode and the mean was 1.3, both worse than valproate.
qs.x: Correct: Read the two lithium bars and the valproate bars side by side. In Figure 1A, 34% of the patients on lithium at 0.8 mmol/L had an episode, against 41% on valproate. In Figure 1B, their mean number of episodes was 0.6, against 0.8. The lithium group was lower on both, so that statement is supported. Why the others are wrong: valproate patients stopped treatment more often (25%) than either lithium group (22% and 18%); valproate's 0.8 mean episodes is far below the 2.1 of the no-stabilizer group, so it did not do worse; and lithium at 0.5 mmol/L, with 61% having an episode and 1.3 mean episodes, did worse than valproate, not better. Trap: Assuming that every lithium bar beats valproate, when the low-level lithium group does not.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the case that lithium itself reduced episodes?
o: Lithium levels stayed stable
Not quite. Stable levels concern monitoring, not cause.
A blinded psychiatrist counted episodes
Not quite. Blinding was already used.
Episodes fell in patients after starting it
Correct: Before-and-after in the same patients removes differences between people.
The lithium groups were larger
Not quite. Bigger groups don't fix self-selection.
qs.x: Correct: The study's main weakness is that people chose their treatments, so the groups differ (paragraph 2 and 4). If you compare each patient's episode rate before and after starting lithium, each person is their own comparison. Differences between people, like years of illness, drop out. A clear drop within the same patients would be hard to blame on who picked lithium. Why the others are wrong: larger lithium groups shrink random error but don't fix bias from self-selection; a blinded psychiatrist was already in place; stable lithium levels speak to monitoring and adherence, not to whether lithium caused the drop. Trap: Mixing up precision (less random error) with freedom from bias.

passages.title: Components of CBT for Insomnia
text: Insomnia is defined by difficulty falling or staying asleep together with daytime impairment. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) combines several parts. Stimulus control rebuilds the association between the bed and sleep: the person gets out of bed when unable to sleep and uses the bed only for sleep. Sleep restriction limits time in bed to the hours actually slept, which builds the homeostatic sleep drive, the pressure to sleep that grows with time awake. Cognitive work addresses beliefs such as "if I sleep badly I cannot function at all." Sedative-hypnotic drugs act quickly but their effects often fade after they are stopped.

Researchers randomly assigned 180 adults with chronic insomnia to six weeks of CBT-I, a sedative-hypnotic drug, or a waiting list. Allocation was by computer in blocks of six, and the person who prepared the assignments was not involved in the treatment. Participants kept daily sleep diaries, and a subset wore actigraphs. The main outcome was sleep onset latency, the time from lights out to sleep. Sleep efficiency is time asleep divided by time in bed. Measurements were taken after six weeks and again six months later. Figure 1 plots sleep onset latency, and Table 1 gives sleep efficiency at 6 weeks.

The researchers noted that a waiting-list group controls for the passage of time and for repeated measurement, but not for the expectation of being treated. A placebo pill group would separate the drug's chemical effect from the belief that one is being treated; it was not included because the funder judged a six-month placebo period unacceptable.

Baseline sleep onset latency was about 48 minutes in all three groups (the first point of each line in Figure 1). Participants and therapists knew which treatment was given; the researcher who analyzed the diaries did not. 14 people in the drug group and three in the CBT-I group left the study early. Among those who completed treatment, 52% of the drug group reported daytime drowsiness, compared with 11% of the CBT-I group.

qs.q: Which part of CBT-I most directly builds the homeostatic sleep drive?
o: Sleep restriction
Correct: Less time in bed means more time awake, so sleep pressure builds.
Cognitive restructuring
Not quite. Cognitive restructuring changes beliefs about sleep, not sleep pressure.
Sleep hygiene advice
Not quite. Hygiene advice is about habits like caffeine, not adding time awake.
Stimulus control therapy
Not quite. Stimulus control rebuilds the bed-sleep association, a learned link.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines the homeostatic sleep drive as the pressure to sleep that grows with time awake. Sleep restriction limits time in bed to the hours a person actually sleeps. Less time lying in bed means more hours awake, so the sleep pressure builds up higher. By bedtime the person falls asleep faster and sleeps more solidly. Why the others are wrong: cognitive restructuring targets worried beliefs like 'if I sleep badly I can't function', not sleep pressure; stimulus control rebuilds the link between bed and sleep, a learned association; sleep hygiene advice covers habits like caffeine and screens, and it doesn't directly add time awake. Trap: Picking the part that sounds most like a bedtime routine instead of the one that adds hours awake.

qs.q: What is the most important finding at six months?
o: The waiting list improved on its own
Not quite. The waiting list stayed at about 45 minutes, near its 48-minute start.
Both treatments failed by six months
Not quite. CBT-I kept its gain at 20 minutes.
Only CBT-I kept its benefit
Correct: At 6 months CBT-I held at 20 minutes while the drug group slid back to 44.
The drug worked better than CBT-I
Not quite. The drug was slightly ahead at 6 weeks, but its benefit was gone by 6 months.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Figure 1. Sleep onset latency is the time from lights out to falling asleep, so lower is better. At 6 weeks the two treatments look alike: 18 minutes for CBT-I and 15 for the drug. At 6 months they split. The CBT-I group stayed at 20 minutes, but the drug group went back to 44, almost the waiting list's 45 and close to the baseline of about 48 (paragraph 4). The skills learned in CBT-I keep working after therapy ends, while the drug's effect fades once it's stopped, as paragraph 1 warned. Why the others are wrong: the drug only edged ahead at 6 weeks and lost its benefit by 6 months; CBT-I didn't fail, it held at 20 minutes; the waiting list stayed at about 45 minutes, so it didn't improve on its own. Trap: Judging a treatment only by its short-term result.

qs.q: Why does the uneven dropout weaken the comparison?
o: Dropout was caused by randomization
Not quite. Randomization sets up the groups. It doesn't make people quit.
Dropout makes the groups larger
Not quite. People leaving makes groups smaller, not larger.
Dropout affected only the waiting list
Not quite. Most dropouts were in the drug group, not the waiting list.
The remaining drug group may be unusual
Correct: 14 left the drug group versus 3 from CBT-I, so those remaining may be unusual.
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment makes the groups alike at the start. But paragraph 4 says 14 people left the drug group and only 3 left CBT-I. If the people who quit the drug were the ones who did badly on it (say, the 52% drowsiness rate drove them out), the people left in the drug group are the ones it suited best. That can make the drug look better than it really is. Uneven dropout like this can undo the fairness that randomization built. Why the others are wrong: dropout makes groups smaller, not larger; randomization doesn't cause people to leave, it only decides where they start; most dropouts came from the drug group, not the waiting list. Trap: Assuming randomization protects a trial from everything that happens after it.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the person analyzing the diaries did not know the group assignments?
o: It blinds the participants too
Not quite. Participants knew their own treatment, so they weren't blinded.
It makes treatment more effective
Not quite. How data are scored doesn't change how well a treatment works.
Expectations cannot shape the scoring
Correct: A blind analyst can't let expectations tilt the scoring of the diaries.
It removes the control group
Not quite. The waiting list is still the comparison group. Blinding doesn't remove it.
qs.x: Correct: Blinding means keeping someone unaware of who got which treatment, so their expectations can't tilt the results. In this study the participants and therapists couldn't be blinded, since you know whether you're in therapy or taking a pill (paragraph 4). The one place blinding was still possible was the analysis. Diary entries can be messy or unclear, and an analyst who knew the groups might, without meaning to, read them in the expected direction. A blind analyst can't do that. Why the others are wrong: the participants still knew their treatment, so they weren't blinded; scoring the diaries doesn't change how well a treatment works; the waiting list is still there as the comparison group. Trap: Treating one kind of blinding as if it covers all the others.

qs.q: What does the waiting-list group's stability over six months show?
o: The waiting list received a placebo
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says no placebo group was included.
Measurement becomes unreliable over time
Not quite. Stable values point to consistent measurement, not unreliable measurement.
The treatments have no real effect at all
Not quite. Both treatment groups dropped to 15 to 18 minutes at 6 weeks.
Insomnia did not improve by itself
Correct: Latency stayed near 47 to 45 minutes, so insomnia didn't improve on its own.
qs.x: Correct: In Figure 1 the waiting list sat at 47 minutes at 6 weeks and 45 at 6 months, barely below the baseline of about 48 (paragraph 4). So without treatment, insomnia didn't get better by itself. That matters: it means the big drop in the treated groups at 6 weeks can't be put down to time passing or to just being measured again, which is exactly what paragraph 3 says a waiting list controls for. Why the others are wrong: the treatments clearly worked at 6 weeks (18 and 15 minutes versus 47); the waiting list got no placebo, and paragraph 3 says a placebo group wasn't included; steady numbers suggest the measurement was consistent, not unreliable. Trap: Mixing up a no-treatment control with a placebo control.

passages.title: Auditory Stream Segregation in a Crowd
text: Sound from several sources arrives at the ear as one pressure wave, so hearing a single voice in a crowd requires the auditory system to assign parts of that wave to separate sources. The resulting perceptual objects are called streams, and the cues that build them are regularities that natural sources tend to obey.

Three cues are well established. Frequency separation matters because a single source usually produces sounds in a limited range, so tones far apart in pitch tend to split into two streams. Rate matters because a fast sequence gives less time to integrate successive tones into one line. And common onset matters because components that begin together usually come from one event.

Segregation is not fixed at the start of a sequence. Listening to an alternating sequence for several seconds makes it more likely to split, a build-up that suggests the system accumulates evidence for two sources rather than deciding once.

Listeners heard sequences of alternating high and low tones and reported whether they heard one stream or two. Frequency separation and presentation rate were varied within listeners, and reports were taken in the first second and after 10 seconds (Figure 1).

Both cues act and build-up acts on top of them. Frequency separation has the larger effect, raising two-stream reports by about 32 points at the slow rate and 57 at the fast rate, while rate contributes 8 to 33 points depending on separation. Every condition shows more splitting after 10 seconds than in the first second.

The build-up itself varies with the strength of the cues. It adds 5 points in the weakest condition and 24 points in the 10-semitone slow condition, which is the ambiguous case where accumulated evidence has the most room to change the outcome.

Two cautions apply. The report is a subjective judgment with no objective criterion, so a listener's willingness to say "two" could shift with the sequence rather than their perception changing. And the sequences were isolated tones in quiet, while real segregation operates on speech and music in noise, where additional cues such as harmonicity and spatial location are available.

qs.q: Why does the build-up over 10 seconds favor an evidence-accumulation account?
o: Perception changes while the stimulus is unchanged
Correct: Perception changes while the sound stays the same, so evidence keeps building.
Listeners heard each sequence more than one time
Not quite. The comparison is within one listening, not across repeats.
The widest separation produces the most splitting
Not quite. That's the frequency cue.
Two streams are reported more at the fast rate
Not quite. That's the rate cue, not build-up.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says segregation isn't decided once at the start. The sequence is exactly the same in the first second and after 10 seconds, yet Figure 1 shows more two-stream reports later in every pair of bars (for example 38% to 62%). If nothing in the sound changed but perception did, the brain must still be gathering evidence and revising its grouping. That's evidence accumulation. Why the others are wrong: more splitting at the fast rate is the rate cue, a property of the sound; more splitting with wider separation is the frequency cue; the comparison is within one listening, first second versus 10 seconds, so how often a sequence was heard isn't what it rests on. Trap: Explaining a change over time with one of the sound cues.

qs.q: In which condition does build-up contribute most, and why?
o: The ambiguous 10-semitone slow-rate condition
Correct: The 10-semitone slow condition gains 24 points. It starts most undecided.
The 2-semitone slow condition, where cues are weakest
Not quite. It gains only 5 points. Weak cues leave little to build on.
The 10-semitone fast condition, where splitting is highest
Not quite. It gains 23 points and is near the ceiling at 94%.
All conditions equally, since time is the same
Not quite. Gains range from 5 to 24 points.
qs.x: Correct: Build-up = after-10-seconds report − first-second report. From Figure 1: 2 semitones slow, 11 − 6 = 5; 2 fast, 29 − 14 = 15; 10 slow, 62 − 38 = 24; 10 fast, 94 − 71 = 23. The 10-semitone slow condition gains the most. Paragraph 6 explains why: at 38% in the first second, listeners are genuinely undecided, so extra evidence has the most room to tip the outcome. Why the others are wrong: the 2-semitone slow condition gains only 5 points, since weak cues give little to build on; the 10-semitone fast condition gains 23, a bit less, because it's already near the top at 94%; the gains clearly aren't equal, they run from 5 to 24 points. Trap: Assuming an effect of time must be the same size everywhere.

qs.q: What is an auditory stream?
o: The pathway from cochlea to auditory cortex
Not quite. That's anatomy, not a perceptual object.
A perceived sound source built from the signal
Correct: A stream is a perceived sound source built from the mixed signal.
The pressure wave that arrives at the eardrum
Not quite. That wave is the mixed input, before separation.
A continuous tone of one single unchanging frequency
Not quite. A stream can contain many frequencies.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says all the sounds around you reach the ear as one mixed pressure wave. The auditory system splits that wave into separate perceived sources, like one voice in a crowd. Each of those perceived sources is a stream, a perceptual object the brain builds from cues in the mixed signal. Why the others are wrong: a stream can contain many frequencies, like a voice, so it isn't one steady tone; the pressure wave at the eardrum is the mixed input that has to be separated, not the stream; the pathway from the inner ear to the cortex is anatomy, not a perceived object. Trap: Mixing up a perceptual object with the physical signal that produces it.

qs.q: By how many percentage points does the wider separation raise two-stream reports at the fast rate in the first second?
o: Not quite. 14 − 6 = 8 is the rate effect at narrow separation.
Not quite. 38 − 6 = 32 is the separation effect at the slow rate.
Not quite. 71 − 38 = 33 is the rate effect at wide separation.
Correct: 71% − 14% = 57 percentage points.
qs.x: Correct: Rise = 10-semitone report − 2-semitone report, both at the fast rate in the first second. From Figure 1: 10 semitones fast = 71% and 2 semitones fast = 14%. Plug in: 71 − 14 = 57 percentage points, matching paragraph 5. Why the others are wrong: 8 points is the rate effect at narrow separation, 14 − 6; 32 points is the separation effect at the slow rate, 38 − 6; 33 points is the rate effect at wide separation, 71 − 38. Trap: Comparing bars that differ in rate instead of in separation.

qs.q: Why does the subjective report limit the conclusions?
o: The sequences were too short to judge
Not quite. 10 seconds is enough to judge.
Listeners cannot judge their own perception
Not quite. Self-report is the only source here, just an imperfect one.
Willingness to say "two" may itself shift
Correct: Willingness to say 'two' could shift, tangled with perception.
Reports were collected only after 10 seconds
Not quite. Reports were taken at both time points.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 notes that 'one or two streams' has no right answer to check against. So if more people say 'two' after 10 seconds, maybe they really hear two, or maybe they've just become more willing to say 'two', their response criterion shifted. The design can't separate a change in perception from a change in willingness to report. Why the others are wrong: listeners' reports are the only access to what they hear here, so self-report is the right tool, just limited; 10-second sequences are long enough to judge; reports were collected both in the first second and after 10 seconds. Trap: Treating a response as a direct readout of perception.

graph.title: Figure 1. Two-stream reports in the first second and after 10 seconds

passages.title: Weber's Rationalization and Bureaucracy
text: Max Weber described rationalization as the spread of calculation, efficiency and formal rules into areas of life once governed by tradition or personal judgment. Bureaucracy, with its written rules, specialized roles and hierarchy, is its clearest form. Weber argued that rationalization raises efficiency but can leave people feeling trapped in an impersonal system, and that formal rules sometimes crowd out the goals they were meant to serve, an outcome later called goal displacement. George Ritzer applied these ideas to modern services, arguing that organizations pursue efficiency, calculability, predictability and control, and that these can come at the cost of personal attention.

Researchers studied the introduction of a standardized electronic checklist at 40 primary care clinics in one health system. The checklist prompted the clinician to record a fixed set of items at every visit and would not close until each field was filled. 20 clinics adopted it in January and the other 20 kept their existing records for that year, with assignment made by the health system according to which clinics had updated computers. The researchers compared the two groups over 12 months using appointment records, chart audits and patient surveys (Table 1).

Patient surveys were sent to a random sample of 50 patients from each clinic, and 61% responded at checklist clinics and 64% at comparison clinics. Burnout was measured with a standard questionnaire given to every clinician at the start and the end of the year; the scores in the table are end-of-year values, and the two groups had started within 0.3 points of each other.

In interviews, clinicians at checklist clinics described spending much of the visit facing the screen and said they sometimes deferred a patient's concern to a later visit in order to complete the required fields. Several said the checklist had caught problems they might otherwise have missed. One clinic in the comparison group began using a shortened checklist of its own in month 9.

qs.q: Which feature of the checklist best illustrates Weber's idea of formal rationality?
o: Clinicians share a building
Not quite. Sharing space isn't a system of rules.
Visits vary in length by patient
Not quite. Varying by patient is the opposite of standardization.
A fixed set of items at every visit
Correct: A fixed set of required items replaces individual judgment with a rule.
Patients choose a clinician
Not quite. Patient choice is personal judgment, not a uniform rule.
qs.x: Correct: Weber's formal rationality (paragraph 1) means decisions run on written, uniform rules instead of tradition or personal judgment. The checklist in paragraph 2 makes the clinician record the same fixed set of items at every visit and won't close until every field is filled. That's a rule replacing the clinician's own judgment about what each visit needs. Why the others are wrong: sharing a building is just shared space, not a rule system; patients choosing a clinician is personal choice, the opposite of a uniform rule; visits varying in length by patient reflects discretion, which is the opposite of standardization. Trap: Treating any organized activity as bureaucratic rationality.

qs.q: Which pair of findings best illustrates goal displacement?
o: More screenings but less listening
Correct: Screenings rose (92%) while listening fell (58%): the rule crowded out the purpose.
Shorter visits with more visits per day
Not quite. Both are efficiency gains, not a lost purpose.
Higher burnout with much longer visits
Not quite. Checklist visits were shorter, 16.5 versus 18.2 minutes.
Higher follow-up calls with higher screening
Not quite. Both are intended results of the checklist.
qs.x: Correct: Goal displacement (paragraph 1) is when following the rule takes the place of the goal the rule was supposed to serve. In Table 1, checklist clinics completed more required screenings (92% versus 71%), but fewer patients felt the clinician listened carefully (58% versus 74%). Paragraph 4 adds that clinicians faced the screen and put off patients' concerns to finish the fields. Filling in the checklist crowded out the care it was meant to support. Why the others are wrong: shorter visits with more visits per day are both efficiency gains, not a lost purpose; more follow-up calls and more screenings are both intended results; visits were actually shorter at checklist clinics (16.5 versus 18.2 minutes), not longer. Trap: Calling any unwanted side effect goal displacement.

qs.q: What most limits a causal interpretation of these results?
o: Patient surveys were the measure
Not quite. Surveys are a reasonable measure here.
The study ran for only 12 months
Not quite. A year is a reasonable study period.
Chart audits were used
Not quite. Chart audits give objective data, a strength.
Clinics were not randomly assigned
Correct: Clinics were chosen by computer upgrades, not at random, so they may differ in other ways.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says clinics got the checklist based on which ones had updated computers, not at random. Clinics with newer computers might also have more funding, more staff or different patients. Any of those could explain the differences in Table 1, so we can't be sure the checklist caused them. Why the others are wrong: patient surveys are a reasonable way to measure whether patients felt listened to; 12 months is a reasonable time span for this question; chart audits give objective data, which is a strength. Trap: Confusing a measurement method with a flaw in the design.

qs.q: How does the comparison clinic that adopted its own checklist in month 9 affect the study?
o: It makes the two groups more alike
Correct: The groups became more alike, so a real effect may look smaller.
It makes the checklist look more effective
Not quite. Shared practice shrinks the gap, so the effect looks smaller.
It invalidates the patient surveys
Not quite. The surveys were still collected and remain valid.
It has no bearing on the results
Not quite. That clinic's data are part of the comparison group.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says one comparison clinic started its own shortened checklist in month 9. Now part of the comparison group is doing something like what the checklist group does. That makes the two groups more alike, so the measured difference between them shrinks. Any real effect of the checklist would be understated, not exaggerated. Why the others are wrong: shared practice narrows the gap, so it makes the checklist look less different, not more effective; the surveys were still collected and remain valid; the clinic's data are in the comparison group, so it does affect the results. Trap: Assuming every flaw must exaggerate the finding.

qs.q: Using Table 1, about how many more minutes per day does a clinician at a checklist clinic spend in visits than a clinician at a comparison clinic?
o: 2 minutes
Not quite. 2 minutes is the gap in visit length per visit (18.2 − 16.5 = 1.7), not the gap in total daily time.
19 minutes
Correct: 16.5 × 21 = 346.5 minutes versus 18.2 × 18 = 327.6 minutes, a gap of about 19.
3 minutes
Not quite. 3 is the gap in visits per day (21 − 18), not in minutes.
36 minutes
Not quite. 36 is 1.7 × 21, which treats the shorter visit as if it were the only change.
qs.x: Correct: Total daily visit time = visit length × visits per day, so work it out for each group and subtract. Checklist clinics: visit length is 16.5 min and visits per clinician per day is 21. Plug in: 16.5 × 21 = 16 × 21 + 0.5 × 21 = 336 + 10.5 = 346.5 minutes. Comparison clinics: 18.2 min and 18 visits. Plug in: 18.2 × 18 = 18 × 18 + 0.2 × 18 = 324 + 3.6 = 327.6 minutes. Difference: 346.5 − 327.6 = 18.9, about 19 minutes. Why the others are wrong: 2 minutes is the per-visit gap (1.7); 3 is the gap in number of visits (21 − 18); 36 is 1.7 × 21, which ignores that comparison clinicians also see fewer patients. Trap: Comparing the visit length alone and forgetting that the number of visits changed too.

passages.title: Size-Exclusion Chromatography with Porous Beads
text: Size-exclusion chromatography separates molecules by size. The column is packed with porous beads; small molecules enter the pores and take a long path, while molecules too large to enter flow around the beads and leave first. The volume at which a protein emerges, its elution volume, therefore decreases as size increases. Proteins larger than the largest pore all leave together in the void volume. Because the method separates by the size and shape of the molecule as it is in solution, it reports the size of an assembled complex rather than of a single chain.

SDS-PAGE separates proteins differently. Sodium dodecyl sulfate coats each chain with negative charge in proportion to its length and unfolds it, and the reducing agent β-mercaptoethanol breaks disulfide bonds. Migration then depends on the mass of the individual chain.

Researchers purified an enzyme from liver. They first calibrated a size-exclusion column with proteins of known mass, then ran their enzyme. They also ran the enzyme on SDS-PAGE, with and without β-mercaptoethanol, beside a ladder of mass standards (Figure 1 shows the size-exclusion results; Table 1 shows the gel bands).

Before the calibration, the researchers checked the column by running a mixture of blue dextran, a very large polymer, and a small dye. Blue dextran emerged at 40 mL, defining the void volume, and the dye at 98 mL, defining the total volume accessible to small molecules. Every protein therefore had to elute between these two values, and a protein that emerged outside that window would indicate that it was binding the beads rather than being separated by size.

The researchers then repeated the size-exclusion run in buffer containing 6 M guanidinium chloride, a denaturant, with a reducing agent. Under those conditions the enzyme emerged at 85 mL, corresponding to about 35 kDa. Enzyme activity was measured in fractions from the original run and appeared only in the fractions around 66 mL.

qs.q: What is the most likely structure of the native enzyme?
o: Four 35 kDa chains, joined in pairs by disulfides
Correct: 140 kDa total, from two 70 kDa disulfide-linked pairs of 35 kDa chains.
A single folded chain of 140 kDa
Not quite. A single 140 kDa chain wouldn't give 70 or 35 kDa bands.
Two 70 kDa chains with no disulfides
Not quite. Reducing agent splits the 70 kDa band, so disulfides are present.
Four 35 kDa chains held by noncovalent forces
Not quite. Without reducing agent a 70 kDa band persists, so disulfides link pairs.
qs.x: Correct: Put the three numbers together (Figure 1 and Table 1). Native mass, from size-exclusion: 140 kDa. SDS-PAGE without reducing agent: one band at 70 kDa. With reducing agent: one band at 35 kDa. SDS breaks the non-covalent contacts between chains but not disulfide bonds (S–S links), so the 70 kDa band is a unit held by disulfides. Breaking those disulfides with reducing agent leaves 35 kDa chains, so each 70 kDa unit is two chains: 2 × 35 = 70. The native enzyme is 140 kDa, so it's two of those units: 140 ÷ 70 = 2, held together non-covalently. That's 4 chains of 35 kDa in all. Why the others are wrong: a single 140 kDa chain would give a 140 kDa band on the gel; two 70 kDa chains with no disulfides wouldn't split to 35 kDa when reduced; four chains held only by non-covalent forces would run at 35 kDa even without reducing agent, not 70. Trap: Reading the native mass as the mass of one chain.

qs.q: Before the calibration, the researchers ran blue dextran and a small dye through the column. What was the main purpose?
o: To mark the two limits that every protein must elute between
Correct: Blue dextran marks the void volume and the dye the total volume, so a protein outside that window signals binding to the beads.
To set the mass scale for the standard proteins that were run afterward
Not quite. The standards of known mass set the mass scale, not these two markers.
To unfold the standard proteins before they were applied to the column
Not quite. Neither marker unfolds anything, and the standards were run in native form.
To measure how much enzyme activity is recovered in the eluted fractions
Not quite. Neither marker is an enzyme or has anything to do with activity.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 explains the check. Blue dextran is a very large polymer, so it is shut out of every pore and emerges first, at 40 mL, which defines the void volume. The small dye enters every pore and emerges last, at 98 mL, which defines the total volume. Every protein has to elute between those values, so a protein outside that window would show it was sticking to the beads instead of being sorted by size. The standards in Figure 1 (45, 78 and 96 mL) and the enzyme (66 mL) all fall inside it. Why the others are wrong: the mass scale comes from the standards of known mass, not from the markers; neither marker unfolds proteins, and the standards were run native; neither marker has any enzyme activity. Trap: Thinking every material run through a column is part of the calibration curve.

qs.q: What does the run in guanidinium chloride with reducing agent show?
o: The 140 kDa form is built from 35 kDa chains
Correct: Fully taken apart, it runs at 35 kDa, so the 140 kDa form is built from 35 kDa chains.
The enzyme is a single 35 kDa chain
Not quite. Natively it runs at 140 kDa, not 35.
Guanidinium chloride cuts the peptide bonds of the enzyme
Not quite. It breaks non-covalent contacts, not peptide bonds.
The column pores shrink in denaturant
Not quite. Pore size is set by the beads and doesn't change.
qs.x: Correct: Guanidinium chloride is a denaturant, which breaks the non-covalent contacts holding chains together, and the reducing agent breaks the disulfide bonds (paragraph 5). With both gone, the enzyme falls apart into single chains, and it came out at 85 mL, about 35 kDa. So the native 140 kDa enzyme, which came out at 66 mL, must be built from 35 kDa chains. Why the others are wrong: the native enzyme runs at 140 kDa, so it isn't a single 35 kDa chain; guanidinium chloride doesn't cut peptide bonds, it only undoes the non-covalent forces; the pore size is fixed by the beads and doesn't shrink. Trap: Treating the pulled-apart result as the protein's normal state.

qs.q: Why is enzyme activity found only near 66 mL?
o: Activity requires the reducing agent itself
Not quite. The native run had no reducing agent.
Activity is destroyed by the column beads
Not quite. Activity was recovered at 66 mL, so the beads didn't destroy it.
Only the assembled complex is active
Correct: Activity comes out with the 140 kDa assembly, so the assembly is the active form.
Small fragments elute before large ones
Not quite. Large molecules come out first, not small ones.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says activity showed up only in the fractions around 66 mL, which is exactly where the native 140 kDa enzyme comes out (Figure 1). Fractions without the assembled complex had no activity. So the active form is the whole folded assembly of four chains, not a single chain. Why the others are wrong: the beads didn't destroy activity, since activity was recovered at 66 mL; large molecules come out first, not small ones; the native run had no reducing agent, so activity can't depend on it. Trap: Ignoring that where activity appears tells you which form of the protein works.

qs.q: Why can SDS-PAGE not report the native mass?
o: SDS-PAGE cannot resolve proteins above 50 kDa
Not quite. It resolves proteins above 50 kDa, like the 70 kDa band here.
SDS unfolds and separates the chains
Correct: SDS unfolds the protein and pulls the chains apart, so it shows chain mass.
SDS adds mass that cannot be corrected
Not quite. SDS binding scales with length, which is what makes mass estimates work.
SDS-PAGE separates by charge alone
Not quite. Charge scales with length, so separation tracks size.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says SDS unfolds proteins and coats each chain with negative charge in proportion to its length. That also breaks the non-covalent contacts holding chains together, so the assembly falls apart and each chain runs by its own mass. The gel shows chain sizes, 70 kDa (disulfide-linked pairs) or 35 kDa, never the 140 kDa assembly. Why the others are wrong: SDS-PAGE can measure proteins above 50 kDa, it shows a 70 kDa band here; SDS binding is proportional to length, which is exactly what makes mass estimates work; because the charge is proportional to length, separation tracks size, not charge alone. Trap: Expecting one method to give both chain mass and assembled mass.

passages.title: Chemotherapy Drugs That Target Dividing Cells
text: Many chemotherapy drugs act on dividing cells. Some damage DNA directly, some block the enzymes that copy or untangle it, and some interfere with the spindle. A cell that cannot repair the damage may undergo apoptosis, a controlled death in which the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into fragments and its remains are cleared, or it may die by necrosis, in which the membrane breaks and the contents spill out and provoke inflammation.

Researchers tested a new compound, drug X, on three cultures: HCT116 colon cancer cells, which divide about every 20 hours; the same line treated to stop dividing but stay alive; and normal colon epithelial cells, which divide about every 48 hours. Cells were exposed for 48 hours. Viability was measured with a dye reduced only by cells with working mitochondria, and the concentration that reduced viability by half (IC₅₀) was calculated from a series of drug concentrations (Figure 1). Apoptosis was measured by a stain that detects cut DNA ends, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release into the medium was measured as a marker of broken membranes (Table 1).

In a second experiment, dividing HCT116 cells were treated with 10 µM drug X for 12 hours and examined by flow cytometry. The fraction of cells with the DNA content of G2/M rose from 18% to 61%. Microscopy showed condensed chromosomes that were not aligned at the metaphase plate, and spindles that appeared short and disorganized.

The researchers also checked that the viability dye was reporting what they intended. They counted cells directly under a microscope after trypan blue staining, which labels cells with broken membranes, and found that the proportion of unstained cells matched the dye result within 5% at every concentration tested.
A caspase inhibitor was added with drug X in a third experiment. Apoptosis at 10 µM fell from 46% to 7%, but viability at 72 hours rose only slightly, from 31% to 38%.

qs.q: What do the three IC₅₀ values suggest about drug X?
o: It is equally toxic to all three cultures
The IC₅₀ values range from 2.1 to 58 µM.
It harms cancer cells regardless of division
Nondividing cancer cells needed about 28 times more drug.
It is more toxic to normal cells
Normal cells' IC₅₀ is about 9 times higher, so they're less sensitive.
It mainly harms rapidly dividing cells
Correct: Dividing cells need only 2.1 µM, versus 58 and 19 µM.
qs.x: Correct: IC₅₀ is the drug concentration that cuts viability in half, so a lower IC₅₀ means the cells are more sensitive. Dividing HCT116 cells: 2.1 µM. The same cells not dividing: 58 µM, about 28 times higher (58 ÷ 2.1 ≈ 28). Normal colon cells, which divide more slowly: 19 µM, about 9 times higher (19 ÷ 2.1 ≈ 9). So the drug hits whatever divides fastest, whether or not it's cancer. Why the others are wrong: it doesn't harm cancer cells regardless of division, since the nondividing cancer cells resisted it; it isn't equally toxic, the IC₅₀ values differ up to 28-fold; and it isn't more toxic to normal cells, since their IC₅₀ is about 9 times higher, meaning they need more drug. Trap: Assuming a drug that kills cancer cells recognizes cancer itself.

qs.q: Which mechanism of action for drug X is best supported by the results of the second experiment?
o: The drug disrupts spindle assembly
Correct: G2/M pile-up, unaligned chromosomes and messy spindles all point to the spindle.
The drug blocks DNA replication in S phase
An S-phase block wouldn't pile cells up with G2/M DNA content.
The drug prevents cells from leaving G1
A G1 block would pile cells up in G1, not G2/M.
The drug stops protein synthesis in all cells
That would harm nondividing cells too, but they were spared.
qs.x: Correct: In paragraph 3, cells with G2/M DNA content (doubled DNA, ready to divide or dividing) rose from 18% to 61%. Under the microscope, chromosomes were condensed, which means the cells had entered mitosis, but they weren't lined up at the metaphase plate, and the spindles were short and messy. The spindle is the fiber machine that lines chromosomes up and pulls them apart. A broken spindle stalls cells in mitosis, exactly this picture. Why the others are wrong: blocking DNA copying in S phase would leave cells with half-copied DNA, not a pile-up in G2/M; a G1 block would pile cells up in G1, not G2/M; and stopping protein synthesis in all cells would hurt nondividing cells too, but they were largely spared. Trap: Picking a DNA-damage mechanism just because many chemotherapy drugs work that way.

qs.q: What explains the low LDH release alongside high apoptosis?
o: HCT116 cells lack LDH
LDH is a common enzyme found in nearly all cells.
The dye assay also measures LDH
The dye and LDH tests are separate measurements.
The drug fails to kill them
The drug clearly kills them; viability fell sharply.
Apoptosis keeps membranes intact
Correct: Apoptotic cells keep their membranes intact, so LDH stays inside.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 describes two ways to die. In apoptosis, the cell shrinks and gets packaged up neatly, so its membrane stays intact and its contents stay inside. In necrosis, the membrane breaks and the contents spill out. LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that lives inside the cell, so it only shows up in the medium if membranes break. For dividing HCT116 cells at 10 µM, apoptosis is high (46%) but LDH release is low (8%), so they died the tidy way. Why the others are wrong: the drug does kill them, viability fell sharply; HCT116 cells do have LDH, it's a common enzyme found in nearly all cells; and the viability dye and the LDH test are separate measurements. Trap: Expecting every kind of cell death to spill the cell's contents.

qs.q: What does the caspase-inhibitor experiment suggest about how drug X kills dividing HCT116 cells?
o: Caspases are not involved in this death
Apoptosis fell from 46% to 7%, so caspases are involved.
The inhibitor makes the drug more toxic
Viability rose slightly, so the drug didn't become more toxic.
Blocking apoptosis does not save them
Correct: Blocking apoptosis barely helped; viability rose only from 31% to 38%.
Apoptosis is the only route of death here
Cells still died with apoptosis blocked.
qs.x: Correct: Caspases are the enzymes that carry out apoptosis. In paragraph 5, blocking them dropped apoptosis from 46% to 7%, so caspases clearly run that death program. But viability at 72 hours barely improved, from 31% to 38%. The drug's damage is still there, so the cells die some other way or never recover. Blocking apoptosis just changes how they die. Why the others are wrong: caspases are involved, since blocking them cut apoptosis from 46% to 7%; the inhibitor didn't make the drug more toxic, viability actually rose a little; and apoptosis isn't the only route, since most cells still died without it. Trap: Assuming that blocking the visible form of death saves the cell.

qs.q: What was the purpose of including HCT116 cells that had been treated to stop dividing?
o: To measure the drug's stability in medium
The passage never measures the drug's stability.
To separate cancer from division rate
Correct: Same cells, different division, so division is the only variable.
To show the dye works without mitochondria
The dye only works in cells with working mitochondria.
To provide a dose–response curve
Every culture gave its own dose-response curve.
qs.x: Correct: Comparing cancer cells with normal cells mixes two differences: the cells are different types, and the cancer cells divide faster. Using the same cancer line in a nondividing state removes the first difference, leaving division as the only thing that changes. Its IC₅₀ jumped from 2.1 to 58 µM, showing that division, not cancer, is what makes cells sensitive. Why the others are wrong: the passage never tests whether the drug is stable in the medium; every culture produced its own dose-response curve, so this one wasn't needed for that; and the viability dye needs working mitochondria (paragraph 2), so it couldn't show the opposite. Trap: Missing why an experiment uses the same cell line twice.

passages.title: Gram-Positive and Gram-Negative Cell Envelopes
text: Bacteria are classified in part by their cell envelope. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer outside the plasma membrane. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and, outside it, an outer membrane whose outer leaflet is made largely of lipopolysaccharide. This extra membrane keeps many compounds out and makes gram-negative bacteria harder to treat.

Antimicrobial peptides are part of innate immunity in many animals. Most are short, carry a positive charge and fold so that nonpolar and charged residues sit on opposite faces. The positive charge draws the peptide to the negatively charged surfaces of bacterial membranes, and the nonpolar face lets it insert into the lipid interior, forming pores. Mammalian plasma membranes have mostly neutral outer leaflets and contain cholesterol, which makes them less attractive targets.

Researchers tested peptide P, a 22-residue peptide with six lysines, against two bacteria and against human red blood cells. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth. Hemolysis was measured as the release of hemoglobin from red blood cells, and membrane permeability was measured with a dye that enters only cells with damaged membranes (Figure 1).

The MIC was read after 18 hours of growth in broth, and each measurement was repeated three times on separate days. Wells with no peptide grew to full density every time, and wells with no bacteria stayed clear, confirming that the medium was not contaminated.

Killing was rapid: at four times the MIC, more than 99% of S. aureus cells were killed within 20 minutes, before the cells could divide. In a serial-passage experiment, S. aureus was grown for 25 days in gradually rising concentrations of peptide P or of ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic that inhibits DNA gyrase. The MIC of ciprofloxacin rose 64-fold over this period, while the MIC of peptide P rose two fold. Adding 150 mM NaCl raised peptide P's MIC against S. aureus from 4 to 32 µg/mL.

qs.q: In Figure 1A, why is peptide P less active against E. coli than against S. aureus?
o: E. coli divides too quickly to be killed
Killing happened within 20 minutes, before division.
E. coli has a thicker peptidoglycan layer
E. coli's peptidoglycan layer is thin. The thick one is in gram-positive cells.
The outer membrane blocks peptide access
Correct: the outer membrane is an extra barrier. Loosening it drops the MIC from 16 to 2 µg/mL.
E. coli membranes carry a positive charge
Bacterial surfaces are negatively charged, which attracts the peptide.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says gram-negative bacteria like E. coli have an outer membrane, an extra lipid layer outside their thin peptidoglycan wall, and it "keeps many compounds out." So peptide P has a second barrier to get through before it reaches the inner membrane it attacks. Figure 1 shows it: the MIC (the lowest concentration that stops growth) is 4 µg/mL for S. aureus but 16 µg/mL for E. coli. When a compound loosens the outer membrane, the MIC drops to 2 µg/mL and permeability rises from 52% to 91%. That points straight at the outer membrane as the obstacle. Why the others are wrong: E. coli's peptidoglycan layer is thin, the thick one belongs to gram-positive S. aureus; bacterial surfaces are negatively charged, which attracts the positive peptide; killing happens fast, within 20 minutes, before cells even divide (paragraph 5). Trap: Assuming the thicker wall must be the bigger barrier.

qs.q: In Figure 1B, why does peptide P damage bacterial membranes but spare red blood cells?
o: Bacterial surfaces are more negatively charged
Correct: the positive peptide is drawn to negatively charged bacterial surfaces.
Bacterial membranes contain cholesterol
Cholesterol is in animal membranes, not bacterial ones.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria
True of mature red cells, but irrelevant. The peptide acts on membranes.
Red blood cells have no plasma membrane
Red blood cells do have a plasma membrane.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains the selectivity. Peptide P has six lysines, which are positively charged amino acids, so the peptide is positive overall. Opposite charges attract, so it gathers on the negatively charged surfaces of bacterial membranes. Mammalian cells have mostly neutral outer leaflets (the outer half of the membrane) and contain cholesterol, which makes them poorer targets. Figure 1B shows the result: at 16 µg/mL, S. aureus permeability is 88% but red blood cell hemolysis (bursting) is only 3%. Why the others are wrong: red blood cells do have a plasma membrane; mature red blood cells do lack mitochondria, but that's beside the point, since the peptide acts on the membrane; cholesterol is found in animal membranes, not bacterial ones. Trap: Looking for a target inside the cell when the peptide acts at the surface.

qs.q: What does the salt result suggest about how the peptide works?
o: Salt makes bacterial membranes thicker
No membrane thickening is described.
Ions shield the charge attraction
Correct: ions screen the charge attraction, so binding weakens and the MIC rises from 4 to 32 µg/mL.
Salt destroys the peptide's amino acids
Salt doesn't break peptide bonds.
Salt provides an alternative nutrient
The MIC measures growth inhibition, not nutrition.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says adding 150 mM NaCl raised the MIC against S. aureus from 4 to 32 µg/mL, so 32 ÷ 4 = 8 times more peptide was needed. Peptide P sticks to bacteria through charge attraction. Dissolved ions like Na⁺ and Cl⁻ crowd around charged groups and screen them, which weakens that pull. The peptide binds less well, so more is needed to stop growth. This matters in practice because blood has a similar salt level. Why the others are wrong: salt doesn't break peptide bonds or destroy amino acids; the passage describes no thickening of membranes; salt isn't a food source here, and the MIC measures stopping growth, not feeding it. Trap: Assuming a higher MIC means the drug was destroyed.

qs.q: Wells with bacteria but no peptide grew to full density every time. What do these wells show?
o: That the medium is itself free of contamination
Not quite. Contamination is checked by wells with no bacteria. These wells have bacteria.
That bacteria grow normally without peptide
Correct: If bacteria thrive without peptide, no growth in the peptide wells can be credited to the peptide.
That the peptide stays stable for 18 hours
Not quite. Wells without peptide say nothing about peptide stability.
That every species has the same MIC value
Not quite. These wells contain no peptide, so they cannot give an MIC for any species.
qs.x: Correct: These are the positive control wells. They show the bacteria can grow in this medium for 18 hours. If a well with peptide stays clear, the peptide stopped the growth, since the same bacteria grew fine without it. The MIC for S. aureus (4 µg/mL) and E. coli (16 µg/mL) in Figure 1A is only meaningful against that growth. Why the others are wrong: contamination is checked by the wells with no bacteria, a different control; peptide stability is not tested by wells that hold no peptide; an MIC needs peptide in the well, so these wells give none. Trap: Mixing up the two controls, growth without drug and sterility without bacteria.

qs.q: Why does rapid killing argue against a mechanism that blocks cell wall synthesis?
o: Killing speed is the same for every mechanism
Mechanisms differ in speed, so timing is a clue.
Wall synthesis occurs only in gram-negative cells
Both gram types build peptidoglycan walls.
Wall-synthesis inhibitors need cells to grow
Correct: wall blockers kill as cells grow and divide, but killing came before division.
Peptidoglycan is not part of the cell wall
Peptidoglycan is the wall's main component.
qs.x: Correct: A drug that blocks cell wall synthesis kills growing cells: as a cell grows and divides without being able to build new wall, it bursts. That takes at least one round of growth. Paragraph 5 says peptide P, at four times the MIC, killed over 99% of S. aureus within 20 minutes, "before the cells could divide." Killing that fast fits direct damage to the membrane, not a slow wall failure. Why the others are wrong: both gram-positive and gram-negative cells build peptidoglycan walls; peptidoglycan is the main part of the wall; different mechanisms kill at very different speeds. Trap: Ignoring timing as a clue to how a drug works.

passages.title: Diagnostic Criteria for ADHD
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is defined by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that begin in childhood, exceed what is expected for the child's developmental level, and cause impairment. A central requirement is that the symptoms appear in more than one setting, which is why evaluations collect ratings from parents and from teachers rather than from either source alone.

The reason for that requirement is diagnostic rather than statistical. Difficulty confined to one setting usually has a cause located in that setting: a mismatch between a child and a particular classroom, an unmanageable schedule at home, or a teacher whose tolerance for movement is low. A disorder of attentional control, by contrast, should follow the child across settings, so cross-setting agreement is evidence that the problem is in the child rather than in the environment.

The treatments act on catecholamine signaling. Stimulants block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, raising their availability in prefrontal circuits that support working memory and inhibitory control. Atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is an alternative that is not a stimulant.

A specialty clinic evaluated 200 children referred for attention problems, collecting standardized rating scales from one parent and one teacher for each child, and recorded whether the child ultimately met full diagnostic criteria after a full evaluation (Figure 1). Children were sorted by whether ratings were elevated at home and at school, at school only, at home only, or in neither setting.

The gradient is steep. Agreement between informants is almost diagnostic on its own, at 96%, while a single elevated informant leaves roughly nine in 10 children not meeting criteria, which is what the cross-setting requirement is designed to accomplish.

Two cautions follow. These are referred children, so the proportions in each group of bars describe a clinic population and not the general population, where the share of children with elevated ratings anywhere is much lower. More importantly, the rating pattern was part of the information available when the diagnosis was made, so the association between agreement and diagnosis is partly circular; an independent diagnostic procedure blind to the ratings would be needed to estimate how well informant agreement actually predicts the disorder.

qs.q: Why does the diagnosis require symptoms in more than one setting?
o: Teachers rate children far more accurately than their parents do at home
Not quite. Neither informant is favored.
The symptoms of this disorder appear only at school
Not quite. The disorder should appear across settings.
Difficulty in only one setting usually has a cause in that setting
Correct: Trouble in one setting usually comes from that setting, not the child.
Two settings provide twice as many symptoms to count
Not quite. It's about where the problem lies, not the count.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains this. If a child struggles in only one place, the cause is usually in that place: a poor fit with a certain classroom, a chaotic schedule at home, or a teacher with low tolerance for movement. A true problem with attention control should show up everywhere the child goes. So requiring more than one setting helps place the problem in the child rather than in the environment. Why the others are wrong: teachers rating more accurately than parents is false, neither informant is favored; two settings giving twice as many symptoms to count misses the point, it's about whether the problem is general; symptoms appearing only at school is exactly the pattern the rule screens out. Trap: Reading a rule meant to locate the cause as just a way to gather more evidence.

qs.q: What is the strongest reason to doubt that informant agreement predicts the diagnosis as well as Figure 1 suggests?
o: All of the children had been referred for attention problems
Not quite. That limits generalization, not the link itself.
The rating scales informed the diagnosis itself
Correct: The ratings were used in making the diagnosis, so the link is partly circular.
One parent and one teacher rated each of the children
Not quite. Two informants is the standard design.
Only 200 children were evaluated at the clinic
Not quite. Sample size affects precision, not circularity.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 points out that clinicians could see the rating scales when making the diagnosis. So agreement between parent and teacher was part of the evidence for diagnosing. Naturally the agreement group then looks very likely to be diagnosed (96%). This is circular: the predictor fed into the outcome. A diagnosis made blind to the ratings would be needed to test the link fairly. Why the others are wrong: only 200 children affects how precise the numbers are, not circularity; all children being referrals limits how far the results apply to the general population, but it doesn't inflate the link; one parent and one teacher is the standard design. Trap: Picking a limit on generalization when the real flaw is that predictor and outcome aren't independent.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitter systems do stimulant medications mainly act on?
o: Dopamine and norepinephrine
Correct: Stimulants block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine.
Acetylcholine and glycine
Not quite. Not the mechanism here.
Serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid
Not quite. Those are targets of other drug classes.
Histamine and glutamate
Not quite. Also not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says stimulants block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine. Reuptake is how a neuron pulls a neurotransmitter back in after release. Blocking it leaves more dopamine and norepinephrine in the synapse, boosting prefrontal circuits for working memory and impulse control. Why the others are wrong: serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) are targets of antidepressants and anti-anxiety drugs; acetylcholine and glycine aren't what these drugs act on; histamine and glutamate aren't either. Trap: Naming the best-known neurotransmitter instead of the ones this drug class targets.

qs.q: Stimulants also improve sustained attention in children without the disorder. Why does that matter for diagnosis?
o: It shows that stimulant medications do not actually work
Not quite. They do improve attention.
It means that medication is unnecessary for diagnosed children
Not quite. Nothing here questions whether it helps diagnosed children.
Response to the drug cannot serve as a diagnostic test
Correct: Everyone improves, so improving can't confirm the diagnosis.
It implies every child meets the criteria for the disorder
Not quite. Improving on a drug isn't a diagnosis.
qs.x: Correct: If a drug improves attention in children with and without the disorder, then improving on it doesn't tell you which group a child is in. The response isn't specific to the disorder. So a trial of medication can't be used to confirm a diagnosis. Why the others are wrong: stimulants not working is the opposite of the finding, they improve attention broadly; every child meeting the criteria doesn't follow, improving on a drug isn't a diagnosis; medication being unnecessary for diagnosed children doesn't follow either, nothing here questions whether it helps them. Trap: Turning a point about specificity into a claim about whether the drug works.

qs.q: Why do 12% of the children rated elevated at school only still meet full criteria?
o: Ratings from schools are sufficient on their own
Not quite. 88% of school-only children didn't qualify.
The criteria require elevation in only a single setting
Not quite. The criteria require more than one setting.
Those children in fact have no symptoms anywhere
Not quite. They met full criteria, so they had symptoms.
A parent may underreport symptoms seen at home
Correct: One parent's rating can miss symptoms that a full evaluation finds.
qs.x: Correct: A rating scale is one person's report, not a direct measurement. A parent might see the child mostly in relaxed, unstructured time, or might be reluctant to report problems. Their score could be low even though the full evaluation finds difficulties at home too. That's how 12% of the school-only group still met full criteria, which require symptoms in more than one setting. Why the others are wrong: the criteria requiring only one setting is false, they require more than one (paragraph 1); school ratings being enough on their own is false, 100 − 12 = 88% of the school-only group did not qualify; those children having no symptoms anywhere is false, they met full criteria. Trap: Treating a rating scale as a direct measure of symptoms rather than as someone's report.

passages.title: The Fundamental Attribution Error
text: When people explain behavior, they weigh dispositional causes, which lie in the person, against situational causes, which lie in the circumstances. The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to favor dispositional explanations for other people's behavior even when the situation is obvious. The actor-observer asymmetry adds that people explain their own behavior more situationally than they explain the same behavior in someone else. One proposed reason is a difference in perspective: an actor looks outward and sees the situation, while an observer looks at the actor.

Researchers tested 240 undergraduates. Each read a short scenario in which a student arrived 20 minutes late to a study group, with no explanation given. In the self condition, participants imagined that they themselves had arrived late. In the other condition, they read about a classmate. Half of the participants in each condition were also told that the campus shuttle had broken down that morning. Participants then rated, from 1 to 7, how much the lateness was caused by the person's character and how much by the circumstances (Figure 1).

The researchers noted that imagining oneself in a scenario is not the same as actually being late, and that a participant who imagines being late may picture a reason without meaning to. To check this, they asked a separate group of 40 participants to describe what they had pictured; 32 reported imagining a specific cause, most often traffic or oversleeping. The researchers argued that this is itself part of the asymmetry: an actor supplies reasons that an observer never sees.

In a second study, participants in the other condition watched a 30-second video filmed from the late student's point of view, showing the empty shuttle stop and the walk to campus. Their character rating fell to 3.2. A third group watched the same scene filmed from across the street, showing the student walking; their character rating was 4.9.

qs.q: Which comparison best demonstrates the actor-observer asymmetry?
o: Other with and without shuttle information
Not quite. Both sets of bars are ratings of someone else, so perspective never changes.
Self versus other, no shuttle news
Correct: Same information, only perspective differs: character rated 2.6 for self versus 5.1 for a classmate.
The two video groups
Not quite. Both video groups judged someone else; only the camera angle differed.
Self with and without shuttle information
Not quite. Both sets of bars are self-ratings, so this changes the information, not the perspective.
qs.x: Correct: The actor-observer asymmetry means we explain our own behavior with the situation but explain the same behavior in someone else with their character. To see it, you need a comparison where only the perspective changes, self versus other, and everything else stays the same. Figure 1 gives that in the two no-shuttle sets of bars: participants rated character as the cause at 2.6 when they imagined being late themselves, but at 5.1 when a classmate was late. Same lateness, same information, about double the character blame for the other person. Why the others are wrong: self with and without shuttle news compares two self-ratings, so it changes the information, not the perspective; other with and without shuttle news has the same problem from the observer side; the two video groups (paragraph 4) both watched someone else, so they vary camera angle within the observer role. Trap: Picking a comparison that changes something else, like information or camera angle, while the perspective stays fixed.

qs.q: What do the camera angle results suggest?
o: Video evidence always reduces blame
Not quite. The across-the-street video left character blame high at 4.9.
The actor-observer effect disappears with video
Not quite. The outside-view group still blamed character at 4.9, so the effect persisted.
People ignore video evidence entirely
Not quite. Ratings changed with camera angle, so the videos mattered.
The actor's viewpoint shifts attribution
Correct: Same scene, different angle: the actor's view gave 3.2, the outside view 4.9.
qs.x: Correct: In paragraph 4, both video groups saw the same event. The only difference was where the camera stood. When the video showed what the late student saw (the empty shuttle stop, the walk to campus), character blame fell to 3.2. When it was filmed from across the street, showing the student walking, character blame stayed at 4.9, close to the 5.1 from the plain observer condition. So seeing the world through the actor's eyes shifts blame toward the situation. That supports the perspective explanation from paragraph 1: actors see the situation, observers see the actor. Why the others are wrong: video doesn't always reduce blame, since the across-the-street video left it high at 4.9; people didn't ignore the videos, because ratings clearly changed with camera angle; the effect didn't disappear with video, since the outside-view group still blamed character at 4.9. Trap: Treating all video as equally informative, when what matters is whose point of view it shows.

qs.q: Why does giving the shuttle information reduce character ratings more in the other condition?
o: Actors always ignore new information
Not quite. Actors' character rating also dropped, from 2.6 to 2.1.
Observers care more about accuracy than actors
Not quite. The study never measured motivation, so this goes beyond the data.
Observers lacked what actors already knew
Correct: Actors already pictured a reason; observers didn't, so the news cut their score more (5.1 to 4.0).
The shuttle information was false
Not quite. The shuttle information was presented as true; nothing suggests otherwise.
qs.x: Correct: Look at how much each group moved in Figure 1. For self, character blame went from 2.6 to 2.1, a drop of 2.6 − 2.1 = 0.5. For other, it went from 5.1 to 4.0, a drop of 5.1 − 4.0 = 1.1, more than twice as big. Paragraph 3 explains why: people imagining their own lateness already pictured a reason (32 of 40 did), so being told about the shuttle added little. An observer starts with no reason in mind, so handing them one changes their judgment a lot. Why the others are wrong: observers caring more about accuracy is a claim about motivation, and the study never measured motivation; actors didn't ignore the new information, since their rating still dropped by 0.5; nothing suggests the shuttle information was false, as it was presented as fact. Trap: Explaining a group difference by motives when the passage points to a difference in information.

qs.q: Even when told about the shuttle, observers rated character at 4.0, above the actors' 2.1. Which conclusion does this best support?
o: The information reduces but keeps the bias
Correct: The rating fell from 5.1 to 4.0 but stayed above 2.1, so the bias shrank but remained.
Situational information has no effect on observers
Not quite. Observers' character rating dropped by 1.1 points, so the information had an effect.
Actors ignore their own character completely
Not quite. Actors rated character at 2.1, not 1, so they didn't ignore it.
Observers are unable to consider situations
Not quite. Observers did adjust when told about the shuttle.
qs.x: Correct: The fundamental attribution error is leaning on character to explain someone else's behavior even when the situation is obvious. When observers heard about the shuttle, their character rating fell from 5.1 to 4.0, so the information helped. But 4.0 is still well above the actors' 2.1 for the very same story (4.0 − 2.1 = 1.9 points). So knowing the situation shrinks the bias but doesn't erase it. Why the others are wrong: situational information did affect observers, since their rating fell by 5.1 − 4.0 = 1.1 points; observers can consider situations, because they adjusted; actors didn't ignore their own character completely, since they rated it 2.1, not the minimum of 1. Trap: Reading a partial change as either no change or a complete fix.

qs.q: Which situation would most likely reduce the fundamental attribution error in everyday life?
o: Watching the person for a longer time
Not quite. Longer watching keeps the observer's outside view, like the 4.9 group.
Being told the person is usually reliable
Not quite. Reliability is information about the person's character, not their situation.
Judging someone from a different culture
Not quite. An unfamiliar culture makes the situation harder to see, which tends to increase the error.
Having been in the same situation
Correct: It gives you the actor's view of the situation, like the point-of-view video.
qs.x: Correct: The passage traces the error to perspective: observers don't see the pressures the actor faces. Anything that gives the observer the actor's view should help, just as the point-of-view video in paragraph 4 dropped character blame to 3.2. Having been in the same situation yourself does exactly that. You know firsthand the constraints the other person is dealing with. Why the others are wrong: being told the person is usually reliable is still information about the person's character, so it keeps the focus on disposition; watching the person longer keeps you in the observer's seat, like the across-the-street video that left blame at 4.9; judging someone from a different culture makes their situation harder to recognize, which tends to make the error worse. Trap: Assuming more observation fixes the bias, when the problem is where you're standing, not how long you look.
