passages.title: Simple Versus Fractional Distillation
text: Distillation separates liquids by exploiting differences in boiling point. Heating a mixture produces a vapor richer in the more volatile component, and condensing that vapor gives a distillate enriched in it. The enrichment achieved in one such cycle is set by the ratio of the components' vapor pressures at the boiling temperature.

One cycle is often not enough. Simple distillation, which condenses the vapor directly, works when the boiling points differ by roughly 25 degrees or more. When they are closer, the vapor is only slightly enriched and the distillate remains a mixture.

Fractional distillation addresses this by inserting a packed column between the flask and the condenser. Vapor rising through the packing repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates, and each cycle enriches it further, so a column of sufficient length can separate components differing by only a few degrees. The number of effective cycles is described as the column's theoretical plates.

Researchers distilled four two-liquid mixtures (Table 1) by simple distillation and by fractional distillation and measured the composition of the first fraction collected (Figure 1). Simple distillation, with no column, served as the comparison for the packed column.

The two methods diverge as the boiling points converge. Simple distillation gives a usable separation at a 44-degree difference and fails at 12 degrees, where the first fraction is only slightly enriched over the starting mixture, while fractional distillation exceeds 90% purity in every case.

The hexane and cyclohexane pair shows why the column matters. A single vaporization enriches the vapor from 50% to 58%, so about eight percentage points per cycle, and reaching 91% requires several such cycles, which the packing supplies within one apparatus.

Two limits should be kept in mind. These purities are for the first fraction, and later fractions are progressively poorer as the flask is depleted of the volatile component, so the yield at a stated purity is lower than the purity alone suggests. And a pair that forms an azeotrope cannot be separated beyond the azeotropic composition by either method, however many plates the column has.

qs.q: Why does fractional distillation succeed where simple distillation fails?
o: The vapor condenses at a lower temperature
Not quite. The condenser only liquefies vapor. That's not the mechanism.
The column raises the mixture's boiling point
Not quite. Boiling points belong to the liquids, not the column.
The packing provides repeated vaporization cycles
Correct: The packing gives many vaporize-condense cycles, each enriching the vapor further.
The mixture is heated more slowly in a column
Not quite. Heating rate doesn't change the enrichment per cycle.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 explains it. The packing in the column makes the vapor condense and boil again many times on its way up. Each cycle enriches the vapor a bit more in the lower-boiling liquid. One cycle might only add a few percent, but many cycles stacked up add a lot. Figure 1 shows it: hexane goes from 58% (one cycle, simple) to 91% (column). Why the others are wrong: the column doesn't change the liquids' boiling points, those belong to the liquids; the condenser just turns vapor back to liquid, its temperature isn't the trick; heating more slowly doesn't change how much each cycle enriches. Trap: Crediting temperature for an improvement that comes from the number of cycles.

qs.q: What does the 58% figure for hexane indicate?
o: One vaporization enriches only slightly
Correct: One vaporization only took hexane from 50% to 58%.
Hexane and cyclohexane cannot be separated
Not quite. The column reached 91%, so they can be separated.
The simple apparatus was assembled wrongly
Not quite. The apparatus worked. One cycle just enriches a little.
Cyclohexane is the more volatile component
Not quite. Hexane is the more volatile one. Its share went up.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says the mixture started at 50% hexane, and one simple distillation gave a first fraction of 58% hexane. That's a gain of 58 − 50 = 8 percentage points from one vaporization. Since hexane and cyclohexane boil only 12 degrees apart, a single cycle barely enriches. You'd need several cycles to get high purity, which the column provides, reaching 91%. Why the others are wrong: they can be separated, the column reached 91%; the simple setup worked fine, it just gives one cycle's worth of enrichment; hexane is the more volatile one, since its share goes up in the distillate. Trap: Reading a weak result as a broken method instead of the size of one cycle's effect.

qs.q: What determines the enrichment achieved in a single cycle?
o: The volume of the distillation flask
Not quite. Flask size affects scale, not enrichment.
The length of the condenser attached
Not quite. The condenser only liquefies the vapor.
The total mass of the mixture placed in the flask to distill
Not quite. Total mass doesn't change the vapor's makeup.
The ratio of the components' vapor pressures
Correct: The ratio of the two vapor pressures sets one cycle's enrichment.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the enrichment from one cycle is set by the ratio of the two liquids' vapor pressures at the boiling temperature. Vapor pressure is how strongly a liquid tends to escape into vapor. The liquid with the higher vapor pressure makes up a bigger share of the vapor, and the ratio sets how much bigger. Why the others are wrong: flask size changes how much you distill, not the vapor's makeup; the condenser only turns vapor back to liquid; the total mass of mixture doesn't change the vapor's composition. Trap: Looking at the equipment for something set by the liquids themselves.

qs.q: By how many percentage points does the column improve the benzene fraction?
o: Not quite. 5 is acetone's improvement, 99 − 94.
Not quite. 10 is methanol's improvement, 98 − 88.
Correct: 96% − 71% = 25 percentage points.
Not quite. 33 is hexane's improvement, 91 − 58.
qs.x: Correct: Improvement = fractional purity − simple purity. From the benzene points in Figure 1 (30 degrees): fractional = 96% and simple = 71%. Plug in: 96 − 71 = 25 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: 5 is acetone's improvement (99 − 94 = 5); 10 is methanol's (98 − 88 = 10); 33 is hexane's (91 − 58 = 33). Trap: Grabbing the biggest improvement in the figure instead of the mixture the question asks about.

qs.q: Why does an azeotrope defeat both methods?
o: Columns cannot be made long enough
Not quite. A longer column only adds cycles that do nothing here.
The components decompose on heating then
Not quite. Decomposition is a separate problem.
Its vapor has the same composition as the liquid
Correct: Its vapor matches the liquid, so no cycle enriches anything.
Azeotropes have no single measurable boiling point at all
Not quite. Azeotropes boil at a definite temperature.
qs.x: Correct: Distillation only works because the vapor has a different makeup from the liquid. An azeotrope is a mixture whose vapor has exactly the same composition as the liquid. So boiling it produces no enrichment at all, and repeating the cycle any number of times still gets nowhere (paragraph 7). More column plates can't help. Why the others are wrong: azeotropes do boil at a definite temperature; breaking down on heating is a different problem; a longer column only adds cycles, and each cycle does nothing at the azeotrope. Trap: Treating a limit set by the mixture's chemistry as if better equipment could fix it.

passages.title: Ogburn's Cultural Lag
text: Sociologists distinguish material culture, the physical objects a group makes and uses, from nonmaterial culture, its beliefs, norms and values. Culture changes unevenly: William Ogburn argued that material culture often changes faster than the norms that govern its use, leaving a culture lag during which a technology is in wide use before shared rules for it exist. Norms themselves vary in strength. Folkways are everyday customs whose violation brings mild disapproval; mores carry moral weight and their violation brings serious sanction; taboos are prohibitions so strong that the act is almost unthinkable.

A society's dominant culture coexists with subcultures, which differ from it without rejecting it, and countercultures, which oppose it. Judging another culture by the standards of one's own is ethnocentrism; understanding practices on their own terms is cultural relativism.

Researchers surveyed 4,000 adults in one country about the use of personal recording devices in public, a technology adopted rapidly over the previous decade. Respondents rated how wrong each act is on a 1 to 7 scale and reported whether they would say something to the person. The acts were recording a street performance, recording a stranger's conversation on a train, recording inside a locker room, and recording a friend without telling them. Figure 1A shows the wrongness ratings and Figure 1B the two percentages.

The researchers noted two limits of the survey. First, what people say they would do is not what they do: self-reported willingness to speak up is usually higher than observed behavior, so the percentages in Figure 1B should be read as attitudes rather than as predictions. Second, the sample was drawn from an online panel, which underrepresents adults without regular internet access, a group that is older and less urban on average.

Respondents aged 18 to 29 rated recording a stranger's conversation at 3.4, while those over 60 rated it at 4.9. In follow-up interviews, many respondents of all ages said they were unsure what the rules were and that no clear etiquette had developed. Researchers in a second country, where recording in public has been regulated for 20 years, found far less disagreement across age groups on the same items.

qs.q: Which act is best described as violating a taboo?
o: Recording a conversation on a train
Not quite. It's rated 4.1, with opinion divided.
Recording a friend without telling them
Not quite. It's rated 3.9, only moderate disapproval.
Recording a street performance openly
Not quite. It's rated 1.4, barely wrong at all.
Recording inside a locker room
Correct: Rated 6.8 of 7, with 92% wanting it banned: the strongest reaction.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 ranks norms by strength: folkways bring mild disapproval, mores bring serious sanctions, and taboos are so strong the act is almost unthinkable. In Figure 1, recording inside a locker room has a wrongness rating of 6.8 out of 7, and 92% want a law against it. That near-total condemnation fits the strongest category best. Why the others are wrong: recording a street performance is rated just 1.4, barely wrong at all; recording a friend without telling them gets a middle rating of 3.9; recording a stranger's conversation on a train gets 4.1, with opinion split. Trap: Ranking acts by how unpleasant they sound instead of by how strongly people react.

qs.q: Which finding best illustrates culture lag?
o: Near-unanimous condemnation of locker-room recording
Not quite. That norm is settled, the opposite of lag.
A low rating for recording a street performance
Not quite. That norm is settled too.
Widespread use with no agreed etiquette
Correct: The technology spread faster than shared rules for using it.
Support for prohibiting locker-room recording
Not quite. A clear rule already exists there.
qs.x: Correct: Ogburn's culture lag (paragraph 1) is the gap when a technology (material culture) spreads before shared rules for using it (nonmaterial culture) catch up. Paragraph 3 says recording devices were adopted rapidly over the past decade, and paragraph 5 says people of all ages weren't sure of the rules and no clear etiquette had developed. Wide use with no agreed etiquette is exactly that gap. Why the others are wrong: near-unanimous condemnation of locker-room recording shows a settled norm, the opposite of lag; the low rating for recording a street performance is also settled; strong support for banning locker-room recording shows a clear rule already exists. Trap: Picking the item with the strongest opinion, when lag shows up as a lack of agreement.

qs.q: What does the age difference on the train item most likely reflect?
o: Different generations learned different norms
Correct: Each generation was socialized with different norms about recording.
Younger adults are less moral in general
Not quite. Nearly everyone condemned locker-room recording (6.8 of 7).
Older adults cannot operate the devices
Not quite. Device skill wasn't measured.
The question was worded unclearly for the older adults
Not quite. Both groups answered the same question.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says people aged 18 to 29 rated recording a stranger's conversation at 3.4, while those over 60 rated it at 4.9, a gap of 4.9 − 3.4 = 1.5 points. People learn norms through socialization in the era they grow up in. Younger people grew up with recording devices everywhere, so they absorbed looser expectations. The gap shows up on an item where no settled rule exists. Why the others are wrong: device skill was never measured; a mean of 6.8 out of 7 for the locker room means nearly everyone, young and old, condemned it, so younger people aren't less moral overall; both age groups answered the same question, so there's no sign it was unclear. Trap: Reading a difference in learned norms as a difference in character.

qs.q: What does the comparison with the second country suggest?
o: Age never affects attitudes
Not quite. Age clearly mattered in the first country.
Formal rules can reduce disagreement
Correct: With long-standing regulation, age groups disagreed far less.
Recording is less common there
Not quite. How often people record there wasn't reported.
Laws always follow public opinion
Not quite. Nothing shows the law followed opinion; the rule came first.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says that in a second country, where recording in public has been regulated for 20 years, age groups disagreed far less on the same items. A clear formal rule gives everyone the same reference point, which closes the gap that culture lag opens. Why the others are wrong: how often people record there was never reported; age clearly mattered in the first country, so 'never' is too strong; nothing shows the law simply followed public opinion, and if anything the long-standing rule came before the agreement. Trap: Assuming laws always just write down an agreement that already exists.

qs.q: In Figure 1B, for which act did the share who would speak up exceed the share who say a law should prohibit it by the widest margin?
o: Recording a street performance
Not quite. 3% versus 2% is a margin of only 1 point.
Recording a stranger's conversation on a train
Not quite. Here the law figure (31%) is higher than the speak-up figure (19%), so the margin is negative.
Recording inside a locker room
Not quite. Here the law figure (92%) is higher than the speak-up figure (61%), so the margin is negative.
Recording a friend without telling them
Correct: 28% would speak up versus 12% for a law, a margin of 28 − 12 = 16 points.
qs.x: Correct: For each act, margin = share who would speak up − share who want a law. Read the two bars for each act in Figure 1B. Street performance: 3 − 2 = 1. Stranger's conversation: 19 − 31 = −12. Locker room: 61 − 92 = −31. Friend without telling them: 28 − 12 = 16. The largest positive margin is the friend, at 16 points. Why the others are wrong: the street performance margin is only 1 point; the train conversation has a negative margin of −12 because more people want a law than would speak up; the locker room margin is −31 for the same reason. Trap: Picking the act with the tallest bars instead of subtracting the two bars for each act.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Mean rating of how wrong each act is (4,000 adults)
Figure 1B. Share who would speak up and share who say a law should prohibit the act

passages.title: Flexibility and Heat Tolerance of Enzymes from Different Climates
text: Enzymes from organisms that live at different temperatures often catalyze the same reaction with the same active-site residues, yet they differ in speed and in heat tolerance. One explanation is that a protein must be flexible enough to move through the conformational changes of its catalytic cycle but rigid enough to stay folded. A protein from a heat-loving organism may be well suited to high temperatures yet sluggish at room temperature, because the same interactions that hold it together also restrict its motion.

To test this idea, researchers purified adenylate kinase, which catalyzes 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP, from a bacterium that grows best at 37 °C (Enzyme M) and from a related species isolated from a hot spring that grows best at 70 °C (Enzyme T). The two proteins share 74% sequence identity, and every residue that contacts the substrates is conserved. Turnover number (kcat) was measured at several temperatures with saturating substrate (Figure 1A). Each value is the mean of three runs that differed by less than 5%.

The researchers also measured the melting temperature (Tm), the temperature at which half of the protein is unfolded, using circular dichroism. Enzyme M had a Tm of 47 °C and Enzyme T had a Tm of 82 °C. Inspection of the Enzyme T crystal structure showed that Glu142, a surface residue far from the active site, forms an ion pair with Arg87. A mutant of Enzyme T in which Glu142 was replaced by glutamine (E142Q) had a Tm of 71 °C. At 40 °C, the kcat of E142Q was 5.8 s⁻¹.

Heat tolerance has practical uses. Enzymes from heat-loving organisms are used in laboratory methods that cycle between high temperatures, such as the polymerase chain reaction, and in industrial processes that run hot to keep reactants dissolved and to limit microbial growth. Engineers who want an enzyme that is both stable and fast at moderate temperatures often start by adding or removing surface ion pairs and then testing how the changes affect Tm and kcat separately.

In a final experiment, Enzyme M was held at 60 °C for 10 minutes in the presence of substrate. Its activity was then measured after the solution was cooled to 30 °C. The rate was 4% of the rate of an unheated sample. When fresh, unheated Enzyme M was added to the heated solution, the rate returned to the expected value.

qs.q: Which explanation of the kcat values of the two enzymes at 20–30 °C is most consistent with the passage?
o: Enzyme T is too rigid to cycle quickly at low temperature
Correct: the interactions that keep it folded also make it too stiff to cycle fast when cool.
Enzyme T makes the reaction less favorable overall
An enzyme changes the rate, not the reaction's ΔG.
Enzyme T is partly unfolded when the temperature is low
Its Tm is 82 °C, so it's fully folded at 20 to 30 °C.
Enzyme T is missing residues that bind substrate
Every residue that contacts the substrate is conserved.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Figure 1A at the low temperatures. At 20 °C, Enzyme M turns over 12 times a second and Enzyme T only 1.5, and 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8. At 30 °C it's 23 against 3.0, again about 8 times. Enzyme T isn't damaged: its melting temperature (Tm, where half the protein unfolds) is 82 °C, so it's fully folded at 20 to 30 °C, and its substrate-binding residues are identical to M's (paragraph 2). Paragraph 1 gives the explanation: the same interactions that hold a heat-loving protein together also make it stiff, so it moves through its catalytic shape changes slowly when it's cool. Why the others are wrong: with a Tm of 82 °C, Enzyme T is folded well below that; every residue touching the substrate is conserved; an enzyme speeds a reaction but can't change how favorable it is (its ΔG). Trap: Assuming a slow enzyme must be damaged or missing part of its active site.

qs.q: To estimate the activation energy of Enzyme T from Figure 1A, which plot should the researchers make?
o: kcat against T, which has a slope of Eₐ/R
kcat rises exponentially with T, so this isn't a straight line.
1/kcat against 1/T, which has a slope equal to Eₐ/R
A double-reciprocal plot belongs to enzyme kinetics, not the Arrhenius equation.
ln kcat against T in kelvin, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
ln k is linear in 1/T, not in T.
ln kcat against 1/T, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
Correct: ln k = ln A − (Eₐ/R)(1/T), a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R.
qs.x: Correct: The Arrhenius equation is k = Ae raised to the power −Eₐ/RT, where k is the rate constant, A is a constant, Eₐ is the activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is the temperature in kelvin. Take the natural log of both sides: ln k = ln A − (Eₐ/R) × (1/T). That has the shape of a straight line, y = b + mx, with y = ln k, x = 1/T, and slope m = −Eₐ/R. So plot ln kcat against 1/T and read Eₐ from the slope. Figure 1B shows that plot for Enzyme T, with kcat on a log axis against 1000 ÷ T: the points fall close to a straight line. Use only temperatures where the enzyme is still folded, below its Tm. Why the others are wrong: kcat rises exponentially with temperature, so kcat against T isn't a straight line; ln k is a straight line against 1/T, not against T; plotting 1/kcat against 1/T is a Lineweaver–Burk-style plot from enzyme kinetics, not the Arrhenius form. Trap: Mixing up the Arrhenius plot with a Lineweaver–Burk plot.

qs.q: What do the results for the E142Q mutant most strongly suggest?
o: The mutation shifts the equilibrium to ATP and AMP
Enzymes and mutations don't change the equilibrium constant.
The Glu142–Arg87 ion pair stabilizes the folded enzyme
Correct: Tm fell by 11 °C while kcat stayed at about 5.8 to 5.9 s⁻¹.
Glu142 is required for the chemical step of catalysis
kcat at 40 °C was unchanged, so it's not needed for the chemistry.
Glutamine side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds
Glutamine's amide forms hydrogen bonds well. It just lacks a charge.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says Glu142 (negatively charged) forms an ion pair, a salt bridge, with Arg87 (positively charged), far from the active site. Swapping Glu for Gln, which is about the same size but has no charge, breaks that pair. Two results follow. The Tm fell from 82 °C to 71 °C, so the enzyme unfolds 82 − 71 = 11 °C sooner. But kcat at 40 °C was 5.8 s⁻¹, essentially the same as wild type's 5.9 s⁻¹ (Figure 1A). So the ion pair holds the protein together but plays no part in the chemistry. Why the others are wrong: if Glu142 did the chemistry, kcat would have dropped; glutamine's side chain can form hydrogen bonds just fine, it just lacks a charge; no enzyme or mutation can shift the equilibrium. Trap: Assuming any residue whose mutation matters must be in the active site.

qs.q: Which observation shows that the loss of Enzyme M activity at 60 °C is due to the enzyme rather than the substrate?
o: Raising substrate levels after heating restored the rate
That would point to the substrate, and it wasn't observed.
Enzyme M activity at 50 °C is lower than at 40 °C
That's the drop being explained, not a test of its cause.
Fresh enzyme added after heating restored the rate
Correct: fresh enzyme restored the rate, so the substrate was fine and the old enzyme was damaged.
Enzyme M is faster than Enzyme T at 30 °C
That compares two enzymes. It doesn't test heat damage.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 describes the test. After heating, the reaction ran at only 4% of normal. That could mean the enzyme was ruined or the substrate was ruined. Adding fresh, unheated enzyme to the same heated solution brought the rate back to normal. If the substrate had been destroyed, new enzyme would have nothing to work on, so the substrate must have survived and the original enzyme was the casualty. That fits Enzyme M unfolding above its Tm of 47 °C. Why the others are wrong: M being faster than T at 30 °C compares two enzymes and says nothing about heat damage; lower activity at 50 °C is the thing being explained, not a test of the cause; adding substrate restoring the rate would point to the substrate, and that wasn't observed. Trap: Picking a result that restates the observation instead of one that tests it.

qs.q: If kcat were measured at 75 °C, how would E142Q most likely compare with wild-type Enzyme T?
o: Higher, because glutamine carries no charge
Losing the charge lowered stability. It didn't raise activity.
The same, because the active site is unchanged
The active site only works while the protein is folded.
Higher, because kcat rises with temperature for both
Rates rise with temperature only while the protein stays folded.
Lower, because most E142Q molecules would be unfolded
Correct: 75 °C is above E142Q's Tm of 71 °C, so most of it is unfolded.
qs.x: Correct: The mutant's Tm is 71 °C (paragraph 3). At 75 °C, that's above its Tm, so more than half of the E142Q molecules are unfolded, and an unfolded enzyme can't catalyze anything. Wild-type Enzyme T has a Tm of 82 °C, so at 75 °C it's still mostly folded and still speeding up with temperature: Figure 1A shows it climbing from 20 to 35 s⁻¹ between 60 and 70 °C. So the mutant should be slower. Why the others are wrong: rates rise with temperature only while the protein stays folded; an identical active site is useless once the protein unfolds; removing the charge made the protein less stable, not more active. Trap: Extending the rise-with-temperature trend past the melting temperature.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Turnover number of Enzyme M and Enzyme T against temperature (mean of three runs)
Figure 1B. Arrhenius plot for Enzyme T (kcat on a log axis against 1000 ÷ T in kelvin)

passages.title: Expected Versus Observed Ratios in a Carrier Cross
text: A cross between two carriers of a recessive allele is expected to produce affected offspring in a quarter of cases, but an observed proportion in a real family rarely matches that figure. The expectation describes the probability for each conception independently, and a small number of conceptions is a small sample from it.

Two further effects move the observed proportion. Incomplete penetrance means some individuals carrying the genotype do not show the phenotype, which lowers the observed proportion of affected offspring without changing the genotype ratio; and ascertainment through an affected child guarantees at least one affected offspring in every family studied, which raises it.
The two biases therefore act in opposite directions, and a study must correct for both before an observed proportion can be compared with the expected quarter.
Offspring were counted in four sets of 240 families each (Figure 1). Each point shows the offspring counted in a set and how many of them were affected.

The prospective sample gave 0.248, close to the expected quarter. Ascertaining families through an affected child raised the proportion to 0.455, and excluding the index child from the count brought it back to 0.249, because the siblings of an affected child are no more likely to be affected than any other offspring of the same couple.
The penetrance sample gave 0.176, which is close to 0.25 multiplied by 0.70, so a reduced penetrance scales the observed proportion rather than changing the shape of the expectation.

Two qualifications apply. The prospective sample counts conceptions that reached birth, and if the genotype causes early pregnancy loss the affected offspring are undercounted in every sample including the prospective one, which would bias all four proportions downward. And the penetrance figure of 70 percent was itself estimated from a separate family study, so the agreement between 0.176 and the predicted 0.175 is partly circular and does not independently confirm the penetrance. An independent estimate would have to come from a different design, such as genotyping a population sample and counting how many carriers of the genotype are unaffected, which does not depend on families having been noticed in the first place.

qs.q: Why does ascertainment through an affected child raise the proportion?
o: Affected children have more affected siblings than expected
Their siblings have the ordinary 1/4 risk.
The bias lowers it
It raises the proportion, to 0.455.
Families with none are missed
Correct: families with no affected child are never found, so they're missed.
The genotype changes with the sampling
Genotypes don't depend on how families were found.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says finding families through an affected child guarantees at least one affected offspring in every family studied. Two carrier parents with a few children might, by chance, have none affected. Those families are never noticed, so they're left out. The sample is then loaded with affected children. Figure 1 shows the effect: 398 affected out of 874, and 398 ÷ 874 = 0.455, far above the 0.248 from the prospective sample (families followed regardless of outcome). Why the others are wrong: siblings of an affected child have the ordinary 1/4 risk, as the corrected value (0.249) shows; genotypes don't change with how a family was found; the bias raises the proportion, not lowers it. Trap: Treating a selected sample as if it were random.

qs.q: Why does excluding the index child restore the expected quarter?
o: Siblings of an affected child carry extra risk
Siblings' risk is the ordinary 1/4.
Other siblings carry ordinary risk
Correct: only the index child was selected. Siblings carry the ordinary 1/4 risk.
Exclusion adds affected offspring
Excluding removes one affected child per family.
The index child was not actually affected
The index child was affected by definition.
qs.x: Correct: Only the index child, the one who brought the family to the study, was guaranteed to be affected. Remove one per family and the rest are ordinary siblings. Find the new counts: 240 families, so 240 index children. Offspring: 874 − 240 = 634. Affected: 398 − 240 = 158. Proportion = affected ÷ offspring = 158 ÷ 634 ≈ 0.249. Check it against 1/4: 634 ÷ 4 = 158.5, so 158 is right on target. Why the others are wrong: the index child was affected by definition; excluding removes one affected child per family, it doesn't add any; siblings don't have extra risk, since each conception has the same 1/4 chance (paragraph 1). Trap: Treating the whole ascertained family as a random sample.

qs.q: Why does reduced penetrance scale rather than reshape the expectation?
o: It multiplies each probability
Correct: 0.25 × 0.70 = 0.175. Genotype ratios stay the same.
It alters the proportion of carriers among the offspring
Carrier proportion is unchanged.
It changes the ratio to 1 in 3
It doesn't make 1 in 3. It gives 0.175.
It reshapes it
It scales the number down, it doesn't reshape it.
qs.x: Correct: Penetrance is the chance that someone with the genotype actually shows the trait. For an affected child, two things must both happen: the child gets two recessive alleles, and the genotype shows. Multiply: P(affected) = P(genotype) × penetrance. The values: P(genotype) = 1/4 = 0.25 for two carriers, and penetrance = 70% = 0.70. Plug in: 0.25 × 0.70 = 0.175, which matches the observed 0.176 (paragraph 6). The genotype ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 hasn't changed; penetrance just multiplies the affected share down. Why the others are wrong: penetrance doesn't change how many children are carriers; it gives 0.175, not 1 in 3; it shrinks the number, it doesn't reshape the pattern. Trap: Mixing up whether a gene shows with whether it's passed on.

qs.q: How many affected offspring would be expected in the prospective sample at full penetrance?
o: That's the reduced penetrance sample.
That's the number observed.
That's the sample found through an affected child.
qs.x: Correct: Expected affected = number of offspring × probability each is affected. From Figure 1, the prospective sample has 892 offspring, and two carriers have a 1/4 chance per child at full penetrance. Plug in: 892 × 1/4 = 892 ÷ 4. Half of 892 is 446, and half of 446 is 223. So 223 are expected, very close to the 221 actually seen. Why the others are wrong: 221 is the number observed, not expected; 156 is the observed count in the 70% penetrance sample; 398 is the count in the sample found through an affected child. Trap: Giving an observed value when an expected one was asked for.

qs.q: Why is the agreement between 0.176 and the predicted 0.175 partly circular?
o: Early pregnancy loss biases the count
Not quite. That's the other qualification, about all four samples.
Penetrance was measured in this sample
It came from a separate study.
The figure came from family data
Correct: the 70% came from family data, so it isn't an independent test.
The agreement is exact
It's close, 0.175 against 0.176, not exact.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the 70% penetrance figure came from a separate family study. If you take a number from family data, plug it in, and it predicts family data, the match partly just reflects where the number came from. It's not a fresh test. The predicted 0.25 × 0.70 = 0.175 against the observed 0.176 looks great, but a truly independent check would use a different design, like genotyping a population sample. Why the others are wrong: early pregnancy loss is the other qualification, about all four samples; the agreement is close (0.175 vs 0.176) but not exact; and the figure wasn't measured in this sample, it came from a separate study. Trap: Taking a prediction as proof when the number was fitted to similar data.

passages.title: Stereotype Threat and Working Memory
text: Stereotype threat is the performance decrement that appears when a person is at risk of confirming a negative stereotype about a group they belong to. The proposed mechanism is not reduced ability or effort but competition for working memory: monitoring one's own performance, suppressing anxious thoughts and worrying about what a poor score would mean all consume the same limited resource the task requires.

The mechanism generates a testable prediction. If threat acts through working memory, then a measure of load taken during the task should rise under threatening conditions and should move inversely with performance, and interventions that reduce threat should lower load as well as raising scores. If load stayed constant while scores moved, the account would be in trouble.

Two interventions are commonly used. Self-affirmation has the person write briefly about a value that matters to them before the task, which is held to reduce the stake the task carries for the self. Explicitly describing the stereotype as unfounded removes the inference a poor score would license.

Students completed the same difficult quantitative test under one of four randomly assigned framings. A concurrent secondary task indexed working memory load, scored so that higher values mean more load (Table 1). Figure 1 shows the proposed mechanism the study tests.

The two columns move inversely across all four conditions, from 62 and 7.8 in the threatening condition to 74 and 5.1 in the puzzle framing, with the two interventions landing in between on both measures. That is the pattern the working memory account predicts.

The correspondence is suggestive but not decisive. Load and score are both outcomes measured at the same time, so a third factor, such as how engaging each framing felt, could move them together, and a mediation claim requires showing that the load change accounts for the score change statistically. The secondary task also competes with the test for resources, so the measurement may itself alter what it measures, and the test was difficult by design, which is the condition under which threat effects are largest and therefore not a general estimate.

qs.q: Which result supports the working memory account?
o: Four different framings were tested in the study
Not quite. The number of conditions is a design choice, not a result.
Load moved inversely with score across the conditions
Correct: Higher load went with lower scores across all four conditions, as predicted.
Scores exceeded 60 points in all conditions
Not quite. True, but it doesn't test the working memory account.
Self-affirmation raised the measured load index in every group
Not quite. Self-affirmation lowered load from 7.8 to 5.6.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says if stereotype threat works by using up working memory, then load should go up when scores go down. Table 1 shows that across all four framings. Threatening framing: score 62, load 7.8. Puzzle framing: score 74, load 5.1. The two interventions land in between on both (72 and 5.6; 71 and 5.9). As one goes up, the other goes down, just as predicted. Why the others are wrong: self-affirmation lowered load to 5.6 rather than raising it; all scores being above 60 is true but doesn't test anything; the number of framings is a design choice, not a result. Trap: Picking a true statement about the table that doesn't actually test the hypothesis.

qs.q: Why does the puzzle framing help?
o: No judgment of ability is implied by the task
Correct: A puzzle implies no judgment of ability, so there's no stereotype to confirm.
The questions have been made easier
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says everyone took the same test.
The time limit for the test has been removed
Not quite. Only the framing differed between conditions.
Anxiety ignores how a task is framed
Not quite. Framing changed load from 7.8 to 5.1.
qs.x: Correct: Stereotype threat comes from the risk of confirming a negative stereotype about your group. If the test is called a measure of ability, a poor score could seem to confirm it, so you start worrying and checking yourself, and that uses up working memory. Call the same test a puzzle, and there's nothing about ability to confirm. In Table 1, load dropped from 7.8 to 5.1 and scores rose from 62 to 74. Why the others are wrong: the questions weren't easier, since paragraph 4 says it was the same test; the time limit wasn't changed, since only the framing differed; framing clearly mattered, since it changed load a lot. Trap: Blaming a framing effect on a change in difficulty.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the account?
o: Load fell under the interventions while scores stayed low
Correct: Load fell but scores didn't rise, which breaks the proposed link.
Students were already aware of the stereotype
Not quite. Knowing the stereotype is needed for threat to happen at all.
Test scores rose after students completed the self-affirmation task
Not quite. Better scores after affirmation fit the account.
Load was highest in the diagnostic framing
Not quite. High load under threat is what the account predicts.
qs.x: Correct: The account says threat lowers scores by using up working memory. Paragraph 2 says the account would be in trouble if load and scores came apart. So the most damaging result is load dropping under the interventions while scores stayed low. That would mean freeing up working memory didn't help performance, so working memory can't be the route. Why the others are wrong: load being highest under the diagnostic framing is exactly what the account predicts; scores rising after self-affirmation also fits it; students knowing the stereotype is a requirement for threat, not a problem for it. Trap: Choosing the most striking result instead of the one that breaks the proposed link.

qs.q: What was randomly assigned in this experiment?
o: The items that appeared on the test
Not quite. Everyone took the same test.
The framing each student received
Correct: Each student was randomly given one of four framings.
The working memory load measure used
Not quite. One load measure was used for everyone.
The group membership of the students
Not quite. Group membership is a trait and can't be assigned.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says students took the same test under one of four randomly assigned framings. So the framing was what got assigned. That's what lets the researchers say framing caused the differences. Why the others are wrong: the test items were the same for everyone; group membership is something a person already has and can't be assigned; there was one load measure, the secondary task, used for everyone. Trap: Confusing the group the study is about with the variable that was actually assigned.

qs.q: Which practical implication follows most directly?
o: Reduce the difficulty of all assessments
Not quite. Difficulty didn't vary in the study.
Separate students by group for testing
Not quite. Separating by group makes group membership more noticeable.
Present assessments as tools for learning
Correct: Calling a test a learning tool removes the ability judgment, like the puzzle framing.
Avoid timed assessments where possible
Not quite. Timing didn't vary in the study.
qs.x: Correct: The best result came from calling the test a puzzle instead of a measure of ability (score 74, load 5.1). In real life, that means presenting tests as tools for learning, feedback to help you improve, rather than a verdict on your ability. That removes the thing a poor score would seem to prove. Why the others are wrong: separating students by group would make group membership more noticeable, which is what feeds threat; difficulty wasn't varied in the study, since the test was the same; timing also wasn't varied, so the study can't support changing it. Trap: Drawing a lesson from a feature the experiment held constant.

graph.title: Figure 1. Proposed path from stereotype threat to lower scores

passages.title: Asch's Line-Judgment Conformity Study
text: Solomon Asch studied conformity by asking participants to judge which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. The task was easy: people working alone were correct almost every time. In the group version, several confederates answered aloud before the participant and gave the same wrong answer on certain trials. About a third of participants' responses matched the wrong majority, and about three-quarters of participants conformed at least once.

Psychologists distinguish two reasons for conformity. Normative influence is the wish to be accepted, which produces public agreement without private belief. Informational influence is the belief that others know better, which changes private judgment as well. Ambiguous tasks favor informational influence, while clear tasks with a visible audience favor normative influence.

Researchers ran a modern replication with 160 participants in four conditions. In every condition, five confederates answered before the participant on 12 of 18 trials, giving a wrong answer on each of those 12, except for the one dissenter described below. In the private condition, the participant wrote answers on a card that the others could not see. In the unanimous condition, all five confederates gave the same wrong answer. In the dissenter condition, the fourth confederate gave the correct answer. In the hard condition, the comparison lines differed by only 1 mm, making the judgment genuinely difficult (Figure 1). Answers were spoken aloud in every condition except the private one.

The researchers also recorded how long each participant took to answer on the critical trials. In the unanimous spoken condition, participants who went along with the majority took about 1.8 seconds longer than those who gave the correct answer, which the researchers read as a sign of conflict between what they saw and what they said.

In interviews afterward, most participants in the unanimous spoken condition said they had seen the correct answer but had not wanted to appear foolish. In the hard condition, most said they had not been sure and had assumed the others saw better.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates normative influence?
o: Hard versus easy judgment, spoken
This changes how hard the task is, which tests informational influence, not the audience.
Spoken versus written, both unanimous
Correct: only the audience differs, and wrong answers fell from 31% to 8%.
Unanimous versus dissenter, spoken
This changes whether the group agrees. Both are spoken, so the audience is the same.
Written versus the hard condition
Two things change at once, the audience and the difficulty.
qs.x: Correct: Normative influence is going along with a group because you want to be accepted, not because you think they're right (paragraph 2). So it depends on the group actually seeing your answer. The cleanest test is to keep everything the same and take away the audience. That's the spoken versus written comparison: both groups faced five confederates who all agreed, and the only change was whether the participant said the answer out loud or wrote it privately on a card (paragraph 3). In Figure 1, wrong answers fell from 31% spoken to 8% written. That drop is the part of conformity that came from wanting to fit in. Why the others are wrong: unanimous versus dissenter changes whether the group agrees, not whether anyone is watching; hard versus easy changes how sure people are, which is about informational influence; written versus hard changes both the audience and the difficulty at once, so you can't tell which one caused the difference. Trap: Picking a comparison where more than one thing changes. A clean test changes just one thing.

qs.q: Why is conformity highest in the hard condition?
o: Uncertainty makes other answers useful
Correct: when people can't tell, others' answers look like evidence. That's informational influence.
The task had no correct answer
One line still matched. It was just hard to see.
Participants wanted acceptance more
The audience was the same as in the unanimous spoken condition.
The group was larger there
Every condition used five confederates.
qs.x: Correct: Informational influence is going along because you think the others know better (paragraph 2). It's strongest when you're unsure. In the hard condition, the comparison lines differed by only 1 mm (paragraph 3), so participants honestly couldn't tell which line matched. When you can't trust your own eyes, other people's answers start to look like useful evidence. Figure 1 shows wrong answers jumped to 46%, the highest of any condition. The interviews in paragraph 5 back this up: people in the hard condition said they weren't sure and assumed the others saw better. Why the others are wrong: every condition used five confederates, so the group wasn't larger; the answers were spoken aloud just like the unanimous spoken condition, so the pressure to be accepted was the same; one line still matched the standard, so a correct answer existed, it was just hard to see. Trap: Blaming every rise in conformity on social pressure. When a task is hard, people often conform because they truly believe the group.

qs.q: Why does a single dissenter reduce conformity so sharply?
o: The dissenter makes the task ambiguous
The task stayed easy and clear.
The dissenter makes the group smaller
There were still five confederates. Only one changed his answer.
Unanimity is what creates the pressure
Correct: losing unanimity cut wrong answers from 31% to 7%.
The dissenter gives the participant new information about the lines
The lines were easy, so participants already knew the answer.
qs.x: Correct: Breaking the group's agreement matters more than how many people are in the majority. In the dissenter condition, the fourth confederate gave the right answer, and wrong answers fell from 31% to 7% (Figure 1). There were still five confederates and the task was still easy, so the only change was that the group was no longer unanimous. One ally shows the participant that disagreeing is allowed, and the fear of standing alone drops away. Why the others are wrong: the group still had five confederates, so it wasn't smaller; the lines were easy to judge, so the participant didn't need new information about them; the task stayed just as clear, so it didn't become ambiguous. Trap: Thinking conformity depends mostly on how many people hold the majority view. A single dissenter can undo most of the pressure.

qs.q: What do the interview responses add to the numerical results?
o: They prove that the participants were lying outright
What people say afterward is evidence, not proof of lying.
They replace the written condition
Self-report is weaker evidence than the written condition, so it can't replace it.
They show the task was impossible
Most answers were correct, so the task was manageable.
They suggest which kind of influence operated
Correct: they separate public agreement (normative) from a real change in belief (informational).
qs.x: Correct: The numbers tell you how often people conformed, but not why. The interviews in paragraph 5 hint at the reason. People in the unanimous spoken condition said they saw the right answer but didn't want to look foolish. That's public agreement without private belief, which is normative influence. People in the hard condition said they weren't sure and assumed the others saw better. That's a real change in what they believed, which is informational influence. So the interviews suggest which kind of influence was at work in each condition. Why the others are wrong: what people say afterward is evidence, but it can't prove anyone was lying; the written condition tests the audience directly, and self-report is weaker evidence, so it can't replace it; most answers were correct (Figure 1), so the task wasn't impossible. Trap: Treating self-report as either worthless or as the final word. It's useful support, not proof.

qs.q: A student concludes from the 31% figure that most people conform. What is the best correction?
o: Only one person conformed in that condition
About 73% conformed at least once, so far more than one person.
The figure counts trials, not people
Correct: 31% counts trials, and 27% of people never conformed at all.
The figure should be 46%
46% is the hard condition, not this one.
Conformity never occurs on easy tasks
Conformity did happen here, on 31% of critical trials.
qs.x: Correct: The 31% in Figure 1 is the share of the critical trials where participants gave the wrong majority answer. It counts answers, not people. A second bar shows that 27% of participants in that condition never conformed at all. So it's wrong to read 31% as "31% of people conform" or as "most people conform." On a typical critical trial, most answers were still correct. Why the others are wrong: 46% is the hard condition, not the unanimous spoken one; conformity clearly did happen on the easy task, on 31% of critical trials; and since only 27% never conformed, about 73% (100 − 27 = 73) conformed at least once, which is far more than one person. Trap: Reading a percentage of trials as if it were a percentage of people. Always check what the number is counting.

graph.title: Figure 1. Conformity in four conditions (n = 40 per condition)

series.name: Wrong answers on the 12 critical trials (%)

passages.title: Le Châtelier's Principle in the Haber Process
text: Le Châtelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting in the direction that partly opposes it. Ammonia is made industrially by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. The equilibrium constant Kp depends only on temperature; pressure and catalysts do not change it. Because the reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants and lowers Kp.

The reaction also has 4 mol of gas on the left and two on the right, so compressing the mixture shifts it toward ammonia. The reaction is slow at low temperature, however, because breaking the triple bond of N₂ has a high activation energy. An iron catalyst lowers that barrier and speeds both the forward and the reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position does not change.

An engineering team measured the percentage of ammonia present at equilibrium under several conditions (Figure 1 shows the yields; Table 1 lists the conditions and the time to reach equilibrium). In each run the starting mixture was one part N₂ to three parts H₂ by moles.

The team also considered what sets the starting ratio. Using one part N₂ to three parts H₂ matches the stoichiometry of the reaction, which gives the highest conversion of both gases; an excess of either one would raise the conversion of the other but leave the excess gas unreacted and circulating through the plant. Hydrogen for the process is usually obtained from methane and steam, a step that is itself energy-intensive, so plants are designed around the cost of hydrogen as much as around the equilibrium yield. Roughly 1% of the world's energy use goes into this one reaction, which supplies the nitrogen in most agricultural fertilizer.

Industrial plants typically run at about 400 °C and 200 atm. The team also noted that ammonia is removed continuously by cooling it to a liquid while the unreacted gases are recycled through the reactor.

qs.q: Why does the ammonia percentage fall as temperature rises?
o: The forward reaction releases heat
Correct: heat acts like a product, so adding heat shifts the reaction back toward N₂ and H₂.
The catalyst stops working when hot
These are equilibrium amounts, which a catalyst doesn't change.
Ammonia decomposes into different products
Ammonia breaks back down into N₂ and H₂, not different products.
Higher temperature lowers the pressure
Pressure is held at 100 atm across these rows.
qs.x: Correct: The reaction gives off heat (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol, paragraph 1), so you can treat heat as a product: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat. By Le Châtelier's principle, adding heat (raising the temperature) pushes the equilibrium back toward the reactants to use up the extra heat. That lowers Kp and the share of ammonia. Figure 1A shows it: 81% at 200 °C, 25% at 400 °C, 5% at 600 °C. Why the others are wrong: these are amounts at equilibrium, and the catalyst doesn't change equilibrium amounts anyway; pressure is held fixed when comparing temperatures; the reverse reaction gives back N₂ and H₂, not different products. Trap: Expecting more ammonia at higher temperature because the reaction goes faster.

qs.q: Why does raising the pressure increase the yield?
o: Pressure liquefies the gases
The reaction happens in the gas phase.
The product side has fewer gas moles
Correct: 4 moles of gas become 2, so higher pressure favors the ammonia side.
Pressure lowers activation energy
Lowering activation energy is the catalyst's role.
Pressure raises the value of Kp
Kp depends only on temperature.
qs.x: Correct: The left side has 1 + 3 = 4 moles of gas, the right side has 2 (paragraph 2). Squeezing the mixture raises the pressure, and Le Châtelier's principle says the system shifts to ease that, toward the side with fewer gas molecules. That's the ammonia side. Figure 1B shows it: 25% at 100 atm, 36% at 200 atm, 47% at 400 atm. Why the others are wrong: Kp depends only on temperature, so pressure moves the position without changing Kp; lowering the activation energy is the catalyst's job; the reaction happens in the gas phase, so pressure isn't liquefying anything in the reactor. Trap: Assuming a bigger yield means a bigger equilibrium constant.

qs.q: Why does industry use 400 °C rather than 200 °C, where the yield is far higher?
o: The catalyst fails at 200 °C
The catalyst works there. It cut months down to 4 hours.
Kp is much larger at 400 °C than it is at 200 °C
Kp is larger at 200 °C, since the reaction is exothermic.
Ammonia is unstable at 200 °C
Ammonia's equilibrium share is highest at 200 °C.
Equilibrium is reached far more slowly at 200 °C
Correct: even with the catalyst, equilibrium takes 4 h at 200 °C versus 20 min at 400 °C, and months without it, so 400 °C trades yield for speed.
qs.x: Correct: At 200 °C the yield is great, 81%, but look at the time columns of Table 1. Without a catalyst it takes several months to get there, and even with one it takes 4 hours. At 400 °C it takes 8 hours without a catalyst and only 20 minutes with one. A plant can't wait months, so it gives up some yield (25 to 36%) for speed. Recycling the leftover gases (paragraph 5) makes up for the lower single-pass yield. Why the others are wrong: Kp is larger at 200 °C, since the reaction gives off heat; the catalyst does work at 200 °C, cutting months down to 4 hours; ammonia's equilibrium share is highest at 200 °C, so it isn't unstable there. Trap: Choosing conditions from the yield alone and ignoring the time columns.

qs.q: Why does removing ammonia as a liquid increase the total amount produced?
o: Liquid ammonia catalyzes the reaction
Liquid ammonia leaves the gas phase. It isn't a catalyst.
Removing ammonia raises Kp
Kp doesn't change at a fixed temperature.
The system shifts to replace it
Correct: removing product drops Q below Kp, so the system makes more ammonia.
Removing ammonia raises the temperature
The ammonia is removed by cooling, not heating.
qs.x: Correct: Pulling ammonia out as a liquid (paragraph 5) lowers its amount in the gas. Now the reaction quotient Q, which is products over reactants, drops below Kp. By Le Châtelier's principle, the system makes more ammonia to get back to equilibrium. Then that ammonia is removed too, and the cycle repeats with the recycled gases. Over many passes, far more of the N₂ and H₂ gets converted than one equilibrium would allow. Why the others are wrong: Kp stays the same at a fixed temperature; liquid ammonia leaves the reaction, it doesn't speed it up; ammonia is removed by cooling, not heating. Trap: Treating one equilibrium percentage as the most you can ever get.

qs.q: How would the catalyst change the time to equilibrium and the yield at 400 °C and 200 atm?
o: Less time and a lower yield
The equilibrium position doesn't move, so the yield can't drop.
Less time and a higher yield
Yield is set by Kp, which only temperature changes.
Less time, same yield
Correct: it speeds both directions equally: 8 h becomes 20 min, and the yield stays 36%.
The same time and a higher yield
A catalyst does change the time. That's its whole job.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the iron catalyst lowers the activation energy (the energy barrier) for both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount. So both directions speed up equally. Equilibrium arrives sooner, but where it ends up doesn't move. Table 1 at 400 °C and 200 atm: 8 hours drops to 20 minutes with the catalyst, while the yield stays 36% (Figure 1B). Why the others are wrong: a higher yield would need a bigger Kp, and Kp depends only on temperature; a catalyst's whole job is to speed up the approach, so the time does change; a lower yield would also mean a different Kp. Trap: Thinking a catalyst makes more product rather than making it sooner.

passages.title: Stereotypes, Prejudice and Discrimination Compared
text: Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination are distinct. A stereotype is a belief about the attributes of a group, prejudice is an evaluative attitude toward the group, and discrimination is behavior that treats people differently on the basis of group membership. A person can hold a stereotype without endorsing it, and can behave in a discriminatory way without reporting a hostile attitude.

That last possibility motivated implicit measures. A reaction-time association task infers the strength of a learned association from how quickly a person pairs group labels with evaluative words, on the premise that such associations operate without deliberate control and so escape both self-presentation and introspective limits. Explicit measures, by contrast, ask directly, and are subject to both.

The principle of correspondence predicts how each should behave. Deliberate, considered actions should be predicted better by explicit attitudes, because the person has time to apply what they endorse. Spontaneous, hard-to-monitor behaviors should be predicted better by implicit associations.

Researchers measured explicit attitudes with a questionnaire, implicit associations with a reaction-time task, and four outcomes in 800 adults, then computed the correlation of each outcome with each measure (Figure 1A). Figures 1B and 1C show two of the pairings for 30 participants each (every point is one person, drawn from the 800, with a best-fit line): explicit attitude against willingness to befriend, and implicit score against seating distance. The outcomes are labeled Befriend (self-reported willingness to befriend), Hiring form (hiring recommendation on a rated form), Seating distance (distance chosen in a waiting room) and Eye contact (duration during conversation).

The pattern is a crossover rather than a contest. The two deliberate, verbal outcomes correlate with the explicit measure at 0.61 and 0.52 and with the implicit score near 0.15, while the two spontaneous nonverbal outcomes reverse that, which is what correspondence predicts and which neither measure would produce on its own.

Several things the figure does not settle matter. All of these are correlations in a single cross-sectional sample, so nothing here shows that changing an association would change a behavior; only manipulating the association could. The figure also gives no information about the test-retest reliability of the implicit measure, a standing criticism of it, and a measure that is unstable over weeks cannot support claims about enduring individual differences even when it predicts behavior on the day of testing.

qs.q: What pattern do the correlations in Figure 1A show, which the steady upward trends in Figures 1B and 1C illustrate for two of the pairings?
o: Each measure predicts the kind of behavior that matches it
Correct: Explicit predicts deliberate outcomes, implicit predicts spontaneous ones.
Explicit self-report measures have no predictive value at all
Not quite. Explicit attitude correlates 0.61 with willingness to befriend.
The implicit score predicts every outcome better than the explicit measure
Not quite. Implicit scores predict the verbal outcomes worse (0.14, 0.19).
The two measures are interchangeable indices of the same attitude
Not quite. Each predicts different outcomes best, so they aren't interchangeable.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3's correspondence principle says deliberate actions should match explicit (stated) attitudes, and quick, hard-to-control behaviors should match implicit associations. Figure 1 shows exactly that crossover. The two deliberate verbal outcomes, willingness to befriend and hiring recommendation, correlate 0.61 and 0.52 with the explicit measure but only 0.14 and 0.19 with the implicit score. The two spontaneous nonverbal outcomes, seating distance and eye contact, flip it: 0.43 and 0.38 with implicit, 0.17 and 0.12 with explicit. Why the others are wrong: the implicit score doesn't predict everything better, since it's weaker for the verbal outcomes; the measures aren't interchangeable, because each predicts a different kind of outcome best; explicit self-report clearly has value, reaching 0.61. Trap: Reading the question as 'which measure is better overall'.

qs.q: Which of the outcomes measured is best described as discrimination?
o: The chosen seating distance in a waiting room
Correct: Sitting farther away is actual behavior toward a person.
Agreement with an item describing a group's attributes
Not quite. Agreeing about a group's traits is a stereotype, a belief.
Self-reported willingness to befriend a stranger
Not quite. That's a reported attitude, not behavior.
The score on the reaction-time association task
Not quite. That's a lab measure, not behavior toward someone.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines discrimination as behavior that treats people differently based on their group. Choosing to sit farther from someone in a waiting room is an actual action toward a person, so it counts. Why the others are wrong: saying how willing you'd be to befriend someone is a reported attitude, not a behavior toward anyone; the reaction-time score is a lab measure of a presumed association, not a behavior toward a person; agreeing with a statement about a group's traits is endorsing a stereotype, which is a belief. Trap: Sorting by how negative something sounds instead of asking whether it's actually behavior.

qs.q: Which standing criticism of implicit measures do these data leave untouched?
o: Whether it relates to nonverbal behavior specifically
Not quite. Seating and eye contact address nonverbal behavior directly.
Whether the measure predicts any behavior at all
Not quite. Correlations of 0.43 and 0.38 show it predicts some behavior.
Whether the measure is stable when a person is retested
Correct: Each person was tested once, so stability over time is untested.
Whether it diverges from what people report explicitly
Not quite. The crossover shows how it differs from explicit reports.
qs.x: Correct: Test-retest reliability asks whether the same person gets a similar score when tested again. Checking that requires testing people twice. Paragraph 6 says the figure gives no information on it, because each person was tested once. So the criticism that implicit scores jump around from session to session isn't answered here. Why the others are wrong: whether it predicts behavior at all is addressed, since it correlates 0.43 and 0.38 with the nonverbal outcomes; whether it differs from explicit reports is addressed by the crossover; whether it relates to nonverbal behavior is addressed by the seating and eye-contact bars. Trap: Picking the most familiar criticism even though the data actually speak to it.

qs.q: Which correlation in Figure 1A is the largest in absolute value?
o: Not quite. 0.19 is one of the smallest values.
Not quite. 0.43 is the top implicit value, but 0.61 is bigger.
Not quite. 0.52 is second largest, below 0.61.
Correct: 0.61, explicit attitude with willingness to befriend, is the largest.
qs.x: Correct: Absolute value means ignore any minus sign and just look at size. Every correlation in Figure 1 is positive, so just find the biggest number. Explicit bars: 0.61, 0.52, 0.17, 0.12. Implicit bars: 0.14, 0.19, 0.43, 0.38. The largest is 0.61, explicit attitude with self-reported willingness to befriend. That makes sense, since both are things people say about themselves in the same session. Why the others are wrong: 0.19 is the implicit score with hiring, one of the smallest; 0.43 is the biggest implicit correlation but still smaller than 0.61; 0.52 is the second largest overall. Trap: Picking the largest implicit correlation because the implicit measure is the new and interesting one.

qs.q: Which change to the design would permit a causal claim?
o: Add a third and a fourth nonverbal behavioral outcome
Not quite. More outcomes are still just correlations.
Measure explicit attitudes twice rather than once
Not quite. Measuring twice speaks to reliability, not cause.
Increase the sample from 800 adults to 2,000 or more participants
Not quite. A bigger sample makes estimates sharper but stays correlational.
Experimentally alter the associations and then measure behavior
Correct: Changing the association yourself is what lets you claim cause.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says every number here is a correlation from one sample at one time, so nothing shows that changing an association would change behavior; only manipulating the association could. To make a causal claim, you have to change the suspected cause yourself and see if the behavior follows. For example, train people on a different association, then measure seating distance and eye contact. Why the others are wrong: a bigger sample makes the correlations more precise but they're still correlations; adding more nonverbal outcomes still just gives more correlations; measuring explicit attitudes twice speaks to reliability, not cause. Trap: Mistaking a more precise correlation for evidence of cause.

passages.title: Tumor Angiogenesis and the Diffusion Limit
text: A cell more than a few hundred micrometers from a blood vessel cannot obtain enough oxygen by diffusion alone, so any mass of tissue larger than that must acquire a blood supply or stop growing. A mass that has not acquired one reaches a size at which cells at the center die as fast as cells at the edge divide, and the mass stops enlarging while remaining alive.

Acquiring a supply involves releasing a factor that causes nearby vessels to grow towards the mass. Release of that factor is itself triggered by low oxygen, so the mass that most needs a supply is the one that signals most strongly for it, and the signal stops when the supply arrives.

Tumor masses were implanted into tissue either with or without an inhibitor of the growth factor, and size, vessel density and the fraction of dying cells were measured over six weeks (Figure 1). In the figure, "low dose" and "high dose" refer to the inhibitor dose, and "oxygen raised" to the high dose with extra oxygen supplied.

Without the inhibitor the masses reached 11 mm with a dense vessel network and only 4% of cells dying. The high dose of inhibitor held them to under 2 mm with almost no vessels and a quarter of cells dying, while the fraction of dividing cells was essentially unchanged across every condition at around 21%.

That the dividing fraction did not change is the central result. The inhibitor did not slow division; it limited the size that could be supported, and the mass stopped enlarging because cells were dying at the center at the same rate as cells were being produced at the edge.

Raising the oxygen available to the tissue in the presence of the high dose allowed the masses to reach 4 mm with the vessel count still at three. Oxygen reached the interior by diffusion from a richer source rather than through new vessels, which separates the supply of oxygen from the growth of vessels as the thing that actually limits size.

Two qualifications apply. Vessels per field counts vessel cross sections in a stained section, and a field at the edge of a mass contains vessels of the surrounding tissue as well as vessels that grew into the mass, so the count at low vessel density is the least reliable. And the dying cell fraction is measured at one moment and depends on how long a dying cell remains recognizable, so a change in that interval would change the fraction without any change in the rate of death.

qs.q: Why does a mass without a blood supply stop enlarging while remaining alive?
o: The whole mass dies at that size
Edge cells survive and keep dividing.
Division ceases in such a mass
The dividing fraction stays near 21%.
New vessels grow into it
It has no blood supply.
Death at the center matches division
Correct: deaths at the center balance divisions at the edge, so net growth is zero.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says oxygen can only diffuse a few hundred micrometers from a vessel. In a mass with no blood supply, cells too far from the edge run out of oxygen and die, while cells at the edge keep dividing. Once the mass reaches a size where the center dies as fast as the edge divides, the net change is zero. The mass stops growing but is still alive. Figure 1C backs this up: even at the high inhibitor dose, about 20% of cells are dividing. Why the others are wrong: division doesn't stop, the dividing fraction stays near 21%; the whole mass doesn't die, the edge cells survive and divide; no new vessels grow in, that's the point. Trap: Assuming a mass that stops growing must have stopped dividing.

qs.q: Why does the passage call the unchanged fraction of dividing cells the central result?
o: It shows oxygen does not affect division
Oxygen was tested separately.
It shows division was not slowed
Correct: division stayed near 21%, so the inhibitor limited size, not division.
It shows the cells became resistant
Size still fell, so there was no resistance.
It shows the inhibitor acted on dividing cells
Not quite. The dividing fraction stayed near 21%, so the inhibitor didn't act on division.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 calls this the central result. Across every condition, the dividing fraction stays at about 21% (20 to 22% in Figure 1C). So the inhibitor didn't slow division. Instead, by blocking new vessels, it limited how big a mass could be kept alive. Cells kept dividing at the edge, but more died in the center: 4% dying with no inhibitor against 26% at the high dose. Why the others are wrong: the inhibitor didn't act on division, the dividing fraction stayed near 21%; the oxygen condition is a separate test and isn't what this result shows; and the cells didn't become resistant, size still fell. Trap: Ignoring the number that didn't change, when it's the one that rules out an explanation.

qs.q: What does adding extra oxygen at the high inhibitor dose allow the researchers to distinguish?
o: Division from death
Division and death were measured everywhere.
The inhibitor's effect from the implantation procedure
Implantation was the same in every condition.
Oxygen supply from vessel growth
Correct: size rose with more oxygen but no new vessels, so oxygen is the real limit.
The low dose from the high dose
Not quite. Only the high dose was tested with extra oxygen, so this condition can't compare doses.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 explains it. At the high inhibitor dose, raising oxygen let masses grow from 1.9 to 4.1 mm (Figure 1A) with almost no new vessels. Oxygen reached the interior by diffusing from a richer supply, not through new vessels. Vessels are normally just how oxygen gets delivered, so this shows the real limit on size is oxygen, not vessels themselves. Why the others are wrong: the implantation procedure was the same in every condition, so nothing separates it; division and death were measured in every condition, so this condition doesn't separate them; and the oxygen condition used only the high dose, so it can't compare the two doses. Trap: Treating a delivery route and the thing it delivers as the same.

qs.q: According to the passage, why is the vessel count least reliable when vessel density is low?
o: Surrounding vessels are included
Correct: neighboring vessels get counted, and at low counts they make up a big share.
The stain fails when vessels are sparse
The passage gives no sign the stain fails.
Dying cells hide vessels at low density
Not quite. The passage doesn't say this. The issue is edge vessels from the surrounding tissue.
Counts were made at only one time point
Not quite. That concern applies to the dying-cell fraction, not the vessel count.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says a field at the edge of a mass includes vessels from the surrounding tissue, not just ones that grew into the mass. That adds a roughly fixed number to every count. When a mass has 34 vessels, a couple of extra ones barely matter. When it has only 3, those extra ones could be most of the count. Why the others are wrong: the passage gives no sign the stain fails when vessels are sparse; it says nothing about dying cells hiding vessels; and the single-moment problem belongs to the dying-cell fraction, not the vessel count. Trap: Assuming an error that adds a fixed amount affects big and small counts equally.

qs.q: How many times larger in diameter is the untreated mass than the high dose mass?
o: That's the high-dose diameter.
That's the difference, 11.4 − 1.9, not a ratio.
That's the untreated diameter.
qs.x: Correct: Times larger = untreated diameter ÷ high-dose diameter. From Figure 1A, the untreated mass is 11.4 mm and the high-dose mass is 1.9 mm. Plug in: 11.4 ÷ 1.9. Check it: 1.9 × 6 = 11.4, so the answer is exactly 6. Why the others are wrong: 11.4 is the untreated diameter itself; 1.9 is the treated diameter; 9.5 is the difference, 11.4 − 1.9 = 9.5, not how many times larger. Trap: Subtracting when the question asks "how many times."
