passages.title: Milgram-Style Obedience Experiments
text: Obedience research asks what makes an ordinary person carry out instructions that harm someone else. In the standard paradigm a participant is told to deliver increasing electric shocks to another person who is in fact a confederate and receives none, and the measure is the fraction who continue to the maximum level on the generator.

Two accounts compete. A dispositional account locates obedience in the person, so the people who continue would be unusually callous. A situational account locates it in the features of the setting: the physical presence of a legitimate authority, the distance of the victim, the absence of visible dissent, and a graded sequence of requests in which each step is barely worse than the one before. The experimental strategy is therefore to hold the task constant and vary one situational feature at a time.

Participants were drawn from the same community sample and randomly assigned across five variations, each identical to the baseline procedure except in the feature named (Figure 1): baseline (authority present, victim in another room), victim seated in the same room, authority giving instructions by telephone, two confederates refusing to continue, and instructions given by an ordinary person with no authority.

Every manipulation moved the rate, and the largest single drop, to 10%, came from watching two other apparently ordinary participants refuse. Making the victim visible cut obedience by 25 points, and removing either the authority's presence or the authority's legitimacy produced similar rates near 20%, which suggests that presence and legitimacy contribute in comparable measure.

What the design can and cannot show is worth separating. Random assignment across variations licenses causal claims about the situational features. The design says nothing, however, about which individuals obey, because personality was not measured; the finding is that the rate is movable, not that dispositions are irrelevant. The procedure also depends on participants believing the shocks were real, and it deliberately imposed severe distress, which is why review boards would not approve it today and why replications use milder analogs.

qs.q: Which variation produced the largest reduction in obedience?
o: The authority gives instructions by telephone
That leaves 21%.
The victim is seated in the same room as the participant
That leaves 40%, a 25-point drop.
Instructions come from an ordinary person rather than an authority
That leaves 20%.
Two confederates refuse to continue
Correct: it falls to 10%, a 55-point drop from 65%.
qs.x: Correct: Read the bars in Figure 1. The baseline is 65%. The lowest number is 10%, when two confederates refused to continue. That's a drop of 65 − 10 = 55 points, the biggest in the figure. Paragraph 4 says the same thing: seeing ordinary peers refuse had the strongest effect. Why the others are wrong: seating the victim in the same room left 40%, a drop of 65 − 40 = 25 points; telephone instructions left 21%; an ordinary person giving orders left 20%. All of those are well above 10%. Trap: Picking the condition that sounds most dramatic instead of reading the numbers.

qs.q: What do the five variations taken together support?
o: Situational features substantially determine the rate
Correct: every single change in the situation moved the rate.
Obedience cannot be studied experimentally
These are experiments, so it clearly can be studied.
Obedience is fixed by stable features of personality
Personality was never varied or measured.
The people who continue are unusually cruel
No trait like cruelty was measured.
qs.x: Correct: The design keeps the task the same and changes one feature of the situation at a time (paragraph 2). Every change moved the obedience rate, from 65% at baseline down to as low as 10%. Since people were randomly assigned to conditions (paragraph 3), the groups were alike, so the differences come from the situation, not from who was recruited. Why the others are wrong: personality was never varied or measured, so we can't say it fixes obedience; the same is true for the claim that people who continue are unusually cruel; and these data come from experiments, so obedience clearly can be studied that way. Trap: Concluding personality doesn't matter at all, when the study simply never measured it.

qs.q: Why is the condition with an ordinary person giving instructions informative?
o: It demonstrates that no one obeys instructions from anybody
One in five still continued.
It provides a measure of how distressed the victim appeared
The victim's behavior was the same in every condition.
It separates legitimacy from the instruction itself
Correct: same orders, no authority, so it isolates legitimacy.
It proves that the authority's presence is entirely irrelevant
The telephone condition shows presence matters too.
qs.x: Correct: In this condition, the orders were the same, but they came from an ordinary person instead of an authority figure. So it pulls apart two things: the instructions themselves and the legitimacy (rightful authority) of the person giving them. Obedience fell from 65% to 20%, so the legitimacy of the authority, not the content of the orders, carries much of the baseline obedience. Why the others are wrong: 20% still continued, about one in five, so people did obey somebody; the telephone condition (21%) shows the authority's presence matters too, so it isn't irrelevant; the victim's behavior was the same in every condition, so this one doesn't measure the victim's distress. Trap: Reading a big drop as if it were zero.

qs.q: Which concept best explains why a present, legitimate authority raises obedience?
o: The authority is physically compelling compliance
No physical force was used.
Responsibility is shifted to the authority
Correct: the authority takes responsibility, so participants feel like tools, not agents.
Participants had not understood the task instructions
Nothing suggests the instructions were misunderstood.
Participants find delivering shocks intrinsically rewarding
The procedure caused severe distress, not enjoyment.
qs.x: Correct: When a legitimate authority is right there and takes responsibility for what happens, participants start to see themselves as carrying out someone else's plan, not as the one causing harm. That shift in responsibility lowers the felt cost of continuing. Paragraph 2 lists the physical presence of a legitimate authority as a key feature, and taking it away (by phone, 21%) or making the instructor ordinary (20%) cut obedience sharply from 65%. Why the others are wrong: nothing suggests participants enjoyed giving shocks, and paragraph 5 says the procedure caused severe distress; no force was used; nothing suggests the instructions were misunderstood. Trap: Looking for a motive to harm when the real mechanism is a shift in who feels responsible.

qs.q: What would these data not establish?
o: That visible dissent by peers reduces obedience sharply
Shown: the rate fell to 10%.
Which individuals are most likely to comply
Correct: no trait of the participants was measured, so it can't say who obeys.
That the legitimacy of the authority affects compliance
Shown: an ordinary person got only 20%.
That victim proximity reduces the rate of obedience
Shown: same-room victim cut the rate by 25 points.
qs.x: Correct: Every condition changed the situation, and nothing about the participants themselves, like personality, was measured (paragraph 5). So the study can tell you which situations raise or lower obedience, but not which people are more likely to obey. Why the others are wrong: seating the victim in the same room cut obedience from 65% to 40%, a 25-point drop, so proximity is established; two refusing confederates cut it to 10%, so dissent is established; an ordinary person giving orders got only 20%, so legitimacy is established. Each of these was tested with random assignment, so the data support all three. Trap: Assuming a well-designed experiment answers every question about its topic.

passages.title: Social Facilitation and Task Difficulty
text: The presence of others changes performance, and the direction depends on the task. Social facilitation is the improvement seen on simple or well-learned tasks when others are present; impairment appears on complex or novel tasks. Zajonc's account is that the presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant. On a well-practiced task the dominant response is the correct one, so performance improves; on a novel task the dominant responses are errors, so performance worsens.

Social loafing is a different phenomenon that is easily confused with it. Loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when contributions are pooled and no one's output can be identified, and its remedy is making individual contributions visible, which is close to the opposite of removing an audience.

Participants completed two tasks either alone in a cubicle or at a desk observed by two silent confederates, with task and audience condition crossed so that each cell had a separate group of participants. Scores are percent correct (Figure 1); each of the four cells had 25 participants. Each point in Figure 1 is one participant, and the legend gives the mean of each cell; 10 participants per cell are plotted, drawn from the full groups.

The crossover is the result. An audience adds 9 points to typing and removes 15 points from the logic puzzle, so the effect of being watched reverses with the nature of the task, which no account positing a single direction of effect can produce.

Arousal was not measured, and that is the gap. The arousal account predicts the crossover, but so does an account in which an audience consumes attention that complex tasks require and simple ones do not, and these data cannot distinguish them. Recording heart rate or skin conductance would show whether arousal rose, and manipulating how much attention the audience demanded, for instance by having observers face away, would separate the two. The between-groups design also means that differences between the people assigned to each cell contribute to the variance, and a within-subject design would be more sensitive if practice effects could be controlled.

qs.q: Why does an audience help typing and hurt the logic puzzle?
o: Arousal improves performance on any task at all
The puzzle score fell by 15 points.
Logic puzzles require no attention to solve
Logic puzzles need a lot of attention.
Arousal strengthens whichever response is dominant
Correct: arousal boosts the dominant response, right for typing, wrong for a new puzzle.
An audience distracts only while typing
Typing improved with an audience, 82 to 91.
qs.x: Correct: Zajonc's idea (paragraph 1) is that having others around raises arousal, your body's level of alertness, and arousal strengthens your dominant response, whatever you're most likely to do. On a well-practiced task like typing, the dominant response is the right keystroke, so an audience helps: 82 alone rose to 91 with an audience, up 91 − 82 = 9 points (Figure 1). On a new logic puzzle, your most likely responses are mistakes, so the same arousal hurts: 64 fell to 49, down 64 − 49 = 15 points. One cause, two opposite effects. Why the others are wrong: logic puzzles need lots of attention, not none; arousal didn't help on every task, since the puzzle score dropped 15 points; typing got better with an audience, so the audience wasn't distracting there. Trap: Expecting an audience to push performance in only one direction.

qs.q: How does social loafing differ from social facilitation?
o: It describes better group performance
It describes less individual effort, not better group performance.
It concerns pooled effort that cannot be identified
Correct: loafing happens when pooled effort can't be traced to any one person.
It requires an audience to be present and watching closely
Being watched reduces loafing.
It occurs only when a task is simple
Loafing isn't limited to simple tasks.
qs.x: Correct: Social loafing is slacking off when everyone's work is pooled together and nobody can tell who did what (paragraph 2). The fix is to make each person's contribution visible. Social facilitation is about being watched while you work on your own task. So loafing is about whether your effort can be identified, not about having an audience. Why the others are wrong: loafing isn't limited to simple tasks; it describes people putting in less effort, not a group doing better; and being watched closely actually reduces loafing, because it makes each person's work identifiable. Trap: Lumping the two together just because both involve other people.

qs.q: Which measurement would best distinguish the arousal account from an attention account?
o: The time each participant spent on the task
Time on task measures effort.
Participants' ratings of how much they liked the task
Liking a task measures preference.
The number of observers present in the room
That changes the manipulation, not the mechanism.
Physiological arousal recorded during each task
Correct: it directly checks whether arousal, the proposed middle step, actually rose.
qs.x: Correct: Both accounts predict the same crossover in scores (paragraph 5), so scores alone can't separate them. The arousal account says something happens in between: arousal rises, then performance changes. That in-between step is called a mediator. If you record arousal directly, with heart rate or skin conductance (sweat on the skin), you can check whether it really rose. The attention account doesn't need arousal to rise at all. Why the others are wrong: changing how many observers are present just makes the manipulation stronger, without showing how it works; time on task measures effort; liking the task measures preference. None of those is the mediator either account proposes. Trap: Making the manipulation stronger instead of measuring the step in between.

qs.q: How could the puzzle result be reduced in a workplace?
o: Allow practice before anyone is observed
Correct: practice makes the right response dominant, so arousal helps instead of hurts.
Add more observers to the room during the task
More observers would strengthen the drop.
Increase the time pressure on the task as well
More pressure raises arousal further.
Require that the task be done in public first
Doing a new task in public is what hurt scores.
qs.x: Correct: Performance on the puzzle got worse with an audience because, on a new task, mistakes are the dominant response (paragraph 1). If people practice first, the correct response becomes dominant. Then the audience's arousal boosts the right answers instead of the wrong ones, just like it did for typing (82 to 91). Why the others are wrong: doing the task in public first is exactly the condition that hurt scores (64 fell to 49); more time pressure raises arousal even further, which strengthens the errors; more observers also raise arousal, which makes the drop worse. Trap: Treating the audience effect as something to put up with, when practice can flip it into a benefit.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the logic puzzle was novel?
o: Novelty makes incorrect responses the dominant ones
Correct: on a new task, wrong responses are dominant, and arousal strengthens them.
Novelty removes arousal from the situation
Novelty doesn't remove arousal.
Novel tasks cannot be scored for accuracy
The puzzle was scored as percent correct.
Novel tasks are easier to perform than well-practiced tasks
Novel tasks are harder, not easier.
qs.x: Correct: The whole account depends on which response is dominant (paragraph 1). On an unfamiliar task, the responses that come to mind first are usually wrong. Arousal from the audience strengthens those wrong responses, so the score drops, from 64 to 49 in Figure 1. If the puzzle were familiar, the right response would be dominant and the audience would help. Why the others are wrong: the puzzle was scored as percent correct, so novel tasks can be scored; novel tasks are harder than practiced ones, not easier; and novelty doesn't remove arousal, the audience still raises it. Trap: Thinking novelty matters because of how the task is scored, when it matters because it changes which response is dominant.

passages.title: Timing the Phases of the Cell Cycle
text: A dividing cell passes through a repeating sequence of stages: a period of growth, a period in which the stored material is duplicated, a second period of growth, and the division itself. The total time is the sum of the four, and the stages differ greatly in length.

Measuring the individual stages requires something that distinguishes them, because a population of cells is distributed among all four at once. The proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to that stage's share of the total time, which converts a single snapshot into timings.
Cell populations were examined in five cultures (Table 1). Figure 1 plots the duplication period listed for each culture against the share of cells duplicating multiplied by the cycle time.

T1 has 30% of its cells duplicating and a cycle of 20 hours, which gives a duplication period of six hours. T2 has the same proportion with a cycle twice as long and a duplication period twice as long, because the proportion fixes the share and not the time.
T3 has twice T1's proportion at the same cycle time and twice the duplication period, and T4 has half the proportion and half the period. The conversion holds in both directions.

T5 is the culture whose figures disagree. It has T1's proportion and T1's cycle time, so its duplication period must be six hours, and it is tabulated as 12. Two of its entries determine the third and contradict it.

The 5% of cells dividing in every culture gives a dividing period of about an hour in the 20-hour cycles, which illustrates how short that stage is relative to the rest despite being the only one visible under a microscope.

The general statement is that a proportion gives a share of the cycle and must be multiplied by the cycle time to give a duration, so two cultures with identical proportions can have very different stage lengths.

Two qualifications apply. The method assumes the population is growing steadily with cells spread through the cycle in proportion to stage length, which fails in a culture recently disturbed. And cells were assigned to stages by appearance and by the amount of stored material, which does not separate the two growth periods from each other.

qs.q: Why is the duplication period in T2 twice as long as in T1?
o: Its cycle is twice as long
Correct: Same 30% share, but of a 40-hour cycle instead of 20.
Its dividing proportion is higher
Both have 5% of cells dividing.
Its dividing stage is longer
The dividing share is 5% in both, so it doesn't explain the difference.
Its proportion duplicating is higher
Both T1 and T2 have 30% of cells duplicating.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the percent of cells in a stage tells you that stage's share of the cycle, not its length in hours. To get hours, multiply the share by the cycle time. T1 and T2 both have 30% of cells duplicating, so duplication takes the same share of the cycle in both. But T2's cycle is 40 hours versus T1's 20. 30% of 20 h = 6 h, and 30% of 40 h = 12 h. Same share, twice the cycle, twice the hours. Why the others are wrong: T2's proportion duplicating isn't higher, both are 30%; its dividing proportion isn't higher, both are 5%; and its dividing stage has the same 5% share, which doesn't explain a longer duplication period. Trap: Reading a percentage of cells as if it were a length of time.

qs.q: Which observation shows that division takes up only a small part of the cell cycle?
o: The dividing stage is visible under a microscope
Not quite. Being visible says nothing about how long a stage lasts.
Only 5% of cells are dividing
Correct: Only 5% of cells are in it, about 1 hour of a 20-hour cycle.
Cycle times range from 20 to 40 hours
Not quite. Cycle time alone doesn't give the share spent dividing.
60% of T3's cells are duplicating
Not quite. That's T3's duplicating share, not the dividing share.
qs.x: Correct: Stage length = share of cells × cycle time. Paragraph 7 says 5% of cells are dividing in every culture. For a 20-hour cycle: 5% = 0.05, and 0.05 × 20 h = 1 h. So division takes about an hour out of 20, a twentieth of the cycle. That's very short compared with the other stages, even though division is the only stage you can actually see under a microscope. Why the others are wrong: being visible under a microscope says nothing about how long a stage lasts; cycle time alone doesn't give the share spent dividing; and 60% is T3's duplicating share, while only 5% of cells are dividing. Trap: Assuming the stage that's easiest to see must last the longest.

qs.q: Why does the passage say the figures for T5 disagree?
o: Two entries fix the third
Correct: 30% of 20 hours is 6 hours, but the listed time is 12.
Its share is twice T1's
Not quite. T5's share duplicating is 30%, the same as T1's.
Its cells are dividing faster
Not quite. T5's dividing fraction is 5%, the same as every culture.
Its cycle is twice T1's
Not quite. T5's cycle is 20 hours, the same as T1's.
qs.x: Correct: Duplication time = share duplicating × cycle time. For T5, share = 30% = 0.30 and cycle time = 20 h. Plug in: 0.30 × 20 = 6 h. Figure 1 shows the point for T5 at 12 h, well above the line, where 6 h is expected. Since the first two numbers fix the third, they can't all be right, and paragraph 5 says the row contradicts itself. Why the others are wrong: T5's cycle isn't twice T1's, both are 20 hours; its share isn't twice T1's, both are 30%; and its cells aren't dividing faster, its dividing fraction is the same 5%. Trap: Treating three numbers as three independent measurements when two of them determine the third.

qs.q: Why does the method fail in a disturbed culture?
o: Disturbance shortens the cycle
The passage's concern is uneven spread, not cycle length.
Disturbance spreads cells more evenly
Disturbance bunches cells up; it doesn't spread them evenly.
The method makes no assumption about spread
The method depends on that assumption (paragraph 9).
Cells may not be spread evenly
Correct: Cells may bunch up instead of being spread in proportion to stage length.
qs.x: Correct: The whole method rests on one assumption (paragraph 9): in a steadily growing population, cells are spread through the cycle in proportion to how long each stage lasts. A recent disturbance, like a shock that pauses many cells at once, bunches cells up at particular stages. Then the percent of cells in a stage no longer matches its share of the time, and the conversion gives wrong answers. Why the others are wrong: disturbance bunches cells up, it doesn't spread them more evenly; the method does assume an even spread, it depends on it; and shortening the cycle isn't the issue raised, the problem is that cells are no longer spread in proportion to stage length. Trap: Using a formula built for a steady population on one that isn't steady.

qs.q: How long is T4's duplication period, in hours?
o: That's T1's duplication time.
That's the percentage of cells, not hours.
That's the whole cycle time.
qs.x: Correct: Duplication time = share duplicating × cycle time. From Table 1, T4's share = 15% = 0.15 and cycle time = 20 h. Plug in: 0.15 × 20. 0.1 × 20 = 2 and 0.05 × 20 = 1, so 2 + 1 = 3 h. That's half of T1's 6 hours, matching half the share (15% versus 30%). Why the others are wrong: 15 is the percentage of cells, not hours; 6 is T1's duplication time; and 20 is the whole cycle time. Trap: Reading the percentage as if it were already in hours.

passages.title: Phases of Bacterial Growth in Batch Culture
text: A bacterial population introduced into fresh medium grows through a sequence of stages. For a time the numbers hardly change while the cells adjust, then they double at a constant interval, then the doubling slows and stops, and finally the numbers fall. Each stage has a different limiting factor.
The stages are distinguished by the doubling interval rather than by the number of cells, because a count alone does not say whether the population is accelerating, steady or declining.

Counts and intervals were recorded through one growth curve (Figure 1). The doubling interval was 36 minutes from 2 to 8 hours and 240 minutes from 8 to 12 hours, with none assigned in the first two hours or after 12 hours. A repeat record of the 2 to 8 hour stage, with the same counts, listed an interval of 240 minutes.
In the first two hours the count is unchanged and no doubling interval can be assigned, because the cells are adjusting to the medium rather than dividing.

From two to eight hours the count rises a thousand fold with a doubling interval of 36 minutes, which is about 10 doublings in six hours. The nutrient is still abundant, so nothing is limiting growth.

From eight to 12 hours the interval lengthens nearly seven fold and the nutrient falls to 5%, which identifies the nutrient as what slows the growth. After 12 hours the count falls with the nutrient exhausted.

The repeat record is the one that conflicts. It covers the same six hours and the same thousand fold rise with a doubling interval of 240 minutes, which would give only one and a half doublings. The interval is determined by the counts and the time.

The general statement is that the stages are defined by rates rather than by counts, and that the rate is calculable from two counts and the interval between them, so it cannot be assigned independently.

Two qualifications apply. Counts were made by plating and counting colonies, which counts only the cells that can form colonies and so understates a population containing damaged cells. And nutrient remaining was measured for one component, so another could have run out earlier.

qs.q: Why can no doubling interval be assigned in the first stage?
o: The count does not change
Correct: the count stays at 1 × 10⁶, so there's no doubling to time.
One can be assigned regardless
Not quite. No doubling happens, so none can be assigned.
The interval is 20 minutes
Not quite. No interval applies. Figure 1 shows a flat line.
The count rises a thousand fold
Not quite. The thousand fold rise is from 2 to 8 hours.
qs.x: Correct: A doubling interval is the time it takes the cell count to double. Paragraph 4 says that in the first two hours, the lag phase, the count stays at 1 × 10⁶ cells per mL because the cells are adjusting to the new medium, not dividing. If the count never doubles, there's nothing to time, so no interval can be assigned (Figure 1: a flat line). Why the others are wrong: the thousand fold rise happens from 2 to 8 hours, not in the first stage; no interval applies here, 20 minutes or otherwise; one can't be assigned, because no doubling happens. Trap: Giving a rate to a period when the quantity isn't changing.

qs.q: Which observation identifies the nutrient as the factor that slows growth from 8 to 12 hours?
o: It rises as growth slows
It falls, it doesn't rise.
The cells run out of oxygen
Oxygen was never measured.
It remains abundant throughout
It falls to 5% by 12 hours.
It falls as growth slows
Correct: it falls from 60% to 5% as the interval stretches nearly seven fold.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 links the two. From 8 to 12 hours, the doubling interval stretches from 36 to 240 minutes, and 240 ÷ 36 ≈ 6.7, nearly seven fold. Over those same hours the nutrient drops from 60% to 5% (Figure 1B). When the slowdown happens exactly as the nutrient runs low, the nutrient is the likely limit. Why the others are wrong: the nutrient doesn't stay abundant, it falls to 5%; it falls as growth slows, it doesn't rise; oxygen was never measured, so the passage can't point to it. Trap: Naming a limiting factor without checking that it changed when the growth rate did.

qs.q: Why does the passage reject the repeat record's doubling interval of 240 minutes?
o: The interval follows from the counts
Correct: 10 doublings in 360 minutes is 36 minutes each, not 240.
Its time span differs
Both cover 2 to 8 hours.
Its counts differ from those of the original
Both rise from 1 × 10⁶ to 1 × 10⁹.
Its nutrient was used up
Its nutrient is at 60%.
qs.x: Correct: The interval can be calculated, not chosen. Number of doublings: 2 raised to the power n = fold rise. A thousand fold rise is 1 × 10⁶ to 1 × 10⁹, and 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 1000, so n ≈ 10 doublings. Interval = time ÷ doublings. The time is 2 to 8 hours = 6 hours, and 1 h = 60 min, so 6 × 60 = 360 minutes. Plug in: 360 ÷ 10 = 36 minutes. The repeat record lists 240 minutes, which would give only 360 ÷ 240 = 1.5 doublings (paragraph 7). Why the others are wrong: its counts are the same as the original record; its time span is the same, 2 to 8 hours; its nutrient is at 60%, not used up. Trap: Treating a rate figure as a separate measurement, when it follows from the counts and the time.

qs.q: Nutrient remaining was measured for one component only. Which added experiment would best test that this nutrient limits growth?
o: Add more of it at 10 hours and see whether growth resumes
Correct: If adding the nutrient restores doubling, that nutrient was the limit.
Count the colonies again after 12 hours without adding anything
Not quite. Counting again repeats the measurement without changing the nutrient, so it cannot test the claim.
Start a second culture with a lower starting count
Not quite. A smaller start changes timing, not which nutrient limits the slowdown.
Measure the doubling interval in the first two hours
Not quite. No interval exists in the first stage, and it would say nothing about the nutrient.
qs.x: Correct: To test whether a nutrient limits growth, change only that nutrient and watch the outcome. At 10 hours the nutrient is down to about 5% and the doubling interval has stretched to 240 minutes (Figure 1). Adding more of it at that point should bring the interval back toward 36 minutes if the claim is right, and should change nothing if another component is the real limit. Why the others are wrong: counting again without changing anything repeats the same measurement; a lower starting count shifts when things happen but not what limits them; the first two hours have no doubling interval to measure. Trap: Choosing a repeat of the measurement instead of a manipulation of the suspected cause.

qs.q: How many doublings does a thousand fold rise represent?
o: That's the power of 10 (10³), not of 2.
Correct: 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 1000.
That's the interval in minutes.
That's the fold rise itself.
qs.x: Correct: Each doubling multiplies the count by 2, so after n doublings the count rises by 2 raised to the power n. Set that equal to the fold rise: 2ⁿ = 1000. Count up: 2¹ = 2, 2² = 4, 2³ = 8, 2⁴ = 16, 2⁵ = 32, 2⁶ = 64, 2⁷ = 128, 2⁸ = 256, 2⁹ = 512, 2¹⁰ = 1024. Since 1024 ≈ 1000, n ≈ 10 doublings, which matches paragraph 5. Why the others are wrong: 36 is the doubling interval in minutes; 3 is the number of zeros in 1000, the power of 10 (10³), not the power of 2; 1000 is the fold rise itself. Trap: Counting powers of 10 instead of powers of 2.

passages.title: Bonding and Bridging Social Capital
text: Social capital refers to the resources a person can draw on through social relationships. The distinction that matters for outcomes is between two kinds. Bonding capital links people who are alike, typically within a family, a congregation or a block, and supplies trust, mutual aid and informal insurance. Bridging capital links people across groups and supplies what a closed circle cannot: information from outside, contacts in other institutions, and routes into labor markets a neighborhood is not already connected to.

The two kinds are not substitutes, and a neighborhood can be high on one and low on the other. A tight community with no outside links is rich in support and poor in access, which predicts resilience without mobility; a neighborhood whose residents have many outside contacts but little internal cohesion may have access without the trust needed to act collectively.

Investigators followed 90 neighborhoods in one metropolitan area for five years. Bonding and bridging indices were built from resident surveys at baseline, neighborhoods were grouped by whether each index fell above or below the metropolitan median, and the change in the employment rate over the five years was recorded from administrative data (Table 1). Figure 1 shows the routes by which each kind of capital is thought to act.

Bridging is what moves employment: the two high-bridging groups gain 2.9 and 4.1 points while the high-bonding, low-bridging group is flat at 0.4. Bonding is not useless, though, because adding it to high bridging raises the gain from 2.9 to 4.1, which is consistent with internal trust helping a neighborhood act on outside information.

Nothing was assigned here. Neighborhoods were classified on characteristics they already had, and the kind of place that develops outside ties is also likely to differ in transit access, in the age and education of its residents, and in how far it sits from areas where employment was growing anyway. A measure of the pathway would help: if bridging capital works through information, then counting job referrals received by residents would show the mechanism directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the employment column.

qs.q: Which kind of capital best predicts employment gains in Table 1?
o: Bonding capital on its own, without outside ties
Not quite. High bonding with low bridging gained only +0.4.
Bridging capital, the ties that link across groups
Correct: Both high-bridging groups gained most, +2.9 and +4.1.
Both indices contributed in equal measure here
Not quite. Bonding alone did little; bridging does most of the work.
Neither index related to employment
Not quite. The groups range from −1.1 to +4.1, a 5.2-point spread.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the employment change column in Table 1. The two high-bridging groups gained the most: +2.9 (low bonding, high bridging) and +4.1 (high on both). The high-bonding, low-bridging group barely moved at +0.4. So bridging capital, the ties that link people across groups, is doing most of the work. Bonding helps too, but only on top of bridging: adding it lifts the gain from 2.9 to 4.1 (4.1 − 2.9 = 1.2 points). Why the others are wrong: bonding alone was nearly flat at +0.4; the indices clearly relate to employment, since the groups range from −1.1 to +4.1, a spread of 4.1 − (−1.1) = 4.1 + 1.1 = 5.2 points; the two don't contribute equally, because high bonding without bridging gained little. Trap: Splitting the difference when the table clearly favors one kind of capital.

qs.q: What does bonding capital typically supply?
o: A household's own financial assets
Not quite. Personal savings are individual wealth, not social capital.
Access to institutions outside the neighborhood
Not quite. Outside access is what bridging capital supplies.
Formal authority over local decisions
Not quite. Formal authority comes from office, not relationships.
Support and mutual aid within a group
Correct: Bonding ties supply trust, mutual aid and support within a group.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says bonding capital links people who are alike, like family, a congregation or a block, and supplies trust, mutual aid and informal insurance. In short, support within a group. That's why paragraph 2 says a tight community with no outside links is rich in support but poor in access. Why the others are wrong: access to outside institutions is what bridging capital supplies; formal authority over local decisions comes from holding office, not from relationships; a household's own savings is individual wealth, not a resource drawn through social ties. Trap: Counting any useful resource as social capital.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects a causal reading of these results?
o: The follow-up period extended over five years
Not quite. Five years is appropriate for employment change.
Employment change was taken from administrative tax records
Not quite. Administrative records are a strength.
Neighborhoods were classified, not assigned, by type
Correct: Neighborhoods were sorted by existing traits, so other differences could explain the gains.
90 neighborhoods were followed for the study
Not quite. 90 neighborhoods is a reasonable number.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says nothing was assigned. Neighborhoods were sorted by traits they already had. Places with lots of outside ties may also have better transit, more educated residents, or be closer to areas where jobs were growing anyway. Any of those could produce the employment gains, so we can't be sure bridging capital caused them. Why the others are wrong: administrative records are a strong, objective source for employment; 90 neighborhoods is a reasonable number to compare; five years is a sensible period for seeing employment change. Trap: Looking for a flaw in measurement when the problem is that the groups weren't assigned.

qs.q: Which type of neighborhood lost employment over the five years?
o: The neighborhoods low on both indices
Correct: Low on both, with a 1.1-point decline.
High bonding, low bridging capital
Not quite. This group gained 0.4 points.
High on both of the two indices
Not quite. This group gained 4.1 points.
Low bonding, high bridging capital
Not quite. This group gained 2.9 points.
qs.x: Correct: Look for a negative number in the employment column of Table 1. Only the low-bonding, low-bridging group has one: −1.1, meaning its employment rate fell by 1.1 points. With neither inside trust nor outside links, these neighborhoods had nothing to cushion them. Why the others are wrong: high bonding, low bridging gained 0.4; low bonding, high bridging gained 2.9; high on both gained 4.1. Trap: Mistaking the smallest gain (+0.4) for a loss.

qs.q: Which additional measure would best show the pathway by which bridging capital acts?
o: The number of job referrals residents received
Correct: Job referrals measure the information flow bridging ties should carry.
The average number of years residents had lived there
Not quite. Years lived there measures stability.
The total number of residents in each neighborhood
Not quite. Population measures size, not information flow.
The median housing price within each neighborhood
Not quite. Housing price measures affluence.
qs.x: Correct: The idea is that bridging capital works by carrying information from outside, like job leads. Paragraph 5 suggests counting the job referrals residents received. That measures the in-between step directly, instead of guessing it from the employment numbers it's supposed to explain. Why the others are wrong: years lived in the neighborhood measures stability, not information flow; median housing price measures how well-off the area is; the number of residents measures size. None of them shows information reaching people. Trap: Adding a reasonable control variable instead of measuring the mechanism.

passages.title: Siting Versus Move-In Explanations of Environmental Injustice
text: Environmental justice research examines whether environmental hazards and benefits are distributed unevenly across groups. Two explanations are debated. In the siting explanation, polluting facilities are built in neighborhoods with less political power. In the move-in explanation, housing near existing facilities is cheaper, so lower-income households move there afterward. The two can be separated only by data that record the order of events.

Researchers linked the locations of 1,100 industrial facilities that report toxic releases to census data for the surrounding tracts across three decades. For each facility, they recorded the characteristics of its tract in the decade before it opened and in the two decades after. They also measured ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and, from a state health registry, the rate of childhood asthma emergency visits. Figure 1A shows tract characteristics before and after siting, and Figures 1B and 1C show the exposure measures.

To check that the comparison tracts were reasonable, the researchers matched each facility tract to a tract in the same metropolitan area with similar population density and distance from the city center, since both affect land cost and the kinds of businesses that locate there. They also repeated the analysis using only facilities that opened in the middle decade, so that a full decade of data was available on each side of the opening, and the pattern was unchanged. Facilities that had closed during the study period were analyzed separately; disparities in those tracts persisted after closure, although PM2.5 in them fell toward the level of the comparison tracts within a few years of closure.

The researchers noted that income and demographic composition in these tracts were already different from comparison tracts before siting and changed only modestly afterward. They also noted that tracts were not assigned at random, that asthma has other causes including indoor allergens and secondhand smoke, and that people who live in a tract today may have moved there recently.

qs.q: What do the before-siting figures most directly address?
o: Whether the facilities comply with rules
Not quite. Regulatory compliance wasn't studied.
Whether PM2.5 causes asthma
Not quite. Air and asthma are in the exposure panels (Figures 1B and 1C), not the before-siting bars.
Whether residents support the facilities
Not quite. Residents' opinions were never surveyed.
Whether disparities came before the facilities
Correct: they show the gaps existed before the facilities, which tests move-in against siting.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 gives two explanations. Siting says facilities get built where people have less political power. Move-in says lower-income families move near facilities later, because housing there is cheaper. Paragraph 1 adds that only the order of events can tell them apart. The before-siting bars in Figure 1A give exactly that order. A decade before any facility opened, those tracts already had lower income (71% of the state median against 99%), more residents of color (46% against 24%) and lower homeownership (41% against 63%). The gaps came first, which points to siting rather than move-in. Why the others are wrong: Whether PM2.5 causes asthma is a health question answered by the exposure panels, not by tract makeup before siting; whether residents support the facilities was never surveyed; whether facilities follow regulations wasn't studied. Trap: Using any disparity as proof of one explanation without checking when it appeared.

qs.q: Why is the modest change after siting important?
o: It argues against later turnover
Correct: income and makeup barely shifted after siting, which argues against later move-in.
It shows the facilities later closed
Not quite. Closures were analyzed separately; this change says nothing about them.
It shows residents were unaffected
Not quite. PM2.5 and asthma visits are higher in facility tracts.
It proves the facilities cause poverty
Not quite. Income was already low a decade before siting.
qs.x: Correct: The move-in explanation predicts that once a facility opens, the tract changes a lot as lower-income families arrive. Figure 1A shows only small shifts. Median income went from 71% to 68% of the state median, a drop of 3 points. The share of residents of color went from 46% to 52%, a rise of 6 points. Those are tiny next to the gaps that already existed before siting (71 against 99 for income, 46 against 24 for residents of color). So the data argue against large turnover after siting. Why the others are wrong: Proving facilities cause poverty can't work, since income was already low before they arrived; saying residents were unaffected ignores the higher PM2.5 (11.8 against 8.1) and asthma visits (34 against 19 per 1,000); a small change in makeup says nothing about whether facilities closed, which paragraph 3 handles as a separate analysis. Trap: Reading a small change in who lives there as no effect on the people who live there.

qs.q: What most limits the conclusion that facility emissions cause the higher asthma rate?
o: The study covered three decades
Not quite. A long study period strengthens it.
Tracts differ in other asthma risks
Correct: other asthma causes like allergens and smoke could differ between tracts.
PM2.5 was measured in both groups
Not quite. Measuring PM2.5 in both groups is a strength.
Asthma visits came from a health registry
Not quite. Registry data are fairly objective, which helps the study.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1C shows 34 childhood asthma emergency visits per 1,000 near facilities against 19 in comparison tracts. To say emissions cause the gap, you'd need to rule out other differences. Paragraph 4 says asthma has other causes, like indoor allergens and secondhand smoke, and those tracts already differ in income and housing. When an outside factor could explain a link, it's called confounding. That's the biggest limit here. Why the others are wrong: Measuring PM2.5 in both groups is a strength, since it allows a fair comparison; asthma visits coming from a state health registry makes them more objective than self-report, not less; covering three decades gives more data over time and strengthens the study. Trap: Picking a design strength when the question asks for a weakness.

qs.q: Which concept best describes the pattern the siting explanation proposes?
o: Voluntary residential mobility
Not quite. People choosing to move is the move-in explanation, not siting.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: ordinary siting decisions produce unequal outcomes without anyone intending it.
The sick role in affected families
Not quite. The sick role is about expectations for people who are ill.
Stereotype threat among residents
Not quite. Stereotype threat is about performance under a negative stereotype.
qs.x: Correct: The siting explanation says facilities end up in places with less political power. Nobody has to intend harm. Ordinary decisions, like picking cheaper land and places where neighbors are less likely to fight back, produce the unequal result. That's institutional discrimination: unequal outcomes created by the normal rules and routines of organizations, not by one person's prejudice. Why the others are wrong: Stereotype threat is when worrying about confirming a negative stereotype hurts someone's performance, such as on a test; voluntary residential mobility describes people choosing to move, which is the move-in explanation, not siting; the sick role is about what society expects from people who are ill. Trap: Assuming unequal outcomes always need someone's intent.

qs.q: Which additional measurement would best strengthen the link between emissions and asthma?
o: Total number of facilities in the state
Not quite. A count of facilities doesn't link exposure to health.
Average income in the state as a whole
Not quite. A statewide average gives no exposed versus unexposed comparison.
The number of workers each facility employs
Not quite. Jobs are a separate outcome from asthma.
Asthma rates before and after opening
Correct: before-and-after rates in the same tracts hold the neighborhood's other features steady.
qs.x: Correct: The weak spot in the asthma finding is that facility tracts differ from comparison tracts in many ways. The fix is to compare each tract with itself. Measure asthma rates before a facility opens and again after. Housing, smoking habits and other fixed features of the neighborhood stay roughly the same, so if asthma rises after opening, emissions become a much stronger explanation. Why the others are wrong: The total number of facilities in the state is just a count and doesn't connect exposure to health; average income for the whole state adds no comparison between exposed and unexposed people; the number of workers each facility employs is about jobs, a different outcome entirely. Trap: Adding data that describe the setting instead of data that test the link.

passages.title: Stages of the Demographic Transition
text: The demographic transition describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. In stage 1, both are high and population grows slowly. In stage 2, death rates fall first, usually because of clean water, sanitation and vaccination, while birth rates stay high, so population grows rapidly. In stage 3, birth rates fall as child survival improves, women gain education and employment, and families move to cities where children cost more to raise. In stage 4, both rates are low and growth is slow. Some countries have entered a stage in which births fall below deaths and the population shrinks without immigration.

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. A TFR of about 2.1 is replacement level in countries with low child mortality. Even when fertility falls to replacement, a population keeps growing for decades because a large share of it is young and entering childbearing years, an effect called population momentum.

These measures have limits. The crude birth and death rates depend on a population's age structure, so a country with many older residents can show a high death rate even when people there live long lives: Country D's rate of 12 per 1,000 reflects its age structure rather than poor health. Comparing countries fairly often requires age-adjusted rates or measures such as life expectancy at birth. The TFR has its own limitation, because it describes the rates of one year rather than the completed families of any real group of women. If women are postponing births to later ages, the TFR of a given year underestimates how many children women who are young that year will eventually have.

Country A built its first national vaccination program 15 years ago, and its death rate has fallen from 20 per 1,000 over that period. Country D's population declined by 0.1% last year despite net immigration of 2 per 1,000. Figure 1 shows the birth and death rates, fertility rate and age structure of the four countries.

qs.q: What is the rate of natural increase in Country A, per 1,000?
o: Not quite. This divides 38 by 12, which is a ratio, not a growth rate.
Not quite. 12 is Country A's death rate alone, not births minus deaths.
Correct: natural increase = births − deaths = 38 − 12 = 26 per 1,000.
Not quite. This adds 38 and 12, but deaths remove people, so subtract them.
qs.x: Correct: The rate of natural increase is how fast a population grows from births and deaths alone, leaving out people moving in or out. The formula is natural increase = crude birth rate − crude death rate. From Figure 1A, Country A's crude birth rate is 38 per 1,000 people and its crude death rate is 12 per 1,000. Plug in: 38 − 12 = 26 per 1,000. If you want it as a percent, 26 per 1,000 is 26 ÷ 1,000 = 0.026, which is 2.6% growth per year. That's fast, and it fits a young country where 44% of people are under 15. Why the others are wrong: 50 adds the two rates (38 + 12), but deaths take people away, so you subtract them; 3.2 divides 38 by 12, which gives a ratio, not a growth rate; 12 is just Country A's death rate on its own. Trap: Mixing up natural increase with total population change, which also counts migration.

qs.q: Which country best fits stage 2 of the transition?
o: Country C
Not quite. Both its rates are low (11 and 9), which is stage 4.
Country B
Not quite. Its birth rate has already dropped to 21, so it's past stage 2.
Country A
Correct: deaths fell from 20 to 12 per 1,000 while births stay high at 38.
Country D
Not quite. Its deaths outnumber births, the shrinking stage beyond stage 4.
qs.x: Correct: Stage 2 of the demographic transition is when death rates drop first, thanks to things like clean water and vaccines, while birth rates stay high. The gap between them makes the population grow fast. Country A fits that exactly. Paragraph 4 says its death rate fell from 20 to 12 per 1,000 after vaccination began, yet Figure 1A shows its birth rate is still 38 per 1,000 and its TFR is 5.1. A very young population, 44% under 15, is another sign of recent high births. Why the others are wrong: Country B's birth rate has already fallen to 21, so it's further along, around stage 3; Country C has low births (11) and low deaths (9), which is stage 4; Country D has more deaths (12) than births (9), the shrinking stage the passage describes at the end of paragraph 1. Trap: Placing a country by its growth rate alone instead of asking which rate has changed.

qs.q: Why would Country B keep growing for decades even if its TFR fell to 2.1 next year?
o: Its young cohort has yet to have children
Correct: 30% are under 15, so many future parents keep births high. That's population momentum.
Replacement fertility causes population growth
Not quite. Replacement fertility leads to a stable size in the long run, not growth.
Fertility rates cannot fall that quickly
Not quite. Fertility can fall fast; several countries have done exactly that.
Its death rate would rise immediately
Not quite. A fertility change wouldn't raise death rates, and they change slowly anyway.
qs.x: Correct: This is population momentum, from paragraph 2. A TFR (total fertility rate) is the average number of children per woman, and 2.1 is replacement level, meaning each couple roughly replaces itself. But Figure 1C shows 30% of Country B's people are under 15. Those kids haven't had children yet. As they grow into their childbearing years, there are simply a lot of parents, so lots of babies get born even if each woman has only about 2. The population keeps growing until that big young group ages through and the age structure evens out. Why the others are wrong: Replacement fertility doesn't cause growth on its own; over time it leads to a stable size; nothing in a TFR change would make death rates jump, and they shift slowly anyway; fertility can drop quickly, and many countries have done it. Trap: Thinking that hitting replacement fertility stops growth right away.

qs.q: What is the most likely consequence of Country D's age structure?
o: A rapidly rising birth rate
Not quite. Its TFR is 1.3, well below replacement; nothing points to a rising birth rate.
More retirees per working adult
Correct: 28% are over 64 against just 13% under 15, so fewer workers per retiree.
A growing labor force over the next decade
Not quite. Only 13% are under 15, so few young people are coming into the workforce.
A falling median age
Not quite. With so many older people and few children, the median age is rising.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Country D's bars in Figure 1C. 28% of its people are over 64, and only 13% are under 15. That's more than twice as many older people as children. So the working-age group is shrinking from below while more people move into retirement. The result is more retirees for every working adult, which puts pressure on pensions and health care. That's why countries in this spot often turn to immigration or later retirement. Why the others are wrong: A growing labor force needs lots of young people coming up, and only 13% are under 15; a rapidly rising birth rate doesn't fit a TFR of 1.3, well below the 2.1 replacement level; a falling median age is backwards, because with so many older people and so few children the median age is going up. Trap: Expecting low fertility to fix itself quickly.

qs.q: Why can Country D's population shrink despite net immigration?
o: Immigration lowers the birth rate
Not quite. Immigrants are often young adults, so they tend to add births, not lower them.
Its death rate is the highest shown
Not quite. Country A also has a death rate of 12, so D's isn't the highest.
Emigration is not counted in net immigration
Not quite. A net figure is arrivals minus departures, so emigration is already in it.
Deaths exceed births by more than 2
Correct: births − deaths = 9 − 12 = −3 per 1,000; adding +2 still leaves −1 per 1,000.
qs.x: Correct: Start with natural change, the formula is births − deaths. From Figure 1A, Country D's birth rate is 9 per 1,000 and its death rate is 12 per 1,000. Plug in: 9 − 12 = −3 per 1,000. Paragraph 4 adds net immigration of +2 per 1,000. Total change = −3 + 2 = −1 per 1,000. To turn that into a percent, divide by 1,000: 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001, which is 0.1%. So the population falls by about 0.1% a year. Immigration helps, but deaths beat births by 3, which is more than the 2 that arrive. Why the others are wrong: Immigration lowering the birth rate is backwards, since immigrants are often young adults who add births; its death rate isn't the highest, because Country A also has 12; net immigration already means arrivals minus departures, so emigration is counted. Trap: Assuming any amount of immigration is enough to stop decline.

passages.title: Colligative Properties and Particle Number
text: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute in a liquid lowers its vapor pressure, raises its boiling point and lowers its freezing point. These are colligative properties: they depend on the number of dissolved particles, not on what the particles are. The changes are ΔTb = iKb·m and ΔTf = iKf·m, where m is molality, Kb and Kf are constants of the solvent, and i is the van 't Hoff factor, the number of particles each formula unit produces in solution. For water, Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol and Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol.
Osmotic pressure follows Π = iMRT, where M is molarity. Because it can be large even for dilute solutions, it is the colligative property used to measure the molar mass of proteins.

Students measured freezing points of aqueous solutions, each prepared at 0.100 mol of solute per kilogram of water: glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), sodium chloride, magnesium chloride and acetic acid (CH₃COOH). Figure 1A shows the drop in freezing point, ΔTf, which is 0 °C minus the measured freezing point, so a ΔTf of 0.186 °C means the solution froze at −0.186 °C. Figure 1B plots each drop against the apparent i calculated from it; the line shows ΔTf = i × 1.86 × 0.100 = 0.186 × i.

Colligative properties are at work in several familiar situations. Salt spread on an icy road lowers the freezing point of the water film, so ice melts at temperatures below 0 °C. Antifreeze in a car both lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the coolant. In the body, the osmotic pressure set by plasma proteins pulls fluid back into capillaries at their venous end, and a low plasma protein level allows fluid to accumulate in the tissues as edema. Each of these depends on the number of dissolved particles rather than on their chemical identity, which is why the van 't Hoff factor matters so much for ionic solutes.

The students noted that the apparent values of i for the salts fall short of the whole numbers predicted from their formulas. In concentrated solutions, oppositely charged ions spend part of their time close together as ion pairs and behave as fewer particles. At 0.0010 mol/kg, the apparent i for NaCl rose to 1.97.

qs.q: Why does 0.100 mol/kg NaCl lower the freezing point more than the same amount of glucose?
o: Ionic solutes bind water tightly
Not quite. Colligative effects count particles. They don't depend on how strongly ions bind water.
Each formula unit gives two particles
Correct: NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so it gives about twice as many particles as glucose.
Glucose evaporates from the solution
Not quite. Glucose is nonvolatile, so it stays in the solution.
Sodium chloride is heavier
Not quite. Mass isn't in ΔTf = iKf·m. Only the particle count matters.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says colligative properties depend on how many particles are dissolved, not on what they are. NaCl is ionic, so each formula unit splits into two ions, Na⁺ and Cl⁻. That means 0.100 mol/kg of NaCl puts close to 0.200 mol of particles into each kilogram of water. Glucose doesn't split, so 0.100 mol/kg of glucose is just 0.100 mol of particles. Twice the particles gives about twice the drop, and Figure 1A shows it: the NaCl bar reads 0.348 °C against 0.186 °C for glucose. Why the others are wrong: being heavier doesn't matter, because molar mass isn't anywhere in ΔTf = iKf·m; how tightly ions hold water isn't what the law counts, it only counts particles; glucose is nonvolatile (it doesn't evaporate), and paragraph 1 is about nonvolatile solutes anyway. Trap: Thinking about how heavy or how strong a solute is, when colligative properties only care about the number of particles.

qs.q: Follow the line in Figure 1B out to i = 3.00. What freezing point would 0.100 mol/kg of a solute with i = 3.00 produce?
o: Not quite. That's i = 1, like glucose. This solute gives three particles.
Not quite. A solute lowers the freezing point, so the answer must be below 0 °C.
Not quite. That uses 1.00 mol/kg, 10 times the molality in the question.
qs.x: Correct: Use the formula from paragraph 1, ΔTf = iKf·m, where ΔTf is how far the freezing point drops. The values are i = 3.00 (given in the question), Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol (paragraph 1, for water) and m = 0.100 mol/kg. Plug in: ΔTf = 3.00 × 1.86 × 0.100. First 3 × 1.86 = 5.58. Then 5.58 × 0.100 = 0.558 (multiplying by 0.1 moves the decimal one place left). So the freezing point drops by 0.558 °C, which is where the line in Figure 1B reaches at i = 3.00. Pure water freezes at 0 °C, so the solution freezes at 0 − 0.558 = −0.558 °C. Why the others are wrong: −0.186 °C is what you get with i = 1, like glucose in Figure 1A, so it ignores the three particles; −5.58 °C uses 1.00 mol/kg instead of 0.100, 10 times too much solute; +0.558 °C has the right size but the wrong direction, because a solute lowers the freezing point. Trap: Getting 0.558 and forgetting it's a drop, so the answer has to be below zero.

qs.q: Why is the apparent i for MgCl₂ 2.70 rather than 3.00?
o: Some ions remain paired in solution
Correct: Some Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ stick together as pairs, and a pair acts like one particle.
The formula produces only two ions
Not quite. MgCl₂ gives three ions: one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻.
MgCl₂ does not dissolve completely
Not quite. MgCl₂ is soluble. The shortfall comes from ion pairing in solution.
The measurement was too early
Not quite. NaCl falls short the same way, so it's a real pattern, not a timing slip.
qs.x: Correct: MgCl₂ splits into one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so the ideal count is 3 particles. Paragraph 5 explains why the MgCl₂ point in Figure 1B sits at i = 2.70: oppositely charged ions spend some of their time stuck together as ion pairs. A pair moves around as one particle, not two, so the solution acts as if it had fewer particles than the formula predicts. Mg²⁺ has a +2 charge, so it pulls on Cl⁻ harder than Na⁺ does, which is why MgCl₂ falls short too. Why the others are wrong: MgCl₂ is a soluble salt, so it does dissolve completely; the formula really does give three ions (one Mg²⁺ plus two Cl⁻), not two; a timing problem wouldn't explain why NaCl falls short in the same way (1.87 instead of 2). Trap: Assuming a salt that dissolves completely must act like the full whole-number count of ions.

qs.q: What does the rise of NaCl's apparent i to 1.97 at 0.0010 mol/kg show?
o: The constant Kf changes with concentration
Not quite. Kf is a property of the solvent, water, so it stays 1.86.
Dilution increases the number of ions
Not quite. Dilution lowers the number of ions per kilogram of water.
Sodium chloride dissociates more at low temperature
Not quite. Only concentration changed here, not temperature.
Ion pairing weakens as the solution is diluted
Correct: In a dilute solution ions meet less often, so fewer pairs form and i gets close to 2.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says ion pairs form in more concentrated solutions. When you dilute, the ions are spread farther apart, so they bump into each other and pair up less often. More of them act as separate particles, and the apparent i climbs toward the ideal value of 2 for NaCl. At 0.100 mol/kg it was 1.87; at 0.0010 mol/kg it's 1.97, nearly 2. Real solutions act more ideally as they get more dilute. Why the others are wrong: dilution lowers the number of ions per kilogram, it doesn't add ions; Kf belongs to the solvent (water), so it doesn't change with how much salt you add; the experiment changed the concentration, not the temperature. Trap: Reading a bigger i as more salt dissolving, when it really means fewer ions are paired up.

qs.q: Why is osmotic pressure the preferred colligative property for finding a protein's molar mass?
o: Proteins cannot be dissolved in water
Not quite. Many proteins dissolve in water.
Osmotic pressure does not depend on particle number
Not quite. Π = iMRT, so osmotic pressure does depend on particle count.
Proteins lower the freezing point most of all
Not quite. Their big molar mass makes molality tiny, so the freezing point barely moves.
Dilute protein still gives usable pressure
Correct: Even a dilute protein solution gives an osmotic pressure large enough to measure.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says osmotic pressure can be large even for dilute solutions. A protein has a huge molar mass, so a few grams of it is only a tiny number of moles. That makes the molality very small, and the freezing point would drop by only thousandths of a degree, too small to measure well. The same small particle count still gives an osmotic pressure big enough to read, so it's the property used to find a protein's molar mass. Why the others are wrong: many proteins dissolve in water just fine; osmotic pressure does depend on particle number, through the iM in Π = iMRT; proteins give tiny freezing point changes, not big ones, because their molality is so low. Trap: Assuming a big molecule makes a big colligative effect, when the effect depends on how many particles there are, not how big they are.

Figure 1B. Measured ΔTf against apparent i (line: ΔTf = i × Kf × m = i × 0.186 °C)

passages.title: Recombination Frequency as a Map Distance
text: Two genes on the same chromosome are inherited together unless a crossover separates them. The frequency with which they are separated increases with the distance between them, so recombination frequency is used as a measure of distance, with 1% recombination defined as one map unit.

The relationship breaks down over long distances. Two genes far apart are separated by a crossover in so many meioses that the observed recombination frequency approaches 50%, the same value expected for genes on different chromosomes, so a large distance cannot be measured directly.

The solution is to measure in short steps and add them. Three-point crosses give the distances between adjacent pairs, and summing the intervals gives a total that exceeds the directly measured frequency between the outer genes, because double crossovers between them restore the original arrangement.
Recombination was measured between four genes in order (Table 1). Figure 1 shows how the intervals are measured and added.

The three adjacent intervals summed to 35.6 map units while the directly measured A to D frequency was 29.4 percent, a shortfall of 6.2 that corresponds to the double crossovers that returned the outer markers to their parental combination. Those were detected by scoring the middle markers.
The interference column records that fewer double crossovers were seen than the product of the single frequencies would predict, so a crossover in one interval reduces the chance of another nearby.

Two qualifications apply. Map distances built by addition assume the gene order is known, and an incorrect order produces a map that is internally consistent and wrong, so the order must be established from the double crossover classes rather than assumed. And recombination frequency is not uniform along a chromosome, with regions near the centromere recombining far less than their physical length would suggest, so a map in these units is a map of recombination rather than of DNA.

qs.q: Why does a directly measured long distance underestimate the true map distance?
o: Recombination is less frequent when far apart
Genes far apart recombine more often, not less.
Interference adds extra crossovers
Not quite. Interference reduces double crossovers.
Map units are defined at 50%
Not quite. One map unit is 1% recombination.
Double crossovers look parental
Correct: two crossovers put the outer genes back in their parental arrangement.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 explains it. A crossover swaps chromosome pieces between two genes, making a recombinant (a new combination). But if two crossovers happen between the same two outer genes, the second swap puts the outer genes back in their original, parental arrangement. Those offspring look like nothing happened, so they're counted as non-recombinant. The farther apart two genes are, the more often doubles happen, so the measured frequency falls short of the true distance. Table 1 shows it: the A to D frequency was 29.4%, but adding the short intervals gives 35.6 map units. Why the others are wrong: interference reduces double crossovers, it doesn't add them; genes far apart recombine more often, not less; and a map unit is 1% recombination, not 50%. Trap: Assuming a measured frequency counts every crossover that happened.

qs.q: Why must the gene order be established rather than assumed when adding distances?
o: Interference changes the gene order
Not quite. Interference affects double crossovers, not gene order.
A wrong order still adds up neatly
Correct: a wrong order still adds up neatly, so neat isn't the same as right.
Addition fails with the wrong order
Addition still works. It just gives a wrong map.
Order cannot be determined from crosses
Order comes from the double crossover classes.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says that adding up intervals produces a map that is internally consistent and wrong if the order is wrong. Whatever order you assume, the numbers still add up neatly, so the math can't tell you the order is right. The order has to come from the data itself: in a three-point cross, the rarest offspring class is the double crossovers, and the gene that switches in that class is the one in the middle. Why the others are wrong: order can be worked out from crosses, using the double crossover classes; adding still works with a wrong order, it just gives a wrong map; and interference affects double crossovers, not the order of genes. Trap: Mistaking neat, consistent numbers for proof they're right.

qs.q: Paragraph 7 says map units follow recombination, not length of DNA. Which added experiment would best test whether map distance tracks physical length in a region near the centromere?
o: Compare each interval's map distance with its length in bases from sequencing
Correct: if map units per base fall near the centromere, recombination is not tracking physical length there.
Repeat the A to D cross with many more offspring, scoring only the two outer genes
Not quite. More offspring tighten the A to D frequency but give no physical length to compare.
Add a fifth gene beyond D and check that its interval also adds to the total
Not quite. Adding intervals checks the arithmetic, not whether units match physical length.
Recalculate interference from the same 214 double crossovers and compare it with the single crossover rate
Not quite. That reuses the same counts and says nothing about physical length.
qs.x: Correct: A map in recombination units is only a map of DNA if map units per base are steady along the chromosome. To test that near the centromere, put the two kinds of measurement side by side: the map distance of each interval and its length in bases from sequencing, in regions near and far from the centromere. If map units per base drop near the centromere, recombination does not track length there. Why the others are wrong: more offspring in the same cross sharpen the A to D frequency without giving any physical length; adding a fifth gene checks the addition, not the match to length; recalculating interference from the same doubles reuses the same data. Trap: Choosing a bigger or repeated version of the same cross when the question needs a second kind of measurement.

qs.q: By how many map units did the sum exceed the direct measurement?
o: Correct: 35.6 − 29.4 = 6.2 map units.
That's just the B-C interval.
That's the direct measurement.
That's the sum, not the difference.
qs.x: Correct: First find the sum of the adjacent intervals from Table 1: A-B is 11.2, B-C is 14.6, and C-D is 9.8 map units. Add them: 11.2 + 14.6 = 25.8, then 25.8 + 9.8 = 35.6 map units. The direct A-D measurement is 29.4%, which is 29.4 map units, since 1% recombination = 1 map unit. Difference = sum − direct = 35.6 − 29.4 = 6.2 map units. That 6.2 is the share hidden by double crossovers (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: 35.6 is the sum itself; 29.4 is the direct measurement; 14.6 is just the B-C interval. Trap: Reporting a total when a difference was asked for.

qs.q: Why does the interference column in Table 1 matter?
o: It measures gene size
It's about non-independence, not gene size.
Interference raises the double count
Interference lowers the number of doubles.
Crossovers are not independent
Correct: fewer doubles than predicted, so one crossover suppresses another nearby.
It reflects low recombination near centromeres
Not quite. That's the second qualification; interference is about doubles.
qs.x: Correct: If crossovers in neighboring intervals were independent, you could predict the double crossovers by multiplying. P(both) = P(crossover in one interval) × P(crossover in the other). Paragraph 6 says fewer doubles were seen than that product predicts. That's interference: one crossover makes another nearby less likely, so the intervals aren't independent. It also tells you not to multiply interval frequencies to predict doubles. Why the others are wrong: low recombination near centromeres is the other qualification, not interference; interference lowers the number of doubles, it doesn't raise it; it measures how crossovers affect each other, not gene size. Trap: Multiplying interval frequencies as if crossovers were independent.

passages.title: Cationic Antimicrobial Peptides and Membranes
text: Many organisms defend themselves with short peptides that kill bacteria by disrupting their membranes rather than by inhibiting an enzyme. Such a peptide is typically cationic and amphipathic: it carries a net positive charge that draws it to the negatively charged bacterial surface, and it folds so that its hydrophobic residues lie on one face and its charged residues on the other.

Once bound, the peptide inserts its hydrophobic face into the lipid interior and disrupts the barrier, and the cell loses its ion gradients and dies. Because the target is the membrane's physical integrity rather than a specific protein, resistance is harder to acquire than it is against a conventional antibiotic.

Selectivity for bacteria over host cells comes from the difference in surface charge. Bacterial membranes carry anionic phospholipids on their outer face, while animal cell membranes present mostly neutral phosphatidylcholine and carry cholesterol, which stiffens the bilayer and resists insertion.

A synthetic peptide was tested against bacteria and red cells under varying salt, and at one acidic pH. Figure 1A plots the minimum inhibitory concentration against bacteria for each salt concentration, with the acidic condition as a separate point, and Figure 1B gives the selectivity ratio. Hemolysis at 64 µg/mL was 2% with no salt, 2% at 50 mM NaCl, 3% at 150 mM NaCl (physiological salt) and 3% at 150 mM NaCl with pH 5.5.

The peptide is 16 times less active at physiological salt than in salt-free medium, while its effect on red cells barely changes, so the selectivity ratio collapses from 32 to 2. Lowering the pH at physiological salt restores much of the activity.

The salt sensitivity is what the electrostatic mechanism predicts: added ions screen the attraction between the cationic peptide and the anionic bacterial surface, and the initial binding step is weakened.

Two qualifications apply. The minimum inhibitory concentration is measured in a defined medium, and serum proteins bind such peptides and reduce the free concentration substantially, so activity in blood is lower than these figures suggest. And a peptide that disrupts membranes is not without a target in the host: the modest hemolysis seen here sets a ceiling on the dose that can be given, which is why selectivity rather than potency is the limiting property.

qs.q: In Figure 1A the minimum inhibitory concentration climbs as the NaCl concentration rises. Why does added salt reduce the peptide's activity?
o: The peptide's hydrophobic face is neutralized by the dissolved ions
Not quite. Ions act on the charged face, not the hydrophobic one.
Ions screen the initial attraction
Correct: Salt ions screen the plus-minus attraction that brings the peptide to the bacterium.
Salt degrades the peptide
Not quite. The peptide stays intact in salt.
Bacteria grow faster in salt
Not quite. Growth rate isn't what was varied.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the peptide is cationic (positive) and is drawn to the negatively charged bacterial surface. Paragraph 6 says added salt ions crowd around those charges and screen them, which shortens the reach of the attraction. The first step, sticking to the bacterium, gets weaker, so it takes more peptide to kill. Figure 1A shows the minimum inhibitory concentration rising from 2.0 µg/mL with no salt to 32 µg/mL at 150 mM NaCl. Why the others are wrong: salt doesn't break down the peptide; bacterial growth rate isn't what changed; and the ions act on the charged face, not the hydrophobic one. Trap: Looking for a chemical change in the peptide when salt just weakens an attraction between charges.

qs.q: Why does the peptide spare animal cells?
o: They repair damage quickly
Not quite. Repair isn't the reason given.
Animal cells lack a membrane for the peptide to disrupt
Not quite. Animal cells have membranes.
They are larger
Not quite. Size isn't the basis.
Their membranes are not anionic
Correct: Their membranes are mostly neutral and contain cholesterol, which resists insertion.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says selectivity comes from surface charge. Bacterial membranes have negatively charged lipids on the outside, which pull in the positive peptide. Animal cell membranes show mostly neutral phosphatidylcholine, so the pull is weak, and they contain cholesterol, which stiffens the membrane and makes it harder for the peptide to push in. Why the others are wrong: size isn't the basis the passage gives; the passage doesn't mention repair; and animal cells do have membranes, they're just harder to attack. Trap: Crediting a host defense instead of the makeup of the membrane.

qs.q: Why is resistance harder to acquire?
o: The peptide kills bacteria too quickly for resistance to develop at all
Not quite. Killing speed isn't the barrier.
Bacteria cannot make peptidases
Not quite. Many bacteria can make peptidases.
The target is physical, not a protein
Correct: The target is the membrane itself, so no single mutation gives resistance.
The peptide is natural
Not quite. Natural origin doesn't matter here.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the peptide attacks the membrane's physical structure, not one specific protein. With a normal antibiotic, one mutation that changes the target protein can be enough for resistance. To escape this peptide, a bacterium would have to rebuild its whole membrane's lipids and charge, which no single mutation can do.
