Why the others are wrong: being natural gives no protection against resistance; bacteria can make peptidases (enzymes that cut peptides), and some do; and how fast it kills isn't the reason. Trap: Assuming a fast killer can't be resisted.

qs.q: How many times less active is the peptide at physiological salt?
o: Not quite. That's the MIC with no salt.
Not quite. That's the MIC at 50 mM salt.
Not quite. That's the MIC at physiological salt.
qs.x: Correct: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest amount that stops bacteria growing, so a higher MIC means less active. "How many times less active" means divide. Factor = MIC at 150 mM salt ÷ MIC with no salt. From Figure 1A, these are 32 µg/mL and 2.0 µg/mL. Plug in: 32 ÷ 2.0 = 16. The peptide needs 16 times as much to work at physiological salt, matching paragraph 5. Why the others are wrong: 2.0 is the MIC with no salt; 32 is the MIC at physiological salt; 8.0 is the MIC at 50 mM salt (and also at pH 5.5). Trap: Giving one MIC when the question asks for a ratio.

qs.q: Why is selectivity the limiting property rather than potency?
o: Potency cannot be improved
Not quite. Potency can be improved.
The peptide also damages host cells
Correct: It also damages host cells, which caps the dose.
A more potent peptide would be degraded faster in the bloodstream
Not quite. Degradation is a separate issue.
Selectivity is easier to measure
Not quite. Ease of measurement isn't the reason.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the peptide also hurts host cells a little, shown by the small amount of red cell bursting (hemolysis). That puts a ceiling on the dose. You can't just give more peptide to make up for salt weakening it, because more peptide also means more hemolysis. So the useful window depends on the ratio between killing bacteria and harming host cells, which is selectivity. At physiological salt that ratio has fallen to 2. Why the others are wrong: potency can be improved; ease of measuring isn't the reason; and degradation in blood is a separate problem. Trap: Chasing more bacterial killing while ignoring harm to the host.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the peptide against bacteria as salt rises (each point is one condition)
Figure 1B. Selectivity ratio (higher is safer) under the same conditions

passages.title: Income Quintiles and Measuring Inequality
text: Describing how unequally income is distributed in a population requires more than an average, because two populations with the same average income can differ greatly in how that income is spread. A common approach is to divide the population into five equal groups by income and report the share each group receives.

The shares sum to a hundred percent by construction, so only four of the five carry independent information. A single summary figure is often calculated from the shares to allow populations to be ranked.
Shares were measured in five populations with equal average incomes. Figure 1A shows the share received by each group and Figure 1B shows the summary index.
BL4 divides income equally, with each fifth receiving a fifth of the total and a summary index of zero. It is included as a reference point rather than as a description of any real population.

BL2, BL1 and BL3 are increasingly unequal, with the highest fifth receiving between a third and nearly three fifths of all income. The summary index rises with the inequality and allows the three to be ranked without comparing all the shares.

The average income is the same in all five populations, which is the point of the comparison. An average conceals the distribution entirely, and two populations can share an average while the poorest fifth of one receives a tenth of what the poorest fifth of the other receives.
BL5 is the population that conflicts. Its shares are identical to BL1's and its summary index matches BL2's. The index is calculated from the shares, so identical shares must give an identical index.

The general statement is that a distribution needs several numbers to describe and one number to rank, that the ranking number is derived from the others, and that an average carries none of this information.

Two qualifications apply. Income was recorded before taxes and transfers, which reduce the measured inequality in most populations. And the groups were formed from household income without adjusting for household size, so a large household and a small one with the same income are treated alike.

qs.q: Why is an average inadequate here?
o: An average describes the distribution
Not quite. An average hides the distribution; it doesn't describe it.
All five averages are equal
Correct: equal averages, yet the incomes are spread out very differently.
It is adequate for this purpose
Not quite. Equal averages hide big differences, so it's not adequate.
The averages differ between populations
Not quite. The passage says all the averages are equal.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says the five populations have the same average income, and that's the whole point. Yet Figure 1A shows their incomes are spread very differently. BL4's lowest fifth gets 20% of all income while BL3's gets only 2%. An average is just the middle point, so it hides how income is shared out. Why the others are wrong: Saying the averages differ is wrong, since the passage says they're equal; saying an average describes the distribution is backwards, because it hides it; calling the average adequate ignores that equal averages here sit on top of huge differences. Trap: Using the center of a distribution to describe its spread.

qs.q: Why do only four of the five shares carry information?
o: All five are needed
Not quite. The fifth share is determined once you know the other four.
Each of the shares is independent of the rest
Not quite. Their total is fixed at 100%, so they aren't fully independent.
None of them carries information
Not quite. Four of the shares do carry information.
They sum to a hundred
Correct: they must total 100%, so the fifth share follows from the other four.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the five shares add up to 100% by construction. That means if you know four, you can work out the fifth: fifth share = 100 − (sum of the other four). For example, if four fifths got 10, 15, 20 and 25, the last must be 100 − 70 = 30. So the fifth doesn't add new information. Why the others are wrong: Saying each share is independent of the rest ignores that their total is fixed at 100; saying all five are needed is wrong, since the last one is already determined; saying none carries information goes too far, because four of them do. Trap: Counting numbers that are tied together as if each were free to vary.

qs.q: Why is BL5 inconsistent?
o: Its index matches BL1's
Not quite. Its index, 0.25, matches BL2's, not BL1's.
Its middle share is too small
Not quite. Its middle share is 17%, the same as BL1's.
Its index follows from its shares
Correct: its shares equal BL1's, so its index should be 0.38, not 0.25.
Its shares differ from BL1's
Not quite. BL5's shares are identical to BL1's.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 explains it. The summary index is calculated from the shares, so if two populations have the same shares, they must have the same index. In Figure 1A, BL5's shares (4, 17 and 45) are exactly BL1's, but in Figure 1B its index is 0.25, matching BL2 instead of BL1's 0.38. A number worked out from other numbers can't differ when the inputs are the same. Why the others are wrong: Saying its shares differ from BL1's is wrong, since they're identical; saying its index matches BL1's is wrong, since it matches BL2's 0.25; saying its middle share is too small is wrong, since it's 17%, the same as BL1's. Trap: Treating a number calculated from others as if it were measured on its own.

qs.q: Which additional measurement would best show how much taxes and transfers change the inequality in these populations?
o: Record income after taxes and transfers too
Correct: the same households measured both ways show directly how much taxes and transfers shift the shares.
Report each population's average income a second time
Not quite. The averages are already equal in all five populations, so they cannot show a change in the shares.
Add a sixth population with exactly equal shares
Not quite. Another population adds a reference point but says nothing about the effect of taxes and transfers.
Divide each population into 10 groups instead of five
Not quite. Finer groups describe the same before-tax income in more detail and do not bring in taxes or transfers.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 9 says income was recorded before taxes and transfers, which reduce measured inequality in most populations. To test how much, you measure the same households a second way, after taxes and transfers, and compare the shares in Figure 1A with the new ones. The only thing that changes is the income definition, so any shift is due to it. Why the others are wrong: Repeating the averages tells you nothing, since they are equal by design; adding a population with equal shares gives another reference but no comparison of the two income definitions; splitting into 10 groups gives finer detail about the same before-tax income. Trap: Adding more detail to the same measurement when the question needs a different measurement.

qs.q: What share does BL3's highest fifth receive as a multiple of its lowest fifth?
o: Not quite. 2% is BL3's lowest-fifth share, not a ratio.
Not quite. That's BL1's ratio, 45 ÷ 4 ≈ 11.
Correct: 58 ÷ 2 = 29.
Not quite. 58% is BL3's highest-fifth share, not a ratio.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks how many times bigger one share is than the other, so divide. The formula is ratio = highest fifth's share ÷ lowest fifth's share. From Figure 1A, BL3's highest fifth gets 58% and its lowest fifth gets 2%. Plug in: 58 ÷ 2 = 29. The top fifth gets 29 times what the bottom fifth gets, the widest gap in Figure 1A. Why the others are wrong: 2 is just the lowest fifth's share, not a ratio; 58 is just the highest fifth's share; 11 is BL1's ratio, 45 ÷ 4 ≈ 11, from a different population. Trap: Reporting a share when the question asks for a ratio.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Share of total income received by the lowest, middle and highest fifth in five populations
Figure 1B. Summary index of inequality calculated for each population

passages.title: X-Linked Recessive Inheritance
text: A gene on the X chromosome is inherited differently in the two sexes because males carry one copy and females two. A recessive allele on the X is expressed in any male who carries it and only in a female who carries two, which is why recessive X-linked conditions are far commoner in males.

The transmission pattern follows from the same asymmetry. An affected male passes his X to all his daughters and none of his sons, so the condition appears to skip a generation and reappear in his grandsons through his daughters.

Female carriers are not always unaffected. One X in each cell is inactivated at random early in development, so a carrier is a mosaic of cells expressing one allele or the other, and the proportion varies between tissues and between individuals.
Enzyme activity was measured in family members (Table 1).

The affected male had 3 percent activity with little variation between tissues, while the two carrier females averaged 52 and 19 percent with ranges spanning 18 to 86 and 9 to 31 percent. The mean activity of a carrier is near half the normal value, but the spread between tissues is what distinguishes a mosaic from a uniform half.
The second carrier's low mean reflects a skewed pattern of inactivation rather than a different genotype, which is why two women with identical genotypes can differ in whether they have symptoms.

Two qualifications apply. Mean activity is calculated across sampled tissues, and the tissues that matter clinically may not be among those sampled, so a woman with a normal mean in blood can have a low value in the organ that produces her symptoms. And inactivation is random at the time it occurs but is then inherited by all descendants of each cell, so a tissue derived from few founder cells shows more extreme values than one derived from many, which contributes to the spread.

qs.q: Why does an affected male have little variation between tissues?
o: He has only one X chromosome
Correct: with one X, every cell uses the same allele, so there's no mosaic.
The male is mosaic
He has one X, so he can't be a mosaic.
His tissues are all derived from one founder cell
His tissues come from many founders, and he has no second X anyway.
His enzyme activity is high
His activity is only 3%.
qs.x: Correct: A male has only one X chromosome. Paragraph 3 says X inactivation shuts off one X in each cell of a female, which makes her a mosaic (a patchwork of cells using different X chromosomes). A male has no second X to choose between, so every cell in every tissue uses the same mutant X. That's why Table 1 shows the affected male at 3% with a tight range of 2 to 4%, while carrier females range widely. Why the others are wrong: his tissues come from many founder cells like anyone's, and it wouldn't matter since he has no choice of X; his activity is low, only 3%; he isn't a mosaic, because he has just one X. Trap: Expecting variation wherever a gene is X-linked.

qs.q: Why can two carriers with the same genotype differ clinically?
o: One of them carries a second mutation elsewhere
The passage says their genotypes are identical.
Their diets differ
Diet isn't mentioned.
Genotype determines everything
Here the same genotype gives different outcomes.
Inactivation is random
Correct: random X inactivation leaves a different share of active normal X in each woman.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraphs 3 and 6 explain it. Early in development, each cell in a female randomly shuts off one of her two X chromosomes. Like flipping a coin in each cell, it usually lands near half and half, but sometimes it's lopsided (skewed). Both carriers in Table 1 have the same genotype, one normal and one mutant X. The first averages 52% activity with no symptoms. The second has more cells using the mutant X, averaging 19%, and is mildly affected. Why the others are wrong: the passage says their genotypes are identical, so a hidden second mutation doesn't fit; genotype alone doesn't decide the outcome here, which is the point; diet isn't mentioned. Trap: Treating genotype as a complete predictor of phenotype.

qs.q: Why does a tissue from few founder cells show extreme values?
o: All tissues have the same number
Tissues come from different numbers of founder cells.
Founder cells inactivate both X chromosomes
Only one X is shut off per cell.
Chance has less to average
Correct: fewer coin flips means more chance of a lopsided result.
It shows less variation
Few founders give more variation, not less.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the X inactivation choice is made once in each founder cell and then copied to all of its descendants. So a tissue grown from many founders averages many coin flips and lands near 50%. A tissue grown from just a few founders averages only a few flips, and a few coin flips can easily come out lopsided. Example: with 2 founders, the chance both pick the mutant X is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, but with 10 founders the chance all pick it is 1/2 multiplied by itself 10 times, about 1 in 1000. Why the others are wrong: only one X is shut off per cell, not both; tissues differ in how many founders they come from; few founders give more variation, not less. Trap: Expecting a random process to average out no matter how few times it happens.

qs.q: What is the width of the skewed carrier's tissue range?
o: That's her mean activity.
Correct: 31 − 9 = 22.
That's the upper end of the range.
That's the other carrier's width: 86 − 18 = 68.
qs.x: Correct: Width of a range = upper value − lower value. From Table 1, the skewed carrier's range is 9 to 31%, so upper = 31% and lower = 9%. Plug in: 31 − 9 = 22 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: 31 is just the upper end of her range; 19 is her mean activity; 68 is the other carrier's range width, 86 − 18 = 68. Trap: Reading an end of the range when its width was asked for.

qs.q: Why can a normal blood value coexist with symptoms?
o: The relevant tissue was not sampled
Correct: the affected organ can have a different pattern from the blood.
Blood is not affected by X inactivation
Blood cells go through X inactivation too.
Symptoms are unrelated to enzyme activity
Symptoms follow activity in the affected tissue.
The assay failed in blood
The test worked.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the X inactivation pattern differs between tissues. Blood is easy to sample, so it's often what gets tested. But a woman's blood might have mostly normal X active, giving a normal reading, while the organ causing her symptoms might have mostly mutant X active. The tissue that matters may just not have been sampled. Why the others are wrong: blood cells go through X inactivation like any other cells; symptoms do follow enzyme activity, just in the affected tissue; nothing says the blood test failed. Trap: Treating one easy-to-sample tissue as if it spoke for the whole body.

passages.title: Push and Pull Factors in Migration
text: Migration is analyzed in terms of push factors at the origin, which drive people to leave, and pull factors at the destination, which attract them. Push factors include conflict, crop failure and unemployment; pull factors include wages, safety and existing networks of earlier migrants. Intervening obstacles, such as distance, cost and legal barriers, determine which of those who want to move actually do.

Two refinements matter. Migration is selective: migrants are typically not a random sample of the origin population but are younger and, for longer moves, better educated, because the costs are paid up front and the returns accrue over a working life. And networks are self-reinforcing, since each earlier migrant lowers the cost of the next move by supplying information, housing and job contacts, which is why flows persist after the original push has eased.

Four origin-destination corridors were compared on the size of the flow and on three correlates measured in the same year (Figure 1). Each point is one corridor, W to Z, and the vertical axis in all three panels is the annual number of migrants per 1,000 people at the origin.

The wage ratio does not order the flows. Corridor Z has the highest ratio at 3.9 and the smallest flow at 2.1 per thousand, while Corridor Y has the lowest ratio at 1.8 and the second largest flow. What does track the flows is the combination of short distance and a high share of households with a prior migrant, which is the obstacles-and-networks account rather than a simple wage account.

Distance and network share are themselves closely related here, since corridors with short distances also have high prior-migrant shares, so the figure cannot separate the two: a corridor that is near may send more people simply because moving is cheap, or because its long history of movement has built the networks. A corridor that was distant but had a high network share would distinguish them, and none of the four provides that combination.

The figures are also one year's snapshot of four corridors, so they describe a cross-section rather than a process, and the wage ratio is an average that says nothing about the wages available to the kind of worker who actually migrates.

qs.q: What does Corridor Z most clearly show?
o: A high wage gap need not produce a large flow
Correct: Z has the highest wage ratio (3.9) but the smallest flow (2.1 per 1,000).
Wage ratios are measured with error
Not quite. Nothing in the passage suggests the wage ratios are mismeasured.
Distance has no relation to migration flows
Not quite. Z is the farthest and has the smallest flow, so distance seems to matter.
Networks are unnecessary for migration
Not quite. Z has the weakest network and the smallest flow, which supports networks.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Corridor Z in Figure 1. It has the biggest wage ratio, 3.9, meaning wages at the destination are almost four times those at home. Yet it has the smallest flow, just 2.1 migrants per 1,000. Paragraph 4 uses this to show that a big wage gap alone doesn't decide how many people move. Z is also the farthest corridor (4,600 km) with the fewest prior migrants (4%), so obstacles and missing networks hold people back. Why the others are wrong: Nothing suggests the wage ratios are measured badly; distance having no relation to flow is backwards, since Z is both the farthest and the smallest flow; networks being unnecessary is backwards too, since Z has the weakest network and the smallest flow. Trap: Treating evidence against one factor as evidence against all factors.

qs.q: Why is migration described as selective?
o: Every member of a household moves together
Not quite. Households often move in part, not all together.
Destinations choose which applicants to admit
Not quite. Admission rules are an obstacle, not what selective means here.
Migrants are younger and often better educated
Correct: younger, better-educated people move because costs come first and payoffs come later.
Only those with networks may move
Not quite. Networks lower costs; they don't decide who is allowed to move.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says migration is selective, meaning the people who move aren't a random slice of the home population. They tend to be younger and, for longer moves, better educated. Why? Moving costs money and effort up front, and the payoff comes over years of work. Younger people have more working years left to earn back the cost, and better-educated people can often earn more at the destination. Why the others are wrong: Destinations choosing which applicants to admit is a legal barrier, which paragraph 1 calls an intervening obstacle, not what selective means; only those with networks being allowed to move is wrong, since networks lower the cost but don't grant permission; whole households always moving together isn't true, as families often move in part. Trap: Reading 'selective' as the destination doing the selecting.

qs.q: Why can these data not separate distance from networks?
o: The two move together across all four corridors
Correct: near corridors always have strong networks, so the two can't be separated.
Network share was reported by households
Not quite. Self-report is a small concern next to the two moving together.
Only four corridors appear in the comparison
Not quite. More corridors with the same pairing still wouldn't separate them.
Distance is reported in kilometers rather than hours
Not quite. The units used for distance aren't what blocks the comparison.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 explains that in every corridor, distance and network share go together. The near corridors (W at 420 km and Y at 310 km) have lots of households with a prior migrant (62% and 48%). The far ones (X at 2,900 km and Z at 4,600 km) have few (11% and 4%). To tell them apart, you'd need a far corridor with a strong network, and none of the four has that. When two variables always move together like this, they're called collinear. Why the others are wrong: Measuring distance in kilometers rather than hours isn't the obstacle; having only four corridors isn't the core issue, because more corridors with the same pairing wouldn't help; households reporting their own network status is a minor concern next to the collinearity. Trap: Treating collinearity as a shortage of data.

qs.q: Why do migration flows often persist after the original push factor eases?
o: Push factors never actually ease at the origin
Not quite. Push factors like conflict and crop failure do ease.
Each earlier migrant lowers the next move's cost
Correct: earlier migrants share housing, jobs and information, so later moves cost less.
Legal barriers fall as flows become established
Not quite. Legal barriers often tighten as flows grow, not fall.
Wage gaps widen once a flow begins
Not quite. A migration flow doesn't make the wage gap wider.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says networks are self-reinforcing. Each person who has already moved helps the next by sharing information, a place to stay and job contacts. That makes moving cheaper and less risky for the people who follow. So once a network exists, the flow can keep going even after the original reason to leave, the push factor, has eased. Why the others are wrong: Wage gaps widening once a flow begins isn't supported, since the flow doesn't drive wages that way; push factors never easing is false, as wars and crop failures do end; legal barriers falling as flows grow isn't what happens, and if anything they often tighten. Trap: Looking for a push that never stopped when the real answer is that moving got cheaper.

qs.q: Which corridor has the largest annual flow per 1,000 at the origin?
o: 2.1, Corridor Z
Not quite. 2.1 is the smallest flow.
7.2, Corridor X
Not quite. 7.2 is the second smallest.
11.9, Corridor Y
Not quite. 11.9 is second largest, below Corridor W's 18.4.
18.4, Corridor W
Correct: 18.4 per 1,000 is the largest flow on the vertical axis.
qs.x: Correct: Read the vertical axis of Figure 1, annual migrants per 1,000 at origin. Corridor W has 18.4, the largest. It pairs a short distance (420 km, the second shortest after Y's 310 km) with the highest share of households with a prior migrant, 62%. That's the obstacles-and-networks pattern paragraph 4 describes. Why the others are wrong: Corridor Z has 2.1, the smallest flow; Corridor X has 7.2, second smallest; Corridor Y has 11.9, the second largest but still below 18.4. Trap: Picking the corridor with the highest wage ratio, which is Z, the one with the smallest flow.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Annual migrants versus wage ratio, by corridor
Figure 1B. Annual migrants versus distance, by corridor
Figure 1C. Annual migrants versus share of households with a prior migrant, by corridor

passages.title: Goffman's Front Stage and Back Stage
text: Erving Goffman described social life in dramaturgical terms. In the front stage, people manage the impression others form of them, following the expectations of the role they are performing. In the back stage, they step out of the performance. Impression management is this ongoing regulation of information about oneself. It includes ingratiation, trying to be liked; self-promotion, trying to be seen as competent; and self-handicapping, creating an obstacle in advance so that failure can be attributed to it rather than to ability.

Researchers studied these behaviors in job interviews. Trained observers coded 160 videotaped interviews for ingratiation, such as complimenting the organization and expressing agreement, and self-promotion, such as describing accomplishments. Interviewers rated each candidate's likability and competence, and reported whether they would recommend a hire. In Figure 1, "ingratiation only" means high ingratiation with low self-promotion, "self-promotion only" the reverse, "both" high on both, and "neither" low on both. Figure 1A shows the mean ratings and Figure 1B the share recommended for hire.

Goffman also described teams, in which several people cooperate to sustain a single performance, and the care taken to keep the back stage out of the audience's view. A restaurant kitchen and its dining room are his standard example: the staff maintain one presentation in front of diners and another behind the door, and the boundary between the two is defended. Goffman argued that the audience usually cooperates in maintaining the performance, overlooking small slips rather than exposing them, because an exposed performance is awkward for everyone present, a courtesy he called protective practice, or tact.

In a second study, 90 students were told they would take a difficult test of intellectual ability. Before the test, they chose between two drugs described to them, one said to improve performance and one said to impair it. Students who had succeeded on an earlier test through clear effort chose the impairing drug 14% of the time, while students who had succeeded on a test whose scoring they could not understand chose it 56% of the time.

qs.q: Which behavior best illustrates self-handicapping?
o: Complimenting the interviewer
Not quite. Compliments are ingratiation, trying to be liked.
Describing one's own past accomplishments in detail
Not quite. Listing accomplishments is self-promotion.
Studying extra hours before the test
Not quite. Extra studying helps performance; it's not an obstacle.
Choosing a drug said to impair performance
Correct: It sets up an excuse ahead of time, so failure can be blamed on the drug.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines self-handicapping as setting up an obstacle ahead of time, so that if you fail, you can blame the obstacle instead of your ability. In the second study (paragraph 4), choosing a drug said to impair performance before a hard test does exactly that. If they do badly, it was the drug, not their intelligence. Why the others are wrong: complimenting the interviewer is ingratiation, trying to be liked; describing your own accomplishments is self-promotion, trying to look competent; studying extra hours makes success more likely, which is the opposite of creating an obstacle. Trap: Confusing an excuse made after failing with an obstacle set up beforehand.

qs.q: Why did uncertain success raise self-handicapping so sharply?
o: They wanted to perform worse
Not quite. The aim is protecting their image, not failing.
They had not actually succeeded
Not quite. Both groups had succeeded on the earlier test.
Unexplained success may not repeat
Correct: Success they couldn't explain might not repeat, so they set up an excuse.
They misunderstood the drug descriptions
Not quite. Nothing suggests the descriptions were unclear.
qs.x: Correct: In paragraph 4, students who had succeeded through clear effort chose the impairing drug only 14% of the time. Students whose earlier success came from scoring they couldn't understand chose it 56% of the time, four times as often (56 ÷ 14 = 4). Those students had a good reputation but didn't know how they'd earned it, so they couldn't be sure of repeating it. Taking the impairing drug gave them a ready excuse that protects their image as able. Why the others are wrong: both groups had succeeded on the earlier test; the goal of self-handicapping is to protect the image, not to do badly; nothing suggests the drug descriptions were confusing. Trap: Reading self-handicapping as wanting to fail.

qs.q: What do the interview results suggest about the two tactics?
o: Each raises a different impression
Correct: Ingratiation raised likability, self-promotion raised competence.
Ingratiation raises competence
Not quite. Ingratiation barely moved competence, 3.9 to 4.1.
Only ingratiation affects hiring
Not quite. Self-promotion alone got 58% recommended versus 41% for ingratiation.
Both tactics raise likability
Not quite. Self-promotion barely moved likability, 3.8 to 4.2.
qs.x: Correct: Compare each tactic used alone against the "neither" bars in Figure 1. Ingratiation alone raised likability from 3.8 to 5.6 (+1.8) but competence only from 3.9 to 4.1 (+0.2). Self-promotion alone raised competence from 3.9 to 5.8 (+1.9) but likability only from 3.8 to 4.2 (+0.4). So each tactic mainly boosts a different impression. Using both got the most hire recommendations, 71%. Why the others are wrong: self-promotion barely moved likability (+0.4), so it isn't mainly a likability tactic; self-promotion alone actually led to more hire recommendations than ingratiation alone (58% versus 41%); ingratiation barely moved competence, 3.9 to 4.1. Trap: Assuming any good tactic improves every impression.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of the interview study?
o: Observers were trained before coding
Not quite. Training makes coding more reliable, a strength.
Interviews were videotaped
Not quite. Taping lets observers code reliably, a strength.
Both likability and competence were rated
Not quite. Rating two impressions adds information.
Behavior was observed, not assigned
Correct: Candidates chose their behavior, so they may differ in other ways too.
qs.x: Correct: In the interview study, candidates chose how to behave. Nobody was assigned to compliment or to self-promote. So candidates who used more tactics might also have been more experienced or more qualified, and that could explain their higher ratings. Only assigning the behavior could pull those apart. Why the others are wrong: videotaping lets observers code reliably, which is a strength; training the observers improves reliability, another strength; rating both likability and competence gives more information. Trap: Picking a strength of the method when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: In Figure 1B, how many percentage points higher was the share recommended for hire when candidates used both tactics than when they used ingratiation only?
o: 49 percentage points
Not quite. 49 is 71 − 22, the gain over using neither tactic, not over ingratiation only.
30 percentage points
Correct: 71% (both) − 41% (ingratiation only) = 30 percentage points.
13 percentage points
Not quite. 13 is 71 − 58, the gain over self-promotion only, not over ingratiation only.
17 percentage points
Not quite. 17 is 58 − 41, which compares self-promotion only with ingratiation only.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for a difference between two bars in Figure 1B, so write it as difference = both − ingratiation only. The bar for both tactics sits at 71% and the bar for ingratiation only sits at 41%. Plug in: 71 − 41 = 30 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: 49 comes from 71 − 22, which compares both tactics with using neither; 13 comes from 71 − 58, which compares both with self-promotion only; 17 comes from 58 − 41, which compares the two single-tactic groups with each other. Trap: Subtracting from the wrong baseline bar, so always check which two bars the question names.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Mean interviewer ratings by candidate behavior (160 interviews)
Figure 1B. Share of candidates recommended for hire, by candidate behavior

passages.title: Crude Birth Rate Versus Total Fertility Rate
text: Fertility is measured in two ways that answer different questions. The crude birth rate counts births per thousand people in a year, and therefore depends on the age structure of the population: a population with many young adults has a higher crude rate even at the same childbearing behavior. The total fertility rate is the number of children a woman would have if she experienced the current age-specific rates throughout her reproductive years, which removes age structure and so permits comparison across populations.

Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 in a low-mortality population, slightly above two because some girls do not survive to reproductive age and because slightly more boys than girls are born. Below replacement, a population shrinks in the long run unless immigration offsets it, though the decline is delayed for decades by momentum from an existing young age structure.

Fertility typically falls as female schooling and labor force participation rise, and several mechanisms are proposed: later age at first birth, greater opportunity cost of time out of work, lower desired family size, and improved access to contraception.

Four regions were compared on fertility and two correlates, each measured in the same year from national surveys (Figure 1). Schooling is on the horizontal axis of both panels, and the regions are numbered 1 to 4 in order of increasing schooling.

The gradient is clean and that is the problem. Schooling and labor force participation rise together across the four regions, from 3.1 years and 19% to 13.9 years and 71%, so the two correlates are nearly collinear and no comparison among these four regions can say which of them is doing the work, or whether a third factor driving both is responsible.

Two further cautions apply. These are four aggregate observations, so any pattern is a relationship among regions rather than among women, and inferring individual behavior from aggregate rates is unreliable. The total fertility rate is also a synthetic measure built from one year's age-specific rates, so it describes a hypothetical woman and can move sharply when births are merely postponed, which is why it can fall below the number of children women eventually have.

qs.q: Which region is nearest replacement-level fertility?
o: Region 1
Not quite. 5.2 is 3.1 above replacement, the farthest of all.
Region 2
Not quite. 3.4 is 1.3 above replacement.
Region 3
Correct: 2.2 is only 0.1 away from replacement at about 2.1.
Region 4
Not quite. 1.5 is 0.6 below replacement.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 children per woman in a low-death population. That's the number where each generation just replaces itself. Now compare each region's total fertility rate in Figure 1A to 2.1. Region 3: 2.2 − 2.1 = 0.1 away. Region 4: 2.1 − 1.5 = 0.6 below. Region 2: 3.4 − 2.1 = 1.3 above. Region 1: 5.2 − 2.1 = 3.1 above. Region 3 is closest by far. Why the others are wrong: Region 1 at 5.2 is far above replacement; Region 2 at 3.4 is well above; Region 4 at 1.5 is well below, so its population will shrink in the long run without immigration. Trap: Assuming the lowest rate is the closest to replacement.

qs.q: Why can this comparison not separate the effects of schooling and paid work?
o: Replacement-level fertility varies between populations
Not quite. Replacement level barely varies and doesn't affect this question.
The two correlates rise together across all four regions
Correct: schooling and paid work rise in step, so their effects can't be pulled apart.
The total fertility rate is measured with error
Not quite. Measurement error isn't what blocks this comparison.
Four regions is too small a number to analyze at all
Not quite. More regions wouldn't help if the two still rose together.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says schooling and paid work rise together across all four regions, from 3.1 years and 19% up to 13.9 years and 71%. When two variables always move in step, they're called collinear. To tell which one matters, you'd need a region where one is high and the other is low. None exists here, so you can't tell schooling's effect from paid work's, or rule out some third factor driving both. Why the others are wrong: Measurement error in the total fertility rate isn't the problem the passage raises; replacement level varies only slightly between populations and has nothing to do with separating the two correlates; four regions being too few misses the point, because even many more regions wouldn't help if schooling and work kept rising together. Trap: Treating collinearity as a sample-size problem.

qs.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
o: Infant deaths per thousand live births in a year
Not quite. That's infant mortality, a death rate.
The share of women who have at least one child
Not quite. That's a different statistic, not the TFR.
Births per thousand people each year
Not quite. Births per thousand people is the crude birth rate.
Children per woman under current age-specific rates
Correct: the children one woman would have at this year's age-specific rates.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines the total fertility rate (TFR) as the number of children a woman would have if she went through her childbearing years at this year's birth rates for each age. It's built from rates at each age, so it doesn't depend on how many young or old people the population has. That's what lets you compare countries fairly. Paragraph 6 calls it synthetic because it describes an imaginary woman, not a real group. Why the others are wrong: Births per thousand people per year is the crude birth rate, which does depend on age structure; the share of women with at least one child is a different statistic; infant deaths per thousand live births is infant mortality, a death rate, not a fertility rate. Trap: Thinking every fertility measure is just a count of births in a population.

qs.q: What would sustained below-replacement fertility imply in the long run?
o: An age structure that remains unchanged
Not quite. With fewer births the population ages, so the structure shifts.
A rising share of dependent children
Not quite. Fewer births means the child share falls, not rises.
Population decline in the absence of immigration
Correct: each generation is smaller, so the population shrinks without immigration.
An immediate decline in population size within a single year
Not quite. Momentum from a young population delays decline for decades.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says below replacement, about 2.1 children per woman, the population shrinks in the long run unless immigration makes up the difference. If women on average have fewer than about 2.1 kids, each generation is smaller than the one before. Over time that adds up to a shrinking population. Why the others are wrong: An immediate decline ignores population momentum, which paragraph 2 says delays the drop for decades while today's large young groups have their own children; a rising share of dependent children is backwards, because fewer births means a smaller child share; an unchanged age structure is wrong, since fewer babies plus long lives make the population older. Trap: Turning a long-run result into an instant one.

qs.q: Why is it risky to infer how individual women behave from Figure 1?
o: Only four of the world's regions were included here
Not quite. That limits coverage, but the real issue is using averages for individuals.
Regional averages need not describe individuals within them
Correct: a pattern among regional averages may not hold for individual women.
Total fertility rates cannot be compared across the four regions
Not quite. Comparing populations is exactly what the TFR is designed for.
Female schooling cannot be measured in survey data
Not quite. Surveys routinely measure schooling.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 points out that Figure 1 has just four data points, each an average for a whole region. A pattern among regions doesn't have to hold among the women inside them. It could be weaker, stronger or even reversed for individuals. So the figure can support claims about regions, not about how any particular woman makes choices. Using group averages to describe individuals is a classic mistake. Why the others are wrong: Total fertility rates not being comparable is backwards, since comparing populations is exactly what the TFR is built for; female schooling not being measurable in surveys is false, as surveys collect it routinely; including only four regions limits how much of the world is covered, but that's a separate issue from the averages problem. Trap: Treating a pattern across groups as if it described the people inside them.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Total fertility rate against mean years of female schooling in four regions
Figure 1B. Share of women in paid work against mean years of female schooling in the same regions

passages.title: Hess's Law and Combining Reaction Enthalpies
text: Enthalpy is a state function, so the enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on the initial and final states and not on the route between them. This is Hess's law, and it allows the enthalpy change of a reaction that is hard to measure to be computed from reactions that are easy to measure.

The method is to combine known reactions so that unwanted species cancel. A reaction may be reversed, which changes the sign of its enthalpy change, or multiplied by a coefficient, which multiplies the enthalpy change by the same factor. Adding the adjusted reactions gives the target reaction and the sum of the adjusted enthalpies gives its enthalpy change.

A common special case uses enthalpies of formation, the enthalpy change for making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states. The reaction enthalpy is then the sum for the products minus the sum for the reactants, with elements in their standard states assigned zero by definition.

Three combustion reactions were measured calorimetrically in order to obtain the enthalpy change for the conversion of graphite to diamond, which cannot be measured directly (Table 1; Figure 1 shows how the reactions connect).

The derivation needs only the first two rows. Reversing the diamond combustion gives +395.4, and adding the graphite combustion of −393.5 cancels the oxygen and the carbon dioxide, leaving graphite converting to diamond with an enthalpy change of +1.9 kJ per mol.

The small positive value is informative. Diamond is slightly higher in enthalpy than graphite, which is why graphite is the standard state of carbon, and the difference is small enough that the conversion is thermodynamically unfavorable by a very narrow margin while being kinetically impossible at ordinary temperatures.

Two points about the method deserve note. The third row is not needed for this target, and including an unnecessary reaction does not change the answer but offers no information either, which is a useful check on whether a chosen route is minimal. And a derived value inherits the uncertainties of every measurement used, so a difference of 1.9 computed from two values near 395 is far less precise than either of them.

qs.q: Why is the derived value far less precise than the measurements?
o: The third reaction was omitted
The third reaction isn't needed for this target.
Calorimetry cannot measure combustion
Calorimetry measured all three combustions.
Only the first two reactions were used in it
Fewer reactions means fewer errors, not more.
A small difference of two large numbers
Correct: 1.9 is a small difference of two numbers near 395, so their uncertainties swamp it.
qs.x: Correct: The graphite-to-diamond value comes from a subtraction: −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ/mol (paragraph 5). Each of those big measured numbers has some uncertainty, say a few tenths of a kJ. When you subtract them, the uncertainties don't cancel, they carry over (and add). A few tenths of a kJ is tiny next to 395 but large next to 1.9, so the result has a much larger error relative to its size (paragraph 7). Why the others are wrong: using only two reactions means fewer errors, not more; the third reaction is genuinely not needed for this target; calorimetry did measure all three combustions. Trap: Assuming a derived value is as precise as the numbers it was built from.

qs.q: Why does reversing a reaction change the sign of its enthalpy?
o: Enthalpy is always positive for products
Enthalpy changes can be either sign.
The reaction absorbs oxygen instead
Reversing changes direction, not which species are involved.
Reversed reactions proceed more slowly
Rate isn't a thermodynamic quantity.
Enthalpy depends on initial and final states
Correct: ΔH = final − initial, and reversing swaps final and initial.
qs.x: Correct: Enthalpy change is ΔH = H(final) − H(initial). Paragraph 1 says enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on where you start and where you end. Running a reaction backward swaps start and end. That flips the subtraction, so you get the same number with the opposite sign. For example, diamond burning gives −395.4 kJ/mol, so making diamond from CO₂ and O₂ would be +395.4 kJ/mol. Why the others are wrong: how fast a reaction goes has nothing to do with its enthalpy; reversing doesn't change which chemicals are involved, just the direction; enthalpy changes can be positive or negative. Trap: Bringing speed into a question about a state function.

qs.q: The derived value is a small difference of two large numbers. Which change to the experiment would most improve its precision?
o: Repeat both combustions several times and average the results
Correct: Averaging repeated measurements shrinks the random uncertainty that carries into the difference.
Add the carbon monoxide combustion to the sum as an extra cross-check on the answer
Not quite. An unneeded reaction adds its own uncertainty, as paragraph 7 says.
Report the answer to more decimal places than the calorimeter actually gives
Not quite. Extra digits look precise but do not make the measurement any better.
Burn much smaller samples of each form so that less heat has to be measured in all
Not quite. A smaller heat is harder to measure well, so relative uncertainty grows.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says a derived value inherits the uncertainty of every measurement used, so a difference of 1.9 computed from two values near 395 is far less precise than either. Since +1.9 = −393.5 + 395.4 (Figure 1), a small error in either large number is a big fraction of 1.9. The best remedy is to measure better: repeat each combustion several times and average, which cuts random error in both numbers before they are subtracted. Why the others are wrong: adding the carbon monoxide reaction brings in one more uncertain number and does not help the target; writing more decimal places only changes how the answer looks; smaller samples release less heat, which is harder to measure accurately. Trap: Choosing something that looks like extra care but adds noise or only adds digits.

qs.q: What enthalpy change results from reversing the diamond combustion?
o: −395.4 kJ per mol
That's the forward direction, before reversing.
−393.5 kJ per mol
That's the graphite combustion.
+1.9 kJ per mol
That's the final derived value, not this step.
+395.4 kJ per mol
Correct: flipping −395.4 gives +395.4 kJ/mol.
qs.x: Correct: Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH and keeps the size (paragraph 2). The diamond combustion in Table 1 is −395.4 kJ/mol. Flip the sign: −(−395.4) = +395.4 kJ/mol. That's the first step in paragraph 5, before adding the graphite combustion to get +1.9. Why the others are wrong: −395.4 is the forward direction, before reversing; −393.5 is the graphite combustion; +1.9 is the final graphite-to-diamond answer, not this step. Trap: Giving the answer to the whole problem instead of the step asked for.

qs.q: What does including the third reaction achieve?
o: It converts graphite into diamond
Only the derived combination converts graphite to diamond.
It improves the precision of the final result
It would add its own uncertainty, not improve precision.
Nothing, since it is not needed here
Correct: the first two rows already give the answer, so it adds nothing.
It provides a necessary intermediate
Carbon monoxide doesn't appear in the target.
qs.x: Correct: The target, graphite → diamond, comes from the first two rows alone (paragraph 5). The third reaction involves carbon monoxide, which isn't in the target at all, so there's nothing for it to cancel or supply. Adding it changes nothing in the answer, and paragraph 7 notes it would only bring in its own uncertainty. Why the others are wrong: it would bring extra uncertainty, so it can't improve precision; carbon monoxide isn't a step on the way from graphite to diamond; only the combined first two rows convert graphite to diamond. Trap: Assuming every number given has to be used.

r: Graphite plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide
Diamond plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide
Carbon monoxide plus half oxygen gives carbon dioxide

graph.title: Figure 1. Enthalpy cycle linking graphite, diamond and carbon dioxide

passages.title: Cognitive Dissonance Versus Self-Perception
text: Cognitive dissonance theory proposes that acting against one's own attitude produces an unpleasant state of tension. People can reduce the tension by changing the attitude so that it fits the behavior. A competing view, self-perception theory, holds that people simply infer their attitudes from their behavior, as an outside observer would, without any tension being involved. One way to separate the two accounts is to give people a different explanation for any tension they feel. If tension drives attitude change, people who can blame their tension on something else should have less need to change their attitude.

Researchers recruited 150 undergraduates who opposed a proposed $400 increase in the student activity fee. Each wrote a persuasive essay in favor of the increase. In the high-choice conditions, the experimenter said that writing the essay was voluntary, although all participants agreed. In the low-choice condition, participants were told the essay was required. Before writing, high-choice participants swallowed an inert capsule described as a memory supplement. One group was told it had no side effects. A second group was told it often makes people feel tense, and a third group was told it often makes people feel relaxed. A control group wrote no essay. Afterward, participants rated their own tension and their attitude toward the fee increase (Table 1).

Self-perception theory makes a different prediction for the capsule conditions. If people simply read their attitudes from their behavior, a story about the capsule should not matter, because the behavior, a freely written essay, was identical across the three high-choice groups. Dissonance theory predicts that the capsule story should matter a great deal, because it changes how people explain the tension they feel. The researchers chose the fee increase because a pilot survey showed that 88% of students opposed it, so writing in favor would be inconsistent with the views of most participants.
Participants were assigned to conditions at random, and the person who scored the attitude scales did not know each participant's condition.

qs.q: Why did the high-choice, no-side-effects group shift its attitude more than the low-choice group?
o: Choosing the act freely creates more dissonance
Correct: choosing freely removes the outside excuse, so tension (6.2) and attitude change (7.9) are higher.
High-choice participants were paid
No payment is described.
Required essays persuade the writer more
The required essay barely moved attitudes, 3.6 against the control's 3.1.
Low-choice participants did not write an essay
They wrote the same essay. It was just required.
qs.x: Correct: Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable tension you feel when your actions clash with your beliefs (paragraph 1). One way to ease it is to change the belief so it fits what you did. In the low-choice group, the essay was required, so participants had a ready outside excuse: "I was told to." Little tension, little change. In the high-choice group, they believed they chose to argue against their own view, so the clash was theirs to explain. Table 1 shows it: tension was 6.2 against 3.1, and attitude rose to 7.9 against 3.6 on the 15-point scale. Why the others are wrong: the required essay barely moved attitudes (3.6, close to the control's 3.1), so it didn't persuade more; nobody was paid; both groups wrote the same kind of essay. Trap: Assuming that saying something always changes your attitude, whether or not you chose to say it.

qs.q: Which interpretation best fits the group told the capsule causes tension?
o: They chose not to write the essay after hearing the warning
Every participant wrote the essay.
The capsule reduced their tension, so dissonance disappeared
Their tension stayed high at 6.0.
The warning made the essay feel compulsory
The essay was still described as voluntary.
They blamed their tension on the capsule
Correct: they blamed their tension on the capsule, so they didn't need to change their attitude.
qs.x: Correct: Misattribution means blaming a feeling on the wrong cause. This group was told the capsule often makes people tense. They felt just as tense as the other high-choice groups (6.0 in Table 1), but now they had an outside explanation: "It's the pill." Since the essay no longer seemed to be the cause of their tension, they had no need to change their attitude. It stayed at 4.0, close to the control's 3.1. Why the others are wrong: their tension stayed high at 6.0, so the capsule didn't calm them; every participant agreed to write the essay (paragraph 2); the choice instructions were the same voluntary ones as in the other high-choice groups. Trap: Assuming that no attitude change means no tension. Here the tension was there, it was just blamed on the capsule.

qs.q: Why did the group told the capsule would relax them show the largest attitude change?
o: The capsule raised their liking for the experimenter
Liking wasn't measured.
The relaxing suggestion made them agree more readily
All high-choice participants agreed to write.
They felt less tension than the other high-choice groups
Their tension was the highest, 6.4.
They blamed even more of their tension on the essay
Correct: expecting calm but feeling tense, they blamed the essay even more, giving 9.6.
qs.x: Correct: This group expected the capsule to calm them down, yet they still felt tense, 6.4, the highest of any group. If a relaxing pill can't explain the tension, the only thing left to blame is the essay they chose to write. They pinned even more of the tension on their own act, so they changed their attitude the most: 9.6 on the 15-point scale, above the 7.9 of the no-side-effects group. Why the others are wrong: all high-choice participants agreed to write, so readier agreement can't explain it; liking for the experimenter was never measured; their tension was the highest, not the lowest. Trap: Expecting a "relaxing" pill to reduce attitude change. What matters is what people think caused their tension.

qs.q: Which result would most weaken the claim that tension drives the attitude change in this study?
o: Low-choice participants report little tension
That fits dissonance theory.
High-choice participants report the most tension
That supports the claim.
Attitudes shift equally in every high-choice group
Correct: equal shifts whatever the capsule story would fit self-perception, not tension.
The control group reports the lowest tension
Both theories expect that.
qs.x: Correct: Self-perception theory says people simply read their attitudes off their behavior, with no tension involved (paragraph 1). All three high-choice groups wrote the same freely chosen essay, so self-perception predicts they'd shift equally, whatever they were told about the capsule (paragraph 3). If that had happened, tension wouldn't be doing any work. Instead, attitudes ranged from 4.0 to 9.6 depending on the capsule story, which favors dissonance. So equal shifts across the high-choice groups would weaken the tension claim. Why the others are wrong: the control having the lowest tension is expected by both theories; low tension in the low-choice group fits dissonance; high tension in the high-choice groups supports the claim. Trap: Picking a result that agrees with the claim when the question asks what would weaken it.

qs.q: A patient who chose a painful and costly rehabilitation program later rates it as more helpful than a patient assigned to the same program. Which process does this most directly illustrate?
o: Effort justification
Correct: a painful, costly effort you chose gets valued more to ease dissonance.
The foot-in-the-door effect
That's agreeing to a big request after a small one.
The fundamental attribution error
That's about explaining other people's behavior.
Self-serving bias
That's about taking credit for success and blaming failure on circumstances.
qs.x: Correct: Effort justification is a kind of dissonance reduction. If you freely choose something painful and expensive, the thought "maybe it wasn't worth it" clashes with your choice. To ease that tension, you value it more. The patient who chose the program has that clash; the patient who was assigned has an outside explanation, just like the low-choice essay writers, so there's less need to justify it. Why the others are wrong: self-serving bias is taking credit for your successes and blaming failures on circumstances; foot-in-the-door is agreeing to a big request after first agreeing to a small one; the fundamental attribution error is blaming other people's behavior on their personality and overlooking the situation. Trap: Choosing a familiar social psychology term that sounds related but describes a different process.

h: Attitude toward fee increase (1 = strongly oppose, 15 = strongly favor)
r: High choice, no side effects mentioned
High choice, capsule said to cause tension
High choice, capsule said to relax

passages.title: Dendritic Integration and the Axon Hillock
text: A neuron receives thousands of synaptic inputs and fires only if their combined effect at the site of initiation is sufficient. The individual potentials are graded and decay as they spread, so an input's influence depends on where on the cell it arrives as well as on its size.

Two kinds of summation combine them. Spatial summation adds inputs arriving at different places at the same time; temporal summation adds inputs arriving at the same place in quick succession, and it works only if the second arrives before the first has decayed, which makes it depend on the membrane time constant.

Inhibition does not simply subtract. An inhibitory input that opens chloride channels near the resting potential produces little voltage change on its own but greatly reduces the effect of excitatory inputs arriving nearby, because it holds the membrane close to rest.
Responses were recorded at the site of initiation (Figure 1). No stimulus triggered an action potential.

Two excitatory inputs together gave 7.4 millivolts against the 8.0 predicted by adding them, a small shortfall. Three proximal inputs with a nearby inhibitory input gave 4.1 against a predicted 18.6, a shortfall of more than 14 mV, although the inhibitory input alone produced almost no voltage change.
The inhibition therefore acts by changing how the excitatory currents are handled rather than by adding a negative voltage, which is why its effect is far larger than its own signal.

Two qualifications apply. The recordings are from the site of initiation, which is where the decision to fire is made, but the same inputs recorded at the soma would give different amplitudes, so the numbers describe one location. And the predicted values assume the inputs are independent, which is not true even for two excitatory inputs because each reduces the driving force for the other, and that is the source of the small shortfall for the two excitatory inputs together.

qs.q: Why does the location of a synaptic input on the dendrite affect its effect at the soma?
o: Distal synapses release less transmitter per vesicle
The passage blames distance and decay, not transmitter release.
The proximal inputs are inhibitory
The proximal inputs are excitatory: they depolarize the cell.
Distal inputs arrive later and summate less
Not quite. Timing isn't the explanation given; signals shrink as they travel.
Signals decay as they spread toward the soma
Correct: Graded potentials fade as they travel, so distal inputs arrive smaller (1.8 vs 6.2 mV).
qs.x: Correct: Synaptic potentials are graded, meaning their size varies, and paragraph 1 says they shrink as they spread along the cell. A dendrite works like a leaky hose: current leaks out the farther it travels. So an input far from the site where firing is decided arrives smaller than the same input nearby. Figure 1 shows it: one proximal (near) input gives 6.2 mV at the initiation site, while one distal (far) input gives only 1.8 mV. Why the others are wrong: the passage never says distal synapses release less transmitter, the difference comes from decay along the way; timing isn't the explanation, the near input is more than three times bigger because of decay; and the proximal inputs here are excitatory, which is why they depolarize the cell. Trap: Treating all synaptic inputs as equal no matter where on the cell they land.

qs.q: Why does the inhibitory input have such a large effect?
o: It destroys the excitatory synapses
The excitatory synapses still work. Their current is just drained away.
Its effect is small
It cut the response from a predicted 18.6 mV to 4.1 mV.
It holds the membrane near rest
Correct: Open chloride channels clamp the membrane near rest and drain away the excitatory current.
It adds a large negative voltage of its own
Paragraph 5 says the inhibitory input alone produced almost no voltage change.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says this inhibitory input opens chloride channels, and chloride's equilibrium potential is close to rest. So on its own it barely moves the voltage. What it does is open a leak, a low-resistance path that drains away the excitatory current before it can depolarize the membrane. This is called shunting inhibition. Figure 1 shows the effect: three proximal inputs predicted to give 18.6 mV gave only 4.1 mV, a shortfall of 18.6 − 4.1 = 14.5 mV, even though the inhibition alone produced almost no voltage change (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: it doesn't add a large negative voltage, paragraph 5 says it produced almost none; nothing destroys the excitatory synapses, they're still working; and a 14.5 mV shortfall is a large effect, not a small one. Trap: Expecting inhibition to work by simple subtraction of a negative voltage.

qs.q: Why do two excitatory inputs fall slightly short of their sum?
o: One of the two inputs is actually inhibitory
Both inputs depolarize the cell on their own, so both are excitatory.
The measurement is imprecise
Paragraph 7 gives a real cause: the inputs reduce each other's driving force.
Each reduces the other's driving force
Correct: Each input depolarizes the membrane and shrinks the other's driving force.
They exceed their sum
7.4 mV is below the predicted 8.0 mV.
qs.x: Correct: Each excitatory synapse lets in current because of a driving force, the gap between the membrane voltage and the voltage the ions are pulled toward. When one input depolarizes the membrane, that gap gets smaller for the other input, so it pushes a bit less current. Paragraph 7 says this is why the inputs aren't truly independent. Figure 1 shows the result: 6.2 + 1.8 = 8.0 mV predicted, but 7.4 mV measured, a small shortfall of 0.6 mV. Why the others are wrong: both inputs are excitatory, since each one depolarizes the cell on its own; the passage gives a physical cause for the shortfall rather than blaming measurement error; and 7.4 is below 8.0, so they fall short of their sum, they don't exceed it. Trap: Assuming inputs that arrive together always add up perfectly.

qs.q: By how many millivolts did the response to both inputs together fall short of its prediction?
o: Correct: 8.0 − 7.4 = 0.6 mV.
Not quite. 7.4 mV is the measured value, not the shortfall.
Not quite. 8.0 mV is the prediction, not the gap.
Not quite. 18.6 − 4.1 = 14.5 mV is the shortfall for the stimulus with inhibition.
qs.x: Correct: The shortfall is a difference: shortfall = predicted − measured. From the "Both together" bars in Figure 1, the predicted value is 8.0 mV and the measured value is 7.4 mV. Plug in: shortfall = 8.0 − 7.4 = 0.6 mV. You can check the prediction too: it's the two single inputs added, 6.2 + 1.8 = 8.0 mV. Why the others are wrong: 7.4 is the measured value itself, not the gap; 14.5 is the shortfall with inhibition (18.6 − 4.1 = 14.5 mV), the stimulus with inhibition; 8.0 is the prediction, not how far the measurement missed it. Trap: Pulling the shortfall for the wrong stimulus.

qs.q: Why do the amplitude values in the table apply only to one recording location?
o: The recordings were made at the soma
Not quite. The passage says they were made at the initiation site.
The inputs were too small to spread
Not quite. They spread and decay; the point is that amplitude depends on where you record.
All sites give the same amplitude
Graded potentials decay as they spread, so amplitudes vary by site.
Amplitudes vary with site
Correct: Graded potentials differ in size from place to place, so the soma would read differently.
qs.x: Correct: Because graded potentials shrink as they spread (paragraph 1), the same input has a different size at every point on the cell. Paragraph 7 says the recordings were taken at the site of initiation, where the decision to fire is made, and that the same inputs recorded at the soma (the cell body) would give different amplitudes. So the numbers in Figure 1 describe that one spot. Why the others are wrong: the recordings were made at the initiation site, not the soma; inputs do spread, they just shrink as they go; and different sites give different amplitudes, which is the whole point of paragraph 1. Trap: Assuming a voltage measured at one point applies to the whole neuron.

graph.title: Figure 1. Depolarization at the site of initiation: measured and predicted by simple addition

passages.title: Ion Channels and the Action Potential
text: Neurons at rest hold a negative membrane potential because the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains ion gradients and because the membrane at rest is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. An action potential begins when depolarization opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, letting Na⁺ rush in. Those channels then inactivate, and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, letting K⁺ leave and returning the membrane toward rest. During the absolute refractory period, enough Na⁺ channels are inactivated that no stimulus can trigger another action potential; inactivation is removed only after the membrane repolarizes.

The action potential is all-or-none: once threshold is reached, its size does not depend on how strong the stimulus was. A stronger stimulus is encoded by a higher firing frequency, not by larger spikes.

Researchers recorded from squid giant axons in solutions of different composition and with channel-blocking drugs. Tetrodotoxin (TTX), from pufferfish, blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels (Table 1).

The researchers also noted why the squid giant axon was chosen. It is up to a millimeter across, wide enough for an electrode to be threaded down its length, and its contents can be squeezed out and replaced with a solution of known composition. This let the original investigators set the concentrations on both sides of the membrane and test directly whether the action potential depends on the ion gradients rather than on some property of the cytoplasm. Axons that large exist because the squid has no myelin and relies on diameter alone for rapid conduction.

In a further experiment, the axon was stimulated twice in quick succession. With a 0.5 ms interval the second stimulus produced no response at any strength; with a 3 ms interval it produced a full-sized action potential when the stimulus was stronger than usual; with a 10 ms interval a normal stimulus sufficed.

qs.q: Why does lowering external Na⁺ reduce the peak of the action potential?
o: A smaller gradient drives less Na⁺ inward
Correct: Less Na⁺ outside means a smaller push inward, so the peak drops from +40 to +22 mV.
The resting potential becomes more negative
Table 1 shows rest stayed at −70 mV.
Fewer Na⁺ channels are present in the membrane
Changing the bath solution doesn't change how many channels are in the membrane.
Na⁺ leaves the cell during the upstroke
During the upstroke Na⁺ rushes in, not out.
qs.x: Correct: At the peak of an action potential, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are wide open, so the membrane voltage heads toward the Na⁺ equilibrium potential: the voltage where the push of Na⁺ down its concentration gradient is exactly balanced. That value depends on how much more Na⁺ is outside than inside. Halve the external Na⁺ and the gradient shrinks, so the equilibrium potential is lower and less Na⁺ rushes in. Table 1 shows the peak dropping from +40 to +22 mV while rest stays at −70 mV. Why the others are wrong: changing the bath doesn't change how many channels sit in the membrane; the resting potential stayed at −70 mV, it didn't get more negative; and Na⁺ flows in during the upstroke, not out. Trap: Mixing up how many channels there are with the driving force pushing ions through them.

qs.q: Why does raising external K⁺ depolarize the resting membrane?
o: K⁺ channels close when external K⁺ rises
The resting shift comes from the K⁺ gradient, not channels closing.
The pump stops working in high K⁺
The pump needs external K⁺ to work, so high K⁺ won't stop it.
The outward K⁺ gradient shrinks
Correct: A smaller K⁺ gradient makes K⁺'s equilibrium potential less negative, and rest follows: −70 to −58 mV.
More Na⁺ enters while at rest
External Na⁺ wasn't changed, so the Na⁺ leak isn't the cause.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the resting membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, so the resting potential sits close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential. That value is set by the ratio of K⁺ outside to K⁺ inside. Double the K⁺ outside and the gradient pushing K⁺ out gets smaller, so the K⁺ equilibrium potential becomes less negative, and the resting potential follows it. Table 1 shows rest moving from −70 to −58 mV. Why the others are wrong: the passage explains rest by the gradient, not by channels closing; the Na⁺ gradient wasn't changed, so Na⁺ leak isn't the cause; and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump actually needs external K⁺ to run, so high K⁺ wouldn't stop it. Trap: Reaching for Na⁺ to explain a resting change when K⁺ is the ion that sets rest.

qs.q: When TEA was applied, the action potential was greatly prolonged. What does this result show about repolarization?
o: Na⁺ channels alone repolarize the membrane
With K⁺ channels blocked, Na⁺ inactivation alone took 7.5 ms to repolarize.
K⁺ channels set the peak of the spike
The peak stayed at about +40 mV with TEA, so K⁺ channels don't set it.
TEA prevents Na⁺ from entering
The upstroke and peak were normal, so Na⁺ still got in.
K⁺ channels end the action potential
Correct: Blocking K⁺ channels stretches repolarization from 1.0 to 7.5 ms.
qs.x: Correct: TEA blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels (paragraph 3). Table 1 shows that with TEA the peak is normal, +41 mV versus +40, but repolarization, the return to rest, takes 7.5 ms instead of 1.0. So K⁺ flowing out through those channels is what brings the membrane back down quickly. Na⁺ channel inactivation helps by stopping the inward current, but on its own it's slow. Why the others are wrong: the peak barely changed (+41 mV), so K⁺ channels don't set it; Na⁺ channels alone can't repolarize quickly, since inactivation without K⁺ current took 7.5 ms; and TEA doesn't stop Na⁺ entry, the normal upstroke shows Na⁺ still rushed in. Trap: Assuming a drug that stretches out the spike must also change how it rises.

qs.q: Why does the second stimulus fail completely at 0.5 ms?
o: The stimulus was too weak
Paragraph 5 says no stimulus strength worked at 0.5 ms.
The membrane is still depolarized
Depolarization alone would move the cell toward threshold, not block it.
Na⁺ channels are still inactivated
Correct: The Na⁺ channels are still inactivated, so this is the absolute refractory period.
K⁺ channels have not yet opened
K⁺ channels open during repolarization. Their timing isn't the block here.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says that after an action potential many Na⁺ channels are inactivated: stuck shut and unable to reopen until the membrane repolarizes. During this absolute refractory period, no stimulus of any strength can fire the cell, because there aren't enough working Na⁺ channels to open. Paragraph 5 shows exactly this: at a 0.5 ms interval, nothing worked. By 3 ms, enough channels had recovered that a stronger stimulus could fire it (the relative refractory period), and by 10 ms a normal stimulus did. Why the others are wrong: being depolarized on its own would bring the cell closer to threshold, not block firing; the stimulus strength didn't matter, no strength worked at 0.5 ms; and K⁺ channels open during repolarization, they aren't what's missing. Trap: Explaining the refractory period by the membrane voltage instead of by the state of the Na⁺ channels.

qs.q: In these experiments, why was the squid giant axon a good choice for testing whether the action potential depends on ion gradients?
o: Its contents could be replaced with known solutions
Correct: Its width lets researchers squeeze out the contents and set the ion concentrations on both sides.
Its thick myelin sheath speeds up the recording
Not quite. The passage says the squid has no myelin and relies on diameter alone.
It fires larger spikes than other neurons do, making the peak easier to measure
Not quite. Nothing in the passage says its spikes are larger; the advantage is access to both sides of the membrane.
It has no voltage-gated K⁺ channels
Not quite. TEA slowed repolarization in this axon, so K⁺ channels are present.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says the squid giant axon is up to a millimeter across. That is wide enough to thread an electrode down its length, and its contents can be squeezed out and replaced with a solution of known composition. So the researchers could set the ion concentrations on both sides of the membrane themselves and test directly whether the action potential depends on the gradients, instead of on some property of the cytoplasm. The independent variable (the ion concentrations) is then under the researchers' control. Why the others are wrong: the squid has no myelin, it relies on diameter alone for fast conduction; spikes are all-or-none, and the passage never says this axon's spikes are larger; and the TEA result shows K⁺ channels are present, since blocking them slowed repolarization from 1.0 to 7.5 ms. Trap: Choosing the answer that sounds like a typical neuron feature instead of the one tied to the experimental setup.

passages.title: Thin Lens Equation and Image Formation
text: A thin converging lens obeys 1/f = 1/do + 1/di, where f is the focal length, do the object distance and di the image distance. Magnification is m = −di/do. A positive di means a real image on the far side of the lens, which can be projected onto a screen; a negative di means a virtual image on the same side as the object, which cannot be projected but can be viewed through the lens. The sign of m tells the orientation: negative is inverted, positive is upright.

A compound microscope uses two lenses. The objective, close to the specimen, forms a real inverted image inside the tube; the eyepiece then acts as a magnifier of that image. Total magnification is the product of the two.

Students varied the object distance for a single converging lens of focal length 10.0 cm by moving an illuminated object along an optical bench, and for each setting they measured the image distance by finding where a sharp image formed on a screen. The image distances are plotted in Figure 1, and Table 1 gives the image height ratio and whether an image appeared on the screen.

The students also noted a practical point about measurement. Finding the sharp image by eye has some uncertainty, and that uncertainty grows when the image is far from the lens, because the image stays acceptably sharp over a longer range of screen positions. They therefore repeated each measurement three times and reported the mean, and they treated the 50.0 cm row, where the image is small and close to the focal point, as the most precise. They also checked the lens by using a distant window as the object: the image then formed 10.1 cm from the lens, confirming the stated focal length within their uncertainty.
In a second part, students replaced the lens with one of focal length 5.0 cm and placed the object 6.0 cm away, then viewed the image formed by that lens through a second lens used as an eyepiece.

qs.q: Where does the image form when the object is 12.0 cm from the 10.0 cm lens?
o: 5.5 cm
This adds 1/10 and 1/12 instead of subtracting them.
22 cm
This adds 10 and 12. The lens equation uses 1/distance, not the distances.
60 cm
−60 cm
