A negative image distance needs the object inside the focal length. 12 cm is outside it.
qs.x: Correct: Use the thin-lens equation, 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. The values are f = 10.0 cm and do = 12.0 cm, and we want di. Move 1/do to the other side: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/12. To subtract fractions, give them the same bottom number. 60 is the smallest number both 10 and 12 go into, so 1/10 = 6/60 and 1/12 = 5/60. Now 1/di = 6/60 − 5/60 = 1/60. Flip both sides: di = 60 cm. It's positive, so the image is real and forms on the far side of the lens, where a screen can catch it. That fits Figure 1: as the object moves toward 10 cm, the image runs farther away. Why the others are wrong: 5.5 cm comes from adding the reciprocals (1/10 + 1/12 = 11/60, which flips to about 5.5 cm) instead of subtracting; 22 cm just adds 10 and 12, but the equation works with reciprocals, not the distances themselves; −60 cm would be a virtual image, and that only happens when the object is closer than the focal length, while 12 cm is farther than 10 cm. Trap: Adding or subtracting the distances themselves instead of their reciprocals (the 1/ numbers).

qs.q: Why can the image at do = 5.0 cm not be projected onto a screen?
o: The object blocks the screen
Nothing forms on the far side to block. The image is virtual, on the object's side.
The lens is too weak there
The focal length is a property of the lens. It stays 10.0 cm no matter where the object is.
It is virtual, on the object's side
Correct: di is −10.0 cm, so the image is virtual, on the object's side. No light meets there for a screen to catch.
The image is far too small to be seen on a screen
Table 1 gives a height ratio of 2.00, so the image is twice the object's size, not tiny.
qs.x: Correct: The last point in Figure 1 has the object at 5.0 cm, which is inside the 10.0 cm focal length, and the image distance comes out as −10.0 cm. Paragraph 1 says a negative di means a virtual image on the same side as the object. Virtual means the light rays leaving the lens spread apart and only seem, to your eye, to come from a point on the object's side. No light actually meets at that point, so there's nothing for a screen to catch. You see it only by looking through the lens, like a magnifying glass, which is why the table says "No" in the screen column. Why the others are wrong: the image is too small to see fails because the table gives an image height ÷ object height of 2.00, so it's twice as tall as the object; the lens is too weak there fails because the focal length belongs to the lens and stays 10.0 cm wherever the object sits; the object blocks the screen fails because no image forms on the far side at all, so there's nothing to block. Trap: Thinking a virtual image is just a dim real image. It's a different thing: the light never actually comes together.

qs.q: What does the row at do = 20.0 cm illustrate?
o: The lens produces no image
Table 1 says the image was seen on the screen, so an image clearly formed.
At do = 2f the image matches the object
Correct: At 2f, 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20, so di = 20 cm and m = −20/20 = −1: same size, inverted.
The focal length equals 20 cm
The passage gives the focal length as 10.0 cm. 20 cm is twice the focal length.
The image is upright at that distance
A real image from one converging lens is inverted. Here m = −1, and the minus sign means upside down.
qs.x: Correct: The focal length is 10.0 cm, so an object at 20.0 cm sits at exactly twice the focal length (2f). Check it with the lens equation, 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. Rearrange: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/20. Give them the same bottom number: 1/10 = 2/20, so 1/di = 2/20 − 1/20 = 1/20, and di = 20 cm. Figure 1 and Table 1 agree: image distance 20.0 cm and height ratio 1.00. Magnification is m = −di/do = −20/20 = −1, so the image is the same size and upside down. This row is the dividing line: objects farther than 2f give smaller real images (the 30.0 and 50.0 cm rows), and objects between f and 2f give bigger ones (the 15.0 cm row). Why the others are wrong: the lens produces no image fails because a sharp image showed up on the screen; the image is upright fails because a real image from one converging lens is always inverted (m is negative); the focal length equals 20 cm fails because the passage gives it as 10.0 cm, and 20 cm is twice that. Trap: Thinking matching distances are a special feature of the lens rather than of putting the object at 2f.

qs.q: Why must the eyepiece be positioned so the objective's image falls just inside its focal length?
o: So the eyepiece forms a real image
A real image would need the object outside the focal length. Your eye's lens makes the image on your retina.
So the two images cancel each other's inversions completely
A magnifier keeps its object's orientation, so the objective's flip stays. Microscope images look inverted.
So the image distance becomes zero
The lens equation never gives an image distance of zero for a real object.
So the eyepiece forms an enlarged virtual image
Correct: An object inside the focal length gives an enlarged virtual image, which is exactly how a magnifier works.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the eyepiece acts as a magnifier of the objective's image. A magnifier only works when its object sits inside its focal length. The last point in Figure 1 shows what happens then: an object at 5.0 cm, inside the 10.0 cm focal length, gives di = −10.0 cm and a height ratio of 2.00. That's an enlarged virtual image you look at through the lens. The eyepiece treats the objective's real image as its own object, so placing that image just inside the eyepiece's focal length turns it into a bigger virtual image for your eye. Why the others are wrong: so the eyepiece forms a real image fails because a real image would need its object outside the focal length, and your eye's own lens is what makes the image on your retina; so the two images cancel their inversions fails because a magnifier's virtual image is upright compared with its object, so the objective's flip stays and the final view is still upside down compared with the specimen; so the image distance becomes zero fails because the lens equation never gives di = 0 for a real object. Trap: Expecting the eyepiece to flip the image back upright.

qs.q: How would a shorter objective focal length change the microscope?
o: Lower magnification with a brighter image
A shorter objective focal length raises magnification, it doesn't lower it.
No change, since magnification depends only on the eyepiece
Paragraph 2 says total magnification is the product of both lenses, so the objective matters too.
Higher magnification at a shorter working distance
Correct: The specimen must sit just outside a shorter f, so it's closer to the lens. More magnification, less working room.
Higher magnification at a longer working distance
A shorter focal length forces the specimen closer to the lens, so the working distance shrinks.
qs.x: Correct: The objective has to form a real image inside the tube, so the specimen must sit just outside the objective's focal length. Figure 1 and Table 1 show the pattern: as the object moves in toward f, the image moves farther away and gets bigger (at 15.0 cm, di = 30.0 cm and the image is 2.00 times as tall). Magnification is m = −di/do, so a large di over a small do means large magnification. With a shorter focal length, the specimen can sit even closer and still throw an image far down the fixed-length tube, so magnification rises. The cost is working distance, the gap between the lens and the slide, which shrinks. Why the others are wrong: higher magnification at a longer working distance fails because a shorter f forces the specimen closer, not farther; lower magnification with a brighter image fails because a shorter f raises magnification; no change fails because paragraph 2 says total magnification is the product of both lenses, so the objective counts too. Trap: Assuming a stronger objective is a free upgrade with no downside.

graph.title: Figure 1. Image distance against object distance for the 10.0 cm lens

passages.title: Central and Peripheral Routes to Persuasion
text: The elaboration likelihood model describes two routes to persuasion. In the central route, people think carefully about the content of a message, so strong arguments persuade and weak ones do not, and the resulting attitude tends to last and to predict behavior. In the peripheral route, people rely on cues such as the source's expertise, attractiveness or the sheer number of arguments, producing attitudes that are easier to change later. Which route operates depends on motivation and ability: personal relevance, a need for cognition and freedom from distraction all push people toward the central route.

Researchers asked 320 undergraduates to evaluate a proposal that their university require a comprehensive examination for graduation. Relevance was manipulated by saying the policy would start next year, affecting the participants themselves, or in 10 years. Argument quality was manipulated by using either strong arguments supported by data or weak ones based on anecdote. Source expertise was manipulated by attributing the proposal to a national commission on education or to a local high school class. Attitudes were rated from 1 to 9, with higher numbers meaning more favor (Table 1).

Distraction was examined in a follow-up with 120 further participants. While reading the proposal, half heard a recording of numbers they had to monitor. Under distraction, the difference between strong and weak arguments shrank by about two-thirds even in the high-relevance condition, while the effect of source expertise grew. The researchers concluded that motivation alone is not enough: a person must also have the capacity to process the message.

Two weeks later, participants rated the proposal again. In the high-relevance group, attitudes had shifted by an average of 0.4 points; in the low-relevance group, by 1.9 points. Participants also completed a need-for-cognition scale; among low-relevance participants who scored in the top quarter, argument quality mattered about as much as it did in the high-relevance group.

qs.q: What does the high-relevance row show?
o: Both variables mattered equally
Quality mattered far more, 4.2 against 0.3.
Argument quality drove attitudes
Correct: quality moved ratings 4.2 points, source only 0.3.
Source expertise drove attitudes
Expertise moved ratings by only 0.3.
Neither variable mattered much
Quality moved ratings by more than 4 points.
qs.x: Correct: Read the high-relevance row of Table 1. With an expert source, strong arguments got 7.6 and weak ones 3.4, a gap of 7.6 − 3.4 = 4.2 points. Now hold quality fixed and change the source: strong arguments got 7.6 from the expert and 7.3 from the nonexpert, only 7.6 − 7.3 = 0.3 points apart. So argument quality drove attitudes. That's the central route, where people think carefully about the message itself (paragraph 1). Why the others are wrong: the expert source moved ratings by only 0.3, so it didn't drive them; neither variable mattering much is wrong because quality moved ratings by more than 4 points; and 4.2 against 0.3 is far from equal. Trap: Assuming the expert always matters. When people care, they look at the arguments.

qs.q: What does the low-relevance row show?
o: Participants ignored the message entirely
Ratings still differed by source, so they paid some attention.
The two rows show the same pattern
The high-relevance row shows the opposite pattern.
Source expertise mattered most
Correct: source moved ratings about 2 points (6.2 against 4.1).
Argument quality mattered more than the source
Quality changed ratings by only 0.1 to 0.4 here.
qs.x: Correct: In the low-relevance row, compare sources with strong arguments: 6.2 from the national commission against 4.1 from the high school class, a gap of 6.2 − 4.1 = 2.1 points. Now compare argument quality with an expert source: 6.2 for strong against 5.8 for weak, only 0.4 apart. So the source mattered most. That's the peripheral route: when people don't care much, they lean on shortcuts like who's talking (paragraph 1). Why the others are wrong: ratings did differ by source, so participants didn't ignore the message; quality changed ratings by only 0.4 here, less than the source's 2.1; the high-relevance row shows the opposite pattern. Trap: Expecting the same factor to win in every condition.

qs.q: Why did low-relevance attitudes shift more over two weeks?
o: High-relevance participants were retested sooner
Both were retested at two weeks.
Peripheral attitudes are less durable
Correct: cue-based attitudes have little support, so they drift (1.9 against 0.4).
They were told that the policy had changed
No new information was given.
Those participants forgot the proposal
Both groups rated it again, so they hadn't forgotten it.
qs.x: Correct: Attitudes formed through the central route rest on reasons people thought through and can recall, so they stick. Attitudes formed through the peripheral route rest on a cue, like who made the proposal, and have little behind them, so they drift (paragraph 1). Paragraph 4 shows this: two weeks later, the high-relevance group had shifted only 0.4 points, while the low-relevance group shifted 1.9. Why the others are wrong: both groups rated the proposal again, so forgetting it doesn't fit; no new information was given to anyone; both groups were retested at the same two-week point. Trap: Blaming a weaker attitude on forgetting the topic instead of on how the attitude was formed.

qs.q: What does the need-for-cognition result add?
o: Only the personal relevance of a message can produce central processing
They showed careful processing without relevance.
Need for cognition made them more persuadable
They responded to strong arguments, not to everything.
Motivation can come from the person, not the message
Correct: people who enjoy thinking process carefully even when it doesn't affect them.
Need for cognition replaces argument quality
They responded to argument quality. The trait didn't replace it.
qs.x: Correct: Need for cognition is a personality trait: how much someone enjoys thinking hard. Paragraph 4 says low-relevance participants high in this trait still responded to argument quality about as much as the high-relevance group did. So the motivation to think carefully can come from the person, not just from the message being personally relevant. Why the others are wrong: these participants responded to argument quality, so their trait didn't replace it; they showed central processing without relevance, so relevance isn't the only way in; and responding to strong arguments, but not weak ones, is careful thinking, not being easier to persuade. Trap: Treating personal relevance as the only route to careful thinking.

qs.q: An advertiser wants an attitude that will still influence a purchase months later. What does the study suggest?
o: Give strong arguments to an interested audience
Correct: careful thinking about strong arguments makes attitudes that last.
Repeat the brand name as often as possible
Repetition is a peripheral cue.
List as many arguments as possible, regardless of quality
Number of arguments alone is a peripheral cue.
Use an attractive celebrity in a brief advertisement
An attractive celebrity is a peripheral cue.
qs.x: Correct: Attitudes that last and guide behavior come from the central route (paragraph 1). That needs two things: an audience that cares enough to think, and arguments good enough to reward that thinking. The two-week retest backs this up: the high-relevance group barely moved (0.4 points), while the low-relevance group drifted 1.9 (paragraph 4). Why the others are wrong: an attractive celebrity is a peripheral cue, like the source's attractiveness in paragraph 1; repeating a brand name is a shortcut, not a reason; and piling on arguments no matter their quality relies on sheer number, which paragraph 1 lists as a peripheral cue. Peripheral tactics can work quickly, but the attitudes fade. Trap: Judging a persuasion tactic only by how well it works right away.

passages.title: Blocking and Prediction in Classical Conditioning
text: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US) comes to elicit a conditioned response. Pairing alone is not sufficient: the conditioned stimulus (CS) must predict the US. If a second cue is added to one that already predicts the US reliably, the new cue gains little control, an effect called blocking, because the US is already fully predicted and nothing new is learned.

Several phenomena follow the same logic. In extinction, the CS is presented without the US and the response declines, but the original learning is not erased: after a rest the response partly returns as spontaneous recovery, and a single pairing can restore it quickly. In latent inhibition, a stimulus presented many times on its own before conditioning is harder to turn into a CS afterward.

Researchers conditioned rabbits to blink in response to a tone paired with a brief puff of air to the eye. The percentage of trials with a conditioned blink is shown for several groups after training. Figure 1 shows the design of each group and Table 1 shows the results.

The researchers chose eyeblink conditioning because the circuit is well mapped. The conditioned response depends on the cerebellum, and lesions of one small region there abolish the learned blink while leaving the unconditioned blink to the air puff intact. That separation lets researchers distinguish a failure to learn from a failure to respond, which behavioral measures alone cannot do. The timing of the pairing also matters: a tone that begins about half a second before the puff produces strong learning, while a tone that begins after the puff produces almost none.

A fifth group was trained with the tone and puff for 30 trials and then given 40 trials of the tone with no puff. Blinking fell from 84% to 11%. After 24 hours in the home cage with no training, the first 10 test trials produced blinking on 38% of trials.

qs.q: Why does the light gain so little control in the blocking group?
o: The tone already predicts the puff
Correct: The tone already predicts the puff, so the light adds nothing new to learn.
The light and puff were never paired
Not quite. Light and puff were paired in phase 2.
The light is far too dim to be noticed
Not quite. The same light drew 58% blinking in the standard group.
Two stimuli cannot be conditioned at once
Not quite. The standard group learned both cues together.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says a cue gets learned only if it predicts the US (unconditioned stimulus, here the air puff) and tells the animal something new. In the blocking group, phase 1 trained the tone alone with the puff, so by phase 2 the tone already predicts the puff perfectly. Adding the light gives no new information, so little is learned about it. Table 1 shows blinks to the light at just 9%. Why the others are wrong: the light being too dim fails because the same light drew 58% blinking in the standard group; the light and puff never being paired is false, they were paired in phase 2; two stimuli not being learnable at once is false, since the standard group learned both tone (62%) and light (58%). Trap: Assuming that pairing a stimulus with a US always produces learning.

qs.q: What does the unpaired control group show?
o: The tone is too quiet to be heard
Not quite. The same tone drew 88% blinking in the blocking group.
The puff is not aversive
Not quite. The puff reliably triggers a reflex blink.
Rabbits cannot blink in response to a tone
Not quite. Other groups blinked to the tone on 62% to 88% of trials.
Pairing, not exposure, produces it
Correct: Same stimuli, no predictive pairing, only 7% blinking. Pairing is what drives learning.
qs.x: Correct: The unpaired control group got the same tone, light and puff, but at random times, so neither cue ever predicted the puff. Table 1 shows blinking stayed near zero: 7% to the tone and 6% to the light. So simply experiencing the stimuli isn't enough. The learning in the other groups comes from the predictive pairing. Why the others are wrong: rabbits not being able to blink to a tone fails because other groups blinked to it on 62% to 88% of trials; the puff not being aversive fails because the puff reliably triggers a reflex blink; the tone being too quiet fails because the same tone produced 88% blinking in the blocking group. Trap: Treating a control group as a weaker copy of the experiment, instead of as the test of one specific idea.

qs.q: Why does the latent inhibition group respond less to the light?
o: The tone blocked the light in that group
Not quite. Blocking needs a pretrained cue; their tone was new in phase 2.
The light was never paired with the puff
Not quite. The light was paired with the puff in phase 2.
The light already predicted nothing
Correct: Pre-exposure taught them the light predicts nothing, which slows later learning.
The group received fewer phase 2 trials
Not quite. Every group had 30 phase 2 trials.
qs.x: Correct: Latent inhibition (paragraph 2) means that a stimulus shown many times on its own, with nothing following it, is harder to condition later. In phase 1 this group saw the light alone, so they learned that the light predicts nothing. After the same 30 pairings in phase 2, Table 1 shows only 14% blinking to the light, compared with 58% in the standard group. Why the others are wrong: the light never being paired is false, it was paired in phase 2; fewer phase 2 trials is false, every group had 30; the tone blocking the light doesn't fit, because blocking needs a cue already trained to predict the puff, and for this group the tone was brand new in phase 2. Trap: Mixing up latent inhibition (pre-exposure to the same cue) with blocking (another cue already predicts the US).

qs.q: What does the return of blinking after 24 hours demonstrate?
o: Spontaneous recovery
Correct: The response came back after rest, so the original learning wasn't erased.
Generalization to a new stimulus
Not quite. The same tone was used, so there's no new stimulus.
Complete extinction of the memory
Not quite. The response came back, so the memory wasn't wiped out.
Acquisition of a new association
Not quite. No pairings happened during the rest.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 describes extinction: after tone-puff training, the tone was given 40 times with no puff, and blinking fell from 84% to 11%. Then, after 24 hours of rest with no training at all, blinking came back to 38%. A response coming back after a rest is called spontaneous recovery (paragraph 2). It shows extinction hides the response; it doesn't erase the original learning. Why the others are wrong: complete extinction of the memory is the opposite, the response came back; generalization means responding to a similar new stimulus, but the same tone was used; a new association needs new pairings, and none happened during the rest. Trap: Thinking extinction means unlearning.

qs.q: A therapist uses exposure therapy for a phobia and warns the patient that fear may return later. Which finding supports that warning?
o: The blocking group responded strongly to the tone
Not quite. That's about a cue that already predicts the puff, not relapse.
The latent inhibition group responded less to the light
Not quite. That's about pre-exposure, not a response returning.
The unpaired group barely responded
Not quite. That shows pairing is needed to learn at all.
Blinking returned after a day of rest
Correct: Extinguished blinking came back after rest, just as extinguished fear can return.
qs.x: Correct: Exposure therapy is extinction in practice: the person faces the feared thing again and again without anything bad happening, and the fear fades. But the paragraph 5 group shows that extinction doesn't erase the original learning. Blinking dropped to 11%, then came back to 38% after a day of rest. In the same way, fear can return later, so the therapist's warning makes sense. Why the others are wrong: the blocking group responding strongly to the tone is about a cue that already predicts the US, not about relapse; the unpaired group barely responding shows that pairing is needed to learn in the first place; the latent inhibition group responding less to the light is about pre-exposure slowing learning. Trap: Picking a result about how learning starts when the question is about a response coming back.

r: Tone, light and puff at random times

passages.title: Foot-in-the-Door Versus Door-in-the-Face
text: Two sequential-request techniques raise compliance with a large request, and they work by different routes. The foot-in-the-door technique begins with a small request that is almost always granted, and the act of granting it shifts the person's view of themselves toward being someone who supports the cause, so the later large request is consistent with that self-image. The door-in-the-face technique begins with an extreme request that is refused, and the subsequent smaller request succeeds through reciprocal concession, because the requester has visibly come down and the target feels obliged to meet them.

The two accounts make different predictions about the requester. A self-image shift travels with the person being asked, so it should survive a change of canvasser. A reciprocal concession is owed to a particular person who made the concession, so it should not transfer.

Canvassers approached 600 households about placing a large yard sign supporting a road-safety campaign. Households were assigned by street block to one of four conditions, and the share agreeing was recorded, along with how long the sign remained in place (Table 1).

Both techniques beat the direct request, and the final row is the informative one. Moving to a different canvasser cuts agreement from 53% to 28%, which a pure self-image account did not predict, while retention remains high at 18 days, close to the 21 days of the same-canvasser petition group and well above the 11 days of the door-in-the-face group.

Retention is the more revealing measure. Agreement can be produced by social pressure in the moment, but a sign that stays up for three weeks suggests a changed view of the issue, and that pattern follows the petition conditions rather than the extreme-request condition. The study has a real weakness: assignment was by street block rather than by household, so blocks could differ in traffic, in prior exposure to the campaign, or in how neighbors influence one another, and canvassers were not blind to condition, which leaves room for differences in enthusiasm to affect the results.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 does the passage treat as most revealing about the two mechanisms?
o: The extreme-request group agreed more often than the direct-request group did at the first visit
That's the door-in-the-face effect itself, not a contrast.
Agreement in the direct-request group was the lowest of the four
That only shows both techniques work.
Agreement fell when a different canvasser made the large request
That complicates the self-image account rather than separating the two.
Retention is long in both petition conditions but short after the extreme request
Correct: signs stayed up 21 and 18 days after petitions, but only 11 after the extreme request.
qs.x: Correct: The two techniques work differently (paragraph 1). Foot-in-the-door changes how people see themselves, which should last. Door-in-the-face works by returning a favor in the moment, which shouldn't last once the canvasser leaves. So look at how long signs stayed up. In Table 1, petition households kept the sign 21 days with the same canvasser and 18 days with a different one, but extreme-request households kept it only 11 days. That's the lasting pattern a changed self-image predicts (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: the direct request being lowest (17%) only shows both techniques work; the extreme request beating direct (44% against 17%) is just the door-in-the-face effect existing; and agreement falling with a new canvasser complicates the self-image account instead of separating the two. Trap: Using the agreement column when the mechanisms differ in what happens afterward.

qs.q: What does the different-canvasser condition suggest?
o: Part of the petition effect depends on the particular requester
Correct: agreement fell 25 points when the canvasser changed.
Sign retention is unrelated to whether the household agreed
Retention stayed high at 18 days.
Reciprocal concession requires the same person to concede
Reciprocal concession explains the extreme-request condition, not this one.
The petition itself had no influence on compliance
28% still beat the direct request's 17%.
qs.x: Correct: With a different canvasser, agreement fell from 53% to 28%, a drop of 53 − 28 = 25 points. But 28% is still above the 17% for a direct request. So the petition does have a real effect, but a big part of it depends on the specific person who made the first request (paragraph 4). Why the others are wrong: 28% beat the direct request's 17%, so the petition still mattered; retention stayed high at 18 days, close to the 21 days of the same-canvasser group, which fits a real change in view; and reciprocal concession is how the extreme-request technique works, not the petition. Trap: Reading a partial drop as total failure.

qs.q: Which sequence defines the door-in-the-face technique?
o: A single large request is made with no preliminary
That's the direct-request control.
A small request is granted first, and then a larger one is made
That's foot-in-the-door.
An extreme request is refused, then a smaller one is made
Correct: a huge request is refused, then a smaller one follows.
Two requests of equal size are made in sequence
Equal requests mean no concession.
qs.x: Correct: Door-in-the-face starts with a request so big that it gets refused. Then the requester backs down to a smaller one. Because the requester visibly came down, the person feels they should meet them partway (paragraph 1). That's called a reciprocal concession. Why the others are wrong: a small request granted first, then a bigger one, is foot-in-the-door, the opposite order; two equal requests involve no backing down, so there's no concession to return; a single large request with nothing before it is the direct-request control. Trap: Mixing up the two techniques because both use two requests. Watch which one comes first: small or huge.

qs.q: Which design feature most threatens the causal interpretation?
o: Only one city's households were approached
That limits generalization, not cause.
Sign removal dates were recorded by the canvassers themselves
That's a measurement concern.
The message on the yard sign was the same throughout
Keeping the message the same is a strength.
Households were assigned by street block, not individually
Correct: whole blocks may differ in ways that look like technique effects.
qs.x: Correct: Households were assigned by street block, not one by one (paragraph 5). That means each condition got whole blocks, and blocks can differ in traffic, in past exposure to the campaign, and in how neighbors influence each other. Those differences could look like effects of the technique. This threatens the cause-and-effect conclusion the most. Why the others are wrong: canvassers recording removal dates while knowing the condition is a measurement worry, but smaller; sampling one city limits how far the results generalize, not whether the cause is right; keeping the sign's message the same is a strength, since it rules out a rival explanation. Trap: Naming the most obvious imperfection instead of the one that breaks the comparison.

qs.q: Which additional measure would most directly test the self-perception account?
o: Total minutes each canvasser spent at the door
That measures canvasser effort.
The number of road-safety yard signs already visible on nearby lawns before the visit
That describes the neighborhood.
Rated agreement that one is the kind of person who supports road safety
Correct: it measures the self-view change the account says drives compliance.
Reported household income in each of the four conditions
Income is a background factor.
qs.x: Correct: The self-perception account says granting the small request changes how people see themselves, toward being someone who supports the cause (paragraph 1). That change in self-view is the proposed mediator, the middle step between the petition and saying yes to the sign. The most direct test is to measure it: ask people how much they see themselves as the kind of person who supports road safety, after the petition and before the big request. Why the others are wrong: household income is a background factor, a covariate, not the mechanism; yard signs already on nearby lawns describe the neighborhood; minutes at the door measure the canvasser's effort. Trap: Adding a reasonable background measure instead of measuring the mechanism itself.

r: Extreme request first, then the sign

passages.title: Reinforcement Schedules and Extinction
text: Operant conditioning strengthens a response that is followed by reinforcement, and the schedule on which reinforcement arrives shapes both how fast the response is emitted and how long it persists once reinforcement stops. Continuous reinforcement follows every response. Ratio schedules reinforce after a number of responses, interval schedules after a period of time, and each can be fixed or variable.

The characteristic patterns follow from what the schedule makes predictable. A fixed-ratio schedule produces rapid bursts with a brief pause after each reinforcement, because the next payoff is a known number of responses away. A variable-ratio schedule produces a high, steady rate with no pause, because any response might be the one reinforced. A fixed-interval schedule produces a scalloped pattern, with responding low early in the interval and accelerating as the time approaches, since early responses cannot be reinforced.

Resistance to extinction follows the same logic. Extinction requires the animal to detect that reinforcement has stopped, and that detection is easy under continuous reinforcement, where a single unrewarded response is already unusual, and hard under a variable schedule, where long unrewarded runs were a normal part of training.

Pigeons were trained to peck a key on one of four schedules until responding was stable, then reinforcement was discontinued and responses were counted until the rate fell below one peck per minute (Table 1).

The two columns dissociate. Fixed ratio 10 and variable ratio 10 deliver reinforcement at the same average cost and produce similar rates in training, 68 and 75, yet differ more than three fold in persistence, 340 against 1,120. Rate of responding during training is therefore not what determines resistance to extinction; predictability is.

Several things the table cannot settle remain. All four groups were run to stable responding rather than for a fixed number of sessions, so the ratio groups received more reinforcements in total, and total reinforcement is itself a candidate explanation for persistence. The extinction criterion is also arbitrary, and a different cutoff would compress or stretch the differences. Pigeons pecking a key for grain also differ from a person persisting at a slot machine in ways the paradigm does not capture, although the schedule logic transfers.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 shows that training response rate does not drive persistence?
o: Fixed ratio 10 against variable ratio 10
Correct: Similar rates (68 vs 75), very different persistence (340 vs 1,120).
Variable ratio 10 against fixed interval 1 min
Not quite. Their rates differ by more than two times (75 vs 31).
Fixed interval against continuous reinforcement
Not quite. Both columns differ again.
Continuous against variable ratio 10
Not quite. Rate and persistence both differ there.
qs.x: Correct: To show that training rate doesn't drive persistence, you need two schedules with about the same rate but different persistence. Table 1 has that in fixed ratio 10 (68 responses per minute) and variable ratio 10 (75 per minute). Close rates, yet 340 versus 1,120 responses before extinction. How much more? 1,120 ÷ 340 ≈ 3.3 times. So rate can't be the cause; predictability is (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: continuous versus variable ratio differ in both rate (22 vs 75) and persistence, so you can't separate them; fixed interval versus continuous also differ in both columns; variable ratio versus fixed interval have rates that differ by more than two times (75 ÷ 31 ≈ 2.4). Trap: Picking the pair with the biggest persistence gap instead of the pair that holds rate steady.

qs.q: Why does responding on a fixed-interval schedule stay low early in each interval?
o: Fixed intervals demand more responses per payoff
Not quite. Only one peck is needed after the interval.
Pigeons are unable to discriminate elapsed time
Not quite. The scallop shows they track time.
Early responses cannot be reinforced
Correct: Early pecks can never pay; the timer, not the count, controls the reward.
Interval schedules deliver no reinforcement at all
Not quite. They reward after each interval.
qs.x: Correct: On a fixed-interval schedule, the first peck after the set time is up gets the reward. Paragraph 2 says pecks early in the interval can never be rewarded. The pigeons learn this, so they hold back early and speed up as the time nears. On a graph this looks like a series of scallops. Why the others are wrong: interval schedules delivering no reinforcement is false, they reward after each interval; pigeons not being able to judge time is false, the scallop pattern itself shows they can; fixed intervals demanding more responses per payoff mixes it up with ratio schedules, only one peck is needed once the time is up. Trap: Mixing up a time requirement (interval) with a count requirement (ratio).

qs.q: A parent occasionally gives in to a child's tantrum. Why does this make tantrums especially persistent?
o: Tantrums are being reinforced continuously
Not quite. Giving in happens only sometimes.
Intermittent reward resists extinction
Correct: Unpredictable rewards make failures feel normal, so the behavior resists extinction.
Giving in functions as a punishment of the tantrum
Not quite. Giving in rewards the tantrum.
Extinction is impossible once a behavior is learned
Not quite. Extinction does happen, as Table 1 shows.
qs.x: Correct: Giving in only some of the time puts tantrums on a variable schedule: the child can't predict which tantrum will work. Paragraph 3 explains why that's so persistent. To quit, the child must notice that rewards have stopped. But on a variable schedule, long runs of failed tantrums were normal, so another run of failures doesn't signal that anything has changed. Table 1 shows the same: variable ratio held out for 1,120 responses, continuous only 60. Why the others are wrong: tantrums being reinforced continuously is false, giving in happens only sometimes; giving in punishing the tantrum is backwards, the child gets what it wanted; extinction being impossible is false, every group in Table 1 extinguished eventually. Trap: Thinking occasional rewards are weak rewards, when they actually build persistence.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure leaves total reinforcement as an alternative explanation?
o: Extinction was defined as a response rate below one peck in any single minute of testing
Not quite. It's an arbitrary cutoff applied equally, not a confound.
12 pigeons were assigned to each of the four schedules
Not quite. Equal group sizes help the comparison.
Reinforcement was grain delivered after a key peck
Not quite. The reinforcer was the same for every group.
Groups were trained to stable responding rather than for equal reinforcements
Correct: Training to stability meant ratio groups earned more rewards in total.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says every group was trained until responding was stable, not for a fixed number of rewards. So groups ended up with different totals; the ratio groups earned more rewards. More total rewards could by itself make a behavior more persistent. That means schedule type and total reinforcement are mixed together (a confound). Why the others are wrong: the extinction cutoff of one peck per minute is arbitrary, but it's applied the same way to every group, so it changes the scale of the numbers, not which group differs; 12 pigeons per group is equal, which helps the comparison; grain after a key peck was the same reinforcer for everyone. Trap: Treating an arbitrary measuring threshold as a confound.

qs.q: Which schedule best describes a slot machine?
o: Variable ratio: an unpredictable play count
Correct: An unpredictable number of plays per payout is variable ratio.
Fixed ratio, paying after set plays
Not quite. Players would learn to count the plays.
Fixed interval, paying after a set wait
Not quite. Payouts don't depend on time passed.
Continuous, paying on every single play
Not quite. Every play would win.
qs.x: Correct: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays. That's a variable-ratio schedule: rewards depend on the number of responses, and the number changes each time. Paragraph 2 says this gives a high, steady rate with no pause, because any play might be the winner. Table 1 shows it's also the most persistent schedule (1,120 responses before extinction), which is why long losing streaks don't stop players. Why the others are wrong: a fixed ratio would pay after a set count, and players would learn to count; a fixed interval would pay based on time, so waiting would work as well as playing; continuous would pay on every play, meaning no losses. Trap: Matching the schedule to how often you win instead of to what decides the win.

passages.title: Bandura on Acquisition Versus Performance
text: Observational learning is the acquisition of behavior by watching a model, without the observer being reinforced. Bandura's analysis separates acquisition from performance: an observer can learn what to do without doing it, and whether the behavior appears depends on the incentives in force at the time. Four processes are involved: attention to the model and retention of what was seen support learning, while the motor capacity to reproduce it and motivation govern performance.

The consequences the model receives matter, and they matter through the observer's expectations rather than through any reinforcement the observer has had. Seeing a model rewarded raises the observer's expectation that the behavior pays; seeing a model punished lowers it. Because the learning is already in place, offering the observer an incentive afterwards should reveal behavior that the punished condition suppressed.

Children watched a short film of an adult performing a sequence of four novel actions with a toy. The model was then rewarded, punished, or neither, in randomly assigned conditions. Each child was observed alone with the toy for five minutes, and then, in a second session, was offered a sticker for showing everything the adult had done. Figure 1 shows the sequence of steps and Table 1 shows the results.

The incentive session is the crux. Without it the three groups differ sharply, from 3.1 down to 0.7 actions, but with an incentive they are nearly identical at about 3.4, which means the punished group had learned the sequence all along and was not performing it.

The design has limits. Children were observed once per session by observers who knew the condition, so scoring was not blind, and the second session always followed the first, so the rise could partly reflect practice or a second opportunity rather than the incentive alone. A group offered the incentive in the first session would settle that. The novel actions also have no meaning outside the study, which is deliberate, since it ensures the children could not have learned them earlier, but it leaves open whether consequences to a model work the same way for behavior a child already knows.

qs.q: What does the incentive session establish?
o: Stickers are a stronger reward than praise
Not quite. Praise was never compared.
The punished group had learned without performing
Correct: The punished group jumped from 0.7 to 3.3 actions, so they'd learned without performing.
The reward condition produced the most learning
Not quite. With an incentive all groups land near 3.4.
Punishment prevented all of the children from learning
Not quite. They showed 3.3 actions once offered an incentive.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 separates acquisition (learning the behavior) from performance (actually doing it). Look at the punished-model group in Table 1: 0.7 actions without an incentive, but 3.3 actions once offered a sticker. You can't show 3.3 of 4 actions you never learned. So these children had learned the sequence all along; they just didn't show it until it paid (paragraph 4). Why the others are wrong: punishment preventing all learning is false, the punished group showed 3.3 actions with an incentive; the reward condition producing the most learning doesn't fit, with an incentive all three groups end up close together (3.5, 3.4, 3.3); stickers beating praise was never tested. Trap: Reading low performance as no learning.

qs.q: Which process carries what was observed forward to a later performance?
o: Attending to what the model was doing
Not quite. Attention is needed while watching but doesn't store the sequence.
Having the ability to perform it
Not quite. Motor ability is used when doing it, not for storing it.
Retention of what the model actually did
Correct: Retention stores the sequence so it can be used later.
Receiving reinforcement for it
Not quite. The children were never reinforced themselves.
qs.x: Correct: Retention means storing what you saw in memory. It's what carries the four actions from the film to the later session with the toy. That's how the punished-model children could show 3.3 actions in the second session, even though they showed only 0.7 in the first. Why the others are wrong: receiving reinforcement isn't needed, the children were never rewarded themselves; having the ability to perform it matters when doing the actions, but it doesn't store them; attending to the model is needed while watching, but attention alone doesn't keep the sequence for later. Trap: Picking reinforcement just because it shows up in most accounts of learning.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure most weakens the conclusion about the incentive?
o: The actions shown in the film were novel ones
Not quite. Novel actions rule out earlier learning.
Children were assigned to conditions at random
Not quite. Random assignment is a strength.
Each session lasted five minutes for every child
Not quite. Equal session length is a control.
The incentive session always came second
Correct: The incentive always came second, so it's mixed up with a second chance.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 and Figure 1 show that the incentive session always came second. So when scores rose, two things had changed at once: there was an incentive, and it was the child's second time with the toy. The rise could partly come from practice or a second chance, not the sticker. The order and the incentive are confounded (mixed together). A group offered the sticker in the first session would separate them. Why the others are wrong: random assignment to conditions is a strength; novel actions are a strength too, since they rule out earlier learning; each session lasting five minutes for every child is a control. Trap: Naming a control as if it were a flaw.

qs.q: Why does seeing a model punished reduce performance?
o: It lowers the observer's expectation of reward
Correct: Seeing punishment lowers the child's expectation that the behavior pays.
Punishment erases the memory of the actions
Not quite. The second session shows the memory survived.
The observer has been punished directly
Not quite. Nothing happened to the child directly.
The observer cannot attend to the model
Not quite. They attended well enough to reproduce it later.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says a model's consequences work through the observer's expectations. Watching the adult get punished tells the child, "doing this brings trouble." That lowers the child's expectation of a good outcome, so they hold back. The learning is still there, which is why the punished group showed 3.3 actions once a sticker was offered. Why the others are wrong: the observer being punished directly is false, nothing happened to the child; punishment erasing the memory is false, the second session shows it was kept; the observer not attending is false, they paid enough attention to reproduce the actions later. Trap: Treating vicarious punishment (seeing someone else punished) as if the observer had been punished.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: Observational learning requires that the child be directly reinforced
Not quite. No child was reinforced, yet all learned.
Consequences to a model affect performance more than learning
Correct: Groups differ by 2.4 actions without an incentive but only 0.2 with one.
Rewarding a model has no effect on behavior
Not quite. The rewarded group showed 3.1 actions versus 0.7.
Children imitate a punished model as readily
Not quite. Without an incentive they showed just 0.7 actions.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the two columns in Table 1. Without an incentive, the groups spread out: 3.1 − 0.7 = 2.4 actions between rewarded and punished. With an incentive, they nearly match: 3.5 − 3.3 = 0.2 actions. So what happened to the model changed whether children showed the behavior, not whether they learned it. Why the others are wrong: observational learning needing direct reinforcement is false, no child was reinforced during learning, yet all learned; children imitating a punished model just as readily is false, they showed only 0.7 actions without an incentive; rewarding the model having no effect is false, the rewarded group showed 3.1 versus 0.7 for the punished one. Trap: Drawing a conclusion from one column when the two columns together tell the story.

passages.title: Nonverbal Communication and Universal Expressions
text: Nonverbal communication includes facial expression, gaze, posture, gesture and paralanguage, the vocal qualities that accompany speech such as pitch, loudness and rate. Two claims about it are often confused. The first is that certain facial configurations associated with basic emotions are recognized above chance across cultures. The second is that the circumstances in which an expression may be shown are learned and vary widely; these are display rules.

The two claims are compatible, and separating them requires comparing kinds of nonverbal signal within the same experiment. A signal whose form is learned within a community, such as an emblematic hand gesture, should be recognized well at home and poorly elsewhere. A signal with a strong biological component should show a smaller drop.

Participants from four widely separated regions viewed the same set of stimuli, which included photographed facial expressions of basic emotions, culture-specific gestures drawn from each of the four regions, silent posture-only video clips, and speech filtered to remove words while preserving tone of voice. Each participant chose from a fixed list of emotion or meaning labels, so chance accuracy was the same throughout (Figure 1). Each point in Figure 1 is one participant (10 per signal type plotted, drawn from the full sample); the legend gives each signal type's mean accuracy in the own and other regions and the mean drop.

The drop, own-region accuracy minus other-region accuracy, is the comparison of interest: 9 points for facial expressions, 11 for posture and 13 for tone of voice. Gestures fall 57 points, while the other three signal types fall between 9 and 13 points, so the design separates a signal whose meaning is conventional from signals that carry a substantial amount of information across cultural boundaries.

The facial expression result supports partial rather than complete universality. Accuracy drops only 9 points but it does drop, and 79% is well above chance yet below the within-region figure, so the data are consistent with a recognizable core shaped by local conventions in labeling. What the design cannot address is the production side: these participants judged expressions, and whether people in the four regions produce the same expressions in the same situations is a separate question, which display rules would be expected to affect strongly. The fixed label list also constrains responses, and a free-response procedure typically yields lower cross-cultural agreement.

qs.q: Which stimulus type shows the strongest cultural specificity?
o: Tone of voice with the words filtered out
Not quite. Tone of voice drops 13 points (81% to 68%).
The culture-specific gestures shown
Correct: 91% − 34% = a 57-point drop, by far the biggest.
Silent posture-only video clips
Not quite. Posture drops 11 points (72% to 61%).
Photographed basic facial expressions
Not quite. Faces drop only 9 points (88% to 79%).
qs.x: Correct: Cultural specificity means a signal is understood well at home but poorly elsewhere. That shows up as a drop of 57 points in Figure 1. Gestures fall from 91% in their own region to 34% in others: 91 − 34 = 57 points. The other signal types drop only 9 to 13 points. A huge drop is what you'd expect from a signal whose meaning is learned within a community, as paragraph 2 says. Why the others are wrong: basic facial expressions drop just 9 points; tone of voice without words drops 13; posture-only clips drop 11. All three keep most of their accuracy across regions. Trap: Looking only at the own-region accuracy on the horizontal axis, where gestures actually score highest.

qs.q: What do the facial expression points support?
o: Faces and gestures behave in the same way
Not quite. Gestures drop 57 points, about six times as much.
No cross-cultural recognition of facial expressions
Not quite. Accuracy in other regions was 79%.
Partial universality, with recognition above chance everywhere but reduced
Correct: 88% to 79% is a real drop but still well above chance.
Complete universality, with no cross-cultural difference in recognition at all
Not quite. There's a 9-point drop, so not completely universal.
qs.x: Correct: Facial expressions are recognized at 88% at home and 79% elsewhere, a drop of 88 − 79 = 9 points. Paragraph 5 reads this as partial universality. It's a real drop, so recognition isn't fully universal, but 79% is still far above chance, so there's a core that crosses cultures. Why the others are wrong: complete universality would mean no drop, but there is a 9-point drop; no cross-cultural recognition can't be right when accuracy elsewhere is 79%; faces and gestures don't behave alike, since gestures drop 57 points, about six times as much (57 ÷ 9 ≈ 6.3). Trap: Forcing an in-between result into one of two all-or-nothing positions.

qs.q: Which concept explains why a felt expression is suppressed in some settings?
o: Display rules
Correct: Display rules are learned norms about when emotions may be shown.
Paralanguage
Not quite. Paralanguage is vocal quality like pitch and loudness.
Basic emotion theory
Not quite. That theory is about the expressions, not when they're shown.
Proxemics
Not quite. Proxemics is about personal space.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines display rules as learned norms about when an expression may be shown, and they vary widely across cultures. If a culture says you shouldn't show sadness in public, a person may feel sad and still hide it. That's a display rule at work. Why the others are wrong: paralanguage is the vocal side of speech, like pitch, loudness and rate; basic emotion theory is about the core facial expressions themselves, not when they're shown; proxemics is about how people use personal space. Trap: Choosing the theory that names the expressions instead of the rule that governs when they're shown.

qs.q: What does this experiment not address?
o: Whether posture alone can convey an emotional state
Not quite. Posture clips reached 72% at home and 61% elsewhere.
Whether tone of voice carries information across regions
Not quite. Tone of voice reached 68% in other regions.
Whether gestures are better recognized in their own region
Not quite. Figure 1 shows gestures at 91% at home.
Whether people in the four regions produce expressions alike
Correct: Only recognition was measured, not how people produce expressions.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says participants only judged expressions. Whether people in the four regions actually make the same expressions in the same situations is a separate question about production. Display rules would likely affect production strongly, but this study can't tell. Why the others are wrong: gestures being better recognized at home is answered in Figure 1 (91% versus 34%); tone of voice carrying information across regions is answered too (68% elsewhere); posture conveying emotion is also answered (72% at home, 61% elsewhere). Trap: Assuming a study of recognizing expressions also covers making them.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure most strengthens the comparison across stimulus types?
o: Accuracy was the dependent measure in every condition
Not quite. A shared measure is needed but doesn't equalize chance level.
All participants saw the same stimuli with the same label list
Correct: Same stimuli and same labels keep chance level equal across types.
All of the participants tested were adults
Not quite. Age doesn't matter for comparing stimulus types.
Participants were drawn from four widely separated regions
Not quite. That's the sampling, not the control.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says everyone saw the same stimuli and chose from a fixed label list, so chance accuracy was the same throughout. That makes the four stimulus types directly comparable. A difference in the drop then reflects the signal, not a difference in procedure or how easy it was to guess. Why the others are wrong: drawing people from four regions is how the sample was chosen, which makes the comparison possible but doesn't control it; using accuracy as the measure everywhere is needed but not enough on its own, since chance level could still differ; all participants being adults doesn't speak to comparing stimulus types. Trap: Naming a sampling choice when the question asks about experimental control.

passages.title: Proximity, Similarity and Attraction
text: Attraction is shaped by several well-documented factors. Proximity raises the chance of interaction and of repeated exposure; similarity in attitudes and values supports liking; reciprocity, the perception that liking is returned, strengthens it; and physical attractiveness influences first impressions more than later ones. The mere exposure effect is the finding that repeated encounters with a stimulus increase liking for it, even when the encounters are brief and the stimulus is not consciously noted.

Proximity ordinarily cannot be studied cleanly, because people choose where to live and the choice correlates with everything that also predicts friendship. A setting in which location is assigned by chance removes that problem, which is why housing lotteries are so useful.

Residents of a newly opened apartment building, whose units were assigned by lottery among applicants, were surveyed after one year. For each pair of residents the survey recorded whether each named the other as a friend, and residents also estimated how often they encountered each other in a typical week (Table 1). Figure 1 outlines the design and the route from distance to friendship that the study tests.

The gradient follows the number of encounters closely, from 41% and 12 encounters for adjacent units down to 6% and 1 encounter for units with no shared route, which is what a mechanism based on repeated exposure and opportunity for interaction predicts.

The lottery is what makes this informative, since residents did not choose their neighbors or their position in the building, so the gradient cannot be explained by people who were already similar having selected adjacent units.

Two limits remain. Encounters were estimated by the residents themselves after the friendships had formed, so people may recall more encounters with those they came to like, which would produce the correspondence between the two columns without encounters having caused anything. The design also cannot separate repeated exposure from opportunity for extended conversation, since both rise together with proximity; a condition in which people passed each other often but could not easily talk, as in a busy corridor, would begin to separate them.

qs.q: Why does the lottery strengthen this study?
o: Encounters were reported by the residents themselves
Not quite. Self-reported encounters are a weakness, not a strength.
The survey was administered after a full year
Not quite. Timing isn't what the lottery fixes.
Four relationships between units were compared
Not quite. Comparing four groups is the design, not the lottery.
Neither neighbors nor location was chosen
Correct: The lottery meant no one chose their neighbors, so selection can't explain the result.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says proximity is usually hard to study, because people choose where to live and that choice is tied to things that also predict friendship. Here, units were assigned by lottery, so residents didn't choose their neighbors or their location. Adjacent residents are no more alike than residents far apart. So the friendship gradient can't come from similar people choosing to live near each other (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: surveying after a year is about timing, which the lottery doesn't affect; residents reporting their own encounters is a weakness, as paragraph 6 says; comparing four unit relationships is part of the design, not what the lottery provides. Trap: Giving randomization credit for fixing a measurement problem.

qs.q: Which mechanism do the encounter data most directly support?
o: Physical attractiveness of neighbors
Not quite. No appearance measure was taken.
Repeated exposure raising liking
Correct: Encounters rise with friendship, from 1 per week (6%) to 12 (41%).
The perceived reciprocity of liking
Not quite. Reciprocity wasn't measured.
Similarity of attitudes between residents
Not quite. Attitudes were never measured.
qs.x: Correct: The mere exposure effect (paragraph 1) says repeated encounters increase liking. Encounters are the only factor measured alongside friendship, and they rise right along with it in Table 1: 1 per week with 6% friends, 4 with 19%, 5 with 22%, and 12 with 41%. That's the pattern repeated exposure predicts. Why the others are wrong: similarity of attitudes was never measured; reciprocity, whether liking is returned, wasn't measured either; no one measured or rated physical attractiveness. Trap: Picking a known cause of attraction that this study didn't measure.

qs.q: Which finding would most complicate the proximity account?
o: Adjacent residents reported the most friendships of all
Not quite. Adjacent residents befriending most is the central prediction.
Residents sharing a stairwell formed some friendships
Not quite. Stairwell friendships fit the account.
Encounter frequency failed to predict friendship
Correct: If encounters didn't predict friendship, the proposed route would break.
Few friendships formed across different stairwells
Not quite. Few cross-stairwell friendships also fit the account.
qs.x: Correct: The proximity account says closeness works by producing encounters, and encounters lead to friendship. If encounter frequency didn't predict friendship at all, that route would be broken, and the friendship gradient would need some other explanation. Why the others are wrong: some friendships forming among stairwell-sharers fits the account, since they meet about 4 times a week; adjacent residents having the most friendships (41%) is the central result the account predicts; few friendships across different stairwells (6%) also fits, since they meet only about once a week. Trap: Picking a prominent result that actually supports the account.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 isolates the effect of floor separation?
o: Same floor four doors apart against the same stairwell
Correct: Both are non-adjacent with a shared route; mainly the floor differs (22% vs 19%).
Adjacent doors against units four doors apart on one floor
Not quite. That changes distance on one floor.
Same stairwell against different stairwells
Not quite. That changes whether a route is shared.
Adjacent doors against different stairwells
Not quite. That changes everything at once.
qs.x: Correct: To isolate floor separation, compare two rows that are similar apart from the floor. 'Same floor, four doors apart' and 'different floors, same stairwell' are both non-adjacent and both share a route, with similar encounter rates (5 and 4 per week). The main difference is crossing a floor. Friendship rates are 22% and 19%, a difference of 22 − 19 = 3 points, so crossing a floor adds very little. Why the others are wrong: adjacent versus four doors apart changes distance along one floor; same stairwell versus different stairwells changes whether a route is shared; adjacent versus different stairwells changes everything at once. Trap: Picking the comparison with the biggest difference instead of the one that changes just one thing.

qs.q: What is the mere exposure effect?
o: Liking that follows being liked back
Not quite. Being liked back is reciprocity.
Liking based on physical appearance
Not quite. Liking based on looks is attractiveness.
Liking that follows from shared attitudes
Not quite. Shared attitudes is similarity.
Liking that grows from repeated encounters
Correct: Repeated encounters alone increase liking.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines the mere exposure effect as repeated encounters with something increasing your liking for it, even when the encounters are brief and you don't consciously notice them. Familiarity alone does the work. Why the others are wrong: liking that comes from shared attitudes is similarity; liking that comes from being liked back is reciprocity; liking based on looks is physical attractiveness. Paragraph 1 lists all three as separate factors. Trap: Using the term for any cause of liking that comes to mind.

h: Share naming the other a friend
r: Adjacent doors on the same floor
