passages.title: Geographic and Practical Barriers to Care
text: Access to medical care depends on where people live as well as on whether they can pay. A service may be free and still be out of reach if the nearest provider is far away, if appointments are available only during working hours, or if the journey requires a car.

Distinguishing these barriers from an inability to pay matters because they call for different remedies. Removing a charge does not help someone who cannot reach the provider, and providing transport does not help someone who cannot afford the fee.
Access was surveyed in five districts (Table 1).
BM1 has a free service, a nearby provider and public transport, and its residents use four appointments a year. BM2 is free and remote with no transport and its residents use about a quarter as many.
BM3 charges and is near, and its usage is similar to BM2's, which shows that a charge and a distance can reduce usage by comparable amounts. The two barriers are not distinguished by their size.
BM4 has both barriers and the lowest usage of the four consistent districts, considerably below either single barrier, so the two do not simply substitute for each other.
BM5 is the row that conflicts. It has a free service, a nearby provider and public transport, which is BM1's situation, and its usage matches the district with both barriers.

The general statement is that access has several independent components, that each can reduce usage on its own, and that a district resembling another on every measured component should resemble it in usage.

Two qualifications apply. Appointments used per person is a measure of use rather than of need, so a district with healthier residents would use fewer appointments without facing any barrier. And distance was measured to the nearest provider of any kind, which may not offer the care a particular person requires.

qs.q: Why does removing a charge not always help?
o: Distance remains a barrier
Correct: BM2 is free but remote with no transport, and usage is just 1.1.
Distance is removed with the charge
Not quite. Charge and distance are separate barriers.
It always helps in every case
Not quite. BM2 is free yet uses only 1.1 appointments a year.
A charge is the only barrier of any kind
Not quite. Distance also cuts usage, as BM2 shows.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says removing a charge doesn't help someone who can't reach the provider. Table 1 shows this with BM2. Its service is free, but the nearest provider is 45 km away and there's no public transport, so people use only 1.1 appointments a year, compared with 4.2 in BM1. The cost is gone, but distance still blocks them. Why the others are wrong: Saying a charge is the only barrier ignores that distance cuts usage too, as BM2 shows; saying distance disappears with the charge is wrong, since they're separate barriers; saying removing a charge always helps ignores BM2, which is free yet little used. Trap: Assuming the barrier that's easiest to remove is the one actually holding people back.

qs.q: What does BM4 show about the two barriers?
o: Either one alone gives the same usage
Not quite. Together they give 0.4, below 1.1 and 1.3 for each alone.
The fee is the only real barrier
Not quite. BM2 has no fee but still uses only 1.1.
They do not substitute
Correct: both barriers together give 0.4, well below either one alone.
They cancel each other out
Not quite. Together they cut usage further, not cancel out.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows BM4 has both barriers, a charge and a distant provider with no transport. Its usage is 0.4 appointments a year. That's well below BM2 (distance only, 1.1) and BM3 (charge only, 1.3). Paragraph 6 says this means the barriers don't substitute for each other, meaning one doesn't simply stand in for the other. They add up, so having both is worse than having either one. Why the others are wrong: Saying either one alone gives the same usage as both misses that 0.4 is much lower than 1.1 or 1.3; saying they cancel each other out is backwards, since together they cut usage further; saying the fee is the only real barrier fails because BM2 has no fee and still uses just 1.1. Trap: Assuming two barriers on the same outcome are redundant.

qs.q: Why is BM5 inconsistent?
o: Its usage is the highest
Not quite. At 0.4, its usage ties for the lowest.
It matches BM1 on every measure
Correct: it matches BM1 on every barrier but uses about a tenth as much (0.4 vs 4.2).
Its provider is 45 km away
Not quite. BM5's provider is 2 km away, not 45.
Its service charges a fee
Not quite. BM5's service is free.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says districts that match on every measured barrier should match in usage. BM5 matches BM1 on all three: free service, 2 km to a provider and public transport. Yet BM5's usage is 0.4, while BM1's is 4.2. Compare them: 4.2 ÷ 0.4 = 10.5, so BM5 uses about a tenth as much. Nothing measured explains that, which is why paragraph 7 calls it the row that conflicts. Why the others are wrong: Saying its service charges a fee is wrong, since it's free; saying its provider is 45 km away is wrong, since it's 2 km; saying its usage is the highest is backwards, since 0.4 ties BM4 for the lowest. Trap: Accepting a number without checking it against the conditions listed beside it.

qs.q: Why is usage not a measure of need?
o: Usage and need are the same thing
Not quite. Usage and need differ; healthy people need less.
It is a measure of need
Not quite. Health differences change usage, so it doesn't measure need.
Need was measured directly
Not quite. Only usage was measured, not need.
Healthier residents use less
Correct: healthier residents use less care without facing any barrier.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 9 says appointments used per person measures use, not need. Need is how much care people actually require. A district full of healthy people would use fewer appointments even with no barrier at all. So low usage doesn't automatically mean poor access; it might just mean fewer people are sick. Why the others are wrong: Saying usage and need are the same misses that healthy people need less; saying need was measured directly is wrong, since only usage was measured; saying usage is a measure of need ignores that differences in health mix into it. Trap: Reading a usage number as if it were an access number.

qs.q: By what factor does BM1's usage exceed BM4's?
o: Not quite. 0.4 is BM4's usage, not the factor.
Not quite. 4.2 − 0.4 = 3.8 is the difference; the question asks for a ratio.
Not quite. 4.2 is BM1's usage, not the factor.
qs.x: Correct: By what factor means how many times bigger, so divide. The formula is factor = BM1's usage ÷ BM4's usage. From Table 1, BM1 uses 4.2 appointments per person per year and BM4 uses 0.4. Plug in: 4.2 ÷ 0.4. To make it easier, multiply both by 10: 42 ÷ 4 = 10.5. BM1's residents use about 10 times as many appointments. Why the others are wrong: 4.2 is BM1's usage, not a comparison; 0.4 is BM4's usage; 3.8 is the difference, 4.2 − 0.4 = 3.8, which tells you how many more, not how many times more. Trap: Subtracting when the question asks for a ratio.

h: Appointments used per person per year

passages.title: Anomers of Cyclic Glucose
text: In aqueous solution, glucose exists almost entirely as a six-membered ring. The C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, forming a cyclic hemiacetal whose C1 becomes a new stereocenter called the anomeric carbon. The two forms produced, α and β, differ only at that carbon: in α-D-glucopyranose the C1 hydroxyl is on the opposite side of the ring from the C6 group, and in β it is on the same side. The ring opens and closes continuously through the straight-chain aldehyde, so the two anomers interconvert, a process called mutarotation.

Because the anomers differ in shape, they rotate plane-polarized light differently. Freshly dissolved α-D-glucose has a specific rotation of +112°, pure β is +19°, and an equilibrium mixture settles at +52.7°.

A reducing sugar is one whose anomeric carbon is free to open to the aldehyde or ketone form, which can then be oxidized. Benedict's reagent, containing Cu²⁺, is reduced by such sugars and forms a brick-red precipitate. When the anomeric carbon is locked in a glycosidic bond, the sugar cannot open and gives no precipitate.
Students dissolved several sugars and measured optical rotation over time and the result of a Benedict's test (Figure 1 shows the rotations; Table 1 lists the sugars and the Benedict's results).

The hemiacetal carbon explains why glucose is a reducing sugar but is also only weakly reactive in the aldehyde form: at equilibrium, less than 0.01% of dissolved glucose is open-chain at any moment. That small fraction is enough for oxidation to proceed, because each molecule that reacts is replaced as the equilibrium re-establishes itself. The same slow exposure of the aldehyde lets glucose react with protein amino groups over time, forming the glycated hemoglobin measured as HbA1c in diabetes care.
Students also hydrolyzed sucrose with dilute acid. The rotation changed from +66.5° to −20° over 30 minutes, and the hydrolyzed solution gave a positive Benedict's test.

qs.q: Why do both pure anomers of glucose reach +52.7°?
o: The solvent rotates light by that amount
Not quite. Water doesn't rotate polarized light.
The ring opens and closes repeatedly
Correct: The ring keeps opening and closing, mixing α and β to the same balance.
Light changes the structure of the sugar
Not quite. Measuring rotation doesn't change the sugar.
Both anomers decompose to the same product
Not quite. Glucose is stable in water.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says glucose's ring keeps opening into the straight chain and closing again. Each time it closes, it can form either α or β. That swapping is called mutarotation. So whichever pure anomer you dissolve, it drifts to the same mix, which rotates light +52.7° (Figure 1). You can work out the mix: if x is the fraction α, then 112x + 19(1 − x) = 52.7, so 93x = 33.7 and x ≈ 0.36. That's about one-third α and two-thirds β. Why the others are wrong: shining light through the sample doesn't change the sugar; glucose isn't breaking down in water; water doesn't rotate polarized light, it isn't chiral. Trap: Thinking a changing rotation means a new chemical is forming, rather than two forms re-balancing.

qs.q: In this study, which variable did the students deliberately change from sample to sample, and which did they measure?
o: They changed the sugar and time; they measured rotation and the Benedict's test
Correct: The sugar and the time were chosen, and the rotation and the test result were the recorded responses.
They changed the optical rotation; they measured which sugar was present
Not quite. The rotation was the thing recorded, not a setting.
They changed the Benedict's result; they measured the time that had passed
Not quite. The test result is an outcome, and the time was set by the students.
They changed the solvent in each sample; they measured the molar mass of each sugar
Not quite. Water was the solvent throughout, and molar mass was not measured.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says the students dissolved several sugars and measured optical rotation over time and the result of a Benedict's test. The sugar itself (and the time of the reading, 0 versus 6 hours) is what they chose. The rotation and the Benedict's result are what they recorded in response. That is the independent and dependent variable split. Comparing sugars that differ in one feature, such as the free or locked anomeric carbon, is what lets the outcomes be tied to that feature (Figure 1, Table 1). Why the others are wrong: rotation and the Benedict's result are outcomes, not settings; the solvent was water for all samples and molar mass was never measured; the time was set by the students, not by the test result. Trap: Swapping the thing you manipulate with the thing you observe.

qs.q: Why does maltose's rotation change only slightly over six hours?
o: Both of its rings open freely
Not quite. One anomeric carbon is locked in the bond.
Acid is needed to mutarotate
Not quite. Glucose mutarotated without any acid.
Maltose does not mutarotate
Not quite. It does mutarotate. Its rotation dropped 8°.
Only one anomeric carbon is free
Correct: One anomeric carbon is free and one is locked, so only part can change.
qs.x: Correct: Maltose is two glucoses joined α1→4 (Table 1). The first glucose's anomeric carbon is locked in that bond. The second glucose's anomeric carbon is free, so it can still flip between α and β. Only half the molecule can change, so the rotation shifts only a little: +138° to +130°, a drop of 138 − 130 = 8°. Glucose, with nothing locked, shifts from +112° to +52.7°, a drop of about 59°. Why the others are wrong: maltose does mutarotate, its rotation changed by 8°; both rings can't open freely, one is locked in the bond; glucose mutarotated in plain water, so acid isn't needed. Trap: Expecting all-or-nothing when the structure allows a partial change.

qs.q: Why does the rotation of hydrolyzed sucrose become negative?
o: Fructose rotates light to the left
Correct: Fructose rotates strongly left, outweighing glucose, giving about −20°.
Hydrolysis destroys all optical activity
Not quite. The rotation is −20°, not zero, so it's still optically active.
Acid itself rotates light
Not quite. Dilute acid doesn't rotate light.
Glucose becomes its mirror image
Not quite. D-glucose doesn't turn into L-glucose.
qs.x: Correct: Acid breaks sucrose into equal amounts of glucose and fructose. Glucose at equilibrium rotates +52.7°. Fructose rotates about −92° (to the left). For a 50:50 mix, the rotation is the average: (52.7 + (−92)) ÷ 2 = (−39.3) ÷ 2 ≈ −20°. That matches the −20° in paragraph 6. Fructose's left rotation outweighs glucose's right rotation, which is why this mix is called 'invert sugar'. Why the others are wrong: the solution still rotates light (−20°, not 0), so optical activity isn't destroyed; D-glucose doesn't turn into its mirror image; dilute acid doesn't rotate light. Trap: Assuming the mix must be positive because glucose is positive.

qs.q: Why does methyl α-D-glucoside give a constant rotation and a negative test?
o: Its anomeric carbon is an acetal
Correct: Its anomeric carbon is an acetal, so the ring can't open.
It has no stereocenters
Not quite. It has several stereocenters. That's why it rotates light.
Methanol prevents oxidation of any sugar
Not quite. The methyl group is bonded, not free methanol.
It is not a carbohydrate
Not quite. It's a glucose derivative, still a carbohydrate.
qs.x: Correct: In glucose, the anomeric carbon is a hemiacetal: bonded to the ring oxygen and to an OH. That arrangement can open up. In methyl α-D-glucoside, the OH is replaced by OCH₃ (a methoxy group), making it an acetal, which is stable in neutral water and can't open. With the ring locked, it can't flip between α and β, so its rotation stays at +158°, and it can't form an aldehyde, so Benedict's is negative (Table 1). Why the others are wrong: it's still a carbohydrate, a glucose derivative; it has several stereocenters, which is why it rotates light; the methyl group is bonded to the sugar, not free methanol in solution. Trap: Missing that hemiacetals open but acetals don't.

graph.title: Figure 1. Specific rotation of each sugar at the start and after 6 hours

passages.title: Acid-Catalyzed Hydrolysis Versus Saponification of Esters
text: An ester can be split into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol by hydrolysis, and the mechanism and outcome differ according to the catalyst. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is a reversible equilibrium that gives the carboxylic acid and the alcohol. Base-promoted hydrolysis, or saponification, gives the carboxylate salt and is effectively irreversible.

The difference in reversibility has a thermodynamic explanation. Under base, the carboxylic acid formed is immediately deprotonated to its carboxylate, which is not electrophilic and cannot be attacked by the alcohol, so the reaction cannot run backwards. Under acid, both products remain capable of recombining, and the position of equilibrium depends on the concentrations present.

A practical consequence is that acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is driven by using a large excess of water, while saponification needs only a stoichiometric amount of hydroxide, since nothing pulls the reaction back. The base is consumed rather than catalytic, which is why the term catalysis is inaccurate for it.

Researchers hydrolyzed methyl benzoate under acid and under base and measured the extent of reaction after four hours (Figure 1; Table 1 lists the conditions and the product isolated). The full-reagent runs, excess water for acid and 1.0 equivalent for base, served as the comparison for the limited ones.

The two conditions respond to stoichiometry quite differently. Under acid, reducing the water from a large excess to five equivalents lowers conversion from 87% to 52% because the equilibrium shifts back, while under base the conversion tracks the hydroxide supplied almost exactly, 96% with one equivalent and 49% with half.

The base result is the signature of an irreversible reaction consuming its reagent. Half an equivalent of hydroxide hydrolyzes about half the ester and then stops, which is what a reaction that cannot reverse and cannot regenerate its reagent must do.

Two further points apply. Recovering the free acid from a saponification requires acidifying the carboxylate afterwards, so the base route involves an extra step even though its conversion is higher. And the rates here are for a methyl ester; a bulkier alkoxy group slows attack at the carbonyl considerably, so these extents of reaction at four hours do not transfer to a tertiary ester.

qs.q: Why does half an equivalent of hydroxide stop at about half conversion?
o: Hydroxide is consumed, not regenerated
Correct: Each hydrolysis uses up one hydroxide, and none comes back.
The reaction equilibrates at 49%
Not quite. Saponification doesn't run backward, so it's not an equilibrium.
Hydroxide becomes less reactive
Not quite. Hydroxide stays just as reactive. It simply runs out.
The ester decomposes after four hours
Not quite. Nothing suggests the ester decomposes.
qs.x: Correct: In saponification, each ester molecule that splits uses up one hydroxide. The product, the carboxylate, can't give that hydroxide back (paragraph 3). So hydroxide is a reagent that gets spent, not a catalyst that gets reused. With 0.5 equivalent, meaning enough hydroxide for half the ester, the reaction splits about half the ester and then stops because it ran out: 49% in Figure 1 (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: it isn't an equilibrium, saponification doesn't run backward; hydroxide doesn't become less reactive, there's just none left; nothing suggests the ester breaks down after four hours. Trap: Mistaking 'ran out of reagent' for an equilibrium.

qs.q: Why is saponification effectively irreversible?
o: Hydroxide is a stronger nucleophile than water
Not quite. Nucleophile strength speeds the forward step. It doesn't block reversal.
The products are insoluble in the solvent
Not quite. Sodium benzoate dissolves in water.
The alcohol evaporates from the mixture
Not quite. Evaporation isn't the mechanism.
The carboxylate cannot be attacked by the alcohol
Correct: The carboxylate isn't electrophilic, so the alcohol can't attack it.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. Under base, the carboxylic acid that forms immediately loses its proton to become a carboxylate (negatively charged). To run backward, the alcohol would have to attack the carbonyl carbon. But the carboxylate's negative charge makes that carbon not electrophilic, meaning it no longer attracts electron-rich attackers. With no way back, the reaction only goes forward. Why the others are wrong: the alcohol doesn't need to evaporate, that's not the mechanism; hydroxide being a strong nucleophile speeds the forward reaction but doesn't block the reverse; sodium benzoate dissolves in water, so it doesn't precipitate out. Trap: Explaining irreversibility by a product leaving, rather than by the product being unreactive.

qs.q: Why does acid-catalyzed hydrolysis need excess water?
o: Water removes the alcohol as it forms
Not quite. The alcohol stays in solution.
It shifts a reversible equilibrium forward
Correct: Water is a reactant, so excess pushes the equilibrium toward products.
Water acts as the real catalyst
Not quite. The acid is the catalyst. Water is a reactant.
The acid is diluted by the extra water
Not quite. Diluting the acid would slow it, not help.
qs.x: Correct: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is a true equilibrium: ester + water ⇌ acid + alcohol (paragraph 1). Adding lots of one reactant pushes the equilibrium toward products. This is Le Chatelier's principle: a system shifts to use up what you add. Water is a reactant, so a big excess of it drives the reaction forward. Figure 1 shows it: 87% with water as solvent, but only 52% with 5 equivalents. Why the others are wrong: the acid is the catalyst, water is a reactant; extra water dilutes the acid, which would if anything slow things down, it isn't the reason; the alcohol stays in solution, water doesn't remove it. Trap: Calling the reactant in excess the catalyst.

qs.q: How much does limiting the water cost in conversion under acid?
o: 3 points
Not quite. 3 is 52 − 49, mixing an acid row with a base row.
35 points
Correct: 87% − 52% = 35 points.
44 points
Not quite. 44 is 96 − 52, mixing a base row with an acid row.
47 points
Not quite. 47 is 96 − 49, the two base rows.
qs.x: Correct: Cost = conversion with excess water − conversion with limited water, both under acid. From Figure 1, excess water gives 87% and 5 equivalents of water gives 52%. Plug in: 87 − 52 = 35 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: 3 compares limited-water acid with half-equivalent base (52 − 49), two different conditions; 44 compares one equivalent of base with limited-water acid (96 − 52); 47 compares the two base rows (96 − 49). Trap: Mixing rows from the acid and base conditions.

qs.q: All four runs used methyl benzoate. Why does that limit what can be concluded about a tertiary ester?
o: A bulkier alkoxy group slows attack, so four-hour extents may not transfer
Correct: Paragraph 7 says bulkier groups slow attack at the carbonyl a great deal.
Tertiary esters cannot be hydrolyzed by acid or by base under any condition at all
Not quite. They can be hydrolyzed, only more slowly.
Methyl benzoate gives a different kind of product from the one a tertiary ester gives
Not quite. Both give a carboxylic acid or carboxylate and an alcohol.
Four hours is always long enough for any ester to reach its final extent of reaction
Not quite. Slower esters would not be finished at four hours.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the rates are for a methyl ester and that a bulkier alkoxy group slows attack at the carbonyl considerably. A tertiary ester has a very bulky group, so after four hours it would likely sit well below the 87% to 96% in Figure 1. The study sampled one kind of ester, so its numbers cannot simply be carried over. That is a limit on generalizing from one sample. Why the others are wrong: tertiary esters can be hydrolyzed, just more slowly; the products are the same types (an acid or its salt plus an alcohol); a slower ester would not be finished at four hours. Trap: Treating results from one example as if they covered the whole class.

passages.title: Torque at a Joint and Muscle Insertion
text: When a body segment rotates about a joint, the relevant quantity is torque: τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point where the force acts and θ is the angle between r and the force. A muscle that inserts close to a joint has a small r, so it must generate a large force to produce a given torque, but a small shortening of the muscle produces a large movement at the end of the limb. Rotational equilibrium requires the sum of torques about any axis to be zero.

Researchers studied elbow flexion in 12 adults. The forearm was held horizontal while the participant supported a weight in the hand. The biceps tendon inserts about 4.0 cm from the elbow joint and pulls nearly vertically on the forearm in this position. The forearm plus hand has a mass of 1.6 kg with its center of mass 15 cm from the elbow, and the hand holds the weight 32 cm from the elbow. Muscle force was estimated from the measured torque, and electromyography (EMG) recorded the electrical activity of the biceps, in arbitrary units (Figure 1). Take g = 10 m/s².
In a second trial, participants held the 2.0 kg mass with the elbow bent so that the forearm was 30° above horizontal. The torque from the loads fell to 7.6 N·m, and the EMG fell in proportion.

The researchers also asked what happens during a slow lowering of the weight, in which the muscle lengthens while still producing force. EMG in that phase was about 30% lower than when the same weight was held still, even though the torque the muscle had to resist was identical. Lengthening contractions are known to produce more force per unit of electrical activity, and they are also more likely to cause muscle soreness the following day.

The researchers noted that the biceps is not the only elbow flexor; the brachialis and brachioradialis also contribute, so the force attributed to the biceps is an overestimate of what that one muscle produces.

qs.q: What torque about the elbow does the 2.0 kg mass alone produce?
o: Not quite. This uses 0.032 m. 32 cm is 0.32 m.
Not quite. That's the forearm's own torque, the 0 kg point in Figure 1A.
Correct: F = 2.0 kg × 10 m/s² = 20 N, and 20 N × 0.32 m = 6.4 N·m.
Not quite. That's the total plotted in Figure 1A, forearm plus weight. Subtract the forearm's 2.4 N·m.
qs.x: Correct: Torque is τ = rF sin θ, and here the weight pulls straight down on a horizontal forearm, so θ = 90° and sin 90° = 1. That leaves τ = rF. First find the force. Weight is F = mg, with m = 2.0 kg and g = 10 m/s² (paragraph 2), so F = 2.0 × 10 = 20 N. Next the distance: the hand holds the weight 32 cm from the elbow. 1 m = 100 cm, so divide by 100: 32 cm ÷ 100 = 0.32 m. Plug in: τ = 0.32 m × 20 N = 6.4 N·m. Check it against Figure 1A: the forearm alone gives 2.4 N·m (the 0 kg point), and 6.4 + 2.4 = 8.8 N·m, which is exactly the 2.0 kg point. Why the others are wrong: 2.4 N·m is the forearm's own torque, the empty-hand point; 8.8 N·m is the total in Figure 1A, forearm plus weight; 0.64 N·m comes from turning 32 cm into 0.032 m, a decimal slip. Trap: Reading the total torque in Figure 1A as if it were the weight's torque alone.

qs.q: Why must the biceps force be so much larger than the weight held?
o: The forearm's mass dominates the load
The forearm adds only 2.4 N·m. The short muscle lever is the real cause.
The biceps pulls at a shallow angle
The passage says the biceps pulls nearly vertically on the horizontal forearm.
Its insertion is much closer to the joint
Correct: the biceps acts at 4 cm and the load at 32 cm, so the muscle needs about 8 times the force.
Muscles convert energy inefficiently
Efficiency is about energy use. The force comes from balancing torques.
qs.x: Correct: Torque is distance times force (τ = rF when the pull is perpendicular). For the forearm to stay still, the muscle's torque has to equal the load's torque. The biceps attaches only 4.0 cm from the elbow, while the hand holds the weight 32 cm out (paragraph 2). Since 32 ÷ 4 = 8, the muscle has one eighth of the distance, so it needs about eight times the force to make the same torque. That's why Figure 1B shows hundreds of newtons of biceps force for a weight of only 20 N. Paragraph 1 says the payoff: a small shortening of the muscle swings the hand through a big arc. Why the others are wrong: how efficiently a muscle turns energy into work doesn't set how much force the torque balance needs; the forearm adds only 2.4 N·m, a minority of the load once a weight is held; the passage says the biceps pulls nearly vertically, so it isn't a shallow angle. Trap: Comparing the two forces without comparing their distances from the joint.

qs.q: What explains the lower torque when the forearm is raised 30°?
o: The masses become lighter
The masses stay the same. Lifting the arm doesn't make anything lighter.
Gravity weakens at that angle
Gravity is the same at every angle. Only its direction relative to the forearm changed.
The distances shorten
Bones don't change length, so the distances from the elbow stay the same.
The perpendicular component falls
Correct: only the part of gravity at right angles to the forearm makes torque, and that's cos 30° ≈ 0.87 of it.
qs.x: Correct: Torque depends only on the part of the force that pushes at right angles to the forearm. Gravity always pulls straight down. When the forearm is horizontal, all of that pull is at right angles to it. Tilt the forearm up 30° and only the cos 30° share of the weight is still at right angles, and cos 30° ≈ 0.87. So the new torque should be 8.8 N·m × 0.87 ≈ 7.6 N·m, which is the value in paragraph 3. Why the others are wrong: the masses don't change when you lift your arm; the bones stay the same length, so the distances to the elbow stay the same too; gravity is the same strength at every angle, it's the direction relative to the forearm that changed. Trap: Hunting for a change in the force or the distance when only the angle changed.

qs.q: What does the EMG trend add to the force estimates?
o: It measures the torque directly
EMG records electrical activity. Torque was worked out from the loads.
It identifies which muscle produces the force
Paragraph 5 says other flexors help, and biceps EMG alone can't split the force.
It shows activation rising with load
Correct: EMG rises from 14 to 91 units as the load grows, showing the biceps is working harder.
It shows the muscle shortens as load rises
The arm was held still, so the muscle wasn't shortening.
qs.x: Correct: EMG (electromyography) records the electrical activity of a muscle, which tells you how hard the nerves are driving it. In Figure 1C the EMG climbs from 14 to 91 units as the load goes up, right alongside the estimated force (60 to 380 N in Figure 1B). That gives independent evidence that the biceps really is working harder, so the force numbers aren't just an artifact of the torque calculation. Why the others are wrong: EMG measures electricity, not torque, so it can't measure torque directly; the arm was held still, so the muscle was holding, not shortening; EMG from the biceps alone can't say how the force is split between the biceps and the other flexors (paragraph 5). Trap: Treating a measure that rises along with force as if it were a direct measure of force.

qs.q: Which added measurement would best test whether the biceps alone supplies the force estimated from torque?
o: Biceps EMG recorded during a slow lowering of the weight
Not quite. Lowering tests a different kind of contraction (paragraph 4). It says nothing about whether other flexors share the load.
EMG from the brachialis and brachioradialis at the same loads
Correct: if those flexors also become more active as the load grows, the biceps cannot be supplying all of the torque.
The 4.0 kg trial repeated in the same 12 adults to check the EMG readings agree
Not quite. Repeating a trial checks how repeatable the EMG is. It can't show who else shares the torque.
Torque measured with a heavier 6.0 kg mass held at the same distance
Not quite. A heavier mass adds one more point to the same curve and keeps the same one-muscle assumption.
qs.x: Correct: The force estimate in Figure 1B comes from dividing the torque by the biceps' 4.0 cm moment arm, so it assumes the biceps supplies all of the torque. Paragraph 5 says the brachialis and brachioradialis also flex the elbow. The direct way to test that assumption is to record from those muscles during the same loads. If their EMG rises with the weight the way the biceps' does, they are carrying part of the torque and the biceps' share is smaller. Why the others are wrong: recording during slow lowering compares a different kind of contraction (paragraph 4) and says nothing about the other flexors; repeating the 4.0 kg trial checks reproducibility, not who shares the load; a 6.0 kg mass only adds one more point to the same curve under the same assumption. Trap: Picking a test that makes the same measurement more precise when the doubt is about the model behind it.

passages.title: Index of Refraction and Snell's Law
text: Light changes direction when it passes between media in which it travels at different speeds. The index of refraction of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium, and the directions of the incident and refracted rays are related by n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

Two consequences matter for imaging. A ray entering a denser medium bends toward the normal, which is how a lens brings parallel rays to a focus, and the focal length of a lens depends on both its curvature and the difference in index between the lens and its surroundings. A lens in water focuses less strongly than the same lens in air.

Beyond a critical angle, a ray passing from a denser to a less dense medium is not refracted at all but totally reflected. The critical angle is given by sin θc = n₂ divided by n₁, so it exists only when the second medium is the less dense one.

A converging lens of fixed curvature was characterized in several surrounding media, and the critical angle at its surface was computed (Figure 1). In the index-matched oil (index 1.52) the lens gave no focus and there was no critical angle, so that medium has no point in the figure.

Both effects follow from the index difference. As the surrounding index rises toward the lens's own 1.52, the focal length grows from 10.0 cm to 153 cm, and when the media match exactly the lens stops focusing altogether because no refraction occurs at its surfaces.

The critical angle also rises with the surrounding index. It rises from 41.1 degrees in air to 75.3 degrees in glycerol and vanishes in the matched oil, since total internal reflection requires the second medium to be less dense and there is no longer any difference to reflect from.

Two points qualify the results. The focal lengths assume rays close to the axis, and a real lens focuses rays far from the axis at a slightly different distance, an aberration that grows with aperture. And an index-matched lens still absorbs and scatters a little light, so it becomes nearly invisible rather than truly so.

qs.q: Why does the lens stop focusing in the matched oil?
o: The oil absorbs the light before it focuses
Paragraph 7 says absorption is slight. It can't explain a total loss of focus.
No refraction occurs at its surfaces
Correct: Both indices are 1.52, so by Snell's law the ray doesn't bend at either surface.
The lens curvature changes in the oil
The curvature belongs to the solid glass and is fixed. The oil can't reshape it.
The focal length becomes negative there
A negative focal length means spreading light out. Here light isn't bent at all, so there's no focus.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 gives Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. If n₁ = n₂, they cancel and sin θ₁ = sin θ₂, so the ray leaves at the same angle it came in. It doesn't bend. A lens focuses only because its curved surfaces bend light, and paragraph 5 says that with the oil at 1.52, the same as the glass, no refraction happens at the surfaces. With no bending, the curve does nothing, so there's no focus. Why the others are wrong: the oil absorbs the light fails because paragraph 7 says the absorption is only slight, nowhere near enough to stop focusing; the lens curvature changes fails because the shape is set by the solid glass and the passage calls it fixed; the focal length becomes negative fails because a negative focal length would mean the lens spreads light out, and here the light isn't bent at all, so there's no focal length to speak of. Trap: Blaming something about the oil other than the one thing that controls bending, the difference in index.

qs.q: Why does the critical angle rise as the surrounding index rises?
o: Total reflection needs a denser second medium
Not quite. Backwards. Paragraph 3 says total reflection needs the second medium to be less dense.
Light travels faster in denser media
Not quite. Backwards. Light slows down in denser media; that's what a higher index means.
The two indices become more similar
Correct: sin θc = n₂ ÷ n₁ climbs toward 1 as the indices get closer, so θc climbs toward 90 degrees.
The lens becomes optically denser too
Not quite. The lens stays at 1.52 for every medium. Only the surrounding medium changes.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 gives sin θc = n₂ ÷ n₁, where n₁ is the denser side (the lens, 1.52) and n₂ is the surrounding medium. As the surrounding index climbs toward 1.52, the ratio climbs toward 1, and the angle whose sine is close to 1 is close to 90 degrees. Check it with Figure 1B: in air, 1.00 ÷ 1.52 ≈ 0.66, which gives 41.1 degrees; in glycerol, 1.47 ÷ 1.52 ≈ 0.97, which gives 75.3 degrees. So the more alike the two indices are, the steeper the ray has to hit before it's totally reflected. Why the others are wrong: light travels faster in denser media is backwards, since paragraph 1 defines the index by how much light slows down; the lens becomes optically denser fails because the lens stays at 1.52 for every medium; total reflection needs a denser second medium is also backwards, since paragraph 3 says the second medium must be the less dense one. Trap: Flipping which side has to be denser for total internal reflection.

qs.q: What does the index of refraction measure?
o: The angle at which the light enters
The angle depends on how the ray is aimed, not on the medium.
How much light slows in a medium
Correct: n = speed in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium, so it tells how much the medium slows light.
How much of the light a medium absorbs
Absorption is a separate property. A clear material can have a high index and absorb very little.
The curvature of each lens surface
Curvature is the lens's shape. The index belongs to the material, whatever shape it's cut into.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines the index of refraction as n = c ÷ v: the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium. Light is fastest in vacuum, so n is always 1 or more, and a bigger n means light slows down more. For example, water's 1.33 means light moves 1.33 times slower in water than in vacuum. That change in speed at a boundary is what makes a ray bend. Why the others are wrong: how much of the light a medium absorbs is a separate property (paragraph 7 treats the lens's slight absorption apart from its index); the curvature of each lens surface is the lens's shape, not a property of the material; the angle at which the light enters depends on how the ray is aimed, not on the medium. Trap: Mixing up a property of the material (its index) with a property of the lens's shape or of the ray.

qs.q: How many times longer is the focal length in glycerol than in air?
o: About 3.4
Not quite. No pair of points in Figure 1A gives 3.4.
About 3.6
Not quite. That's water against air: 36.4 ÷ 10.0 = 3.64. The question asks about glycerol.
About 4.2
Not quite. That's glycerol against water: 153 ÷ 36.4 ≈ 4.2. The question asks about air.
About 15
Correct: 153 cm ÷ 10.0 cm = 15.3, so about 15 times longer.
qs.x: Correct: Find each focal length in Figure 1A, then divide. Ratio = focal length in glycerol ÷ focal length in air. Figure 1A gives 153 cm in glycerol and 10.0 cm in air. Plug in: 153 cm ÷ 10.0 cm. Dividing by 10 just moves the decimal one place left, so the answer is 15.3. The cm cancel, so it's a plain number, about 15. The lens focuses about 15 times more weakly in glycerol because glycerol's index (1.47) is so close to the glass's (1.52). Why the others are wrong: about 4.2 compares glycerol with water (153 ÷ 36.4 ≈ 4.2); about 3.6 compares water with air (36.4 ÷ 10.0 = 3.64); about 3.4 doesn't match any pair of points in Figure 1A. Trap: Grabbing two neighboring points instead of the two media the question names.

qs.q: Why do the tabulated focal lengths hold only near the axis?
o: The index varies across the lens
Not quite. The glass is uniform. The effect comes from the curved shape, not the material.
Off-axis rays are absorbed in the lens
Not quite. Off-axis rays pass through the lens too. They just focus in a different place.
Focal length cannot be measured precisely
Not quite. Figure 1A reports focal lengths to a tenth of a centimeter. The limit is which rays, not precision.
Off-axis rays focus at a different distance
Correct: Rays far from the axis focus at a slightly different distance, and this aberration grows with aperture.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the focal lengths assume rays close to the axis, the line through the center of the lens. With a real curved lens, rays passing near the edge are brought to a focus at a slightly different spot (for a converging lens, a bit closer to it). This is called spherical aberration, and it gets worse as the aperture, the open width of the lens, gets bigger, because more edge rays get through. So a single focal length only describes the near-axis rays. Why the others are wrong: off-axis rays are absorbed fails because they pass through the lens too, they just focus in a different place; the index varies across the lens fails because the glass is uniform, and the effect comes from the curved shape; focal length cannot be measured precisely fails because Figure 1A reports it to a tenth of a centimeter, and the limit here is about which rays you're talking about, not measuring skill. Trap: Blaming absorption or a flaw in the glass for what is really an effect of the lens's shape.

passages.title: Elastic Energy Stored in a Stretched Tendon
text: A tendon stretched by a small amount behaves approximately like a spring, with the force rising in proportion to the extension, so the energy stored is one half times the stiffness times the extension squared. That stored energy is returned when the tendon recoils, which is why tendons contribute to the efficiency of running.

The return is not complete. Some of the stored energy is dissipated as heat within the tissue, and the fraction returned is called the resilience. A tendon with a resilience of 0.93 returns 93% of the energy put into it and loses the rest, which appears as a difference between the loading and unloading curves.

The spring approximation holds only for small extensions. Beyond a few percent of its length a tendon stiffens as collagen fibers align and then, at greater extensions, begins to fail, so neither the proportional relationship nor the energy expression applies in that region.

Researchers loaded a tendon of 20 cm rest length cyclically at a single fixed rate. The extension was the variable they set (2, 4, 6 and 8 mm), and for each setting they measured the peak force and the energy stored and returned (Figure 1). No other tendon or loading rate was used as a comparison.

The spring description holds at the smaller extensions and then fails. Doubling the extension from 2 to 4 mm quadruples the stored energy, as the squared relationship requires, and the force doubles, but at 6 and 8 mm the force rises faster than proportionally and the stored energy exceeds the spring prediction.

Resilience falls in the same region. It holds at 0.93 for the first two extensions and then falls to 0.90 and 0.80, so the tendon both stiffens and dissipates more as it is stretched further, and the 8 mm cycle loses more than a joule as heat.

Two limits apply. The measurements come from a cyclic test at one rate, and tendon stiffness depends on how fast it is loaded, so a faster cycle would give higher forces at the same extension. And an isolated tendon lacks the muscle in series with it that shares the extension in life, so the extensions here do not correspond directly to joint angles.

qs.q: Which observation shows the spring approximation failing?
o: The tendon is 20 cm long at rest
Rest length is a fixed property. It says nothing about spring behavior.
Energy stored rises with extension
Stored energy rises with stretch for a perfect spring too.
Force rises faster than proportionally
Correct: a spring would give 1,200 N and 1,600 N at 6 and 8 mm, but the tendon gives 1,250 and 1,800 N.
Resilience is 0.93 when small
Steady resilience at small stretches is the region where the spring model works.
qs.x: Correct: A spring obeys F = kx, meaning force rises in proportion to the stretch (x). Test that with Figure 1A. From 2 mm to 4 mm the stretch doubles and the force doubles too, 400 N to 800 N, so the spring rule holds there. If it kept holding, 6 mm would give 3 × 400 = 1,200 N and 8 mm would give 4 × 400 = 1,600 N. Instead Figure 1A shows the tendon at 1,250 N and 1,800 N, more than proportional. That's the tendon stiffening as collagen fibers line up (paragraph 3). Why the others are wrong: stored energy rising with stretch is expected for a spring too, so it doesn't show failure; resilience of 0.93 at small stretches describes the region where the spring picture works; the 20 cm rest length is just a fixed property of the tendon. Trap: Looking at the energy curves when the spring test is about force being proportional to stretch.

qs.q: What does the fall in resilience represent?
o: More energy dissipated as heat
Correct: a smaller fraction comes back, so more of the stored energy turns into heat.
An error in the force measurement
The forces follow a consistent pattern, so there's no sign of a measurement error.
A reduction in the energy stored
Stored energy rose at every extension, from 0.40 J to 6.70 J.
A change in the tendon's rest length
Rest length stayed at 20 cm. Resilience is about energy returned.
qs.x: Correct: Resilience is the fraction of stored energy that comes back when the tendon recoils (paragraph 2). Whatever doesn't come back is lost inside the tissue as heat. So when resilience falls from 0.93 to 0.80, a bigger share of the energy is being turned into heat. At 8 mm in Figure 1B, 6.70 J is stored and only 5.36 J returns, so 1.34 J becomes heat. Why the others are wrong: stored energy went up at every step, from 0.40 J to 6.70 J, so it didn't fall; the tendon's rest length doesn't change in this test; the forces fit the trends in paragraph 5, so nothing points to a measurement error. Trap: Reading a falling ratio as a falling amount stored, when it's the returned share that dropped.

qs.q: Why do tendons improve the efficiency of running?
o: They convert heat into movement
Heat is the energy lost. Tissue can't turn it back into motion.
They shorten the stride
The passage never ties tendons to stride length.
They reduce the muscle force
Tendons pass the muscle's force along. They don't reduce it.
Stored energy is returned on recoil
Correct: energy stored when the tendon stretches comes back as it recoils, saving muscle work.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says a stretched tendon stores energy like a spring and gives most of it back when it recoils. When your foot lands, the tendon stretches and stores energy. As you push off, it snaps back and returns that energy, so your muscles have less work to do on each step. With a resilience of 0.93, 93% of the stored energy comes back. Why the others are wrong: tendons pass the muscle's force on to the bone, they don't reduce it; nothing in the passage says tendons shorten the stride; heat is energy lost, and a tendon can't turn heat back into movement. Trap: Thinking the energy lost as heat can be recovered.

qs.q: How much energy is lost as heat in the 8 mm cycle?
o: Not quite. That's the 2 mm cycle: 0.40 − 0.37 = 0.03 J.
Not quite. That's the 4 mm cycle: 1.60 − 1.49 = 0.11 J.
Not quite. That's the 6 mm cycle: 3.65 − 3.29 = 0.36 J.
Correct: 6.70 J stored − 5.36 J returned = 1.34 J lost as heat.
qs.x: Correct: Energy lost is energy stored minus energy returned. From the 8 mm points in Figure 1B, stored = 6.70 J and returned = 5.36 J. Subtract: 6.70 J − 5.36 J = 1.34 J. Check with resilience: 5.36 ÷ 6.70 = 0.80, which matches Figure 1C, and 1 − 0.80 = 0.20 of 6.70 J is 0.20 × 6.70 = 1.34 J. That's the "more than a joule" in paragraph 6. Why the others are wrong: 0.03 J is the 2 mm cycle (0.40 − 0.37); 0.11 J is the 4 mm cycle (1.60 − 1.49); 0.36 J is the 6 mm cycle (3.65 − 3.29). Trap: Doing the right subtraction on the wrong extension.

qs.q: Why can't the extensions in this isolated-tendon test be read directly as joint angles in a living limb?
o: Extension is unrelated to joint movement
They are related, just not directly, since the muscle shares the stretch.
Tendons do not act across joints
Tendons do act across joints in life.
Muscle in series shares the extension
Correct: in the body the muscle in series takes part of the stretch, so tendon stretch isn't the joint angle.
Joint angles cannot be measured precisely
Joint angles are measured routinely. The issue is the missing muscle.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 gives the reason. In the body, a tendon is attached end to end (in series) with a muscle. When a joint bends, the total stretch is shared between the muscle and the tendon, so you can't read the tendon's own stretch straight off the joint angle. This test used a tendon removed from that setup, with no muscle attached. Why the others are wrong: joint angles are easy to measure, so precision isn't the issue; tendons do act across joints in the living body; stretch and joint movement are related, just not directly, because the muscle takes part of it. Trap: Assuming a result from isolated tissue carries straight over to the whole limb.

passages.title: Gap Junctions Between Cells
text: Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells through channels wide enough to pass ions and small molecules up to about a kilodalton. They make a group of cells electrically continuous and allow metabolites and second messengers to be shared, while excluding proteins and nucleic acids.

The channels are gated rather than permanently open. They close when the cytoplasmic calcium rises or the pH falls, which are both signs of injury, so a damaged cell is isolated from its neighbors instead of draining them.

Coupling is measured in two ways that report different things. Passing current between cells measures the electrical conductance of the junctions; injecting a dye measures whether a molecule of that size can pass, and a junction can conduct current while excluding a dye that is too large.
Coupling was measured in four conditions (Table 1), and Figure 1 shows how the two injury signals close the junctions.

Acidifying the cytoplasm to pH 6.4 cut the conductance from 18.4 to 0.9 nanosiemens and abolished dye transfer, and restoring the pH restored the conductance to 16.8. Raising calcium at normal pH produced the same closure, showing that the two signals act independently.

The large dye failed to pass in every condition including the normal one, which sets an upper bound on the channel's permeability rather than reporting anything about gating. A measurement that is negative in the control cannot detect a change.

Two qualifications apply. Conductance is measured between a pair of cells, and in a tissue each cell is coupled to several neighbors, so the conductance of one pair does not predict how far a signal spreads through the sheet. And the acidification was produced by changing the external carbon dioxide, which also acidifies the extracellular space and changes several membrane conductances, so the measured fall includes a contribution from channels other than the junctions. A cleaner experiment would acidify the cytoplasm alone with a weak acid loaded into the pipette, which affects one cell of the pair and leaves the extracellular space at its normal pH.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why gap junctions close around an injured cell?
o: Injury lowers cytoplasmic calcium, which closes the channels
Not quite. Injury raises calcium, and it's the rise that closes the channels.
Injury raises cytoplasmic pH, which closes the channels
Not quite. Injury lowers pH. A falling pH is the closing signal.
The channels are destroyed by injury
They reopen on recovery, back to 16.8 nS.
Rising calcium and falling pH each close the channels
Correct: injury raises calcium and lowers pH, and both close the channels.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says gap junction channels are gated, meaning they can open and close. They close when calcium inside the cell rises or the pH falls, and both happen when a cell is injured. Closing cuts the damaged cell off so it doesn't drain ions and small molecules from its healthy neighbors. Table 1 shows each signal works: acid drops conductance from 18.4 to 0.9 nS, and raised calcium drops it to 1.2 nS. Why the others are wrong: injury raises calcium, it doesn't lower it; injury lowers pH, it doesn't raise it; and the channels aren't destroyed, conductance came back to 16.8 nS once the pH was restored. Trap: Mistaking a protective closure for damage to the channel.

qs.q: Why can the large-dye results not be used to show that acidification closes the junctions?
o: The large dye was too small to be affected by gating
Not quite. The large dye was too big to pass at all, not too small.
The large dye did not pass even in the normal, open-channel cells
Correct: it never passed, even in the normal control, so it can't show a change.
It passed only in the normal condition
It passed in no condition, normal included.
Dye transfer measures conductance, not permeability
Not quite. It's the other way around. Current measures conductance, and dye shows whether a molecule of that size can pass.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 points out that the large dye didn't pass in any condition, including the normal one where the channels are open. A test can only show a change if it can come out positive in the control. Since the large dye fails even with the channels fully open, its failure in the acid or calcium conditions tells you nothing about closing. It only shows the channel's size limit, which paragraph 1 puts at about a kilodalton. Why the others are wrong: the large dye wasn't too small to be affected, it was too big to pass at all; it didn't pass in the normal condition either, it passed in none; and it's current that measures conductance, while dye shows whether a molecule of that size can get through. Trap: Leaning on a measurement that's already negative in the control.

qs.q: The conductance of a single cell pair does not predict how far a signal spreads through a sheet of coupled cells because:
o: spread does not depend on conductance
Spread does depend on conductance, just not one pair's alone.
junctions in a sheet are closed at rest
They're open at rest: 18.4 nS.
dye transfer, not current, determines spread
Not quite. Electrical spread depends on conductance. The issue is that one pair is only one link.
each cell is coupled to several neighbors, not just one
Correct: each cell has several neighbors, so spread depends on the network.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 notes that conductance was measured between just two cells. In a tissue, each cell connects to several neighbors, so a signal spreads through a network. How far it goes depends on the whole web of connections, not on one link. So one pair's 18.4 nS can't tell you how far a signal will travel through the sheet. Why the others are wrong: spread does depend on conductance, just not on one pair's alone; the junctions are open at rest, 18.4 nS in the normal condition; and electrical spread depends on conductance, not on dye transfer. Trap: Stretching one connection's measurement to a whole network.

qs.q: By what factor did acidification reduce the conductance?
o: That's the acidified conductance, not a factor.
That's the raised calcium conductance.
That's the normal conductance, not a factor.
Correct: 18.4 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 20.4, about 20.
qs.x: Correct: By what factor means divide: factor = normal conductance ÷ acidified conductance. From Table 1, normal is 18.4 nS (nanosiemens, a unit of how easily current passes) and acidified is 0.9 nS. Plug in: 18.4 ÷ 0.9. To clear the decimal, multiply top and bottom by 10: 184 ÷ 9. Nine goes into 180 20 times, leaving 4, and 4 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.44, so 184 ÷ 9 ≈ 20.4, about 20. The units cancel, so it's just a number. Why the others are wrong: 0.9 is the acidified conductance itself; 18.4 is the normal conductance; 1.2 is the raised calcium conductance, from a different row. Trap: Giving a conductance when the question asks for a ratio.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might the drop in conductance after acidification overstate how much the gap junctions closed?
o: CO₂ also acidifies the extracellular space around the cells
Correct: CO₂ acidifies both sides, changing other membrane conductances too.
Acidification also raised cytoplasmic calcium
Not quite. Calcium was raised in a separate condition, at normal pH.
A weak acid was loaded into only one cell
Not quite. That's the cleaner experiment the passage proposes, not what was done.
Conductance was measured in only one cell pair
Not quite. That limits how far you can generalize to a sheet, but it doesn't inflate the drop.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the acid was made by changing the CO₂ outside the cells. CO₂ crosses membranes easily and forms acid on both sides, so the space outside the cells turns acidic too. That changes the current through several other channels in the cell membranes, not just the gap junctions. So part of the drop from 18.4 to 0.9 nS comes from those other channels. A cleaner test would acidify the inside of one cell with a weak acid from the pipette. Why the others are wrong: calcium was raised in a separate condition at normal pH, not by the acid; loading a weak acid into one cell is the cleaner experiment the passage suggests, not what was done; and measuring one pair limits generalizing to a sheet but doesn't inflate the drop. Trap: Pinning the whole measured change on the channel you care about.

passages.title: Balancing Torques in a Lever System
text: A body at rest requires both zero net force and zero net torque. The second condition is what makes a lever analysis possible: taking torques about a chosen point, the sum of the clockwise torques equals the sum of the anticlockwise torques, and a point can be chosen so that an unknown force contributes no torque and drops out of the equation.

The lumbar spine is often analyzed this way. With the trunk bent forward, the weight of the upper body acts at a long distance from the lumbar pivot while the erector spinae muscles insert close to it, so the muscle must exert a force many times the weight it supports in order to balance the torques.

The compressive force on the disc is then the sum of the muscle force and the supported weight, which is why the compression is far larger than the weight involved. Reducing the moment arm of the load, by holding it close to the body, reduces both the required muscle force and the resulting compression.

A 70 kg person was analyzed lifting a 20 kg load at two trunk angles and two load positions, plus one bent condition with no load (Figure 1). The four conditions were upright with the load held close, bent 60° with the load held close, bent 60° with the load at arm's length, and bent 60° with empty hands.

Both geometry and load matter, and geometry matters more. Bending with the load close raises the muscle force from 780 to 2,030 N, and extending the arms raises it further to 3,590 N without any change in the weight being lifted.

The no-load bar isolates the trunk's own weight. Bending forward with nothing in the hands already requires 1,240 N of muscle force, so most of the compression in the loaded bent condition comes from supporting the upper body rather than the 20 kg load, whose weight is under 200 N.

Two limits apply. The analysis treats the erector spinae as a single muscle with one moment arm, while several muscles with different lines of action contribute, so the computed force is an aggregate. And it is a static analysis, and lifting involves acceleration, so a rapid lift produces forces above those tabulated for the same posture.

qs.q: Why is the compressive force so much larger than the weight lifted?
o: Compression includes the person's weight
Not quite. The spine supports only the upper body, not the whole body weight.
The muscle has a short moment arm
Correct: the muscle's tiny moment arm forces it to pull very hard, and that pull squeezes the disc.
The load is held away from the body
Not quite. That's true in only one condition, but compression is large in every condition.
The disc is weaker than the muscle
Not quite. Disc strength isn't part of the torque balance.
qs.x: Correct: For the trunk to stay still, the muscle's torque (distance × force) must balance the load's torque. The erector spinae muscles attach very close to the lumbar pivot, while the upper body and load act much farther out (paragraph 2). A short distance means the muscle has to pull very hard to make the same torque. Then paragraph 3 says the disc gets squeezed by the muscle force plus the weight it supports, so a huge muscle force means huge compression. In the bent, load-close condition, 2,030 N of muscle force gives 2,710 N on the disc. Why the others are wrong: the strength of the disc never enters the torque calculation; holding the load at arm's length is only one of the four conditions, but compression is large in all of them; only the upper body's weight is supported at the lumbar spine, not the whole body. Trap: Explaining a lever result by how strong the tissue is.

qs.q: What does the no-load condition establish?
o: The load contributes nothing at all
Not quite. The load adds 2,030 − 1,240 = 790 N of muscle force.
The moment arm changes with load
Not quite. The load moment arm is 26 cm in both bent conditions, with or without the load.
Bending forward is safe without a load
Not quite. The passage measures forces. It doesn't judge safety.
Most compression comes from body weight
Correct: 1,240 N of muscle force with empty hands, more than the 790 N the load adds.
qs.x: Correct: The last condition in Figure 1A is bent 60° with nothing in the hands, and it still needs 1,240 N of muscle force. With the 20 kg load held close, it needs 2,030 N. So the load adds 2,030 − 1,240 = 790 N, while the trunk's own weight accounts for 1,240 N, the larger part. Paragraph 6 says the same thing: most of the demand comes from holding up the upper body. Why the others are wrong: the load clearly adds something, 790 N; the passage never judges whether bending is safe; the moment arm in Figure 1B is set by posture and anatomy, and it's 26 cm with or without the load. Trap: Reading the biggest contribution as the only contribution.

qs.q: Why is a pivot point chosen deliberately in such an analysis?
o: The pivot must be where the weight acts
Here the weight acts far from the pivot. That's what gives it torque.
Only one pivot ever gives the correct answer
Every valid pivot gives the same answer. Some just make the math easier.
An unknown force can be made to drop out
Correct: a force acting through the pivot has zero distance, so it makes no torque and drops out.
Torque is defined only about a joint
Torque can be calculated about any point.
qs.x: Correct: Torque is distance × force, where the distance is measured from the pivot to where the force acts. If a force acts right at the pivot, its distance is zero, so its torque is zero. Paragraph 1 uses this trick: pick the pivot where an unknown force acts, and that force drops out of the torque equation, leaving fewer unknowns to solve for. Why the others are wrong: torque can be taken about any point, not only a joint; the pivot doesn't have to be where the weight acts, and here the weight acts far from it; any valid pivot gives the same answer, the choice just makes the algebra easier. Trap: Thinking the choice of pivot changes the physics, when it only changes the algebra.

qs.q: How much extra muscle force does holding the load at arm's length require?
o: That's the load held close versus no load: 2,030 − 1,240.
That's bent versus upright with the load close: 2,030 − 780.
Correct: 3,590 N − 2,030 N = 1,560 N, with only the load position changed.
That compares arm's length with no load: 3,590 − 1,240.
qs.x: Correct: Extra force is the difference between two conditions that differ only in where the load is held. Both are bent 60° with the 20 kg load. From Figure 1A, load close = 2,030 N and arm's length = 3,590 N. Subtract: 3,590 N − 2,030 N = 1,560 N. Nothing about the load changed, only its moment arm, which grew from 26 cm to 77 cm. Why the others are wrong: 790 N is the load held close compared with no load (2,030 − 1,240); 1,250 N is bending versus standing upright with the load close (2,030 − 780); 2,350 N compares arm's length with the no-load condition (3,590 − 1,240), which changes the load too. Trap: Comparing two conditions that differ in more than one thing.

qs.q: Why does a rapid lift exceed these values?
o: The moment arms lengthen when moving
Moment arms depend on posture, not speed.
Acceleration adds to the force required
Correct: accelerating the trunk and load needs extra force beyond the static balance.
Muscles are weaker at higher speeds
That's about what the muscle can do, not what the lift demands.
Static analysis overestimates force
For a fast lift the static values are too low, not too high.
qs.x: Correct: The analysis behind Figure 1 is static, meaning everything is assumed to be at rest, so the torques just balance. Paragraph 7 points out that a real lift involves speeding up (acceleration). By Newton's second law, speeding something up needs a net force, so the muscle has to pull harder than it would just to hold the same posture still. That makes a rapid lift produce larger muscle and disc forces than Figure 1 shows. Why the others are wrong: moment arms depend on posture, not on how fast you move; how strong a muscle is at speed is about its capacity, not about how much force the lift demands; the static numbers are too low for a fast lift, not too high. Trap: Getting backwards which way a static analysis is off.

passages.title: Decibels and the Logarithmic Sound Scale
text: Sound intensity is power per unit area and spans an enormous range in hearing, so it is reported on a logarithmic scale. The sound level in decibels is 10 log of the ratio of the intensity to a reference intensity of 10⁻¹² watts per square meter, which is approximately the faintest audible sound at 1,000 hertz.

Two consequences of the logarithm matter. Each factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 decibels, so 20 decibels represents a hundred fold intensity difference rather than a doubling, and a doubling of intensity adds about 3 decibels. Adding a second identical source therefore raises the level by 3 decibels, not by the level of that source.

Intensity also falls with distance from a point source. Power spreads over the surface of a sphere, so intensity falls as the inverse square of the distance, and each doubling of distance reduces the level by about 6 decibels.

Researchers measured the sound from one machine at distances of 1 m, 2 m and 4 m in an open field. They then switched on a second identical machine beside the first and measured again at 1 m, using the single machine at 1 m as the baseline for comparison. Figure 1A plots the intensity against distance, with the inverse-square prediction drawn as a curve and the two-machine reading as a separate point; Figure 1B gives the sound level in each condition.

Both rules appear. Each doubling of distance divides the intensity by four and lowers the level by 6 decibels, from 80 to 74 to 68, and adding the second machine doubles the intensity and raises the level by 3 decibels, from 80 to 83.

The second result is the counterintuitive one. Two machines each producing 80 decibels together produce 83 decibels rather than 160, because levels are logarithms of intensities and it is the intensities that add.

Two limits should be noted. The inverse square relationship assumes free spread in the open, and indoors reflections return energy so that the level falls more slowly with distance than the rule predicts. And the decibel scale as used here describes intensity rather than perceived loudness, which rises more slowly still, so a 10-decibel rise is usually judged as about a doubling of loudness rather than as a 10-fold increase.

qs.q: Why do two 80-decibel machines produce 83 rather than 160 decibels?
o: Intensities add, not the levels
Correct: Intensity doubles (1.0 to 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m²), and 10 log 2 ≈ 3 dB, so 80 + 3 = 83.
One machine is further from the meter
Not quite. Both machines were side by side at 1 m.
Decibels cannot exceed 100 in air
Not quite. There's no 100 dB cap. Much louder sounds exist.
The machines interfere destructively
Not quite. No cancellation is assumed. Figure 1A shows the intensity doubled.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 defines the level as L = 10 log(I ÷ I₀), with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². Because the level is a log, what adds when two machines run is the intensity, not the decibels. Figure 1A: one machine at 1 m gives I = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m², and two machines give 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m², exactly double. Doubling I adds 10 log 2 to the level. log 2 ≈ 0.3, so 10 × 0.3 = 3 dB. So 80 + 3 = 83 dB, matching Figure 1B. Why the others are wrong: the machines interfere destructively fails because nothing in the passage suggests cancellation, and the measured intensity did double; one machine is further from the meter fails because both were at 1 m, side by side; decibels cannot exceed 100 in air fails because there's no such cap, and loud sounds go well past 100 dB. Trap: Adding decibels as if they were intensities. They're logs, so you add the intensities first.

qs.q: Why does the level fall 6 decibels per doubling of distance?
o: The source becomes quieter with distance
The machine's power output doesn't change. The same power just covers more area.
Air absorbs the sound in proportion to the distance
Air absorption is a much smaller, separate effect. The 6 dB comes from spreading.
Intensity falls as the inverse square
Correct: Double the distance and the sphere's area grows 4 times, so I drops to 1/4, and 10 log(1/4) ≈ −6 dB.
Sound travels more slowly further away
Sound speed in air is essentially constant. Speed doesn't set intensity here.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says the power from a point source spreads over a sphere, whose area is 4πr². So I = P ÷ (4πr²). Doubling r makes the area 2² = 4 times bigger, so the intensity is 1/4 as big. In decibels the change is 10 log(1/4) = −10 log 4. log 4 ≈ 0.6, so 10 × 0.6 = 6 dB lost. Figure 1A shows it: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 1 m drops to 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ W/m² at 2 m (1.0 ÷ 4 = 0.25, and 0.25 × 10⁻⁴ is the same as 2.5 × 10⁻⁵), and the level drops from 80 to 74 dB. Why the others are wrong: air absorbing sound in proportion to distance is a real but much smaller effect, and it wouldn't give a neat 6 dB per doubling; the source becoming quieter fails because the machine's power output doesn't change; sound traveling more slowly fails because the speed of sound in air stays essentially constant with distance. Trap: Blaming the air or the source for what is just the same power spreading over a bigger area.

qs.q: What does the reference intensity represent?
o: Approximately the faintest audible sound
Correct: 10⁻¹² W/m² is about the faintest sound heard at 1,000 Hz. It sets 0 dB.
The intensity produced by one machine
One machine gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 1 m, which is 10⁸ times the reference (80 dB).
The threshold at which damage begins
Hearing damage starts at much higher levels, around 85 dB or more with long exposure.
The intensity of a conversation
A conversation is around 60 dB, a million times more intense than the reference.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the reference intensity, I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m², is about the faintest sound you can hear at 1,000 Hz. Plug it into L = 10 log(I ÷ I₀): if I = I₀, the ratio is 1, log 1 = 0, so L = 0 dB. So 0 dB doesn't mean silence; it means a sound right at the edge of hearing, and every other level is counted up from there. Why the others are wrong: the intensity of a conversation is far higher, around 60 dB, a million times the reference; the threshold where damage begins is higher still, around 85 dB or more with long exposure; the intensity of one machine is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 1 m, which is 10⁸ times the reference (dividing powers of 10, subtract the exponents: −4 − (−12) = −4 + 12 = 8), giving 80 dB. Trap: Thinking the zero of the scale is an ordinary sound rather than the faintest one you can hear.

qs.q: Using the curve in Figure 1A, by what factor does the intensity rise from 4 m to 1 m with one machine?
o: About 2
Not quite. A factor of 2 is what the second machine adds, not a change in distance.
About 4
Not quite. That's one halving of distance. 4 m to 1 m is two halvings: 4 × 4 = 16.
About 12
Not quite. No pair of points in Figure 1A gives 12.
About 16
qs.x: Correct: Intensity factor = I at 1 m ÷ I at 4 m. Figure 1A gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 1 m and 6.3 × 10⁻⁶ W/m² at 4 m. Plug in: (1.0 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (6.3 × 10⁻⁶). Divide the front numbers: 1.0 ÷ 6.3 ≈ 0.159. Dividing powers of 10, subtract the exponents: −4 − (−6) = −4 + 6 = 2. That gives 0.159 × 10² = 15.9, about 16. The inverse square rule predicts the same thing: going from 4 m to 1 m shrinks the distance by a factor of 4, so the intensity rises by 4² = 4 × 4 = 16. Why the others are wrong: about 2 is the effect of switching on the second machine; about 4 is what a single halving of distance does (2 m to 1 m), but 4 m to 1 m is two halvings, so 4 × 4 = 16; about 12 doesn't match any pair of points in Figure 1A. Trap: Using a factor of 4 for a four fold change in distance. The rule squares it, so it's 16.

qs.q: Why might results from this open-field measurement not hold if the study were repeated indoors?
o: Intensity rises with distance indoors
The level still falls with distance indoors, just more slowly than 6 dB per doubling.
Reflections return energy to the listener
Correct: Reflected sound adds to the direct sound, so the level drops more slowly than the rule says.
Sound is absorbed fully by the walls
Walls reflect much of the sound. Full absorption would actually make the room act like open air.
The decibel scale does not apply indoors
The decibel scale is just a way of writing intensity. It works anywhere.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says the inverse square rule assumes free spread in the open, where sound goes out once and never comes back. Indoors, walls, floor and ceiling reflect sound back toward the listener. That reflected energy adds to the sound arriving straight from the source, so the level falls more slowly than 6 dB per doubling of distance. Why the others are wrong: sound absorbed fully by the walls fails because if walls soaked up everything there'd be no reflections and the open-field rule would roughly hold, and real walls reflect a lot; intensity rises with distance indoors goes too far, since paragraph 7 says the level still falls, just more slowly; the decibel scale not applying indoors fails because the scale is just a way of writing intensity and works anywhere. Trap: Turning "falls more slowly" into "rises."
