Figure 1B. Sound level in each condition

passages.title: Poiseuille's Law and Vessel Radius
text: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid tube, Poiseuille's law gives Q = πΔPr⁴ ÷ (8ηL), where Q is flow, ΔP the pressure difference, r the radius, η the viscosity and L the length. The fourth-power dependence on radius means small changes in vessel diameter have large effects on flow. Resistance is R = 8ηL ÷ (πr⁴), and for a given pressure difference, flow is inversely proportional to resistance. Vessels in series add their resistances directly; vessels in parallel combine so that the total resistance is less than that of any one branch.

Researchers studied an isolated rabbit artery preparation perfused with a salt solution at a fixed pressure difference of 60 mmHg. Vessel radius was measured by microscopy, and flow was collected and weighed. Drugs were added to the bath to change the smooth muscle tone of the vessel wall; Figure 1 shows the radius, flow and viscosity in each of four conditions.

The vessel was then replaced by one of the same radius but twice the length, and flow at baseline fell to 80 µL/min. In a final trial, the single vessel was replaced by four parallel vessels, each with half the original radius, and total flow was 40 µL/min.

In the body, the arterioles contribute most of the resistance in the circulation, which is why small changes in their smooth muscle tone have large effects on blood pressure and on how blood is distributed among organs. The capillaries are narrower still, but there are so many of them in parallel that their combined resistance is modest, and their total cross-sectional area is far larger than that of the aorta, so blood moves through them slowly enough for exchange to occur.

The researchers noted that blood is not a Newtonian fluid: its viscosity depends on the shear rate and on hematocrit, and in vessels narrower than about 300 µm the red cells line up near the center, which lowers the effective viscosity.

qs.q: Why did a 16% fall in radius cut flow by half?
o: Flow depends on the fourth power of radius
The pressure difference fell
Not quite. The pressure difference was held at 60 mmHg the whole time.
Norepinephrine also raised the viscosity
Not quite. Viscosity stayed at 1.0 with norepinephrine in Figure 1C.
The vessel became longer as it narrowed
Not quite. The vessel's length didn't change. Only the radius did.
qs.x: Correct: Poiseuille's law (paragraph 1) says flow Q is proportional to r⁴, the radius to the fourth power. Here viscosity, length and pressure stayed the same, so only the radius matters. From Figure 1A, the radius went from 200 µm to 168 µm, and 168 ÷ 200 = 0.84, which is the 16% fall. Raise that to the fourth power: 0.84 × 0.84 = 0.7056 ≈ 0.71, and 0.71 × 0.71 ≈ 0.50. So flow should drop to about half: 160 × 0.50 = 80 µL/min, matching the measured 80. Why the others are wrong: viscosity stayed at 1.0 with norepinephrine (Figure 1C); the pressure difference was held at 60 mmHg throughout; the vessel's length didn't change, only its radius. Trap: Expecting flow to drop by the same 16% as the radius.

qs.q: By Poiseuille's law, what flow would a tripling of viscosity alone predict?
o: 13 µL/min
This divides by 12, which has no basis in the law.
53 µL/min
Correct: η is in the denominator, so tripling it gives 160 ÷ 3 ≈ 53 µL/min.
160 µL/min
Viscosity is in the formula, so flow can't stay the same.
480 µL/min
This multiplies by 3. Thicker fluid flows less, so divide.
qs.x: Correct: In Poiseuille's law, Q = πΔPr⁴ ÷ (8ηL), viscosity η sits on the bottom of the fraction. That means flow is inversely proportional to viscosity: triple η and flow drops to one third. Baseline flow is 160 µL/min and the viscosity goes from 1.0 to 3.0 (Figure 1C, dextran bar), so the new flow = 160 ÷ 3 ≈ 53 µL/min. That matches the measured 53, so the law works here. Why the others are wrong: 480 µL/min multiplies by 3 instead of dividing, but thicker fluid flows less, not more; 160 µL/min would mean viscosity has no effect, yet it's right there in the formula; 13 µL/min divides by 12, which has no basis in the law. Trap: Treating viscosity like radius, when it pushes flow in the opposite direction.

qs.q: Why did flow halve when the vessel length doubled?
o: Longer vessels have smaller radii
The new vessel's radius was matched to the old one.
Resistance is proportional to length
Correct: R grows in step with L, so doubling L doubles R and halves flow.
Pressure is lost at the junctions
It was a single vessel, so there were no junctions.
The fluid cooled along the way
The passage doesn't describe any temperature change.
qs.x: Correct: Resistance is R = 8ηL ÷ (πr⁴) (paragraph 1), and length L is on top, so resistance rises in direct proportion to length. Doubling L doubles R. With the pressure difference fixed, flow = pressure ÷ resistance, so twice the resistance gives half the flow: 160 ÷ 2 = 80 µL/min, exactly what paragraph 3 reports. Why the others are wrong: the new vessel had the same radius as the old one; it was a single vessel, so there were no junctions to lose pressure at; nothing in the passage says the temperature changed. Trap: Thinking length matters as strongly as radius, when length is to the first power and radius to the fourth.

qs.q: Why did four parallel half-radius vessels carry less flow than the single vessel?
o: Parallel vessels always raise resistance
Parallel paths lower resistance. Here they just can't offset the 16-fold rise.
Flow cannot be measured in parallel vessels
Flow was measured: 40 µL/min.
The pressure difference is divided among branches
Every parallel branch feels the full pressure difference.
Each branch has 16 times the resistance
Correct: each half-radius vessel has 2⁴ = 16 times the resistance, and four in parallel give 16 ÷ 4 = 4 times.
qs.x: Correct: Start with one small vessel. Resistance goes as 1 ÷ r⁴, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Now put four of those in parallel. For identical vessels in parallel, the total resistance is one vessel's resistance divided by how many there are: 16 ÷ 4 = 4. So the bundle has 4 times the original resistance, and flow drops to one quarter: 160 ÷ 4 = 40 µL/min, matching paragraph 3. Why the others are wrong: adding parallel paths lowers resistance, it just couldn't make up for the 16-fold rise here; each parallel branch feels the full pressure difference, it isn't split; flow was measured, at 40 µL/min. Trap: Assuming more vessels always means more flow.

qs.q: Why might results from this salt-solution preparation not carry over exactly to blood flow in the body's small arterioles?
o: Arterioles have no pressure difference across them
Arterioles have the largest pressure drop in the circulation.
Blood's viscosity is not constant
Correct: blood's viscosity isn't constant. It changes with shear rate, hematocrit and vessel size.
Arterioles are not cylindrical
Arterioles are roughly cylinders. Blood's changing viscosity is the problem.
Blood flow in arterioles is always turbulent
Flow in arterioles is usually smooth (laminar).
qs.x: Correct: Poiseuille's law assumes a Newtonian fluid, meaning one with a fixed viscosity, flowing through a rigid tube. Paragraph 5 says blood breaks that rule: its viscosity changes with the shear rate (how fast neighboring layers slide past each other) and with hematocrit (the share of blood that's red cells). In vessels narrower than about 300 µm, red cells crowd to the center, which lowers the effective viscosity. Real vessel walls also stretch, so they aren't rigid. Why the others are wrong: arterioles have the biggest pressure drop in the circulation, not none (paragraph 4); flow in arterioles is normally smooth (laminar), not turbulent; arterioles are roughly cylinders. Trap: Using an idealized equation without checking whether its assumptions hold.

Figure 1B. Measured flow at a fixed 60 mmHg pressure difference
Figure 1C. Perfusate viscosity relative to water

passages.title: Critical Concentration for Amphiphile Clusters
text: A molecule with a water liking head and a water avoiding tail stays dispersed in water at low concentration and assembles into clusters above a particular concentration. Below that concentration, adding more molecules raises the number dispersed. Above it, adding more raises the number of clusters and leaves the dispersed concentration almost unchanged.

Several measurable properties therefore change their behavior at the same concentration. The surface tension of the solution falls as the dispersed concentration rises and stops falling once it stops rising, and the solution begins to dissolve water avoiding substances only once clusters exist.

Four detergents were characterized by the concentration at which assembly begins and by two properties measured above and below it (Figure 1). Figure 1A plots the assembly concentration against tail length on a logarithmic axis, and the curve shows a four-fold drop for every two added carbons.

The reference has a 12 carbon tail and begins assembling at 8.2 mM. Q1, Q2 and Q3 have tails of 10, 14 and 16 carbons and begin assembling at 33, 2.1 and 0.5 mM, so each pair of added carbons lowers the concentration about four fold.

The surface tension above the assembly concentration is nearly identical in all four, at 37 to 39 millinewtons a meter, because above that concentration the dispersed concentration has stopped rising and it is the dispersed molecules that lower surface tension.

Q4 has the same tail and the same assembly concentration as the reference but dissolves almost no oil. Its clusters form and do not take up a water avoiding substance, which shows that the two properties are not the same measurement: assembly can be detected by surface tension while the interior of the cluster fails to accommodate oil.

A detergent chosen to dissolve a water avoiding substance therefore cannot be selected on the assembly concentration alone, and the amount dissolved has to be measured. Tail length predicts the assembly concentration reliably and the dissolving capacity only loosely.

Two qualifications apply. The assembly concentration was identified as the point at which the surface tension curve changes slope, and the change occupies a range of concentrations rather than a point, so each figure is the center of a short interval. And oil dissolved was measured at twice the assembly concentration for each detergent, which is a different absolute concentration for each, so the comparison is at matched excess rather than matched concentration.

qs.q: Why does surface tension stop falling above the assembly concentration?
o: It continues to fall
Not quite. It levels off. It's nearly constant above assembly.
Surface tension depends on tail length
Not quite. All four read 37 to 39 mN/m above it, whatever the tail.
The dispersed concentration stops rising
Correct: Extra molecules go into clusters, so the dispersed concentration stops rising.
Clusters lower the surface tension of the solution strongly
Not quite. Dispersed molecules lower surface tension, not the clusters.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says surface tension is lowered by the dispersed molecules, the single detergent molecules floating free in the water. Below the assembly concentration, each added molecule stays dispersed, so the dispersed concentration rises and surface tension keeps dropping. Above it, extra molecules join clusters instead (paragraph 1), so the dispersed concentration stops rising. With no more dispersed molecules coming in, surface tension levels off. That's why all four detergents sit at 37 to 39 mN/m above it (Figure 1B). Why the others are wrong: the clusters aren't what lower surface tension, the dispersed molecules are; tail length doesn't matter above assembly, since all four read nearly the same; surface tension doesn't keep falling, it stays nearly constant. Trap: Giving the clusters credit for something the free molecules do.

qs.q: What does Q4 show?
o: It shows the two properties coincide
Not quite. It shows the two properties come apart, not that they match.
Its assembly concentration is abnormal
Not quite. Its assembly concentration, 8.0 mM, is normal.
Its tail length differs from the reference
Not quite. It has 12 carbons, the same as the reference.
Assembly and dissolving differ
Correct: Q4 forms clusters normally but dissolves almost no oil, so the two properties differ.
qs.x: Correct: Q4 has the same 12-carbon tail as the reference and starts assembling at about the same concentration (8.0 versus 8.2 mM), so its clusters form normally. But it dissolves only 0.2 mg/mL of oil, against 4.1 for the reference (Figure 1C). Paragraph 6 draws the lesson: forming clusters and dissolving oil are two different things. You can see the clusters form through surface tension even when their insides can't hold oil. Why the others are wrong: its assembly concentration, 8.0 mM, is normal; its tail is 12 carbons, the same as the reference; it shows the two properties split apart, not that they always go together. Trap: Treating two properties that usually go together as if they were one measurement.

qs.q: Why is tail length a loose predictor of dissolving capacity?
o: Q4 breaks the relationship
Correct: Q4 has the reference's tail yet dissolves almost no oil.
All four dissolve the same amount of oil
Not quite. Q4 dissolves only 0.2 mg/mL, far less than the rest.
It is a tight predictor
Not quite. Q4 shares the reference tail and still fails, so it's loose.
Tail length does not predict assembly either
Not quite. Tail length predicts assembly well, about four-fold per two carbons.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Figure 1C. Tails of 10, 12, 14 and 16 carbons (Q1, reference, Q2, Q3) all dissolve about the same, 4.0 to 4.2 mg/mL. So tail length barely changes dissolving. Then Q4 has the same 12-carbon tail as the reference but dissolves only 0.2. Knowing the tail length didn't let you predict that. Paragraph 7 sums it up: tail length predicts the assembly concentration reliably and the dissolving capacity only loosely. Why the others are wrong: tail length does predict assembly well, each extra pair of carbons cuts it about four-fold; the amounts aren't all equal, Q4 dissolves only 0.2; it isn't a tight predictor, since Q4 shares the reference tail and still fails. Trap: Assuming a structure rule that works for one property works for another.

qs.q: Oil dissolved was measured at twice each detergent's own assembly concentration, not at one shared concentration. Why is that a sound design choice?
o: Each is compared at the same excess over its own assembly point
Correct: At one shared concentration, some detergents would not have formed clusters yet, so the comparison would be unfair.
It guarantees that all four detergents contain exactly the same number of clusters
Not quite. Cluster numbers still differ between detergents. The choice only matches how far past assembly each one is.
It forces the surface tension to be identical in all four solutions
Not quite. Surface tension is a separate measurement, and it is nearly equal above assembly for another reason.
It removes the need to measure each assembly concentration first
Not quite. You must know each assembly concentration to know what 'twice' means.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 8 says oil dissolved was measured at twice the assembly concentration for each detergent. The assembly concentrations differ a lot, from 0.5 mM for Q3 to 33.0 mM for Q1 (Figure 1A). A single shared concentration such as 5 mM would be above the assembly points of Q2 and Q3 but below those of the reference, Q4 and Q1, so those three would have no clusters yet and would look like poor oil solvents for the wrong reason. Measuring at twice each detergent's own assembly concentration puts every one the same distance past its start, so clusters exist in all of them. Why the others are wrong: this choice does not equalize the number of clusters; surface tension is a separate measurement, nearly identical above assembly (Figure 1B) for a different reason; the assembly concentration still has to be measured first to know what 'twice' means. Trap: Calling a comparison fair because the concentrations match, when matching how far each is past its own assembly point is what matters.

qs.q: On the logarithmic axis of Figure 1A, by what factor does Q1's assembly concentration exceed Q3's?
o: Not quite. 0.5 mM is Q3's concentration alone.
Not quite. 16 is Q3's number of tail carbons.
Not quite. 33 mM is Q1's concentration alone.
qs.x: Correct: Factor = Q1's assembly concentration ÷ Q3's assembly concentration. From Figure 1A, Q1 = 33.0 mM and Q3 = 0.5 mM. Plug in: 33.0 ÷ 0.5. Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2, so 33.0 × 2 = 66. The units cancel, giving a factor of 66. That fits paragraph 4: Q1 to Q3 is three steps of two carbons, and about 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, close to 66. Why the others are wrong: 0.5 is Q3's concentration by itself; 33 is Q1's concentration by itself; 16 is the number of carbons in Q3's tail. Trap: Quoting a number from the graph instead of dividing.

Figure 1B. Surface tension above the assembly concentration
Figure 1C. Oil dissolved at twice the assembly concentration

passages.title: The Continuity Equation in a Narrowed Tube
text: An incompressible fluid in steady flow carries the same volume per second past every cross-section of a tube, so the product of area and speed is constant: a narrowing raises the speed in inverse proportion to the area. Because area varies with the square of the radius, halving a radius quadruples the speed.

Bernoulli's relation then links speed to pressure. Along a streamline, the sum of the static pressure, the kinetic term and the height term is constant, so where the fluid speeds up the static pressure falls. A constriction therefore shows a higher speed and a lower pressure than the wide sections on either side.

This holds only while the flow remains smooth. Above a critical speed the flow becomes turbulent, energy is dissipated in eddies, and the pressure drop along the tube exceeds what Bernoulli's relation predicts, so the relation describes the ideal case and underestimates real losses.

Flow of a test fluid with the density of water but 20 times its viscosity, which keeps the flow smooth to higher speeds, was measured through a tube with a constriction at two flow rates, 50 mL/s and 400 mL/s. Figure 1 shows the speed and static pressure in the wide section and in the constriction, and Table 1 gives the radius and the flow character.

The continuity relation holds throughout. The constriction has one quarter the area and the speed is four times greater at both flow rates, 63.7 against 15.9 and 509 against 127 cm/s, which is what conservation of volume requires.

The pressure behaves as predicted only at the lower rate. At 50 mL/s the constriction shows a small pressure drop consistent with the speed increase, while at 400 mL/s the flow turns turbulent and the pressure falls by 14.8 kPa, more than the 12.2 kPa the kinetic term accounts for.

Two points qualify this. The pressures are static pressures measured at the wall, and a reading taken facing the flow would include the kinetic term and behave quite differently. And blood is not strictly incompressible or Newtonian, and in vessels of small diameter its effective viscosity falls, so these relations describe large vessels better than capillaries.

qs.q: Why does the speed quadruple in the constriction?
o: Area varies with the square of the radius
Correct: half the radius means a quarter of the area, so the speed must be 4 times higher.
Viscosity is lower in narrow tubes
That's a separate effect in blood, not the reason for continuity.
The fluid is compressed as it enters
The fluid is incompressible, so it can't be squeezed.
Pressure simply pushes the fluid faster there
Pressure falls in the constriction. It doesn't push the fluid faster there.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 gives the continuity rule: area × speed stays the same along the tube, because the same volume passes each point every second. Area of a circle is A = πr², so area goes with the radius squared. The constriction's radius is 0.50 cm against 1.00 cm, half as big, so its area is (½)² = ¼ as big. To push the same volume through a quarter of the area, the fluid must go 4 times faster. Figure 1A confirms it: 15.9 × 4 = 63.6 ≈ 63.7 cm/s. Why the others are wrong: pressure actually falls in the constriction, so it isn't pushing the fluid faster there; the fluid is incompressible, so it can't be squeezed; lower viscosity in narrow tubes is a separate effect in blood, not the reason for continuity. Trap: Explaining the speed-up by the pressure drop, which is a result of the speed-up, not its cause.

qs.q: Why does the pressure drop exceed the prediction at the higher rate?
o: The fluid becomes compressible there
The fluid stays incompressible at both flow rates.
Turbulence dissipates energy in eddies
Correct: eddies turn some energy into heat, which Bernoulli's relation doesn't include.
The radius decreases even further at high speed
The tube is rigid, so its radius doesn't change.
The kinetic term grows with speed
The kinetic term is already in the 12.2 kPa prediction. The extra drop comes from turbulence.
qs.x: Correct: Bernoulli's relation assumes the fluid's energy is conserved along its path (paragraph 2). In turbulent flow, the fluid churns into eddies (swirls), and that turns some of its energy into random motion and heat. That lost energy shows up as an extra pressure drop. At 400 mL/s the constriction is turbulent (Table 1), and paragraph 6 says the pressure fell 14.8 kPa when the speed change alone accounts for 12.2 kPa. Why the others are wrong: the tube is rigid, so the radius doesn't shrink further; the kinetic term (the speed part) is already in the 12.2 kPa prediction, so it can't explain the extra; the fluid stays incompressible. Trap: Picking the term the prediction already includes.

qs.q: Why was the same constriction tested at both 50 mL/s and 400 mL/s?
o: Continuity can only be checked if the area is measured at two different flow rates
Not quite. Continuity holds at each rate by itself, so a second rate isn't needed to check it.
The higher rate makes the fluid compressible, which is needed to test Bernoulli's relation
Not quite. The fluid is incompressible at both rates. Bernoulli's relation is tested without squeezing it.
The smooth lower rate is a comparison for the higher rate where turbulence appears
Correct: setting a smooth-flow case beside a turbulent one shows where Bernoulli's prediction stops working.
Averaging the two rates removes the error from using a viscous test fluid
Not quite. Nothing is averaged in Figure 1, and the viscous fluid is there to keep flow smooth longer.
qs.x: Correct: To show that turbulence is what breaks Bernoulli's prediction, you need a case where it holds to compare with a case where it fails. At 50 mL/s the flow is smooth and the constriction shows the small pressure drop the speed increase predicts (Figure 1B, 101.1 kPa to 100.9 kPa). At 400 mL/s the flow is turbulent and the drop is 14.8 kPa, bigger than the 12.2 kPa the kinetic term accounts for (paragraph 6). The only thing changed is the flow rate, so the difference points at turbulence. Why the others are wrong: continuity already holds at each rate on its own, so a second rate isn't needed for it; the fluid is incompressible at both rates; nothing is averaged in Figure 1, and the viscous fluid is used to keep flow smooth to higher speeds. Trap: Thinking a second condition is there for extra data when it is there as a comparison.

qs.q: What is the pressure drop across the constriction at 400 mL/s?
o: 0.2 kPa
That's the drop at 50 mL/s: 101.1 − 100.9.
1.7 kPa
That compares the two wide sections: 101.1 − 99.4.
14.8 kPa
Correct: 99.4 kPa − 84.6 kPa = 14.8 kPa.
16.3 kPa
That compares the two constrictions: 100.9 − 84.6.
qs.x: Correct: Pressure drop = pressure in the wide section − pressure in the constriction, both at the same flow rate. From the 400 mL/s bars in Figure 1B: wide = 99.4 kPa, constriction = 84.6 kPa. Subtract: 99.4 − 84.6 = 14.8 kPa. Paragraph 6 reports the same number. Why the others are wrong: 0.2 kPa is the drop at 50 mL/s (101.1 − 100.9); 1.7 kPa compares the two wide sections at different flow rates (101.1 − 99.4); 16.3 kPa compares the two constrictions at different flow rates (100.9 − 84.6). Trap: Comparing bars from different flow rates instead of within one.

qs.q: Why would a pressure reading facing the flow behave differently?
o: It would be identical to the static value
It would be higher than the static value, by the kinetic term.
It would be unaffected by the speed
It depends directly on speed through the kinetic term.
It could not be measured at all
Readings facing the flow are routinely taken.
It would include the kinetic term
Correct: stopping the fluid turns its kinetic energy into pressure, which the static reading leaves out.
qs.x: Correct: The pressures in Figure 1B are static pressures, measured at the wall, where the fluid slides past without being stopped (paragraph 7). A probe facing into the flow stops the fluid that hits it, and that fluid's kinetic energy (energy of motion) turns into extra pressure. So a facing reading adds the kinetic term to the static pressure. It would be higher than the static value and would rise as speed rises, even where the static pressure falls. Why the others are wrong: facing readings are taken all the time; it wouldn't match the static value, it'd be higher; it depends strongly on speed, not weakly. Trap: Treating every pressure reading in a moving fluid as the same thing.

Figure 1B. Static pressure at the wall at each flow rate

passages.title: Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle
text: A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Whether it floats therefore depends on the comparison of densities: a body less dense than the fluid floats with part of its volume above the surface, and the submerged fraction equals the ratio of the body's density to the fluid's.

Apparent weight follows from the same principle. A body weighed while submerged reads less than in air by exactly the buoyant force, so measuring both gives the displaced volume and hence the body's density without knowing its shape.

Human body composition is estimated this way. Fat is less dense than water and lean tissue is denser, so a person's whole-body density predicts the proportion of fat, provided the air in the lungs is accounted for, since trapped air lowers the measured density and inflates the estimate of fat.
Objects and a person were weighed in air and submerged in fresh water (Figure 1).

The method works from the difference of two weights. The aluminum block loses 10.0 N when submerged, which corresponds to a displaced volume of about 1,020 cm³ and a density of 2.70 g per cubic centimeter, and the bone sample loses two thirds of its weight, giving 1.50.

The two lung conditions show the correction that matters. With the lungs emptied the person's density is 1.03 g per cubic centimeter and they sink slowly; with the lungs filled the apparent weight is negative, meaning the buoyant force exceeds their weight and they float, and the computed density of 0.96 is not a density of tissue at all.

Two limits are worth noting. Residual air remains in the lungs even after a maximal exhalation and must be measured separately or estimated, and an error there translates directly into an error in the fat estimate. And the relationship between whole-body density and fat proportion assumes fixed densities for fat and lean tissue, which vary with age and with bone mineral content.

qs.q: Why is the lungs-filled density not a tissue density?
o: Trapped air is counted as part of the body
Correct: lung air adds volume without mass, pulling the computed density below that of the tissue itself.
The scale cannot read negative weights
The negative reading is real: buoyancy exceeds weight, so the person floats.
Lung tissue is denser than other tissue
The air in the lungs, not lung tissue, lowers the result.
Water enters the lungs during the test
The lungs hold air, not water.
qs.x: Correct: The density calculation divides mass by the whole volume inside the body's outline. With full lungs, that volume includes a lot of air, which adds space but almost no mass. That drags the computed density down to 0.96 g/cm³, lower than water and lower than any real tissue. Paragraph 6 says it directly: that number isn't a tissue density at all. Why the others are wrong: the negative apparent weight (−29.4 N) is real, it means buoyancy is bigger than weight, so the person floats; the lungs hold air, not water; how dense lung tissue is isn't what changes the result, it's the air inside. Trap: Treating a computed number as a property of the tissue when the measurement included something else.

qs.q: Why does weighing in air and in water give the density?
o: The scale reads more accurately when the object is in water
The scale's accuracy doesn't change in water.
Apparent weight tracks density
Apparent weight depends on both mass and volume, not density alone.
Water has a density of exactly one
Water's density makes the math easy, but buoyancy is the principle.
The weight lost equals the displaced fluid
Correct: the weight lost equals the weight of displaced water, which gives the volume.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. Underwater, the scale reads less than in air by exactly the buoyant force, and the buoyant force equals the weight of the water pushed aside. Water's density is known, so the weight of water pushed aside tells you its volume, which is the object's volume. Then density = mass ÷ volume. For the aluminum: 27.0 N − 17.0 N = 10.0 N lost, and 27.0 ÷ 10.0 = 2.70, so it's 2.70 times as dense as water, 2.70 g/cm³. Why the others are wrong: a scale isn't more accurate underwater; water's density being about 1 g/cm³ makes the math easy, but the principle is buoyancy; apparent weight depends on both mass and volume, not density alone. Trap: Picking a convenient number instead of the physics behind it.

qs.q: What determines the fraction of a floating body that is submerged?
o: The depth of the fluid
Water depth doesn't change how a floating object sits.
The total mass of the body
Mass alone doesn't set it. Same material, same fraction.
The ratio of the two densities
Correct: the submerged fraction = body's density ÷ fluid's density.
The shape of the body
Shape affects stability, not the fraction underwater.
qs.x: Correct: A floating body sinks until it pushes aside its own weight in fluid. Working that out, the fraction underwater = body's density ÷ fluid's density (paragraph 1). For example, something 0.9 times as dense as water floats with 0.9 of its volume under the surface. Why the others are wrong: a heavier object of the same material floats with the same fraction submerged, so mass alone doesn't set it; shape affects whether it tips over, not how much is under; the depth of the water doesn't matter as long as the object can float freely. Trap: Thinking a big object floats differently from a small one made of the same stuff.

qs.q: How much weight does the bone sample lose when submerged?
o: That's the bone's apparent weight underwater, not the loss.
Correct: 6.0 N − 2.0 N = 4.0 N lost to buoyancy.
That's the bone's weight in air.
That's the aluminum block's loss: 27.0 − 17.0.
qs.x: Correct: Weight lost = weight in air − apparent weight underwater. From the bone sample bars in Figure 1A: in air = 6.0 N, submerged = 2.0 N. Subtract: 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 N. That 4.0 N is the buoyant force. It also gives the density: 6.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.50 g/cm³, matching Figure 1C, and 4.0 ÷ 6.0 = ⅔, the "two thirds of its weight" in paragraph 5. Why the others are wrong: 2.0 N is what the scale reads underwater, not the loss; 6.0 N is the weight in air; 10.0 N is what the aluminum block loses (27.0 − 17.0). Trap: Reporting one of the readings instead of the difference between them.

qs.q: Why does residual lung air limit the fat estimate?
o: An error in it feeds straight into the result
Correct: a wrong residual-air volume shifts the tissue volume, so the error passes straight into the fat estimate.
It affects only the reading taken with the lungs filled
Residual air is present in both conditions, including emptied lungs.
Residual air has the density of tissue
Air is far less dense than tissue. That's why it matters.
Residual air cannot be measured
It can be measured separately, as the passage says.
qs.x: Correct: Even after breathing out as hard as you can, some air (the residual volume) stays in the lungs (paragraph 7). The method has to subtract that air's volume to get the tissue volume. If the residual volume is guessed wrong, the tissue volume is wrong, so the density is wrong, and the fat estimate built on that density is wrong by the same amount. Why the others are wrong: residual air can be measured separately, the passage says so; air is far less dense than tissue, which is why it matters; residual air is there in both lung conditions, not just the filled one. Trap: Assuming a correction matters only in the condition where the quantity is biggest.

Figure 1B. Weight in air and apparent weight submerged: the person at two lung volumes
Figure 1C. Density computed from the two weights

passages.title: The Membrane as an RC Circuit
text: A patch of neuronal membrane behaves like a resistor and a capacitor in parallel. The lipid bilayer separates charge and acts as a capacitor; the ion channels provide a resistive path. When a steady current is injected, the membrane voltage does not jump but approaches its final value along an exponential curve, V(t) = V_final × (1 − e raised to the power of −t/τ), where the membrane time constant τ = RC. The voltage reaches about 63% of its final value after one time constant.

The final voltage change is set by Ohm's law, ΔV = IR, where R is the membrane resistance. Opening more channels lowers R, so the same current produces a smaller voltage change and the membrane responds faster. Myelin adds layers of membrane in series, which lowers capacitance per unit length and raises resistance across the wall.

Researchers injected 0.2 nA of current into cultured neurons through a microelectrode and recorded the voltage change at the injection site (Figure 1). The calculated membrane capacitance was 400 pF in the control, channel blocker and channel opener conditions, and 1,600 pF in the neuron with a larger surface area.

These properties explain why a neuron does not respond instantly to its inputs. A brief synaptic current produces a voltage change that rises and decays over several milliseconds, so inputs arriving close together in time add up, a process called temporal summation. A membrane with a long time constant sums inputs over a longer window, which makes the cell more sensitive to steady input but slower to follow rapid changes. The researchers measured summation directly by injecting pairs of brief current pulses 5 ms apart and found that the second pulse produced a larger voltage change in the blocker condition than in the control.

The researchers also measured how far a voltage signal spread along a process from the injection point. The signal fell to 37% of its starting size after 0.6 mm in control neurons and after 0.85 mm in neurons whose membrane resistance had been doubled by a channel blocker.

qs.q: Why does the channel blocker double the voltage change?
o: The blocker increases membrane capacitance
Capacitance stayed at 400 pF.
The blocker shortens the time constant
The time constant got longer, 20 to 40 ms.
Fewer open channels raise resistance
Correct: fewer open channels raise R from 50 to 100 MΩ, so ΔV = IR doubles.
The blocker increases the injected current
The current was fixed at 0.2 nA by the experimenter.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 gives Ohm's law for the membrane: ΔV = IR. Blocking channels shuts some of the paths ions use to leak across the membrane, so resistance goes up, from 50 to 100 MΩ in Figure 1C. The injected current stayed at 0.2 nA. With the same I and twice the R, ΔV = IR doubles: 10.0 mV becomes 20.0 mV. Why the others are wrong: the experimenter fixed the current at 0.2 nA; capacitance stayed at 400 pF, since it depends on membrane area, which didn't change; the time constant got longer, from 20 to 40 ms, not shorter. Trap: Looking for a change in current when it was the resistance that changed.

qs.q: What is the membrane resistance in the control condition, in megaohms?
o: This multiplies 0.2 and 10. Ohm's law divides voltage by current.
That's the time constant, 20 ms, not a resistance.
Correct: 10 mV ÷ 0.2 nA = 10⁻² V ÷ (2 × 10⁻¹⁰ A) = 5 × 10⁷ Ω = 50 MΩ.
Off by a factor of 10, usually from a slip converting mV or nA.
qs.x: Correct: Ohm's law for the membrane is ΔV = IR, so R = ΔV ÷ I. From the passage and Figure 1A, ΔV = 10.0 mV and I = 0.2 nA. Change both to base units first. 1 mV = 10⁻³ V, so 10.0 mV = 10 × 10⁻³ V = 1 × 10⁻² V. 1 nA = 10⁻⁹ A, so 0.2 nA = 0.2 × 10⁻⁹ A = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ A. Now divide: R = (1 × 10⁻²) ÷ (2 × 10⁻¹⁰). Divide the front numbers, 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5, and subtract the exponents, −2 − (−10) = −2 + 10 = 8. That gives 0.5 × 10⁸ Ω, which is the same as 5 × 10⁷ Ω (make the front number 10 times bigger and the exponent 1 smaller). Last, change ohms to megaohms. 1 MΩ = 10⁶ Ω, so divide by 10⁶ (subtract 6 from the exponent): 5 × 10⁷ ÷ 10⁶ = 5 × 10¹ = 50 MΩ, which matches Figure 1C. Why the others are wrong: 2 multiplies the two numbers (0.2 × 10) instead of dividing voltage by current; 20 is the time constant in milliseconds from Figure 1B, not a resistance; 500 is off by a power of 10, which usually comes from a slip when converting mV or nA. Trap: Dividing millivolts by nanoamps without changing them into volts and amps first, which makes it easy to lose a power of 10.

qs.q: Why does the larger neuron have the same time constant as the blocker condition?
o: Lower resistance, higher capacitance
Correct: R fell to 25 MΩ while C rose to 1,600 pF, and 25 × 1,600 = 100 × 400.
Larger neurons always respond more slowly
Its τ equals the blocker condition's, so size alone doesn't decide it.
Its capacitance is unchanged by the size
Capacitance rose four times, from 400 to 1,600 pF.
Current spreads faster in large cells
Response speed here is set by τ = RC.
qs.x: Correct: The time constant is τ = RC (paragraph 1). The larger neuron has more membrane, so its capacitance is four times higher: 1,600 pF against 400 pF. More membrane also means more channels, so its resistance is lower: 25 MΩ. Multiply: 1 MΩ = 10⁶ Ω and 1 pF = 10⁻¹² F, so τ = (25 × 10⁶) × (1,600 × 10⁻¹²). Front numbers: 25 × 1,600 = 40,000 = 4 × 10⁴. Exponents: 6 + (−12) = −6. So τ = 4 × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ = 4 × 10⁻² s = 0.04 s = 40 ms. The blocker condition gives 100 MΩ × 400 pF, and 100 × 400 = 40,000 too, so also 40 ms. Why the others are wrong: its time constant equals the blocker's, so bigger cells aren't always slower; capacitance rose four times with the bigger area; speed of response here is set by τ, not by how fast current spreads. Trap: Assuming the time constant depends on cell size alone.

qs.q: Why does a signal spread farther when membrane resistance is doubled?
o: The axon's internal resistance falls
The blocker acts on the membrane, not on the inside of the axon.
The injected current was increased
The current was fixed at 0.2 nA.
The capacitance of the membrane falls
Capacitance stayed at 400 pF.
Less current leaks across the membrane
Correct: higher membrane resistance means less current leaks out, so more travels along.
qs.x: Correct: Current injected at one point has two choices: travel along the inside of the process, or leak out across the membrane through open channels. Doubling membrane resistance (paragraph 5) means less leaks out, so more current keeps going along the process before the signal fades. That's why the signal reached 37% of its size at 0.85 mm instead of 0.6 mm. Why the others are wrong: the blocker acts on membrane channels, not on the resistance of the inside (cytoplasm); capacitance stayed at 400 pF; the injected current was fixed at 0.2 nA. Trap: Thinking how far a signal spreads depends only on the inside of the process.

qs.q: How does myelin speed conduction, in terms of these properties?
o: It lowers capacitance and raises resistance
Correct: lower C means less charge to move, and higher R means less leak.
It raises capacitance so charge builds faster
Higher capacitance would slow the voltage change.
It lowers the resistance of the axon's interior
Myelin wraps the outside. It doesn't change the axon's interior.
It increases the current each channel passes
Channels are concentrated at the nodes, but each passes the same current.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says myelin wraps many layers of membrane around the axon, in series. Stacking layers lowers capacitance, C, so less charge has to move to change the voltage, and the voltage changes faster. It also raises resistance, R, across the wall, so less current leaks out and the signal spreads farther along the axon. Together, the depolarization reaches the next node (the gap in the myelin) quickly. Why the others are wrong: higher capacitance would mean more charge is needed, so the voltage would change more slowly; myelin wraps the outside, it doesn't change the inside; channels are packed at the nodes, but each channel works the same. Trap: Assuming myelin works by making ions move faster.
