passages.title: Measuring Copper in Tap Water Electrochemically
text: Copper is an essential trace element, but dissolved Cu²⁺ above about 2 mg/L (roughly 3 × 10⁻⁵ M) in drinking water can cause nausea, and long exposure can damage the liver. Because copper enters tap water mainly from household pipes, inexpensive field tests are useful. One approach uses a galvanic cell whose voltage depends on the Cu²⁺ concentration.

A student group built a cell from a zinc strip in 1.0 M Zn(NO₃)₂ and a copper strip in the test solution. The two beakers were joined by a U-tube salt bridge filled with KNO₃ in agar, and the strips were connected to a high-resistance voltmeter so that almost no current flowed during readings. The relevant half-reactions are:

Under these conditions, the Nernst equation for the cell at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, where Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. The students first measured standard solutions to make a calibration curve (Figure 1), then tested a sample of tap water from an old building and a second sample that had been concentrated 1000-fold by evaporation.

The group noted two limits of the method. First, the calibration assumes that the solutions are dilute enough for concentration to stand in for activity; in more concentrated solutions, ions interact and the measured voltage drifts from the prediction. Second, other dissolved metal ions that are easily reduced, such as Ag⁺, could also deposit on the copper strip and distort the reading. Neither was expected to matter for household water, but the group ran each sample in triplicate and discarded any run that drifted by more than 2 mV over one minute.

The concentrated tap-water sample gave a reading of 1.055 V. As a control for the role of the salt bridge, the students removed it and laid a glass rod across the two beakers; the voltmeter then read 0.000 V. Finally, they left one cell connected through a small resistor for 6 hours and noted that the voltage slowly fell, the copper strip gained mass, and the zinc strip lost mass.

qs.q: What is the approximate Cu²⁺ concentration of the concentrated tap-water sample?
o: Not quite. That would read about 1.025 V, below the 0.010 M reading.
Not quite. That would read about 1.085 V, above the 0.10 M reading of 1.071 V.
3 M
Not quite. That would read above 1.10 V, higher than any reading in Figure 1.
qs.x: Correct: Use the Nernst equation from paragraph 4: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. The values: E° = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 0.34 + 0.76 = 1.10 V (subtracting a negative is adding); n = 2 electrons; Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1.0/[Cu²⁺]; E = 1.055 V (paragraph 6). First, 0.0592 ÷ 2 = 0.0296 V. Plug in: 1.055 = 1.100 − 0.0296 log Q. Move things around: 0.0296 log Q = 1.100 − 1.055 = 0.045, so log Q = 0.045 ÷ 0.0296 ≈ 1.5. Log just reads off the exponent of 10, so Q is 10 raised to 1.5, about 32. Then [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 ÷ 32 ≈ 0.03 M. Figure 1 agrees: 1.055 V sits about halfway between 1.040 V (0.010 M) and 1.071 V (0.10 M), and halfway on a log scale is 0.03 M. Undo the 1000-fold concentration: 0.03 ÷ 1000 = 3 × 10⁻⁵ M in the tap water, right at the level of concern in paragraph 1. Why the others are wrong: 0.003 M would read about 1.025 V, below 1.040 V; 0.3 M would read about 1.085 V, above the 0.10 M reading of 1.071 V; 3 M would read above 1.10 V. Trap: Interpolating halfway in concentration (0.055 M) instead of halfway in log concentration.

qs.q: Why does each 10-fold drop in [Cu²⁺] lower the voltage by about 30 mV rather than 59 mV?
o: Two electrons move per copper ion reduced
Correct: n = 2, so 0.0592 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.030 V per 10-fold change.
The salt bridge absorbs half of the potential
A salt bridge carries ions. It doesn't divide the voltage.
The zinc half-cell offsets half of the change
[Zn²⁺] was held at 1.0 M, so the zinc side doesn't change.
Only half of the Cu²⁺ ions reach the electrode
The equation uses concentration, not how many ions reach the electrode.
qs.x: Correct: In the Nernst equation the log term is multiplied by 0.0592/n, where n is the number of electrons moved per ion. Both half-reactions here move 2 electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu and Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn), so n = 2. Then 0.0592 ÷ 2 = 0.0296 V, about 30 mV for each 10-fold change in Q. Figure 1 shows it: 1.071 − 1.040 = 0.031 V and 1.040 − 1.012 = 0.028 V per step. The 59 mV figure is for one-electron reactions. Why the others are wrong: [Zn²⁺] stayed at 1.0 M, so the zinc side contributes no change; the equation uses concentration, not how many ions reach the metal; a salt bridge carries ions and doesn't split the voltage. Trap: Using 59 mV per 10-fold change for every cell.

qs.q: In the control trial with a glass rod in place of the salt bridge, which statement best explains the 0.000 V reading?
o: The glass rod would short-circuit the two half-cells
Glass is an insulator, so it can't short anything.
Charge can no longer be balanced by ion movement
Correct: without an ion path, charge builds up in each beaker and the circuit is open.
Zn²⁺ ions are no longer able to reach the copper electrode
Zn²⁺ isn't meant to reach the copper electrode.
Electrons can no longer travel through the bridge
Electrons travel through the external wire, not the bridge.
qs.x: Correct: As the cell runs, zinc atoms become Zn²⁺, adding positive charge to the zinc beaker, and Cu²⁺ becomes copper metal, removing positive charge from the copper beaker. Without a fix, charge would build up and stop the reaction at once. The salt bridge fixes it by letting ions (here K⁺ and NO₃⁻) drift between the beakers to keep each one neutral. A glass rod carries no ions, so the circuit is broken and the meter reads 0.000 V (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: electrons travel through the wire, never through the salt bridge; Zn²⁺ isn't supposed to reach the copper electrode at all; glass is an insulator, so it can't short the cell. Trap: Thinking the salt bridge carries electrons.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the voltage fell while the cell ran for 6 hours?
o: The zinc strip became smaller and less reactive
Electrode size isn't in the Nernst equation.
The reaction became nonspontaneous after 1 hour
E stayed positive while falling, so the reaction was still spontaneous.
Q rose as Cu²⁺ was used up and Zn²⁺ formed
Correct: [Cu²⁺] fell and [Zn²⁺] rose, so Q went up and E went down.
E° fell as copper metal plated onto the strip
E° is fixed for the half-reactions. It doesn't change as the cell runs.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says the copper strip gained mass and the zinc strip lost mass. So Cu²⁺ was turning into copper metal, lowering [Cu²⁺], and zinc was turning into Zn²⁺, raising [Zn²⁺]. Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺], so a bigger top and smaller bottom make Q rise. In E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, a bigger Q means more is subtracted, so E falls. It would reach zero only at equilibrium. Why the others are wrong: E° is a fixed property of the half-reactions and doesn't change during a run; the size of the electrode doesn't appear in the Nernst equation; the voltage was falling slowly but still positive, so the reaction was still spontaneous. Trap: Treating E° as if it were the voltage at any moment.

qs.q: Which change would make the cell's voltage respond more strongly to each 10-fold change in [Cu²⁺]?
o: Raising [Zn²⁺] in the zinc beaker from 1.0 M to 2.0 M
This shifts every reading equally but leaves the change per 10-fold step the same.
Using a copper strip with twice the surface area
Electrode area affects current, not the Nernst slope.
Using a longer salt bridge with more KNO₃
Bridge length affects resistance, not the Nernst slope.
Running the cell at a higher temperature
Correct: the slope is 2.303RT/nF, which grows with absolute temperature T.
qs.x: Correct: The 0.0592 V in the Nernst equation is really 2.303RT/F worked out at 298 K, which is 25 °C, where R is the gas constant, T is the absolute temperature and F is Faraday's constant. T is on top, so a warmer cell has a bigger number there and a steeper change in voltage for each 10-fold change in [Cu²⁺]. Why the others are wrong: a bigger copper strip lets more current flow but doesn't change the equilibrium voltage; raising [Zn²⁺] shifts every reading by the same amount, but each 10-fold step still changes E by the same 30 mV; a longer salt bridge changes the resistance, not the Nernst slope. Trap: Mixing up shifting the whole calibration line with making it steeper.

graph.title: Figure 1. Calibration of the Zn–Cu cell: measured voltage against [Cu²⁺] (log scale), with the Nernst prediction

passages.title: Self-Esteem and Domains of Self-Concept
text: Self-esteem is a global evaluation of one's own worth. Self-concept is the broader set of beliefs a person holds about themselves, organized into domains such as academic ability, appearance, athletic competence and social acceptance. The two are related but not the same: self-concept supplies the content and self-esteem is an overall appraisal drawn from it.

How the appraisal is drawn is the interesting part. The weighting is not equal across domains. A person's global self-esteem depends most on the domains they consider important, so poor self-rated athletic ability lowers self-esteem in someone for whom sport matters and leaves it untouched in someone for whom it does not. This is why two people with identical domain profiles can differ in global self-esteem.

Social comparison supplies much of the domain content. A student's academic self-concept depends less on absolute attainment than on standing relative to the immediate comparison group, which is why the same student can hold a higher academic self-concept in an average school than in a selective one.

Investigators surveyed 1,100 adolescents, measuring global self-esteem, self-rated competence in four domains, and how important each domain was to the respondent, then computed the correlation of each domain with global self-esteem separately among those who rated it important and those who did not (Figure 1).

The pattern is the same in all four domains: a domain is strongly related to global self-esteem among people who care about it and weakly related among those who do not, which is the weighting account in a single figure.

Two limits are worth stating. Importance and competence were both reported by the respondent at the same sitting, so a person may call a domain important partly because they do well in it, which would produce the pattern without any weighting. And nothing in a cross-sectional survey shows direction, since low self-esteem could lead a person to dismiss domains in which they struggle, a protective move that would also produce the observed split.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the weighting account?
o: Appearance correlates most strongly with self-esteem of the four
That's a ranking, not a test of weighting.
Domains correlate equally whatever their importance
Correct: equal correlations would mean importance does nothing.
Self-esteem is lower on average in adolescence
That's about the level, not the structure.
Competence ratings correlate across domains
That's about overlap between domains.
qs.x: Correct: The weighting account says a domain affects your overall self-esteem only as much as you care about it (paragraph 2). Its evidence is the gap in Figure 1: correlations are high when a domain is rated important (0.41 to 0.54) and low when it isn't (0.04 to 0.21). A correlation shows how closely two things move together. If the correlations were the same whether or not people cared about a domain, importance would make no difference and the account would have nothing to explain. Why the others are wrong: appearance having the strongest correlation is just a ranking, not a test; average self-esteem being lower in adolescence is about the level, not how it's built; and competence ratings overlapping across domains is a separate question. Trap: Choosing a noticeable feature of the figure instead of the result that actually tests the claim.

qs.q: How does self-concept differ from self-esteem?
o: It is the content rather than the overall appraisal
Correct: self-concept is the content. Self-esteem is the overall verdict.
It applies only to academic performance
It covers several domains.
It is fixed in early childhood and does not change afterward
Both can shift over time.
It cannot be measured by self-report
Both are measured by self-report.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 draws the line. Self-concept is the whole set of beliefs you hold about yourself, organized into areas like school, looks, sports and friendships. Self-esteem is one overall judgment of your worth, drawn from that content. Self-concept is the content; self-esteem is the verdict. Why the others are wrong: self-concept isn't fixed in childhood, since paragraph 3 shows it shifts with your comparison group; it covers several domains, not just academics; and both are measured by self-report questionnaires, as in this survey. Trap: Treating the broader idea as if it were a narrower piece of the other.

qs.q: Why can the same student hold a higher academic self-concept in an average school?
o: Self-concept does not depend on performance
It depends on performance relative to peers.
Academic ability itself rises in that setting
Ability stays the same. It's what's being judged.
Grading is more generous in average schools
Grading isn't the mechanism described.
The comparison group sets the standard
Correct: the comparison group sets the standard.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says academic self-concept depends less on how well you actually do and more on how you stack up against the people around you. This is social comparison. The same grades put a student near the top in an average school but in the middle or lower in a selective one. The student hasn't changed; the comparison group has. Why the others are wrong: grading practice isn't the mechanism described; the student's actual ability stays the same, it's what's being judged; and self-concept does depend on performance, just relative performance. Trap: Looking for a change in the student when the change is in who they're compared with.

qs.q: Which alternative explanation does this survey leave open?
o: Four domains is too few to study the self
More domains would show the same split.
Appearance clearly matters a great deal to most adolescents
That fits the account.
People may call a domain important when they do well
Correct: people may rate a domain important because they do well in it.
Global self-esteem is one overall evaluation
That's the definition, not an alternative.
qs.x: Correct: Importance and competence were reported at the same time by the same person (paragraph 6). So a teen might call a domain important partly because they're good at it. That alone would make the correlation higher among those who rate it important, with no weighting going on. It's a rival explanation the survey can't rule out. Why the others are wrong: appearance mattering to most adolescents fits the weighting account, so it's not an alternative; global self-esteem being one overall judgment is just the definition; and adding more domains wouldn't change this logic. Trap: Mistaking a feature of the concept for a rival explanation.

qs.q: Which domain shows the largest gap between the two bars?
o: 0.31, social acceptance
0.52 − 0.21 = 0.31, the smallest gap.
0.36, appearance and academic ability
Both are 0.36, just short of 0.37.
0.37, athletic competence
Correct: 0.41 − 0.04 = 0.37, the largest gap.
0.41, the athletic importance correlation
0.41 is one correlation, not a gap.
qs.x: Correct: Subtract the unimportant bar from the important bar in each domain in Figure 1. Appearance: 0.54 − 0.18 = 0.36. Academic ability: 0.47 − 0.11 = 0.36. Athletic competence: 0.41 − 0.04 = 0.37. Social acceptance: 0.52 − 0.21 = 0.31. The largest gap is 0.37, for athletic competence. Why the others are wrong: social acceptance's 0.31 is the smallest gap; appearance and academic ability tie at 0.36, just short of 0.37; and 0.41 is a single correlation, not a gap between bars. Trap: Reading one bar instead of subtracting the two.

graph.title: Figure 1. Correlation of each domain with global self-esteem, by importance

passages.title: Faraday's Law in Electrolysis
text: Electrolysis uses an external supply to drive a redox reaction that would not occur spontaneously. The amount of substance transformed follows from the charge passed: charge is current times time, and 1 mol of electrons carries 96,500 coulombs, so the moles of electrons equal the charge divided by that constant.

Converting electrons to product requires the stoichiometry of the half-reaction. Depositing a mole of silver from Ag⁺ requires 1 mol of electrons, a mole of copper from Cu²⁺ requires two, and a mole of aluminum from Al³⁺ requires three, so the same charge deposits very different masses of the three metals.

Competing reactions reduce the yield. Water can be reduced to hydrogen at the cathode and oxidized to oxygen at the anode, so in aqueous solution a metal whose reduction is less favorable than that of water cannot be plated at all, and one that competes with water is plated with less than complete efficiency.
A current of 2.00 A was passed for 30.0 minutes through three solutions containing silver (1 electron per ion), copper (2) and nickel (2) ions (Figure 1).

The charge passed is the same in every case. Two amperes for 1,800 seconds is 3,600 coulombs, or 0.0373 moles of electrons, which deposits 0.0373 moles of silver but only 0.0187 moles of copper or nickel because each of those ions requires two electrons.

Efficiency falls as the competing reaction becomes more favorable. Silver plates at essentially 100% while nickel reaches only 75%, the remainder of the charge going to hydrogen evolution, which is visible as gas at the cathode and is why nickel plating is run under controlled conditions.

Two points qualify this. The expected masses assume all the charge goes to the intended reaction, so a measured efficiency below 100% is calculated against that assumption rather than measured independently. And the efficiency depends on current density and pH as well as on the metal, so the nickel figure describes these conditions rather than nickel plating in general.

qs.q: Why does the same charge deposit fewer moles of copper than silver?
o: Copper plates less efficiently
Efficiency is a small, separate effect. The 2-to-1 electron count is the main reason.
Copper is heavier than silver
Copper is the lighter metal, and the question is about moles anyway.
Each copper ion requires two electrons
Correct: each Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons and each Ag⁺ needs 1, so copper gets half the moles.
Copper solutions are a good deal more dilute
Concentration wasn't varied in this experiment.
qs.x: Correct: The charge passed sets the moles of electrons, and that's the same in every beaker: 0.0373 mol (paragraph 5). Then the half-reaction decides how many electrons each atom needs. Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag takes 1 electron per atom, so 0.0373 mol of electrons makes 0.0373 mol of silver. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu takes 2 per atom, so the same electrons make only 0.0373 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.0187 mol of copper. Why the others are wrong: copper atoms are actually lighter than silver atoms, and the question is about moles, not mass; copper's efficiency (95.8%) is close to 100% and is a separate, small effect; concentration wasn't varied, and it doesn't set the moles deposited anyway. Trap: Explaining a counting (stoichiometry) result by mass or efficiency.

qs.q: Where does the missing charge go in the nickel experiment?
o: Into oxidizing the nickel
Oxidation happens at the anode, not where the nickel plates.
Into reducing water to hydrogen
Correct: about a quarter of the charge reduces water to hydrogen gas at the cathode.
Into depositing a nickel oxide
No oxide product is described.
Into heating the solution
Heating doesn't use up electrons in a redox reaction.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says water can also be reduced at the cathode, making hydrogen gas. Nickel's reduction competes with water's, so part of the charge goes to making hydrogen instead of nickel metal. The efficiency is 75.2% (Figure 1B), so about 100 − 75 = 25%, a quarter, of the charge went to hydrogen, which shows up as bubbles at the cathode (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: heating the solution doesn't use up electrons in a redox reaction; oxidizing nickel would happen at the anode, the other electrode, and doesn't explain charge missing at the cathode; no nickel oxide is mentioned. Trap: Blaming the missing charge on a process that doesn't use electrons at that electrode.

qs.q: What does one faraday of charge correspond to?
o: 1 mol of electrons
Correct: one faraday is 1 mol of electrons, about 96,500 C.
1 mol of ions in solution
The amount of ions in solution isn't related to the faraday.
One ampere for one second
One ampere for one second is one coulomb, not one faraday.
1 mol of deposited metal
Moles of metal depend on how many electrons each ion needs.
qs.x: Correct: One faraday is the charge carried by 1 mole of electrons, about 96,500 coulombs (paragraph 1). How much metal that makes depends on the half-reaction: 1 faraday makes 1 mol of silver (1 electron each) but only ½ mol of copper (2 electrons each). Why the others are wrong: moles of metal depend on how many electrons each ion needs, so 1 faraday isn't always 1 mol of metal; one ampere for one second is one coulomb, a tiny fraction of a faraday; the amount of ions in solution has nothing to do with the faraday. Trap: Treating a mole of electrons as a mole of product.

qs.q: How many moles of electrons were passed in each experiment?
o: That's the moles of copper, half the electrons since each Cu²⁺ takes 2.
That's the current in amps.
That's the charge in coulombs. Divide by 96,500 to get moles.
qs.x: Correct: First find the charge with Q = It, current times time. The values: I = 2.00 A and t = 30.0 min (paragraph 4). Change minutes to seconds: 1 min = 60 s, so multiply: 30.0 × 60 = 1,800 s. Plug in: Q = 2.00 A × 1,800 s = 3,600 C. Now moles of electrons = Q ÷ F, where F = 96,500 C per mole. So 3,600 ÷ 96,500 ≈ 0.0373 mol. Why the others are wrong: 0.0187 is the moles of copper deposited, half the electrons because each Cu²⁺ takes 2; 2.00 is the current in amps; 3,600 is the charge in coulombs, before dividing by 96,500. Trap: Stopping at the charge instead of converting it to moles of electrons.

qs.q: Why is the efficiency figure not an independent measurement?
o: Efficiency cannot exceed 100%
That's a separate point, not why it isn't independent.
Masses cannot be weighed very accurately here
The masses were weighed to 0.01 g.
It is computed against an assumed yield
Correct: the expected mass is calculated, assuming every electron made metal.
Current was not held constant
The current was held at 2.00 A.
qs.x: Correct: Efficiency = mass deposited ÷ mass expected. The mass deposited is weighed, but the mass expected is calculated from the charge, assuming every electron went into making metal (paragraph 7). So the percentage compares a measurement with a calculation based on an assumption. Nobody measured the hydrogen separately to confirm where the rest of the charge went. Why the others are wrong: the masses were weighed to 0.01 g, which is precise enough; the current was held at 2.00 A; whether efficiency can go above 100% is a different point. Trap: Treating a calculated percentage as if it were measured directly.

graph.title: Figure 1A. Mass of metal expected and mass actually deposited after 3,600 C
Figure 1B. Current efficiency (mass deposited ÷ mass expected)

passages.title: Self-Efficacy Versus Self-Esteem
text: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out a specific action in a specific situation. It is not global self-worth; a person can hold high self-efficacy for public speaking and low self-efficacy for swimming. The distinction matters because self-efficacy predicts behavior in the domain it refers to, while global self-esteem predicts it weakly.

Four sources are proposed, and they are not interchangeable. Mastery experience, the direct experience of succeeding at a graded version of the task, is held to be the strongest, because it supplies evidence that is hard to discount. Vicarious experience works through observing a model, and depends on the observer judging the model to be similar to themselves. Verbal persuasion works through what a credible other says. The fourth source is the interpretation of physiological arousal: a racing heart read as fear lowers efficacy, while the same arousal read as readiness does not.

80 adults enrolled in a beginners' swimming course were randomly assigned to one of four confidence-building sessions held before their first attempt in deep water. Self-efficacy was rated on a 10-point scale immediately after the session, and completion of the deep-water swim was recorded (Table 1).

Mastery comes first, as the theory's claim that it is the strongest source predicts, and the two columns move together, which is what the construct predicts: efficacy ratings should track behavior in the same domain.

Three limits deserve note. The relaxation condition manipulated the level of arousal rather than its interpretation, so it does not test the fourth source as the theory states it; a condition reframing arousal as readiness would. Self-efficacy was also rated after the session but before the swim, so the ratings may partly reflect how encouraging each session felt rather than a stable belief. Finally, randomization was to session type, not to the outcome measure, and the instructor who recorded completions knew which session each participant had received.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 fits the theory's ranking of the four sources?
o: Graded mastery produced the highest rating and the highest completion rate
Correct: mastery led on both the rating (7.9) and completion (78%).
Relaxation training outperformed every other approach tested
It ranked third.
The four approaches produced essentially identical results
Completion ranged from 44% to 78%, a 34-point spread.
Verbal encouragement outperformed watching a similar peer succeed at the task
It ranked last on both measures.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 ranks mastery experience, actually succeeding at an easier version of the task, as the strongest source of self-efficacy. Table 1 agrees on both measures. Graded mastery in shallow water gave the highest efficacy rating (7.9) and the highest completion rate (78%). Verbal encouragement came last on both (5.1 and 44%). Why the others are wrong: relaxation training ranked third, not first; verbal encouragement was below watching a peer on both columns; and the approaches clearly differed, with completion ranging from 44% to 78%, a gap of 78 − 44 = 34 points. Trap: Checking only one column before deciding the ranking fits.

qs.q: Why does the modeling condition use a peer judged to be similar?
o: Observing a similar peer eliminates physiological arousal
Arousal is a separate source.
Similarity makes the model's success feel relevant to the observer
Correct: a similar model's success feels like evidence about yourself.
Similar peers are generally able to give much more accurate instruction
Modeling is watching, not instruction.
Peers who are similar swim faster than expert models do
Speed isn't what matters.
qs.x: Correct: Vicarious experience works by inference: "If someone like me can do it, so can I" (paragraph 2). That inference only holds if the model is comparable to you. Watching an Olympic swimmer wouldn't tell a beginner much about their own chances. A similar peer's success becomes real evidence about what you can do. Why the others are wrong: modeling is watching, not being taught, so the quality of instruction isn't the point; arousal is a separate source of self-efficacy; and how fast the peer swims has nothing to do with the mechanism. Trap: Explaining a vicarious effect by how good the advice was.

qs.q: Why does the relaxation condition fail to test the fourth source as the theory states it?
o: Arousal cannot be manipulated in a swimming course
Relaxation did change arousal.
Physiological arousal is unrelated to self-efficacy
The theory ties them together.
Relaxation training requires more than one practice session to work
The number of sessions isn't the issue.
The theory concerns how arousal is interpreted, not its level
Correct: the theory is about how arousal is read, not how much there is.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the fourth source is how you interpret physiological arousal. A racing heart read as fear lowers efficacy, but the same racing heart read as readiness doesn't. Relaxation training lowers the amount of arousal instead of changing how it's read. So it tests a different claim (paragraph 5). A proper test would reframe arousal as readiness. Why the others are wrong: the number of sessions isn't what the theory is about; arousal can be changed in a swimming course, and relaxation did change it; and the theory explicitly ties arousal to self-efficacy as one of its four sources. Trap: Accepting a condition as a test just because it involves the same body signal.

qs.q: In Table 1, how do the mean self-efficacy ratings relate to the share completing the swim?
o: Higher ratings came with higher completion
Correct: ratings of 7.9, 6.4, 5.6 and 5.1 line up with completion of 78%, 61%, 50% and 44%.
Ratings rose as completion fell
Not quite. The approach with the top rating also had the top completion rate, 78%.
Ratings and completion were unrelated across approaches
Not quite. The ranking of the four approaches is the same on both measures.
Only the shallow-water approach differed on either measure
Not quite. The other three also differ, with ratings of 6.4, 5.6 and 5.1.
qs.x: Correct: Self-efficacy is the belief that you can do a specific task, and the theory says it should track behavior in that same domain (paragraph 1). In Table 1, the mean self-efficacy ratings are 7.9, 6.4, 5.6 and 5.1, and the shares completing the swim are 78%, 61%, 50% and 44%. Both lists run in the same order, from graded mastery down to verbal encouragement, so higher ratings come with higher completion. Why the others are wrong: ratings did not rise as completion fell, since the top rating sits with the top completion; the two measures rank the approaches identically, so they are not unrelated; and all four approaches differ on both measures, not just the shallow-water one. Trap: Looking at the biggest number in one column and ignoring whether the other column moves with it.

qs.q: Which feature of this trial most limits the conclusion drawn from the completion column?
o: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four session types
Random assignment is a strength.
20 adults were assigned to each of the four conditions
Equal groups help.
The instructor recording completions knew the assigned condition
Correct: an instructor who knew the condition recorded the outcome.
Self-efficacy was rated on a 10-point scale
The rating scale is adequate.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 5 says the instructor who recorded completions knew which session each person had attended. Whether a shaky deep-water swim counts as "completed" takes some judgment. An instructor who expects the mastery group to do well might encourage them more or judge them more generously. That alone could create group differences in the completion column, even if beliefs didn't change. This is unblinded outcome assessment. Why the others are wrong: random assignment is a strength; a 10-point rating scale is fine for self-efficacy; and 20 people in each condition is balanced, which helps. Trap: Naming a feature that protects the study instead of the one that leaves it open to bias.

passages.title: Erikson's Adolescent Identity Crisis
text: Erikson described development as a sequence of eight psychosocial stages, each posing a conflict whose resolution shapes what follows. The adolescent stage is identity versus role confusion, and it is followed in young adulthood by intimacy versus isolation, then generativity versus stagnation in midlife and integrity versus despair in late life. The sequencing claim is substantive: a person who has not formed a workable sense of who they are is held to be at a disadvantage in forming close relationships, because intimacy requires something to share.

Marcia operationalized the adolescent stage with two dimensions, exploration of alternatives and commitment to a choice, which cross to give four statuses. Achievement combines exploration with commitment. Moratorium is active exploration without commitment. Foreclosure is commitment without exploration, typically to a path adopted from family. Diffusion is neither.

Clinicians conducted semistructured interviews with 60 young adults aged 20 to 24 about career plans and values, and two raters classified each participant by status with disagreements resolved by discussion (Figure 1 shows how the statuses are defined and Table 1 how common each was).
The distribution is unremarkable for this age range, with moratorium and achievement most common, which is what a model placing identity work in the late teens and early twenties would expect.

What the design cannot do is test Erikson's sequencing claim, and that is its central limit. Status was measured once, in one age band, with no measure of the subsequent stage, so there is no way to ask whether identity achievement predicts later intimacy. Adding a measure of intimacy and following the same people forward would test it directly. Classification by interview also depends on the raters, and although two raters were used with disagreements resolved, agreement before discussion was not reported, so the reliability of the classification is unknown. The sample is small for estimating four proportions, and nothing here establishes that the four statuses are stable categories rather than positions a person moves through.

qs.q: Which status describes commitment without exploration?
o: Achievement
That has both exploration and commitment.
Moratorium
That's exploration without commitment.
Foreclosure
Correct: committed without exploring, often to a path taken from family.
Diffusion
That has neither.
qs.x: Correct: Marcia's model crosses two questions (paragraph 2): has the person explored alternatives, and have they committed to a choice? Foreclosure is commitment without exploration, often taking on a path straight from family without examining other options. In Table 1, it's the only status with "No" for exploration and "Yes" for commitment. Why the others are wrong: moratorium is the reverse, exploring without committing; achievement has both exploration and commitment; diffusion has neither. Trap: Picking a status by how settled the person sounds instead of checking both dimensions.

qs.q: Which Eriksonian conflict follows identity versus role confusion?
o: Intimacy versus isolation
Correct: it's the young-adult stage right after identity.
Generativity versus stagnation
That's the midlife stage.
Industry versus inferiority
That comes earlier, in childhood.
Ego integrity versus despair
That's the final stage.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 lays out Erikson's later stages in order. Identity versus role confusion comes in adolescence, then intimacy versus isolation in young adulthood, then generativity versus stagnation in midlife, and finally integrity versus despair in late life. So the next one is intimacy versus isolation. Erikson's idea is that you need a sense of who you are before you can share yourself in a close relationship. Why the others are wrong: industry versus inferiority comes before identity, in childhood; generativity versus stagnation is the midlife stage; ego integrity versus despair is the last stage. Trap: Choosing a later stage just because it sounds more grown-up.

qs.q: Why can this study not test the sequencing claim?
o: Only four identity statuses were used
Four is the standard scheme.
The interviews followed a semistructured format
That's a reasonable method.
Participants were aged 20 to 24
That's the right age range.
No measure of the following stage was taken
Correct: intimacy, the next stage, was never measured.
qs.x: Correct: Erikson's sequencing claim is that how you resolve identity affects the next stage, intimacy (paragraph 1). To test that, you'd need to measure intimacy in the same people, ideally following them forward. This study measured identity status once, in one age group, and never measured intimacy at all (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: four statuses is the standard Marcia scheme; semistructured interviews are a reasonable way to classify status; and ages 20 to 24 is exactly when identity work is expected. Trap: Naming a weakness in the method when the real gap is a variable that was never measured.

qs.q: Which status is the most common in this sample?
o: 17%, diffusion
17% is the smallest share.
24%, foreclosure
24% is third.
28%, achievement
28% is second.
31%, moratorium
Correct: 31%, the largest share.
qs.x: Correct: Read the "Share of sample" column of Table 1 and find the largest number. Moratorium is 31%, achievement 28%, foreclosure 24%, and diffusion 17%. The biggest is moratorium at 31%. That fits paragraph 4: in the early twenties, many people are still actively exploring without having settled. Why the others are wrong: diffusion is the smallest at 17%; foreclosure is third at 24%; achievement is second at 28%, just behind moratorium. Trap: Choosing achievement because it's the status the model treats as the goal.

qs.q: What would most improve confidence in the classifications themselves?
o: Increasing the sample from 60 to 200
That sharpens the proportions, not the coding.
Resolving every disagreement by discussion
That's what was already done.
Reporting rater agreement before discussion
Correct: agreement before discussion measures how reliable the coding is.
Using three clinicians, not two
More raters without an agreement figure leaves the same gap.
qs.x: Correct: Reliability means how consistently a measure gives the same result. Paragraph 5 says the two raters resolved disagreements by discussion, but their agreement before discussing was never reported. Agreement reached by talking it over doesn't tell you whether two people would independently classify the same person the same way. Reporting how often they agreed before conferring is the number that shows how reliable the classification is. Why the others are wrong: resolving disagreements by discussion is what was already done; going from 60 to 200 people makes the proportions more precise but doesn't check the coding; and a third rater without an agreement figure leaves the same gap. Trap: Adding more effort to a procedure instead of reporting the statistic that checks it.

graph.title: Figure 1. How exploration and commitment combine into the four identity statuses

passages.title: Exponential Decay and Half-Life
text: Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of a single nucleus but highly regular in bulk. The number of decays per second is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, so the quantity falls exponentially and is characterized by a half-life: the interval over which half the nuclei remaining at any moment decay.

Positron emission tomography depends on this. A positron-emitting nucleus is incorporated into a molecule the body takes up, and the positron annihilates with a nearby electron to produce two photons traveling in opposite directions. Detecting both lets the scanner place the annihilation on a line, and many such lines reconstruct an image.

The half-life sets the logistics of the scan. Too short and the tracer decays before it can be delivered and taken up; too long and the patient carries an unnecessary dose after the images are acquired. The commonly used positron emitters span nearly two orders of magnitude in half-life for this reason.

Researchers followed four positron emitters from the moment of production and calculated the fraction of each that remained at 20 and 110 minutes (Figure 1). The nuclides are used for blood flow (oxygen-15), receptor imaging (carbon-11), glucose metabolism (fluorine-18) and cardiac perfusion (rubidium-82).

Fluorine-18 retains 88% of its activity after 20 minutes while oxygen-15 retains about one tenth of 1%, which is why fluorine-18 tracers can be produced centrally and shipped while oxygen-15 must be made beside the scanner.
The two shortest-lived nuclides are not plotted at 110 minutes because the remaining fraction is far below anything detectable, not because the decay law has ceased to apply.

Two points qualify the comparison. The physical half-life is not the whole story, because the tracer is also cleared from the tissue biologically, and the effective half-life is shorter than the physical one. And the choice of nuclide is constrained by chemistry as well: a nuclide is only useful if it can be attached to a molecule the body handles in the way the study requires.

qs.q: Why must oxygen-15 be produced beside the scanner?
o: Regulations forbid shipping
The half-life, not a rule, is what limits it.
It cannot be attached to molecules
It's routinely attached to molecules, such as labeled water.
Its photons are too weak to detect
Every annihilation gives the same photons, whatever the nuclide.
Almost none of it survives transport
Correct: with a 2.04-minute half-life, only 0.00112 is left after 20 minutes.
qs.x: Correct: Oxygen-15's half-life is only 2.04 minutes (Figure 1 legend). In 20 minutes that's 20 ÷ 2.04 ≈ 9.8 half-lives, and halving about 10 times leaves roughly 1 ÷ 1,000 of the start. Figure 1 shows 0.00112 left, about one tenth of 1% (paragraph 5). Any trip from a central factory would leave almost nothing, so it has to be made right beside the scanner. Why the others are wrong: oxygen-15 is attached to molecules all the time, for example in labeled water used for blood flow; every positron annihilation gives the same photons, so oxygen-15's aren't weaker; the limit comes from the physics of the half-life, not from shipping rules. Trap: Looking for a chemical or legal reason when the half-life explains it.

qs.q: Why does detecting both photons locate the annihilation?
o: One photon arrives much later
They arrive at nearly the same moment.
Their energies differ with the position
Both photons have the same energy.
They travel in opposite directions
Correct: the photons fly back to back, so the pair defines a line through the event.
Each photon carries position data
A photon carries no record of where it came from.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 explains it. When a positron meets an electron, they annihilate and make two photons that fly off in exactly opposite directions. If detectors on opposite sides of the scanner catch both at nearly the same moment, the annihilation must have happened somewhere on the straight line joining those two detectors. Many such lines from many events cross each other and build up the image. Why the others are wrong: a single photon carries no record of where it came from; both photons have the same energy, so energy doesn't mark position; they arrive at nearly the same time, not one much later. Trap: Thinking the location is stored in one photon instead of in the geometry of the pair.

qs.q: Why is the effective half-life shorter than the physical one?
o: The dose is reduced before injection
Dose size doesn't change any half-life.
The body also clears the tracer
Correct: decay and the body's clearance both remove tracer, so activity falls faster.
The scanner degrades the tracer itself
The scanner only detects photons. It doesn't use up the tracer.
Decay accelerates inside the tissue
Decay isn't changed by the chemical surroundings.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 gives the reason. Two things remove tracer from the tissue at once: the nuclei decay (the physical half-life), and the body clears the molecule by breaking it down or excreting it (biological clearance). With two ways of losing activity working together, the activity drops faster than decay alone would make it. That faster combined rate is the effective half-life, so it's shorter than the physical one. Why the others are wrong: radioactive decay isn't changed by the chemical surroundings; the scanner only detects photons, it doesn't use up the tracer; the size of the dose doesn't change any half-life. Trap: Assuming the physical half-life alone sets how long the tracer stays.

qs.q: By what factor does fluorine-18 exceed carbon-11 in fraction remaining at 110 minutes?
o: That's carbon-11's fraction, not the ratio.
That's the ratio of half-lives, 110 ÷ 20.4, not of fractions remaining.
That's fluorine-18's half-life in minutes.
qs.x: Correct: "By what factor" means divide. From the 110 min points in Figure 1: fluorine-18 = 0.500 and carbon-11 = 0.0237. Divide: 0.500 ÷ 0.0237 ≈ 21.1. So fluorine-18 keeps about 21 times as much. You can check carbon-11's number: 110 ÷ 20.4 ≈ 5.39 half-lives, and halving 5.39 times leaves about 0.024. Why the others are wrong: 0.0237 is carbon-11's fraction itself, not a ratio; 5.39 is the ratio of the half-lives (110 ÷ 20.4), which isn't the same as the ratio of what's left; 110 is fluorine-18's half-life in minutes. Trap: Dividing the half-lives instead of the fractions remaining.

qs.q: Why are the shortest-lived nuclides left blank at 110 minutes?
o: Decay stops after many half-lives
Not quite. Decay never stops. It just leaves too little to measure.
Those short-lived nuclides were simply never measured
Not quite. They were measured. Both have values at 20 minutes.
The graph has no room for them
Not quite. Graph space isn't the reason. The amount is undetectable.
The remaining fraction is undetectable
Correct: after about 54 or more half-lives, what's left is far below detection.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 says the blanks are there because the remaining fraction is far too small to detect, not because decay stops. For oxygen-15, 110 minutes is 110 ÷ 2.04 ≈ 54 half-lives, and halving 54 times leaves an unimaginably tiny amount. Rubidium-82 is even worse: 110 ÷ 1.25 = 88 half-lives. The exponential decay law still applies the whole time. Why the others are wrong: decay keeps going, it never just stops; these nuclides were measured, they have values at 20 minutes; the missing points aren't about graph space. Trap: Reading a blank as a sign that the decay law broke down.

graph.title: Figure 1. Fraction of activity remaining after production (log scale: exponential decay plots as a straight line)

passages.title: Hydrogen Emission Lines and the Bohr Model
text: The light emitted by a heated gas is not continuous but confined to particular wavelengths, and each element has its own pattern. This was known long before any explanation existed, and it was the hydrogen pattern, with its simple arithmetic regularity, that the first successful atomic model was built to reproduce.

That model assigns the electron to orbits of fixed energy, with the energy of the level inversely proportional to the square of an integer. Light is emitted when the electron moves from a higher level to a lower one, and the photon carries exactly the energy difference, so the wavelengths are determined by differences between two of these levels.

The arrangement explains why the lines crowd together toward short wavelengths: the levels themselves converge as the integer rises, so transitions from high levels differ little in energy. It also explains why the spectrum of each element differs, since the level pattern depends on the nuclear charge and on the other electrons present.
Hydrogen emission lines ending on the second level were measured and compared with the model (Table 1).

The agreement is within 0.1 nanometer in every row, which is why the model was accepted despite its arbitrary postulates. The spacing between successive lines shrinks from 170 nanometers between the first two to 24 nanometers between the last two, converging on the series limit.
The series limit corresponds to a transition from an unbound electron to the second level, and no line appears beyond it, only a continuum, because the initial energy is then no longer quantized.

Two limitations matter. The model reproduces hydrogen but fails for atoms with more than one electron, where the repulsion between electrons is not accounted for, and it offers no reason why the orbits should be stable at all. And it predicts single lines where careful measurement finds closely spaced components, which required a later treatment to explain.

qs.q: Why do the emission lines crowd together at short wavelengths?
o: The electron moves faster up there
The electron's speed doesn't set the line spacing.
Short wavelengths resist resolving
The crowding is in the light, not an instrument limit.
More transitions exist up there
It's the converging levels, not the number of transitions.
The energy levels converge further up
Correct: energy goes as 1 ÷ n², so high levels bunch together and their lines nearly overlap.
qs.x: Correct: In this model, a level's energy goes as 1 ÷ n², where n is the level number (paragraph 2). As n grows, 1 ÷ n² shrinks more and more slowly: 1/9, 1/16, 1/25, 1/36. So the high levels bunch up close together. Jumps down to level 2 from neighboring high levels then differ very little in energy, which means their wavelengths are almost the same. Table 1 shows it: the gap between the first two lines is 656.3 − 486.1 ≈ 170 nm, but between the last two it's 434.0 − 410.2 ≈ 24 nm. Why the others are wrong: the bunching is in the light itself, not a limit of the instrument; the electron's speed doesn't set the line spacing; it's the energy levels getting closer, not the number of transitions, that squeezes the lines. Trap: Blaming the instrument for a pattern the energy levels require.

qs.q: Why does a continuum appear beyond the series limit?
o: The gas becomes opaque at that point
Opacity isn't involved.
The initial energy is unquantized
Correct: a free electron can have any energy, so the emitted photons form a continuous range.
Levels above the limit are too close
There are no bound levels above the limit.
The detector response broadens there
The light itself is continuous. The detector isn't the cause.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 6 explains it. Each line comes from a jump between two levels, and bound levels have fixed energies, so the photons come out at fixed wavelengths. At the series limit the electron starts out free, not bound to the atom. A free electron can have any energy at all. So the photons it gives off when captured into level 2 can have any energy above 3.40 eV, which shows up as a smooth spread (continuum) instead of separate lines. Why the others are wrong: the gas becoming opaque has nothing to do with it; there are no bound levels beyond the limit to crowd together; the detector isn't causing it, the light itself is continuous. Trap: Explaining a smooth spectrum as crowded lines, when it comes from a starting energy that isn't fixed.

qs.q: Why does each element give a different line pattern?
o: Its level energies are different ones
Correct: nuclear charge and the other electrons set each element's energy levels.
Different elements emit different photons
That just restates the observation.
Each element emits at its own temperature
Temperature changes brightness, not where lines fall.
Heavier atoms move more slowly in a gas
Motion only broadens lines slightly. It doesn't set their positions.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says the energy levels depend on the nuclear charge and on the other electrons present. Each element has a different number of protons and a different set of electrons, so its levels sit at different energies. The photons carry the energy differences between levels, so a different set of levels gives a different set of wavelengths, like a fingerprint. Why the others are wrong: temperature changes how bright the lines are, not where they fall; atoms moving in the gas only blur (broaden) lines slightly, they don't place them; saying different elements give different photons just repeats the question. Trap: Accepting a restatement of what's observed as the explanation.

qs.q: How much does the line spacing shrink across the series?
o: Those are transition energies in eV.
170 to 24 nm
Those are the predicted and observed series limit.
Those are line positions, not the gaps between them.
qs.x: Correct: Line spacing is the gap between neighboring wavelengths, so subtract. From Table 1's observed wavelengths, first gap: 656.3 − 486.1 = 170.2 nm, about 170 nm. Last gap between tabulated lines: 434.0 − 410.2 = 23.8 nm, about 24 nm. So the spacing shrinks from about 170 nm to about 24 nm, roughly 7 times smaller (170 ÷ 24 ≈ 7.1). Why the others are wrong: 656 to 410 nm are the positions of the lines, not the gaps between them; 1.89 to 3.02 are transition energies in eV; 364.6 and 364.7 nm are the predicted and observed series limit. Trap: Quoting where the lines are instead of the gaps between them.

qs.q: Why was the model nevertheless replaced?
o: It required far too much computation
The model's math is simple. Computation wasn't the issue.
Its hydrogen predictions were inaccurate
Its hydrogen predictions match to four figures.
It fails for multi-electron atoms
Correct: it can't handle repulsion between electrons in multi-electron atoms.
Spectral lines were later found continuous
Spectral lines are still discrete.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 lists the problems. The model works for hydrogen, which has one electron, but it fails for any atom with more than one electron because it ignores how electrons repel each other. It also gives no reason why the orbits should be stable, and it predicts single lines where careful measurement finds closely spaced pairs. Why the others are wrong: its hydrogen predictions match the measurements to four figures (Table 1), so they weren't inaccurate; spectral lines are still discrete, separate lines; the math is simple, so computation wasn't the problem. Trap: Assuming a replaced model must have been wrong for the case it was built for.

passages.title: Carbon-14 Dating
text: Carbon-14 is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic ray neutrons strike nitrogen. It mixes into atmospheric carbon dioxide and enters the food chain, so a living organism holds carbon with the same carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio as its environment. At death the intake stops and the carbon-14 begins to decline with a 5,730-year half-life.

A date therefore follows from measuring the surviving ratio and comparing it with the living value. Because the decline is exponential, the measurable range is set by how small a ratio can be distinguished from background, which in practice limits the method to roughly 50,000 years, or about nine half-lives.

The method rests on an assumption that the atmospheric production rate has been steady. It has not been exactly steady, and the record is corrected using tree rings and other independently dated material, which is why a raw radiocarbon age and a calibrated calendar age are reported separately.

Researchers dated four archaeological samples. For each one they measured the carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio and compared it with a modern standard, living material whose ratio is set at 1.00, so the age of the sample was the variable being compared and the fraction of the modern ratio was what they measured. Figure 1 plots the fraction remaining against each sample's raw age, and Table 1 gives the half-lives elapsed and the calibrated ranges.

The fraction remaining falls smoothly with age, and each sample's raw age follows from the number of half-lives its fraction represents. The calibrated ranges diverge increasingly from the raw ages for older samples, by about 2,500 years at the wooden post and 4,500 at the bone.
The divergence is systematic rather than random, since it reflects the known history of atmospheric carbon-14 rather than any error in the individual measurement.

Two cautions attach to the method. Contamination with modern carbon raises the apparent ratio and makes a sample look younger, and because the effect is proportionate it matters far more for old samples: 1% modern carbon has almost no effect on the linen but shifts the bone by thousands of years. And the date obtained is the date the organism stopped exchanging carbon, which for a wooden post is when the tree grew rather than when the post was set.

qs.q: Why does the method stop working past about 50,000 years?
o: Older samples contain no carbon at all
Old samples still contain plenty of ordinary carbon.
The half-life itself changes
Half-lives are constant.
Carbon-14 decays completely by then
Exponential decay never reaches zero. It keeps halving.
Too little carbon-14 remains to measure
Correct: after about 9 half-lives only about 0.2% is left, too close to background to measure.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the limit is set by how small a ratio can be told apart from background, the small signal detectors pick up even with no sample. 50,000 years is about 9 half-lives (50,000 ÷ 5,730 ≈ 8.7). Halving 9 times leaves (½)⁹ = 1/512 ≈ 0.002 of the original, about two tenths of a percent. That tiny signal is hard to tell from background, and every extra half-life halves it again. Why the others are wrong: exponential decay never reaches exactly zero, it just keeps halving; the half-life is constant; old samples still contain plenty of ordinary carbon-12. Trap: Treating a detection limit as if the isotope had completely vanished.

qs.q: In Figure 1, the bone fragment retains far less carbon-14 than the linen. Why does contamination matter more for old samples?
o: The surviving signal is far smaller yet
Correct: the old sample's signal is so small that a little modern carbon makes a big relative change.
Old samples absorb carbon more readily
Uptake isn't the mechanism. The small remaining signal is.
Contamination is heavier when old
The amount isn't larger. Its relative effect is.
The half-life is less reliable at age
The half-life doesn't change with age.
qs.x: Correct: Contamination adds a fixed amount of modern carbon-14, and what matters is how that compares with what's left in the sample (paragraph 7). The linen keeps 0.805 of the modern ratio, so adding about 0.01 barely changes it (0.805 to about 0.807), a shift of only a couple of decades. The bone keeps only 0.0154, so adding 0.01 raises it to about 0.025, roughly two thirds more. That's about 0.7 of a half-life, or roughly 4,000 years younger. Why the others are wrong: old samples don't soak up carbon more easily, that isn't the mechanism; the amount of contamination isn't larger in older samples; the half-life doesn't change with age. Trap: Thinking a fixed amount of contamination shifts every date by the same amount.

qs.q: Why are raw and calibrated ages reported separately?
o: The two describe different samples
Both ages refer to the same sample.
Raw ages are measured less precisely
Precision is similar. The difference is the atmospheric correction.
Calibration uses another half-life
Calibration uses the same 5,730-year half-life.
Production has not been truly constant
Correct: atmospheric carbon-14 production hasn't been perfectly steady, so raw ages are corrected.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says the raw age assumes carbon-14 has always been made in the atmosphere at a steady rate. It hasn't been exactly steady. So scientists compare against tree rings and other material dated a different way, and use that history to correct the raw age into a calendar age. Reporting both keeps the measurement and the correction clear. Why the others are wrong: both have similar precision, that isn't the difference; calibration uses the same 5,730-year half-life; both ages describe the same sample. Trap: Reading calibration as a fix for measurement error, when it corrects for the changing atmosphere.

qs.q: How many half-lives has the bone fragment undergone?
o: That's the fraction remaining, not the number of half-lives.
That's the wooden post's value.
Correct: (½)⁶ = 1/64 ≈ 0.0156, so 0.0154 is just over 6 half-lives.
That's the raw age in years: 6.02 × 5,730.
qs.x: Correct: After n half-lives, the fraction left is (½)ⁿ. The bone's fraction is 0.0154 (Figure 1). Try whole numbers: (½)⁶ = 1 ÷ 2⁶ = 1 ÷ 64 ≈ 0.0156. That's just a bit more than 0.0154, so n is just over 6: the table gives 6.02. Then the raw age is 6.02 × 5,730 years ≈ 34,500 years, matching the table. Why the others are wrong: 0.0154 is the fraction left, not the number of half-lives; 2.24 is the wooden post's value; 34,500 is the raw age in years, which is half-lives times 5,730. Trap: Mixing up the number of half-lives with the years they add up to.

qs.q: Why is the post's date not the date the structure was built?
o: Calibration shifts the date forward
Calibration corrects the atmospheric record, not the building date.
It dates when the tree was growing
Correct: it dates when that wood grew and stopped exchanging carbon.
Wood cannot be dated by this method
Wood is a standard sample for this method.
The post was contaminated after burial
Contamination is a separate issue.
qs.x: Correct: Carbon dating gives the date the organism stopped taking in carbon (paragraph 7). For wood, each ring stops exchanging carbon once it's laid down while the tree grows. So the date tells you when that wood grew, which could be decades or centuries before someone cut the tree and set the post. Why the others are wrong: wood is one of the most common materials dated this way; contamination is a separate problem that would make it look younger, not explain this gap; calibration corrects for the atmosphere's history, not for when the timber was used. Trap: Taking the age of a material as the date of the event it was used in.

graph.title: Figure 1. Carbon-14 remaining (log scale) versus raw radiocarbon age; the line is the ideal decay with a 5,730-year half-life

passages.title: Enantiomers and Chirality Centers
text: A molecule is chiral if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, and the commonest cause is a carbon bearing four different groups. The two mirror-image forms, enantiomers, have identical melting points, boiling points, densities and solubilities in ordinary solvents, because every interaction they make with an achiral environment is identical.

They are distinguished only by something that is itself chiral. Plane-polarized light is rotated in opposite directions by the two forms, and a chiral reagent, a chiral solvent or a chiral surface interacts with them differently, which is what makes separation possible at all.

This is why biology discriminates between them. An enzyme's active site is chiral, so two enantiomers of a substrate bind with different affinities and react at different rates, and a drug's two enantiomers can differ in potency, in metabolism and in toxicity.
A racemic drug was analyzed by several methods (Table 1).

The two achiral methods give a single peak or fraction, as the identical physical properties require, while both chiral methods separate the enantiomers cleanly. The chiral acid works by converting the pair into two salts that are not mirror images of one another and therefore differ in solubility.

The salts formed in that last method are diastereomers rather than enantiomers, and diastereomers differ in physical properties such as solubility, which is what makes the separation possible with ordinary crystallization.

Two qualifications apply. Chiral chromatography separates but does not by itself say which peak is which, so an independent assignment is needed, usually by comparison with a sample of known configuration. And the biological difference between enantiomers is not always large: some drugs are given as the racemate because the two forms are comparable in effect, and separating them would add manufacturing cost without any clinical benefit, so the decision is made case by case rather than as a rule.

qs.q: Why does ordinary chromatography give one peak?
o: Silica binds all organic compounds with equal strength
Not quite. Silica sorts by polarity, and both enantiomers have the same polarity.
The surface is achiral
Correct: Silica is achiral, so it holds both enantiomers exactly the same.
The enantiomers co-elute by chance
Not quite. It's not chance. Mirror symmetry guarantees identical behavior.
They have the same molecular mass
Not quite. Same mass doesn't stop separation of other compounds.
qs.x: Correct: Enantiomers are mirror-image forms of a molecule. Paragraph 1 says every interaction they have with an achiral (non-handed) environment is identical. Silica, the surface in ordinary chromatography, is achiral (Table 1). So it grabs both enantiomers exactly the same, they travel at the same speed, and they come out together as one peak. It's like a plain round peg: your left and right hands grip it the same way. Why the others are wrong: they don't come out together by luck, it's guaranteed by their mirror symmetry; having the same mass doesn't stop separation, plenty of same-mass compounds separate on silica; silica doesn't hold all compounds equally, it sorts them by polarity, but both enantiomers have identical polarity. Trap: Thinking a single peak is a coincidence when it's forced by symmetry.

qs.q: Why does a chiral acid allow crystallization to work?
o: It forms diastereomeric salts
Correct: It forms diastereomeric salts, which differ in solubility.
It destroys one enantiomer
Not quite. Both enantiomers are recovered.
It raises the melting points of both salts by the same amount
Not quite. An equal change in both would separate nothing.
It changes the configuration
Not quite. The drug's configuration stays the same.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraphs 5 and 6 explain it. Mix the racemic drug (a 50:50 mix of both enantiomers) with one pure enantiomer of an acid, and you get two salts. Those salts are not mirror images of each other, so they're diastereomers. Diastereomers are just different compounds, with different physical properties, including solubility. So one salt crystallizes out before the other, and you can separate them by ordinary crystallization. Why the others are wrong: the acid doesn't destroy either enantiomer, both are recovered as separate solids; the configuration of the drug doesn't change; if both salts' melting points changed by the same amount, they'd still be alike and nothing would separate. Trap: Thinking the chiral reagent changes the molecules, when it just pairs them into salts that are different from each other.

qs.q: Why can two enantiomers differ in toxicity?
o: Enantiomers are metabolized by completely different organs
Not quite. The same organs handle both. The difference is in protein binding.
Their protein targets are chiral
Correct: The proteins they bind are chiral, so each form binds differently.
One is more reactive chemically
Not quite. They react the same way in achiral surroundings.
They differ in solubility
Not quite. Enantiomers have identical solubility in ordinary solvents.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says an enzyme's active site is chiral, because proteins are built from chiral amino acids. Receptors are the same. A chiral binding site fits one enantiomer better than the other, like a right-handed glove fits your right hand. So the two forms bind differently, react at different rates and can differ in potency, metabolism and toxicity. Why the others are wrong: enantiomers have identical solubility in ordinary solvents (paragraph 1); they react the same with achiral chemicals, so neither is simply more reactive; they're handled by the same organs, the difference is how the chiral proteins there bind each form. Trap: Hunting for a physical difference between enantiomers when the difference comes from the chiral body.

qs.q: How many of the four methods separate the enantiomers?
o: Not quite. That leaves out one of the two chiral methods.
Correct: Only the two chiral methods separate them.
Not quite. Ordinary chromatography on silica gives one peak.
Not quite. The two achiral methods don't separate them.
qs.x: Correct: Read Table 1's 'Separates enantiomers' column. Ordinary distillation: no. Ordinary chromatography: no. Chiral chromatography: yes. Crystallization with a chiral acid: yes. That's 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 2. Both successful methods use something chiral, which fits paragraph 2: only something chiral can tell enantiomers apart. Why the others are wrong: 1 misses one of the two chiral methods; 3 would add ordinary chromatography on silica, which gives a single peak; 4 counts both achiral methods too. Trap: Assuming any chromatography separates enantiomers, when only the chiral kind does.

qs.q: Why is an independent assignment needed after chiral chromatography?
o: The method destroys the sample
Not quite. The sample isn't destroyed.
Chiral columns give the two peaks in a random order each time
Not quite. The order is reproducible. It just isn't labeled.
The peaks are not resolved
Not quite. The peaks are cleanly separated.
Retention order does not reveal configuration
Correct: The order they come out doesn't tell you their configuration.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says chiral chromatography separates the two enantiomers into two clean peaks, but it doesn't tell you which peak is which. The order they come out doesn't reveal their 3D arrangement (configuration). To label the peaks, you run a sample whose configuration is already known and see which peak it matches. Why the others are wrong: the peaks are cleanly resolved (Table 1: two peaks); the method doesn't destroy the sample; the order is the same each time on a given column, it just doesn't say which form is which. Trap: Assuming that separating two things also tells you which one is which.

passages.title: Resonance Structures and Electron Delocalization
text: When more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn for the same arrangement of atoms, the molecule is not any one of them and does not alternate between them. The real structure is a single one in which the electrons are spread over the atoms involved, and the drawn structures are a device for describing that distribution with lines and dots.

Delocalization lowers the energy, and the stabilization is largest when the contributing structures are equivalent. The carbonate ion, with three equivalent structures, has three identical carbon-oxygen bonds of a length between that of a double and a single bond, and no evidence of one being different from the others.

The consequences are measurable. Benzene's six carbon-carbon bonds are all the same length, intermediate between those of ethane and ethene, and its heat of hydrogenation is far less exothermic than three isolated double bonds would predict, the shortfall being the delocalization energy.

Researchers measured bond lengths and hydrogenation enthalpies for four species and compared each measured value with a prediction built from ordinary localized bonds. Ethene and cyclohexene, which have ordinary localized double bonds, served as the control species for judging benzene and the carbonate ion (Table 1).

Benzene's hydrogenation releases 208 kilojoules per mole against the 360 predicted from three cyclohexene double bonds, a shortfall of 152 kilojoules that measures its delocalization energy. Its bonds are all 139 picometers, between the 133 of a double bond and the 154 of a single one.
The carbonate ion's three bonds are likewise identical, at 129 picometers, which is shorter than a carbon-oxygen single bond and longer than a double one.

Two qualifications apply. The equivalence of the drawn structures is a sufficient condition for strong delocalization but not a necessary one, and a molecule whose contributing structures differ in energy is still stabilized, only less so. And bond lengths intermediate between single and double are evidence of delocalization but are not proof of it on their own, since other effects such as hybridization also shift bond lengths.

qs.q: Why does benzene release less energy on hydrogenation than predicted?
o: The products are less stable
Not quite. The product is ordinary cyclohexane.
Hydrogenation is incomplete
Not quite. The hydrogenation goes to completion.
Delocalization stabilized the starting material
Correct: Delocalization makes benzene start lower in energy, so less is released.
Benzene has fewer than three double bonds to hydrogenate
Not quite. It takes up three H₂, one per drawn double bond.
qs.x: Correct: Hydrogenation adds H₂ across the double bonds to make cyclohexane. One cyclohexene double bond releases 120 kJ/mol (Table 1), so three would predict 3 × 120 = 360 kJ/mol. Benzene actually releases only 208 kJ/mol (paragraph 5). Both routes end at the same product, so the gap has to be at the start: benzene begins lower in energy because its electrons are spread around the ring (delocalized), which stabilizes it. Starting lower means less energy to release on the way down. Why the others are wrong: the product is ordinary cyclohexane, nothing unusual about it; the reaction goes all the way; benzene does take up three H₂, one per double bond drawn. Trap: Looking for something odd in the product when the special one is the starting material.

qs.q: Why are all three carbonate bonds identical?
o: The structures alternate rapidly
Not quite. The ion doesn't flip between structures. It's one blended structure.
The ion rotates fast enough to average the bonds out
Not quite. Rotation doesn't change bond lengths.
Each oxygen carries one charge
Not quite. The spread-out charge results from delocalization. It isn't the cause.
The electrons are delocalized
Correct: The electrons are spread over all three bonds, so they're identical.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says resonance structures are just drawings; the real molecule is one structure with the electrons spread out. In carbonate, CO₃²⁻, you can draw the double bond to any of the three oxygens, and all three drawings are equal (paragraph 2). The real ion has the extra electrons shared over all three C–O bonds, so each bond is the same: 129 pm, between a single and a double bond (paragraph 6). Why the others are wrong: the ion doesn't flip quickly between the drawings, it's always the one blended structure; the charge being spread over the oxygens is a result of the delocalization, not its cause; spinning a molecule doesn't change its bond lengths. Trap: Picturing resonance as the molecule rapidly switching between the drawn forms.

qs.q: Why is equivalence not a necessary condition?
o: Equivalence is always present
Not quite. Many molecules lack equivalent structures.
Unequal structures still delocalize
Correct: Unequal structures still delocalize electrons, just with less stabilization.
Delocalization occurs only in rings of alternating single and double bonds
Not quite. Delocalization happens in many systems, like carbonate.
Unequal structures are invalid
Not quite. Unequal structures are still valid contributors.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says equal resonance structures are enough for strong delocalization, but they're not required. If a molecule's drawn structures differ in energy, the electrons still spread out and the molecule is still stabilized, just less so. Equal structures give the biggest effect, not the only effect. Why the others are wrong: many molecules don't have equal structures, so equivalence isn't always present; unequal structures are still valid drawings that contribute; delocalization happens in many systems, not only rings like benzene, for example carbonate. Trap: Turning the condition for the biggest effect into a requirement for any effect.

qs.q: What is benzene's delocalization energy from these data?
o: 120 kJ/mol
Not quite. 120 is one cyclohexene double bond.
152 kJ/mol
Correct: 360 − 208 = 152 kJ/mol.
208 kJ/mol
Not quite. 208 is benzene's measured value, not the gap.
360 kJ/mol
Not quite. 360 is the predicted value, not the gap.
qs.x: Correct: Delocalization energy = predicted energy released − measured energy released. Predicted: three cyclohexene double bonds, each releasing 120 kJ/mol (Table 1), so 3 × 120 = 360 kJ/mol. Measured for benzene: 208 kJ/mol. Plug in: 360 − 208 = 152 kJ/mol. That's how much more stable benzene is than three separate double bonds would make it (paragraph 5). Why the others are wrong: 208 is benzene's measured enthalpy, not the gap; 360 is the predicted enthalpy, not the gap; 120 is cyclohexene's value for one double bond. Trap: Quoting one enthalpy when the question asks for the difference between two.

qs.q: A researcher concludes that a molecule is delocalized from its intermediate bond length alone. Why is that conclusion weak?
o: Bond length depends only on the atoms joined, never on the electrons
Not quite. Bond length depends on the electrons too.
All bonds are intermediate
Not quite. Most bonds aren't in-between.
Other effects also shift lengths
Correct: Other effects, like hybridization, also change bond length.
Bond lengths cannot be measured
Not quite. Bond lengths are measured precisely.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 7 says an in-between bond length fits delocalization but doesn't prove it on its own. Other things change bond length too. Hybridization is one: a bond to an sp² carbon is shorter than the same bond to an sp³ carbon, even with no delocalization. So a bond length between single and double could have more than one cause, and you need other evidence, like the hydrogenation energies, to be sure. Why the others are wrong: bond lengths are measured precisely; most bonds aren't in-between, they match normal single or double lengths; bond length depends on the electrons as well as the atoms, which is exactly why delocalization changes it. Trap: Treating one piece of supporting evidence as proof.
